Furthermore, regarding the first line of the three-line verse, it generally enumerates both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). Then follows [the subsequent discussion].
The three phrases separately clarify the contaminated (*sāsrava*) [dharmas] that lead to further existence; the subsequent eight phrases cite and clarify the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

Within these eight phrases, the first phrase separately clarifies the conditioned uncontaminated (*saṃskṛta-anāsrava*), while the remaining seven phrases separately clarify the unconditioned uncontaminated (*asaṃskṛta-anāsrava*).

Among these seven phrases, the first mentions the number of unconditioned [factors], the second lists the names of the unconditioned, and the final five distinguish the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the unconditioned.

Regarding the explanation of the verses, there are nine parts in total: first, the explanation of the initial phrase; second, the explanation of the remaining three phrases, beginning with "What are the contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*)?
This section contains five sub-divisions: first, the question, "What are the contaminated phenomena?"; second, the citation of the second phrase of the verse as the answer;

third, the explanation of the meaning of "contaminated" using the third phrase of the verse, beginning with "For what reason?"; fourth, [the definition]; and fifth, the exclusion of the Path (*mārga*).
Why are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) said to be with outflows (*sāsrava*)? Because the various afflictions (*kleśa*) increase (*anuśerate*) within all other conditioned phenomena.
Thus, the *Miśraka-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* states: "That which increases the various afflictions is called 'with outflows' by the Noble Ones.

Regarding the second clause [of the definition], the reason for excluding the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) is that the five [categories of] afflictions do not increase therein; the meaning of this is referred back to what will be explained later.
Although there are five phrases, they are combined to form the second section, which provides a separate explanation of the contaminated (*sāsrava*).

From here below is the third section, providing a separate explanation of the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), which contains nine parts: first, a summary of the preceding and an inquiry regarding the subsequent;

second, the citation of the fifth and sixth lines of the verse as the response; third, "What are the three? and so forth, which explains the seventh line of the verse; fourth, this [section on] emptiness...

The section beginning with "Emptiness, etc. concludes [the discussion of] the five untainted [factors]. The section beginning with "In brief, regarding what has been explained" explains the eighth phrase, *ākāśa-asamskrta* (unconditioned space).

The section beginning with "Cessation through deliberation" explains the ninth phrase, *pratisamkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through deliberation); it takes disjunction (*visamyoga*) as its intrinsic nature.
When all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are distanced from that which binds them, one realizes liberation according to the measure of the phenomena bound. No [further]...

Regarding the term "analytical cessation" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), the following explains its name: "analysis" (*pratisaṃkhyā*) refers to discernment, which is a specific differentiation of wisdom (*prajñā*)—namely, the functional capacity of patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*).

It is so called because "seeking" is termed "view" (*darśana*), "decisive determination" is termed "knowledge," and "discernment" is termed "wisdom. Wisdom is able to individually discern the objects of the Four Noble Truths:
the truth of suffering is to be known, the truth of origination is to be abandoned, the truth of cessation is to be realized, and the truth of the path is to be cultivated.

The Truth of Cessation is that which is realized through the Truth of the Path; it is the state of extinction attained through the power of discernment cultivated by wisdom, and is termed "cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

For example, a chariot drawn by oxen is called an "ox-cart"; in this case, the word "power" is omitted from the phrase "attained through the power [of discernment]," and the two words "drawn by" are omitted from the metaphor.
Thus, it is stated in this way. Regarding the seventh point, "all contaminated phenomena," the following explains the tenth [point].
Within this section there are seven points: first, the question: "Are all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena identical in their cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)?
Second, the answer: "No. Third, the inquiry: "Why is this so? Fourth, the citation of a verse for explanation: "It varies according to the objects of bondage (*bandhana-vastu*";

that is, it corresponds to the measure of each individual object of bondage, such as each atom (*paramāṇu*), and the same applies to the unconditioned objects of disjunction (*visaṃyoga-vastu*"); for each individual atom of form (*rūpa*) and so forth, there is one [disjunction]. Fifth... [and so on].
First, there is the single acquisition of each individual phenomenon—such as perception, feeling, mind, mental factors, and so forth—as well as their arising, abiding, change, and cessation;
the dissociated [formations], and the unconditioned. Fifth, if this were not the case, the Sarvāstivāda would raise a counter-objection against the Saṃmitīya:

if the measure of the phenomena that are disjoined from bondage did not correspond to the measure of the objects to which they are bound, then at the moment one realizes the cessation of the afflictions abandoned through the vision of suffering, [the disjunction would not occur].
One should realize the cessation of all other afflictions abandoned through the four remaining doors, because analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is a single entity.
If this were so, then cultivating the remedies for the remaining four doors would be useless. The Sāmmitīyas ask:

"If the entities of dissociation (*visamyoga*) were distinct, then cessation would have multiple substances. It would then possess homogeneous counterparts (*sabhāga*). Based on what principle is it that cessation has no homogeneous counterparts? (7)

The *Sarvāstivāda* replies: "Based on the cessation of multiple entities, when they are viewed in relation to one another, there is no sense of being a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for themselves, nor do they act as a homogeneous cause for others;
therefore, the Sūtra states this [without implying that] there is no cessation of multiple entities of the same kind. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, fascicle 72, states:
"The 'abandonment' (*prahāṇa*) and so forth of the three realms are simply the aforementioned unconditioned liberation (*asaṃskṛta-vimukti*), which is taken here as its own [nature]."

The essence of these three realms is identical; their difference exists only in terms of conventional designation (*prajñapti*). If one considers them from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there is no distinction. What is meant by "difference in terms of conventional designation"?

That which is the separation from the fetter of greed is called the "realm of detachment" (*virāga-dhātu*); the severing of the remaining eight fetters is called the "realm of abandonment" (*prahāṇa-dhātu*);
and the cessation of all other entities that are bound by the fetters of greed and so forth is called the "realm of cessation" (*nirodha-dhātu*). For what reason are there three?
The distinctions among the realms (*dhātu*) are as follows: contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are, in brief, of three types.

First, those that are fettering (*bandhana*) but not defiling (*saṃkleśa*). Second, those that are both fettering and defiling. Third, those that are neither, being the phenomena conducive to the abandonment of the fetters and defilements.

The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) realized through the abandonment of these three types of phenomena is, respectively, termed the realm of abandonment (*prahāṇa-dhātu*), and so forth. Other masters state that it refers exclusively to the abandonment of the fetters.

Regarding the existence or non-existence of a distinct unconditioned entity (*asaṃskṛta*) for the severance of the fetters (*saṃyojana*), some say that for the severance of the eight fetters that have an object (*sālambana*), there is a distinct unconditioned entity;
for the severance of others, it is not so. They further state that the unconditioned entities realized by these three types [of paths] are, respectively, called "severance" (*prahāṇa*) and so forth.

Other masters say that there is a distinct unconditioned entity only for the severance of those fetters that are defiling (*kliṣṭa*); for the severance of others, it is not so. Those masters state that feeling (*vedanā*) has an object in relation to the eight [fetters].

The three types of unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) realized through the severance of the fetter of craving with its conditions, the fetter of craving with its conditions, and other matters, are respectively called "severance" (*prahāṇa*), and so forth.

This is because the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is attained separately for each specific matter to which one is bound; thus, among the three explanations, the first is considered the correct interpretation.
It states that the three realms of severance and so forth are simply the division of the previously mentioned unconditioned liberation, taking it as their own essence.
Regarding the objects of bondage, one attains liberation as an unconditioned state (*asaṃskṛta*).

Just as when a person who is bound becomes free from their bonds, one speaks only of that bound person attaining liberation, rather than speaking of the liberation of the binder through the severing of the bonds;

so too, while the substance of the three realms (*tridhātu*) differs according to conventional designation (*prajñapti*), if one examines them in terms of actual reality (*vastu*), each is individually non-existent. Thus, even the substance of the three realms is ultimately non-existent, being merely a conventional designation.
What is the distinction? It is called "differentiation by way of conventional designation" (*prajñapti-paryāya-bheda*). That is to say, regarding each individual atom (*paramāṇu*) and so forth:

from the perspective of being free from the bond of attachment, it is termed the "realm of detachment" (*virāga-dhātu*); from the perspective of severing the remaining eight fetters (*saṃyojana*), it is termed the "realm of abandonment" (*prahāṇa-dhātu*);

and from the perspective of the cessation of the substantial entities bound by all nine fetters such as attachment, it is termed the "realm of cessation" (*nirodha-dhātu*). There is a second [type of differentiation] which remains.

The Master says that only the abandonment of the *anuśayas*, *paryavasthānas*, and *upakleśas*—which are distinct [from other fetters]—is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); for the abandonment of the remainder is not so.

He explains that the *anuśayas*, *paryavasthānas*, and *upakleśas* have objects (*sālambana*): the *saṃyojanas* have eight objects, the *anunaya-saṃyojana* has nine objects, and the remaining bound entities are abandoned.
The unconditioned realized through the abandonment of these three types is called "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*) and so forth, respectively; in the third realm (*dhātu*), there is a remainder.
The Master [Vasumitra] says that only the abandonment of the defiling fetters of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), while the abandonment of the others is not so;
that Master asserts that craving has eight fetters as its objects, the fetters have craving as their object, and the fetters have other matters as their objects.

The unconditioned realized through the abandonment of these three types is called "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*) and so forth, respectively, for the three realms. The latter two Masters both maintain that one attains [the fruit] individually according to the specific matter to which one was bound.

Regarding the distinct natures of the three realms as unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the commentator now evaluates the views of the masters. He adopts the position of the first master: one attains the cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) individually for each specific object to which one is bound;

thus, while it is conventionally said that there are distinctions within the three realms based on these respective cessations, in terms of the actual reality (*dravya*) of the cessation itself, there is no difference.

Therefore, among the three explanations, the first is the most excellent. Furthermore, since the pervasive afflictions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) of suffering and origination constitute the same bond, when the [afflictions] below suffering are severed...

Although at the time of the ten proclivities (*daśa-anuśaya*) one is bound by the fetters of the lower realm of origination (*samudaya*) which have not yet been severed, it is said that the fetters of the lower realm of suffering (*duḥkha*) and so forth have attained dissociation (*visamyoga*).
This is because when one is bound by the fetters of one's own category (*sva-bīja*), one attains liberation from those very fetters upon their immediate departure;
just as a person is said to have attained liberation when they are freed from the shackles and chains immediately upon their own body, even though the proclivities of other categories remain distant.

To speak of liberation while one has not yet departed from bondage is like a person in prison who, although not yet having left the prison gate or its distant chains, is said to be "already liberated" because they have abandoned the immediate shackles upon their own body.
It is the same with the nine grades of fetters within the gateway of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*):
when the first grade is severed, one is said to have attained liberation from the immediate bond of that specific grade, even though the remaining eight grades are still distant.
Although the fetters have not yet been severed, it is said that upon the first stage of defilement being abandoned, one attains liberation and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

The remaining eight stages may be understood by analogy. Only when the nine grades of the fetters binding defiled form and the other non-defiled five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are exhausted is the object bound said to be liberated.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 31, states in its critique:
One should state it thus: as many as are the entities of the tainted (*sāsrava*) dharmas, so many are the entities of their cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
This is because for as many entities as there are to which one is bound, there are that many entities of disjunction (*visamyoga*). Question:

It is already known that the measure of cessation through deliberation corresponds to the number of things to which one is bound. When sentient beings realize this cessation through deliberation, do they realize it collectively as one, or individually?
If it is argued that they are realized [simultaneously], what fault is there? Both positions entail errors. If they were realized together as one, why would *nirvāṇa* be called an "unshared dharma"?
Furthermore, if this were so, when one sentient being attains *nirvāṇa*, all sentient beings should likewise attain it;
if that were the case, liberation would occur spontaneously without effort. On the other hand, if they are realized individually, how could *nirvāṇa*...

The designations for "nirvāṇa" differ according to their distinct categories. Furthermore, how should one interpret the Sūtra which states that the liberation of a Tathāgata is no different from the liberation of other Arhats?

One should respond as follows: when all classes of sentient beings realize cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), they all realize a single [cessation]. Question: If this is so, why is nirvāṇa called an "unshared dharma"? Answer: Nirvāṇa...

Although its essence is actually shared, it is designated as "unshared" (asādhāraṇa) by way of its acquisition (*prāpti*), because the acquisition of disjunction (*visamyoga-prāpti*) arises individually within the distinct mental continua of each sentient being.
Question: When one sentient being attains *nirvāṇa*, why do all other sentient beings not likewise attain it?
Answer: If there is the acquisition of *nirvāṇa* within a person's body, they are said to have attained *nirvāṇa*; if there is none, they have not.
It is not so; therefore, there is no single moment in which all sentient beings attain nirvāṇa.

Other teachers say that when various classes of sentient beings realize analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), they each realize it individually. Question: If this is so, why is nirvāṇa said to be "of a different kind" (*visabhāga*)?

Answer: It is stated thus because it excludes a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*); that is to say, analytical cessations have no homogeneous causes, and for this reason they are called "not [of a] similar kind."
Regarding the question: "If there is no homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for non-sentient things, how do you distinguish them from cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)?

Furthermore, since the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe-dharmajñāna-kṣānti*) lacks a homogeneous cause, it too should be called a 'non-homogeneous dharma' (*visabhāga-dharma*).

Why, then, are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) called 'homogeneous,' while only *nirvāṇa* is said to be 'non-homogeneous'? The answer is: Although the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering lacks a homogeneous cause, it is nevertheless able to...

Because they act as similar causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) for one another, they are also called "similar nirvāṇa. Otherwise, furthermore, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are called "similar" because they are subsumed within the three categories of aggregates, elements, and bases;
they similarly follow the three time periods; they similarly possess arising and ceasing; they similarly possess the grades of inferior, middling, and superior;
they similarly possess priority and posteriority; they similarly arise from causes; and they similarly produce effects. Therefore, they are called "similar nirvāṇa. Otherwise, it would not be so.

Regarding the term "dissimilar" (*visabhāga*): furthermore, among all phenomena (*dharmas*), only nirvāṇa is both wholesome (*kuśala*) and permanent (*nitya*); others are not so. Therefore, it is called "dissimilar. That is to say, while other phenomena may be either wholesome or impermanent, or neither wholesome nor permanent, nirvāṇa alone possesses both the qualities of being wholesome and permanent. For this reason, it is uniquely designated as a "dissimilar phenomenon. [Question: What is the meaning of "dissimilar"? [Answer: It means that it does not belong to the same category (*asabhāga*). Just as the eye-faculty is dissimilar to the ear-faculty and so forth, nirvāṇa is dissimilar to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). Furthermore, because it is dissimilar to all other phenomena, it is called "dissimilar. Specifically, all conditioned phenomena are characterized by arising and ceasing;

they are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self. Nirvāṇa is the cessation of these characteristics; it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), peaceful, and sublime. Because it is utterly distinct from the nature of conditioned phenomena, it is called "dissimilar. Moreover, regarding the three types of phenomena—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—the wholesome and unwholesome are mutually dissimilar, and the indeterminate is dissimilar to both. Among these, nirvāṇa is exclusively wholesome and exclusively unconditioned. Since no other phenomenon is both wholesome and unconditioned, nirvāṇa alone is termed a "dissimilar phenomenon. This concludes the inquiry.
How is the statement in the Sūtra to be reconciled when it says that the liberation of a Tathāgata is no different from the liberation of other Arhats?
The answer is: although the liberations within the bodies of the three vehicles differ, they are said to be no different because their excellence and permanence are the same.
Furthermore, this demonstrates that within a single continuum there are the paths of the three vehicles, which equally realize liberation—this being said in comparison with others.
The liberations realized through personal experience differ from one another; yet within a single body, there exist the natures of the three vehicles, all of which equally realize liberation.
Since one may give rise to the noble path by relying on any of these vehicles in order to attain this nirvana, the critique states:
"They should not speak in that way; rather, they should speak thus: among all sentient beings, universally, within each and every contaminated phenomenon (*sāsrava-dharma*),"

All together realize a single essence of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), because it was previously stated that the measure of cessation through deliberation corresponds to the number of objects with which one is bound.
For this reason, the previous statement is logically sound. Question: Is the essence of cessation through deliberation also realized regarding external things?

If one were to say "no," what would be the fault? If that were so, then for one who has realized the essence of cessation through deliberation, there would be no possession (*prāpti*) of external phenomena.

How, according to the meaning, is that cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) accomplished? Furthermore, how should one interpret the Sūtra when it says, as the Venerable Śāriputra stated:

"I have severed all craving and attained internal liberation"? If cessation through deliberation is not attained regarding external things, how then is the teaching of the Sūtra to be reconciled, such as:
"Because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are severed, it is called the 'element of abandonment' (*prahāṇa-dhātu')"? (1)

Because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are abandoned, it is called the "element of abandonment" (*prahāṇadhātu*); because all conditioned phenomena are extinguished, it is called the "element of extinction" (*nirodhadhātu*). One should answer as follows:
even among external objects, analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is attained. Question:

If that is so, since there is no sense of "possession" (*prāpti*) regarding external objects, how can one attain analytical cessation with respect to them? Answer: Although there is no possession of external objects, nevertheless, with respect to them...

If there is one who attains *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through deliberation) yet does not possess the eight faculties—such as the past and future life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and so forth—and if it is likewise the case for external objects that one attains *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* with respect to them, what contradiction is there?

Furthermore, how is the statement in the *Sūtra* to be reconciled, such as when the Venerable Śāriputra said: "I have severed all cravings and attained internal liberation"? [The answer] says: with respect to...
Because one attains liberation regarding the internal aggregates, it should be known that one also attains liberation regarding the external.

Furthermore, because the liberation of external objects depends upon the internal for its attainment, it is also called "internal"; that is, one must first cultivate the path within the internal body to attain it.

Furthermore, because the attainment of the liberation of external objects is itself internal, it is also called "internal"; that is, the attainment of that [liberation] is subsumed within the internal aggregates. Furthermore...
Because one attains that cessation by severing internal afflictions, it is also called "internal.

This is because the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) existing among external objects is attained only after severing the internal afflictions that bind them; therefore, the Sūtra says, "one attains internal liberation.

Other masters state that analytical cessation cannot be obtained among external objects, for analytical cessation is attained solely through the severance of the bonds of the various afflictions that bind [the mind].

Question: If that is so, how should one interpret the Sūtra which says, "Because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are abandoned, it is called the element of abandonment (*prahāṇadhātu*)," and so forth?
Answer: That Sūtra should have said, "Because [some] conditioned phenomena are abandoned, it is called the element of abandonment," and so forth;
it should not have used the term "all. As for the fact that it does say "all," it should be understood that this refers to a partial "all," meaning:
"All" is of two kinds: first, partial all; second, total all. That sutra speaks only of partial all.
Some say that although there is cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) among external things, it cannot be apprehended.
[The author] critiques this, saying: One should not speak in such a manner. It would be better to say it does not exist rather than to say it exists but cannot be apprehended. Since...
If it cannot be attained, why is such useless cessation required? One should rather say that it both exists and can be attained. Why is this so?
All contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) have, from beginningless time, been bound by afflictions (*kleśa*) and have not attained liberation.
If the afflictions are severed, one becomes dissociated from them and thereby attains liberation—just as when a person who has been bound is later released.

The term "liberation" (vimukti) does not refer to [the release from] ropes and the like; rather, since liberation is realized with respect to that which binds, one also attains liberation regarding external objects.
Were it otherwise, it would contradict what is stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*. As it says: "What are the dharmas to be realized?
Answer: all wholesome dharmas. Although there is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) within external objects, it cannot be attained [therein].

If it were the case that one could realize the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of wholesome dharmas, it would contradict that teaching; therefore, analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is also obtainable externally.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 32, asks: "Between analytical cessation and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which is more numerous?
Some state: "Analytical cessation is more numerous, while non-analytical cessation is fewer. Why is this? Because analytical cessation applies to dharmas of the three time periods."

Since non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is acquired only with respect to future dharmas that are not destined to arise, some teachers say that non-analytical cessation applies to both contaminated (sāsrava) and uncontaminated (anāsrava) dharmas, whereas analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) applies only to contaminated dharmas.
Those who speak thus should state that non-analytical cessation is more extensive and analytical cessation is less so. Why? Because non-analytical cessation is like conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta).
The number of analytical cessations (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) corresponds exactly to the number of contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*);

were it otherwise, if those phenomena capable of arising were to not arise [due to the attainment of a path], one would not obtain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Although the quantity of the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of these two types of cessation is thus, regarding their acquisition (*prāpti*), there should be four permutations (*catuṣkoṭika*):
there are phenomena for which one obtains analytical cessation but does not obtain non-analytical cessation, and so forth.
Question: Do all classes of sentient beings acquire non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) collectively or individually? Answer: This is not fixed.

Regarding the non-analytical cessation of shared phenomena (sādhāraṇa-dharma), it is acquired collectively; regarding the non-analytical cessation of unshared phenomena (asādhāraṇa-dharma), it is acquired individually.
Furthermore, when ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) each abide in a particular realm (gati), they acquire the phenomena of other realms moment by moment.

Non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) occurs because, when objects such as forms cease moment by moment, the visual consciousness and other cognitions that take them as objects never arise again;
this is likewise true for those who abide in a single destiny (*gati*), realm (*dhātu*), stage (*bhūmi*), or location (*sthāna*). Question:

By virtue of which wholesome dharmas do practitioners attain non-analytical cessation regarding the various evil destinies? Answer: Either through generosity (*dāna*), or through ethical discipline (*śīla*), or...

Whether by means of the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), the wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), or the wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), practitioners attain the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding the various evil destinies (*apāya*).
Question: Is this non-analytical cessation of the three evil destinies attained simultaneously, or is it attained separately?
Answer: Some say that it must be attained simultaneously. Question: If that is so, how is it that Devadatta has already attained the non-analytical cessation of two evil destinies?

Is it not the case that [the state of] extinction is not hell? Answer: For him, with respect to hell, except for one birth, all other births and both evil destinies are simultaneously attained as non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Question: Since one birth has been excluded, does this not mean that there is separately the attainment of the remainder? Other masters say:

If, regarding generosity, morality, learning, and so forth, one attains non-analytical cessation in the evil destinies, whether individually or collectively, it conforms to the stage of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).

If one attains [the *niyāma*] partially, does one not necessarily attain it in its entirety? One might ask: "Does Devadatta not attain the *anuloma-nirvedhabhāgīya*? According to this explanation, at the stage of *kṣānti*, one attains the preceding stages in their entirety;

however, those that were previously indeterminate are excluded. It has already been stated that one attains the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding the miserable realms (*apāya*); now, the attainment of non-analytical cessation regarding the happy realms (*sugati*) shall be explained.

At the time of the supreme patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*), one attains it with the sole exception of seven births among humans and gods in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and each individual birth in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
In each respective birth, one attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding all other births.

When a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) proceeds toward the fruit of a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), if they do not enter meditative absorption, they attain non-analytical cessation regarding six births in the desire realm at the time of the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*).

If they do enter meditative absorption, they attain non-analytical cessation regarding six births in the desire realm only upon reaching the sixth path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*). This is the case for the once-returner.

When one who is destined for the fruit of non-returner does not enter meditative absorption, they attain the analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding one more birth in the desire realm during the stage of the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*).
If, however, they do enter absorption, they must reach the ninth path of immediate succession (*anantarya-mārga*) to attain the analytical cessation regarding one more birth in the desire realm.

At that time, they also attain the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding all births in the desire realm. One who is of the nature of non-retrogression (*avinipātadharman*) is free from the first dhyāna.

For one who does not emerge from meditative absorption while being stained [by defilements], non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is attained regarding birth in the first dhyāna during the stage of the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*).

If, however, one does emerge from absorption, it is only upon reaching the ninth path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) that non-analytical cessation is attained regarding birth twice in the first dhyāna;

at that time, analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is attained regarding all births in the first dhyāna. As for one of the "nature of falling away" (*parihāṇa-dharman*), [this occurs] when they are free from...

When one is defiled by the first dhyāna, whether the meditative absorption has arisen or not, at the time of the ninth path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga), one attains the analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) of all births in the first dhyāna, but does not attain non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), because it is possible to fall back and be reborn there.

This should be understood to apply similarly up until the abandonment of the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana). As for those of the non-falling nature (anāvartika-dharman), they abandon the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).

When one does not arise from meditative absorption while remaining immersed in defilement, one attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding birth in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) during the stage of the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*).

If, however, one does arise from absorption, it is only upon reaching the ninth path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) that one attains non-analytical cessation regarding birth in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
at that time, one attains analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding all births. If...

Regarding those of the nature of falling back (*parihāṇadharman*): when they are free from the defilements of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), if they do not enter meditative absorption, they attain the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) regarding the birth [of defilements] in the eight stages at the time of the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*).
If they do enter absorption, they must reach the ninth path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*) to attain the non-analytical cessation regarding the birth in the eight stages;
at that time, they have already attained analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) regarding all births. This has been explained.
It should be explained that one attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding the acquisition of birth.

At the time of the supreme patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*), one attains non-analytical cessation regarding the acquisition of the afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) within the three realms. Upon entering the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), one attains analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding those [afflictions] according to the uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*).

As for those of the non-retrogressive type (*aparihāṇa-dharman*) on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), when they become free from the defilement of desire, it occurs at the stage of preparatory effort (*prayoga*) for those who do not enter meditative absorption (*samāpatti*).
When proceeding toward the path, one attains the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm;

if one has entered meditative absorption, one attains that non-analytical cessation at each respective moment of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*). At that time, one also attains the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of those afflictions.

For one of the "nature of falling away" (*parihāṇa-dharman*), this occurs at the time of becoming free from the defilements of the desire realm, whether or not one has entered meditative absorption, at each respective moment of the uninterrupted path.
At that time, one attains the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of those afflictions, but does not attain their non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

This should be explained accordingly for each stage up to the abandonment of attachment to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). Question: At what time do those subject to regression (*parihāṇadharman*) attain the non-analytical cessation of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)? Some say:

It is at the time when one who is resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) refines their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) and attains the state of one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*). Others say: It is at the time of liberation.

When one attains the state of immovability (*akopya*) through the refinement of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the afflictions (*kleśa*) abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are non-analytical cessations (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

The commentary states: It should be explained as follows: when one has attained the certainty that those afflictions will never again arise, one obtains the non-analytical cessation of those afflictions.

Having already explained the non-analytical cessation regarding the acquisition of afflictions, it is now necessary to explain the non-analytical cessation regarding the acquisition of the Noble Path (*ārya-mārga*).
For one who follows by faith (*śraddhānusārin*), there is the attainment of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding the path of following the Dharma (*dharmānusāri-mārga*).
For one who follows the Dharma, there is the attainment of non-analytical cessation regarding the path of liberation through faith-follower conviction (*śraddhādhimukti-vimukti-mārga*).

For one who is resolved through faith-follower conviction, if they definitely rely on the path of faith-follower conviction to attain the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*), there is the attainment of non-analytical cessation regarding the path of "one who has attained vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*). For one who has attained vision...

When one attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) during the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) at the stage of being resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), one becomes one liberated by occasion (*samaya-vimukta*).
If one is definitively established in the path of liberation by occasion and attains non-analytical cessation, one becomes one who has reached the ultimate.

When one attains non-analytical cessation during the path of liberation not by occasion (*asamaya-vimukta*), one becomes one liberated not by occasion (*asamaya-vimukta*). Regarding the lineage of the Śrāvaka (*śrāvaka-gotra*)...
When one attains certainty in the path of the śrāvaka, one obtains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding the paths of the Buddha and the pratyekabuddha;
when one of the pratyekabuddha lineage attains certainty in the path of the pratyekabuddha, one obtains non-analytical cessation regarding the paths of the Buddha and the śrāvaka;

when one of the Buddha lineage attains certainty in the path of the Buddha, one obtains non-analytical cessation regarding the paths of the pratyekabuddha and the śrāvaka, as well as the fruit of arhatship.

There are six types of spiritual lineages (*gotra*). If one belonging to the lineage of those subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) reaches the ultimate by means of the path of falling away, they attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding the five higher paths.

If one belonging to the lineage of those who reflect (*cetayitṛdharman*) reaches the ultimate by means of the path of reflection, they attain non-analytical cessation regarding the four higher paths and the one lower path.
This continues up to the lineage of those capable of penetration (*prativedhanādharman*), if they reach the ultimate by means of the path of penetration...

Regarding "ultimately": one attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) with respect to the upper single path and the lower four paths; one who belongs to the immovable lineage (*akopya-gotra*) attains non-analytical cessation with respect to the lower five paths. Question:
If non-analytical cessation is attained at the time of spiritual advancement (*viśeṣa-gamana*), why is this cessation not considered a fruit of the Path?
Answer: Because the Path is not cultivated for the sake of this cessation. Rather, it is cultivated for the sake of *nirvāṇa* and for the sake of detachment from defilements (*virāga*).
One diligently cultivates the Path; because of this cultivation of the Path, one attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding the evil destinies and so forth.

If one were to cultivate the Path for the sake of this specific cessation, one would not attain this cessation regarding the evil destinies and so forth. This is because it is impossible to attain non-analytical cessation regarding the evil destinies without having developed a profound sense of weary revulsion (*nirvid*) toward cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
Therefore, non-analytical cessation is not designated as a fruit of the Path.
Although there have been seven preceding sections, these are combined as the seventh [section] explaining the tenth phrase. Below this, the eighth section explains the eleventh and twelfth phrases;
herein there are three parts: first, a summary of what has already been explained regarding *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through deliberation);

second, the citation of the root verse concerning the distinct attainment of *apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation not through deliberation) which eternally obstructs future arising dharmas; third, the explanation of the root verse, stating that *apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* is capable of...
The permanent obstruction of the arising of future dharmas, which differs from the preceding [cessation], is called "cessation not through deliberation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
This is because its attainment does not depend on the discernment of wisdom, but rather arises solely from the deficiency of conditions. To illustrate this with a specific case:

when the eye—assisted by attention—is exclusively focused on one visible form, the other four sense objects (*viṣaya*) that are not being apprehended cease and pass into the past; thus, the five consciousnesses would have had the five past objects as their conditions.
The body and so forth, abiding in the future, will ultimately never arise because their conditions are fixed; thus, they cannot arise with respect to other objects.

Furthermore, because those five consciousnesses cannot take past objects as their objective supports—since such objects are not present—non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is attained with respect to these five consciousnesses and the like.
Regarding the ninth [category], two types of cessation are attained with respect to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*); one should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Regarding certain phenomena, one attains only analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); these are all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena of the past and present, as well as those of the future that are destined to arise.

Regarding certain phenomena, one attains only non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); these are future phenomena that are not destined to arise, as well as uncontaminated conditioned (*anāsrava-saṃskṛta*) phenomena.
Regarding certain phenomena, one attains both types of cessation; these are future contaminated phenomena that are not destined to arise, because they will not arise.

One attains non-analytical cessation because [those dharmas] are with outflows (*sāsrava*), and one attains analytical cessation [for those that are not]. Alternatively, regarding certain dharmas, one does not attain either of the two cessations:
namely, all uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dharmas of the past and present, as well as future dharmas destined to arise, because they are uncontaminated, they do not attain analytical cessation;
and because they are future and not destined to arise, they do not attain non-analytical cessation.
The three preceding verses generally clarify the nature of tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena;

from here, the following twenty-two verses specifically clarify the tainted and untainted phenomena within the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*). Within this section, the first two verses generally clarify the five aggregates.

Regarding the second verse, "Form consists only of the five sense faculties," etc., the five aggregates are specifically clarified. Within these first two verses, the initial verse provides a general summary.

The second verse-line specifically elucidates the contaminated (*sāsrava*) aggregates within the section on the "Exposition of the Contaminated and Uncontaminated Aggregates. Following the preceding prose, it first concludes the previous discussion and poses a question;

next, it presents the verse as the answer. Within this, the first two lines generally define the essence of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), while the latter two lines enumerate the various names for the conditioned:

(1) world-path (*loka-vartman*), (2) basis of speech (*abhilāpa-adhiṣṭhāna*), (3) existence (*bhava*), (4) departure (*niḥsaraṇa*), and (5) thing (*vastu*). This concludes the explanation of the verse.
Based on the Chinese text, there are eight distinct sections. First, the explanation of the second phrase: "Thus, these five dharmas... and so forth, which explains the first phrase.

Because they are produced by the collective action of a gathering of various conditions (*pratyaya*), and because they are brought about by those various conditions, they are called "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*).

Not even the slightest dharma arises from a single condition; therefore, they are produced by a multitude of conditions. Although dharmas of the future have not yet been acted upon by a multitude of conditions...

Because they are of the same category as those [dharmas] of the past and present, there is no contradiction in their existence in the future, just as a calf drinking milk is called "milk" and wood being burned by fire is called "wood.
Even before it has been consumed or burned, it is still called milk or wood; thus, that which is being consumed or burned belongs to the category of milk and wood.
Third, regarding the path of time (*adhvan*): these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are also called the path of time; the past is that which has already traversed, and the present...
The nature of that which is currently practicing, will practice in the future, and is practicing within the paths of the three times of these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
The *Nyāyapraveśa* states: "Because the five aggregates, such as form, are phenomena subject to arising and ceasing, they circulate through the paths of the future, present, and past.

Furthermore, although those phenomena that have not yet arisen do not arise due to the deficiency of conditions, they are nonetheless established [as conditioned] because they belong to that same category."
The term "world-path" (*loka-mārga*) is likewise not erroneous; for it is swallowed up by impermanence (*anitya*).

Impermanence is a worldly phenomenon (*loka-dharma*), and the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, are swallowed up by this worldly phenomenon of impermanence; therefore, they are called the "world-path. Master Paramārtha says:
"A journey of ten thousand *li* proceeds and proceeds without ceasing until it finally reaches its end; the five aggregates are likewise [consumed] by impermanence."

That which is swallowed and consumed ultimately perishes. The four [commentators] explain that based on this, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are called the "basis of names" (*nāma-āśraya*).

"Name" refers to speech; that which is the basis of this speech is precisely the meaning of arising simultaneously with name and speech, because these phenomena arise together with speech and thus serve as the basis for speech.
In this way, the basis of speech fully encompasses all eighteen realms (*dhātu*) of conditioned phenomena. If...
If it were not so, it would contradict what is stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*. That treatise states: "It is based on the eighteen *dhātus*. Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* says:
"Alternatively, it is called the 'basis of speech' (*vāk-saṃniśraya*). 'Speech' refers to vocal sound, or that which is capable of speaking;

this is the specific differentiation within the continuity of vocal sound. It is named after its basis, yet it possesses the meaning of being inclusive, as it fully encompasses the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), just as the Sūtra says: 'It is based on existence.'"
The third, fourth, and fifth [categories] are well-explained by this through the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*, which states: "They are based on what is subsumed within the five aggregates. One might ask:
"Does it not also state that they arise based on the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)? Why is that meaning not established as being "based on"? Because that meaning and its name do not coexist logically.
As it is said: "Being 'based on' means the name and its meaning coexist. If the meaning and the name can be spoken of together, then it is so.

This is established as a basis for expression (*vāda-niśraya*). Since the meaning of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and the name of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) cannot be spoken of together—because they lack a common referent—it is not established as a basis for expression.
The fifth [explanation] concerns "possessing separation" (*saviyoga*). "Separation" (*viyoga*) means being eternally separated from all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).

Because it possesses that separation, it is called "possessing separation. The sixth [explanation] concerns "possessing a basis" (*savastuka*). It is "possessing a basis" because it has a cause; thus, "basis" (*vastu*) here carries the meaning of "cause" (*hetu*), as explained below.
Among the five topics, the seventh explains the meaning of "clinging" (abhiniveśa); the Vaibhāṣika masters transmit it thus;
and the eighth concludes that such categories as these are synonyms for conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta).

From here below, the second section of verses clarifies the various names for the contaminated aggregates (*sāsrava-skandha*). In this passage, first the preceding [topic] is restated to introduce the subject; next, the root verses are presented:

(1) the aggregates of grasping (*upādāna-skandha*), (2) those with contention (*saraṇa*), (3) suffering (*duḥkha*), (4) origin (*samudaya*), (5) the world (*loka*), (6) the locus of views (*dṛṣṭi-sthāna*), and (7) the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*).
Following this, the root verses are explained. Within that [explanation], there are eight parts. First, the explanation of the name "aggregates of grasping": herein, first, a question is posed.

Regarding the question of where this designation "with-outflows" (sāsrava) is established, the subsequent answer is as follows: it is established in relation to the aggregates of grasping (upādānaskandha).

Since the term "aggregate" (skandha) applies to both that which is with-outflows and that which is without-outflows, the aggregates with-outflows are also called simply "aggregates. Alternatively, there are those which are merely aggregates but not aggregates of grasping, namely, the uncontaminated formations (anāsrava-saṃskāra).
Regarding the latter explanation of "grasping" (upādāna): it is named "grasping" because it refers to afflictions (kleśa), and these afflictions "moisten" (lubricate) karma.

Because one takes up a self through grasping (*upādāna*) when undergoing rebirth, the aggregates (*skandha*) arise from grasping; since they are named after their cause, they are called "aggregates of grasping" (*upādānaskandha*).

This is like fire made of grass and chaff: although the fire is not the grass or chaff themselves, because it arises from the grass and chaff and is named after its cause, it is called "grass-and-chaff fire.

Similarly, according to the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, [the aggregates are so named] because they arise from outflows (*āsrava*), or because the aggregates belong to grasping; since they are named after that to which they belong, they are called "aggregates of grasping. Just as...

The sovereign and his subjects are named after the sovereign; the sovereign and his subjects are likewise included within the *Leakage-Base* (*āsravasthāna*) according to the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*.

Thus, the aggregates (*skandha*) are driven by afflictions (*kleśa*). For example, due to hatred, desire, and so forth, there arise actions such as killing; this is like the aggregates following the graspings (*upādāna*), or like a king’s subjects following the king’s commands.

Alternatively, because the aggregates arise from graspings, they are designated by the name of their cause; thus they are called "aggregates of grasping" (*upādānaskandha*), like a tree of flowers and fruit.
A tree is not named after its flowers or fruits; it is named "a flower-fruit tree" based on its fruit.

This is consistent with the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, which states that because [defilements] arise from them, they are explained in two ways as being "with contention" (*saraṇa*), which is easily understood. Furthermore, according to a third interpretation, they are "with contention" because they oppose the noble mind of patience regarding suffering and wisdom regarding suffering.

As stated in the verses of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*: "The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) are constantly sought by the noble ones. Therefore, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) that accord with the noble mind are "with outflows" (*sāsrava*).

Because it is suffering, it contradicts the Noble Ones' minds; this is the first explanation. Because it can summon subsequent suffering, it is the origin (*samudaya*); this is the second explanation. Regarding the world (*loka*):

first, because its nature arises and ceases moment by moment, it is inherently subject to destruction; second, because it is contaminated (*sāsrava*) and has an antidote path (*pratipakṣa-mārga*) that destroys it—possessing these two meanings, it is called "the world.
The Truth of the Path is exclusively destructive, whereas the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is not destructible in either way; therefore, it is supramundane (*lokottara*).
Regarding the sixfold analysis of the "locus of views" (*diṭṭhāyatana*), the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:

"Alternatively, they are called 'loci of views' because the five views, such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), abide within them, as their latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) increase in accordance with them. [Objection: Is it not the case that all defiled afflictions (*āsrava-kleśa*) increase in accordance with [the locus]?

[Response: Although this principle exists, those various views [alone] increase in accordance with all aspects, at all times, and without distinction regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
Because the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of greed and so forth increase through firm adherence and immovability, they are not like doubt or delusion (*moha*).

This is because those [tendencies] such as greed exist in all modes but not at all times, whereas delusion exists at all times; and while doubt is without distinction [in its occurrence], it lacks firm adherence.
Therefore, among the outflows (*āsrava*), they are not called "bases of views" (*dṛṣṭisthāna*). The commentary explains: the five views possess four characteristics.
1. They take all five types [of objects] as their object; 2. they arise spontaneously at all times; 3.

they possess only the characteristic of arising spontaneously and have no further distinctions; 4. they are firmly adhered to and immovable. Because the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase in accordance with these four meanings, all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are designated as "bases of views" (*dṛṣṭi-sthāna*).
Craving (*rāga*) and the others, however, are not like this; for by that term "craving," etc., hatred (*dveṣa*) and so forth are also included.
Because pride (*māna*) takes ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), six stains (*mala*), and five objects as its conditions, it possesses the sense of being "of all kinds" (*sarvākāra*);
however, because it lacks the sense of arising spontaneously at all times, the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* states: "Greed, hatred, and pride cannot arise without seeing, hearing, or reflecting;
they flare up due to specific conditions. Although delusion (*moha*) arises spontaneously at all times, it is not without distinctions.
The non-associated ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*) and the ignorance associated with the five views (*dṛṣṭi*) arise spontaneously at all times;
however, the ignorance associated with greed, hatred, pride, the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), and the six stains (*mala*) does not arise spontaneously at all times.

Because there is this distinction, it is not the case that there is no difference between them. Although doubt (*vicikitsā*) arises spontaneously at all times, [it differs from the aforementioned types].
7. Arising without distinction, wavering, indecisive, and not firmly adhering—therefore, the outflows (*āsrava*) are not designated as "that greed" and so forth;
this is the seventh [point]. 8. The delusions and karma of the three realms of existence (*tri-bhava*) constitute the cause, while the four types of neutral states (*avyākṛta*) constitute the basis;
both are subsumed within the three realms of existence. 9. Conclusion: These and others are the specific names for the outflows (*sāsrava*).

The two preceding stanzas generally clarify the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); from here on, twenty stanzas specifically clarify the five aggregates, as well as the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*).

Among these, the first five and a half stanzas specifically clarify the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and its inclusion within the bases and elements; the next two stanzas clarify the two feelings (*vedanā*), which receive and experience according to contact;

the following one and a half stanzas specifically clarify the mutual inclusion of the [remaining] three aggregates, the bases, and the elements; and "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) refers to name (*nāman*).
The first two lines of the following verse clarify that the aggregate, base, and element of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha-āyatana-dhātu*) are mutually inclusive;
the next line of verse explains how all phenomena are subsumed under one aggregate, one base, and one element because their objects, consciousnesses, and categories are identical;
the final line of verse explains the bases of the eye, ear, and nose, as well as the two elements, the six groups, the gateways of arising, and the lineages.
One verse explains the meaning of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), stating the reasons for establishing these three categories;

one verse explains the reason for establishing the aggregates of feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) separately; eight and a half verses explain why the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is not included among the aggregates;

one and a half verses explain the sequence of the aggregates, bases, and elements according to their coarseness, defilement, vessel-like nature, and so forth; and one verse explains the distinctions between them.
Regarding the "Distinct and Supreme" section, one line of verse explains the names of the bases (*āyatana*), which are both general and specific (11).

Regarding the "Muni’s Collection of Dharma Aggregates," four lines of verse subsume the various names of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*). Within the first five and a half lines, the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and its corresponding bases and elements are specifically elucidated;
herein, there are five parts: first, one and a half lines of verse list the eleven types of form in general; second, two and a half lines of verse distinguish the five [sensory objects].
The first half-verse, "The faculties are of three types of matter; the objects are two or twenty," distinguishes the matter of the five sense-fields.
The next three verses distinguish the matter of non-informative form (*avijñapti-rūpa*).

Within this, the latter half-verse, "The faculties and their objects," shows how the aggregate of matter (*rūpaskandha*) is subsumed within the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*). The first half-verse enumerates the eleven kinds of matter in general, as the text states.

The second half-verse may be explained as clarifying the nature of the five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*) as form (*rūpa*). Within this passage, the first verse concludes the preceding section and introduces the current topic;
it then presents the root verse and subsequently provides an explanation of that root verse. This explanation consists of two successive parts. Regarding the first part, it states:

"That" refers to the consciousnesses of the five objects—form and so forth—as mentioned in the immediately preceding text; these are the consciousnesses that take those five objects as their objective supports (*ālambana*), and they are the cognizers of those five objects.
The five kinds of pure matter (*rūpaprasāda*) upon which consciousness relies should be understood as being, respectively, the five faculties beginning with the eye.
To prove that the five faculties are pure matter, a scriptural passage is cited below, which can be understood according to the text. Second, regarding the alternative explanation:

"or again, 'those'" refers to the five faculties beginning with the eye mentioned in the preceding text; "consciousness" refers to the five consciousnesses beginning with the visual consciousness, which rely upon those [faculties].
The five faculties (*pañcendriya*) are the five kinds of translucent matter (*rūpaprasāda*) that serve as the bases for the five consciousnesses;

this is the meaning of their being the supports (*āśraya*) for the five consciousnesses, such as eye-consciousness. This subsequent explanation is consistent with the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*, which states:
"What is the eye-faculty? It is defined by its nature as the translucent matter that serves as the support for eye-consciousness. Thus, it is known that [the definition] refers to that.

Regarding the visual consciousness and so forth that depend upon the eyes and other [faculties]: the five faculties are the supports for the consciousnesses that depend upon them, and the pure matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) which serves as the support for those consciousnesses that depend upon the five faculties constitutes the nature of the five faculties.
Next, one verse-line distinguishes the five objects (*viṣaya*). Within this passage, first there is a summary of what preceded and an introduction of what follows;

next, the root verse is presented; and finally, the root verse is explained. Among these, there are six [sections], the first of which explains the object of form (*rūpa-viṣaya*). Within that section, first...
The verse states that there are two types of form (*rūpa*); the commentary explains one as "manifest" (*varṇa*), which is twofold: color and shape.
There are four primary manifest colors—blue, yellow, red, and white—and eight secondary manifest colors, namely smoke, cloud, dust, mist, shadow, glare, light, and darkness;
these eight are variations of the four primary manifest colors. Because the latter eight colors are either blue, yellow, red, or white, they are subsumed within the former four.
Because the latter eight types of form are distinguished from the former four types of form, the latter eight are the differentiated forms of the former four.
Furthermore, the four types of form not subsumed under the latter eight are indeed subsumed within the former four;
just as all twelve divisions of the scriptures are collectively termed *sūtra*, so too the scripture states that a *sūtra* begins with "Thus have I heard" and continues until its conclusion.
This concludes the joyful acceptance and practice; thus, the distinctions among the eleven classes of *sūtra* follow.
As for those not subsumed within these eleven classes, they are subsumed solely within the first class, the *sūtra* class. Herein, the correlation between the four and the eight is likewise:
there are eight forms of shape, beginning with "long" and ending with "irregular."

The preceding section explains the two types of matter (*rūpa*) mentioned in the verse; from here on, it explains the twenty varieties of matter. Within this, there are five parts: first, stating the number;

second, listing the names of the twenty, beginning with blue and yellow; third, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "Some say that matter consists of twenty-one types, with the color of space (*ākāśa-varṇa*) as the twenty-first.
This is a specific differentiation of the matter of the space-element (*ākāśa-dhātu*), which is consistent with this text. [The remaining parts follow.]
Question: Other masters claim that within empty space there is a single visible form (*varṇa*) called "the color of the space-element" (*ākāśadhātu-rūpa*).

The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that during the day it is covered by the color of light, and at night it is covered by the color of darkness; because it is not included among the preceding twenty types of matter, it constitutes the twenty-first.
However, according to the subsequent passage, the color of the space-element is subsumed under the aforementioned colors of light and darkness; therefore, there are only twenty.

Regarding this, "the correct" (*samyak*) and so forth below distinguishes the twenty types of material forms (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*). Here, "the correct" refers to the equality of shape. The *Karmasiddhiprakaraṇa* states:
"Seeing a face that is level and even gives rise to the perception of correctness; seeing a face that is uneven gives rise to the perception of incorrectness. The commentary explains:
"This means that when the various parts of the face are equal, it is called a 'correct face'; when the parts of the face are uneven and unequal, it is called [an incorrect face]."

The rising vapor from the earth in an inauspicious state is called "mist" (*nīhāra*); this can be understood as such. The heat of the sun is named "light" (*prabhā*), while the heat of the moon and other sources is named "clarity" (*āloka*).
Master Paramārtha stated that "light" possesses two meanings: first, it illuminates from afar; second, it carries a sensation of heat.

Because the heat of the sun possesses both [meanings], it receives the name "light. The heat of the moon, stars, fire, medicinal herbs, precious jewels, lightning, and so forth, all likewise [possess these qualities].
The two names [moon and fire] do not possess both characteristics: although the moon and stars can illuminate from afar, they do not carry the sensation of heat;
although fire carries the sensation of heat, it does not illuminate the four continents from afar. Medicinal herbs and the like lack both of these meanings.

When clouds obstruct the sun and form a shadow, other colors are visible within it due to their manifestation; this is called "shadow. When Mount Sumeru obstructs the sun and forms a shadow, [the same applies].
Other forms within it are obscured and no longer visible; this is called "darkness" (*andhakāra*). Because other forms are easily understood, the treatise does not explain them further. Question:

What is the difference between "long" (*dīrgha*) and "high" (*unnata*), and what distinguishes "short" (*hrasva*) from "low" (*avanata*)? Answer: The *Karmasiddhiprakaraṇa* states: "When one sees many [parts] on one side, the cognition of 'long' arises;
when one sees few [parts] on one side, the cognition of 'short' arises; when one sees [parts] equally on all four sides, the cognition of 'square' (*caturaśra*) arises."
When the perception of roundness encounters a protrusion, the cognition of "high" arises; when the perception of roundness encounters a depression, the cognition of "low" arises.

The commentary explains: length and shortness are based on the external features of the four sides of a form; high and low are based on the central position of the form—protruding in the center is called "high," and depressed in the center is called "low.

The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The vapor of fire is called smoke; the vapor of dragons is called clouds; the vapor of the earth is called mist; when the wind blows these fine [particles], they become fog."
Regarding the fourfold classification of "having color" (*varṇa*) and "having shape" (*saṃsthāna*): first, there are those that have color but lack shape.
This refers to the blue, yellow, red, white, shadow, light, radiance, and darkness [of the physical sense-fields]. The Master Satyasiddhi says:
"For example, in the heavens, the lapis lazuli ground is purely blue, and the golden ground is purely yellow; such are the four [colors] found in the heavens."
The ground of jewel-like color is like the light of the sun; it possesses only manifest color (*varṇa*) and lacks shapes such as length and so forth.

Alternatively, there may be places where color exists but shape does not—referring to a portion of length and so forth. Regarding the nature of bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*), the commentary explains:

among the various shapes such as long and short, bodily intimation consists of one specific portion of shape, and not of the inherent length or shortness found in other objects. Now, [the question arises]: what is this?
Karmic form-color (*karma-rūpa*) also lacks shape-color apart from manifest colors such as blue and yellow; one cannot speak of having shape while lacking manifest color.
Furthermore, other [forms] such as length and so forth do not exist apart from blue and yellow. Why is it that wherever there is shape, there must necessarily be manifest color? Answer:
Other non-karmic forms, such as length and so forth, exist spontaneously and eternally; because they are necessarily co-nascent with blue and yellow, wherever there is shape, there is manifest color.

Regarding informative action (*vijñapti-karman*), its form arises from the mind; it possesses the nature of bodily action (*kāya-karman*) and manifests as non-actional in nature. It does not necessarily arise simultaneously [with the mind], so how could it serve as an example?

Alternatively, there are instances where the sphere of matter (*rūpāyatana*) possesses both shape (*saṃsthāna*) and color (*varṇa*). As for the remaining matter, the commentary states: "The rest are non-actional matter;
shape must arise simultaneously with color, and therefore it possesses both shape and color. The *Mahāvibhāṣā* says: "There is matter that has no shape."
This refers to blue, yellow, red, white, light, shadow, brightness, and darkness; that which has form but no color refers to the body;
that which possesses action-color, color, and form refers to the twelve kinds such as long, short, square, round, beautiful, ugly, high, low, smoke, clouds, dust, and mist.
According to the interpretation of Master Paramārtha, these—non-action, length, and so forth—are all identical to blue, yellow, and the others.
If that which possesses form and visibility were to consist of both form and visibility, there would necessarily be sixteen types;

however, since it is stated here that there are only twelve types, we know that all [colors] such as blue, yellow, red, and white are subsumed under "possessing color" (*varṇa*) but not under "possessing form" (*saṃsthāna*). Now, let us further explain the three phrases:

the first eight types of color are called "possessing visibility" (*sanidarśana*) because their specific characteristics are distinct and manifest; they are not [called "possessing form"] because they lack coarse physical substance.

Because it obstructs light to form a shadow, it is formless. For example, while shadows such as long or short exist when light is obstructed by objects like length, shadows produced by obstructing light from objects like blue or yellow do not possess the colors blue or yellow.
The body possesses "action-color" (*karmaja-rūpa*) and has a physical substance;

it consists of colors such as square or round, and because it obstructs light, it produces shadows that are square or round. Therefore, it possesses form, yet it does not coexist with [the primary] retribution-color (*vipāka-rūpa*).

That which can be distinguished by its characteristics and named is called "manifest" (*sanidarśana*). The remaining twelve kinds of non-karmic form have manifest characteristics and can be known as "manifest";
they possess coarse physical substance and obstruct light, thus producing the twelve kinds of shadows. Therefore, they are "with form.
The eight kinds, such as square, round, and so forth, if they are karmic form, are subsumed under the second category of the three natures; if they are not karmic, they are not.

Visible form (*rūpa*) is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and is subsumed under the third category. The first eight types are invariably the first category. Smoke, clouds, dust, and mist belong exclusively to the third category.
Fifth, other masters state that only the visible form of light possesses color (*varṇa*) but lacks shape (*saṃsthāna*). In this passage there are four points:
first, other masters establish that only the visible form of light possesses color but lacks shape, because among the two types of light—[light and darkness]—it is [the former].

Because forms such as length and so forth cannot be perceived [independently], yet in the world we directly perceive that shadows, darkness, and colored surfaces—which are blue, yellow, red, or white—possess length and the like;
therefore, the two masters of the treatises ask: "How can a single substantial entity possess both color (varṇa) and shape (saṃsthāna)? Third, other teachers explain:
"Since both [color and shape] can be known within this same single substance, 'that which exists therein' (tad-asti) has the meaning of being apprehended by two cognitions."
There is no sense of two distinct objective bases; this is the point refuted by the four masters.

If that were so, then within bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*), there would also have to be the sense that two cognitions—of color and shape—arise separately. There is no sense of two distinct objective bases. The *Nyāyānusāra* states:

"Among colors (*varṇa*), only blue, yellow, red, white, shadow, light, brightness, and darkness are perceivable as color; among shapes (*saṃsthāna*), it is bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) [that is perceivable]."

Since its nature is such that only its shape (*saṃsthāna*) can be discerned, while other visible forms (*rūpa*) have both color (*varṇa*) and shape discernible, how could one thing possess two essences?

This is not a fault, as it is not what our school asserts. This will be further examined in the "Exposition of Karma" (*Karmapada*). Thus far, the objective field of form (*rūpaviṣaya*) has been explained.

From here below begins the second section, which distinguishes the object of sound (*śabda-viṣaya*). This section contains four parts: first, stating the number that there are only eight kinds of sound;
second, listing their names, beginning with "those with appropriation" (*upātta*); third, explaining that those caused by appropriated primary elements (*mahābhūta*) constitute the definition;

and fourth, clarifying that sound caused by appropriated primary elements refers to vocal sounds and the sounds produced by hands and other such means. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "Appropriated primary elements refers to..."

Those comprised within the category of sentient beings in the present age—such as those that are nurtured (*aupacayika*), those that are of uniform outflow (*naiṣyandika*), and those that are matured (*vipākaja*) on the various levels (*bhūmi*)—are the opposite of these and are termed "appropriated" (*upātta*).
Among these, sound has two types caused by the great elements (*mahābhūta*):

namely, that produced by the application of effort (*prayoga*) belonging to the class of sentient beings, and that which arises otherwise without depending on such application. Furthermore, regarding that produced by the application of effort belonging to the class of sentient beings...

There are two kinds: first, those produced by the application of the hands and so forth; second, those whose intrinsic nature is informative action (*vijñapti-karman*). This vocal informative action further has two types:
namely, that which arises dependent on names and that which does not depend on names. That which arises dependent on names further has two types:
first, the determinate (*vyākṛta*) and second, the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Those that do not depend on names are likewise of these two types.
There is a distinction among sounds based on whether they have appropriated primary elements (*upātta-mahābhūta*) as their cause or unappropriated primary elements as their cause.
Those caused by unappropriated primary elements are also of two kinds: first, those produced through the volitional effort (*prayoga*) of sentient beings;

second, those generated by the agitation of the elements. The former refers to sounds such as those of conchs, shells, bells, and drums; the latter refers to sounds emitted by wind, forests, rivers, and so forth. That which belongs to the category of sentient beings is speech (*vāc*).

Sounds such as those of hands and other such sounds are "non-sentient"; these various sounds that produce pleasure in hearers are called "agreeable sounds," while those contrary to this are called "disagreeable.

Among these eight [types of sound], only the first two are logically consistent, because sounds categorized as sentient and non-sentient have as their causes the great elements (*mahābhūta*) that are, respectively, appropriated (*upātta*) and unappropriated (*anupātta*).
