Since they are included [within the same category], one should likewise be able to speak of "agreeable" and so forth regarding visible forms (*rūpa*) and the rest; why then is this [distinction] applied only to sound?

Visible forms and the rest should also be said to have both appropriated (*upātta*) and non-appropriated (*anupātta*) primary elements (*mahābhūta*) as their cause. This is indeed how it should be stated;

however, because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the sense-base of sound is difficult to discern, it is spoken of only in terms of its causes as being of two kinds. It is not so for visible forms and the rest.
Therefore, it is not said that [sound] is included among those things that are not appropriated (*anupātta*).

In this treatise, since only sounds produced by the agitation of the elements are cited—such as the sounds emitted by forests, rivers, and so forth—the sounds arising from the volitional activity (*prayoga*) of sentient beings, such as those from conchs, shells, bells, and drums, are omitted.
"Sentient being names" refers to vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*), because vocal intimation necessarily belongs to sentient beings.
This is because it is a combination of names, phrases, and syllables. Other sounds, such as those of hands and so forth, are different from these sounds of sentient beings;

this is explained in the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*. Sounds belonging to the category of sentient beings have appropriated (*upātta*) great elements as their cause, whereas sounds not belonging to the category of sentient beings have non-appropriated (*anupātta*) great elements as their cause.
Fourth, other masters state that sound can arise from both appropriated and non-appropriated great elements.
Regarding the statement that sound produced by the conjunction of causes such as hands and drums serves as an example, the Master [Vasubandhu] refutes it below:
"If you do not admit that a single atom of visible form (*rūpa-paramāṇu*) is composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), then sound should likewise be so. The *Nyāyānusāra* asks:

"Is it not the case that there are sounds that arise with the great elements—both those possessed of sensory appropriation (*upātta*) and those devoid of it—as their cause, such as the sound produced by the conjunction of hands and drums?"
Regarding the production of sound, there are no such sounds as "two [sets of] four great elements" because each possesses its own distinct result.
Furthermore, it would entail the fallacy that two sets of four great elements, though identical in attaining a single result, would constitute simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) for one another.

Although the two sets of four great elements—whether appropriated (*upātta*) or non-appropriated (*anupātta*)—strike against one another and both act as causes to produce their respective sounds, those sounds each depend upon their own respective bases.

Therefore, three distinct entities are not established. Although there may be two sounds produced by the mutual impact of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of a hand—which is appropriated (*upātta*)—and a drum—which is non-appropriated (*anupātta*), these two sounds cancel each other out;
one can only perceive one or the other, and their distinct characteristics cannot be easily discerned.
Thus, the sphere of sound (*śabdāyatana*) consists of only two types.

The preceding section explained the sense-sphere of sound (*śabda-āyatana*). Below this, the third section explains the sense-sphere of taste (*rasa-āyatana*). This passage contains three parts: first, a summary of what preceded and an introduction to what follows;

second, the enumeration of the categories; and third, the listing of their names. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "The reason for explaining them out of order is to demonstrate that there is no fixed sequence in the arising of consciousness with respect to those objects."

From here below is the fourth section, the explanation of the base of fragrance (*gandha-āyatana*). This section has three parts: first, a summary of what preceded and an introduction to what follows;

second, stating the number—that there are four kinds of fragrance; third, listing their names. The *Nyāyapraveśa* (Treatise on Reasoning) states that "equal" and "unequal" refer to the fact that they increase or decrease based on the differences between individual bodies.

Some say it refers to the difference between being weak or intense. The present treatise states that there are three kinds of fragrance: pleasant fragrance, unpleasant fragrance, and neutral fragrance.
Foul odors and neutral odors: if they can nourish the sense faculties (*indriya*) and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), they are called pleasant odors;
those contrary to this are called foul odors. Those that lack the functions of these two are called neutral odors.

Alternatively, those produced through the predominance of meritorious karma are called pleasant odors, while those produced through the predominance of sinful karma are called foul odors. There are only four [types].

That which is produced by the power of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) is called "equal fragrance" (*sama-gandha*). Although this is a dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*), it also possesses differentiation;

therefore, that which is produced solely by the power of the primary elements is also subsumed under the category of the dominant fruit of sentient beings (*sattvādhipati-phala*). The commentary explains:

"That which is weak is called 'equal' because it is prevalent, while that which is intense is called 'unequal' because it is rare—just as among worldly people, those without wisdom are many, while those with wisdom are few."

Regarding humans who are similar in name and so forth, those with wisdom are few and thus surpass the multitude; having already explained the sphere of odor (*gandhāyatana*), the sphere of tangibility (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*) shall now be explained.

Within this text there are four parts: first, connecting the preceding to the subsequent; second, stating the number, which is eleven; third, listing the names; and fourth, defining their characteristics.

Among these eleven, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) will be explained later in the text. As for smoothness, roughness, lightness, and heaviness— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the structure and content up to that point.*
The text can be understood as follows: being oppressed by the sensation of cold, one necessarily desires warmth; thus, the desire for warmth is used to explain the sensation of cold.
The desire for food is termed "hunger," and the desire for drink is termed "thirst. These are all instances of designating the effect by the name of the cause;

therefore, it is said that when a person does not eat, the stomach becomes distended and empty, causing the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*) to stir and produce a tactile sensation that gives rise to the desire for food.
The desire for food is called "hunger," just as when a person does not drink and their lungs and stomach become parched, the fire-element (tejas) is agitated, giving rise to contact;

the arising of this contact within the body is termed the "desire to drink. The desire to drink is called "thirst. These are mental factors (*caitta*) and do not pertain to [the primary] contact itself.

Contact is the cause of hunger and thirst; because the name of the effect is established based on the cause, contact is designated by the names "hunger" and "thirst. As a verse states, which is cited below:
The verse establishes the name of the effect based on the cause to prove that the essence of the Buddhas’ appearance in the world is not itself pleasure;

rather, because it can produce pleasure, the name of the effect is applied to the cause, and thus the appearance of the Buddhas is called "pleasure. Other cases are likewise so. The *Nyāyapraveśa* (*Tattvārtha-śāstra*) states:

"The desire for food is called hunger; the desire for drink is called thirst. How could this be contrary to the definition of contact (*sparśa*), given that desire is a mental factor (*caitta*)? For...

Because the name of the effect is established based on the cause, there is no fault of contradiction. As for other points not yet mentioned, the categories of "weakness" (*hīna*) and so forth are subsumed within this [discussion] and thus are not explained separately.

"Oppression" (*paritāpa*) is not distinct from "smoothness" (*ślakṣṇatva*); "strength" (*bala*) is simply "roughness" (*karkaśatva*); and "weakness" (*hīna*) is included within the natures of "softness" (*mṛdu*), "warmth" (*uṣṇa*), and "lightness" (*laghu*).
Regarding the four [qualities] within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), they are distinguished by way of their respective realms; specifically, within the form realm, hunger and thirst do not exist.

Because it has the nature of contact-food (*sparśāhāra*), there is something remaining; the nine contacts of that realm, such as clothing, individually have no weight in *zhu*, and thus cannot be weighed.
However, when accumulated in great quantity, they do possess weight in *zhu*, and therefore can be weighed.

The preceding section has provided a detailed explanation of the five locations; hereafter, the sixth section clarifies the general and specific ways in which the five consciousnesses apprehend their objects. This passage contains four parts:

first, it concludes the previous discussion by noting that various types of *rūpāyatana* (form bases) have already been explained herein; second, it explains the general and specific ways in which visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) apprehends its object.

At times, visual consciousness arises in relation to a single object, meaning that at such moments, it individually cognizes each distinct thing; at other times, visual consciousness... [text fragment ends].

Regarding the statement that "arising is due to many objects": this means that at such a time, one does not individually discern [the objects] separately; it should be understood that this applies to the three types—armies, forests, and mountains—as observed from a distance.
One should know that the same applies to the consciousnesses of the ear, nose, tongue, and so forth. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle ten, asks:
"Does the eye-consciousness arise by taking a single form as its object, or does it arise by taking many forms as its object? If it takes a single form..."
How is it explained that [the eye] can produce visual consciousness? As it is said, visual consciousness can take five colors as its object.
If visual consciousness is produced by taking many colors as its object, why is there not a duality of cognitions? If there were a duality of cognitions, there would be multiple entities. Answer:
Visual consciousness is produced by taking a single type of color as its object. Question: If that is so, how can it take five colors as its object?
The Venerable Sthavira Āyuṣman Suśruta replied: "Because the perception of the objects occurs with such rapidity, the Buddha said they are perceived simultaneously, like a whirling firebrand;
yet in reality, it does not form a complete circle. Buddhadeva said:

"Because one does not discern [the individual] forms, it is said they are perceived simultaneously, like observing a grove of trees. Furthermore, others say: "Just as the five colors can produce the vision of color, when one perceives a single color, it is called 'seeing'."
Regarding the five colors: furthermore, if various colors are gathered together, one perceives many colors and a single consciousness arises;
if the colors are distinct, one perceives a single color and a single consciousness arises. Regarding the olfactory base (*gandhāyatana*), there are four kinds. Question:

Does a single fragrance serve as the condition for the arising of nose-consciousness, or do multiple fragrances serve as the condition? If it were by depending on a single fragrance that nose-consciousness arises, it would be as in the present case.
If one can smell a hundred kinds of blended incenses at once, and if the olfactory consciousness arises by taking many fragrances as its object, how is it that there are not two minds?
One should answer: it is by taking a single fragrance as its object that the olfactory consciousness is produced. Question:
If this is so, would it not be impossible to smell a hundred kinds of incenses at once? Answer: Some say that the hundred kinds of incenses produce a single [blended] fragrance.
Regarding the arising of nose-consciousness (*ghrāṇavijñāna*), it is said as follows: when many fragrances are gathered together, one smells many fragrances and a single consciousness arises;
if the fragrances are distinct, one smells a single fragrance and is able to produce a single consciousness. Regarding the conditions for perceiving form (*rūpa*), there were four masters:
first, Vasumitra, who held that [the eye] perceives only distinct [atoms]; second, Buddhadeva, who held that it does not clearly perceive the whole but clearly perceives the distinct [parts].
Regarding the third master’s view on the fivefold dependent origination of color being distinct from the single color, as stated in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*:

"The combination of blue and yellow colors gives rise to a dependently originated derivative color (*upādāya-rūpa*). This is the doctrine of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, not the tenet of the Sarvāstivāda school.

According to the fourth master in the subsequent section on the dependence of fragrance, this is the position of the commentator (*pūrvapakṣa-vādin*). When various colors aggregate, many colors are seen arising within a single consciousness. If...

If colors are distinct, then seeing one color gives rise to one consciousness; whether taken collectively or individually, both cases are either fully cognized or not fully cognized—this is the correct position of the commentator.
The first master holds that [consciousness] perceives only the distinct [colors]; the second master holds that collective seeing is not clearly cognized while distinct seeing is clearly cognized;
the third master holds that when different colors are perceived, one word expresses the seeing of many. None of these are the correct positions; in this present text, they are treated as identical.

In the fourth section of the *Vibhāṣā*, the definitive position of the commentators (*viniścaya-vādin*) explains that body-consciousness (*kāya-vijñāna*) takes a maximum number of objects because the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) are diverse;

thus, it differs from the four preceding objects. Regarding this, two masters offer explanations: the first master says that body-consciousness arises by taking a maximum of five tangibles as its object;
the second master says it arises by taking all eleven tangibles collectively as its object. The Master of the Treatise (*śāstrakāra*) raises an objection: if...
Since those five consciousnesses take their objects collectively, they should apprehend common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) rather than specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Why, then, does the Sūtra state that the five consciousnesses apprehend only specific characteristics and not common characteristics? The second master’s rebuttal is as follows:

This is because the Sūtra permits the five groups of consciousness to apprehend specific characteristics with respect to the twelve bases (*āyatana*), but it does not mean they apprehend them with respect to the eleven types of tangible objects (*spraṣṭavya-vastu*).
If it is the case that [the object] has its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its sphere, what fault is there? The *Mahāvibhāṣā* asks:

"Does a single tangible (*spraṣṭavya*) serve as the condition for the arising of body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*), or do multiple tangibles serve as the condition? It answers: "Eleven kinds of tangibles can give rise to eleven kinds of body-consciousness.
Furthermore, others say: "Five tangibles can give rise [to it]. If this is so, why is it not called a cognition that takes a collective sphere (*samastālambana*) as its object?

Because they belong to the same sphere of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*), they are not called "objects of collective perception. [The author] critiques this, saying: One should not speak in such a manner;
rather, it is as previously stated. The *Samyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* asks: "How many types of tangibles can give rise to body-consciousness?

Some say that from roughness to thirst [all can]. Others say that five types of tangibles can give rise to it: the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and roughness, and so on, up to hunger and thirst. Furthermore, others say...
These eleven types [of factors] give rise to body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) and so forth; because they are the objects of body-consciousness, there is no fault.

The Dharma Master Kōng (Kong) says that while the *Abhidharmahṛdaya* and the *Abhidharmakośa* contain only differing explanations, it may be that what was briefly cited earlier in the *Hṛdaya* represents the correct meaning.
Regarding the reason why the various treatises differ, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* follows a prior question, asking: "Does it take a single touch (*spraṣṭavya*) as its object?"

Regarding the statement that "many tangibles serve as conditions for the arising of body-consciousness" because it was previously asked how "a single tangible serves as a condition for the arising of body-consciousness," the answer given—that eleven tangibles give rise to eleven kinds of body-consciousness—means precisely that a single consciousness arises conditioned by a single tangible.
Next, another master says: "Just as among tastes, if the tastes are distinct, one tastes a single flavor."

If one consciousness were produced by contact with the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), since these are not distinct entities, the derived matter of touch must necessarily possess all four great elements;
thus, at the very least, five types of touch would be required to produce consciousness. Since this calculation is unreasonable, it is refuted as previously stated.
As the critics maintain, if touch alone can already produce eleven [types of consciousness], then it goes without saying that when accompanied by other factors, they arise together.
The *Śāstraviniścaya* (Treatise on Abandonment), following the preceding text, states: "There are times when visual consciousness arises due to multiple objects;

if at such times there is no conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*), one should know that the same applies to auditory and other consciousnesses, because the first four consciousnesses clearly take [multiple objects] collectively.

It then analogizes this to the body-consciousness, stating: "If the body-consciousness arises from a maximum of five types of tangibles, this collective maximum would not be appropriate [if it were limited]."

Furthermore, there is another master who asserts that [the object] is complete with eleven factors capable of producing body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*). This is because he reconciles the general and specific categories to harmonize with the correct principle;

thus, he concludes later by asking, "What fault is there in this? According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, since it refers to the maximum number of general conditions, it says that eleven factors can produce body-consciousness.
However, if one considers the minimum number of specific conditions, even then eleven types of contact (*spraṣṭavya*) give rise to eleven instances of body-consciousness.

Regarding consciousness, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states below that the body and its objects are not fixed: the body sometimes takes the four great elements as its object, sometimes takes what is derived from them as its object, and sometimes takes both the primary and derived elements as its object.

Since it is established that these can take distinct objects, we know that the eleven [sense organs] also obtain distinct objects, unlike the former masters who held that the primary and derived elements do not take distinct objects and must therefore take all five [elements]. The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* follows the preceding question.

The question is asked: "How many types of tangibles can give rise to body-consciousness? The first master replies: "Seven. Because the derived tangibles (upādāya-spraṣṭavya) possess distinct differences, each one—from roughness to thirst—can individually give rise to it;
however, because the primary elements (mahābhūta) do not differ from one another, they are not said to do so. The second master says:

"Because the seven derived tangibles possess their own distinct differences, while the primary elements and the derived tangibles are necessarily not different [in their capacity as a basis], five tangibles can give rise to it."

Regarding the third master’s statement following the discussion on the five contacts (*sparśa*), he says: "If we rely on the collection of all contacts, there are eleven kinds capable of giving rise to body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*);
why then speak of only five? This is an alternative explanation based on the preceding text;

while the interpretations differ, according to the underlying principle, if many contacts collect together, then eleven contacts produce a single consciousness. However, if one relies on their distinct individuality, they each take a single [object] as their condition.
The statement that tactile contact gives rise to a single body-consciousness is no different from what was said regarding the [other] four objects.

Fifth, it clarifies the sequence in which the two consciousnesses of the body and tongue apprehend their respective objects. In the text, the initial question is: "Since the two objects of the body and tongue faculties arrive simultaneously and consciousnesses do not arise concurrently, which consciousness arises first?
The answer below states: "Whichever object is more powerful, its corresponding consciousness arises first; if the two objects are equal..."
The tongue-consciousness arises first because, due to long-standing habituation since beginningless time, the desire for food draws the body forward and causes it to continue;

furthermore, among the objects of food, the consciousness of flavor is predominant, and thus the tongue-consciousness arises first. Although the nine subtle particles of sound are not separated from one another, when color and sound are separated, one perceives them individually;

likewise, when wind blows, the subtle fragrance alone gives rise to nose-consciousness. Therefore, there is no need to explain [the sequence] regarding the two objects of touch and taste, as they both arise when in contact with the sense organ.
One must investigate the sequence of the arising of consciousness because it is not fixed.
Thus ends the third section, consisting of one verse, which analyzes the five objective spheres (*viṣaya*) as form (*rūpa*).

Below this, the fourth section consists of three verses that next analyze non-informative form (*avijñapti-rūpa*); therein, the first verse correctly defines the characteristics of non-informative form, while the subsequent two verses provide the reasons.
The treatise on the generation and differentiation of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) consists of three parts:
first, a summary of what preceded and an introduction of what follows; second, the presentation of the root verses;
and third, the commentary on the root verses. Within the latter, there are ten sections; the first restates the distracted mind and explains the distracted mind.

1. "The former" refers to this concentrated mind as opposed to other distracted minds. 2. "The two cases of non-mind" refer to entering the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*);
in these two attainments, unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) does not function, and in the retribution of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-vedanīya-vipāka*), unmanifest form does not function;

therefore, they are not mentioned. 3. "The word 'etcetera' (*ādi*) is cited to explain and indicate that it includes distracted minds, as well as non-distracted concentrated minds and states of non-mind."

1. Regarding the possession of mind (*sacittaka*), within these four stages, the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) is constantly active. 2. The first of the four explanations for "flowing along" (*anuvartin*):

it is said that the unmanifest arises once and continues in a similar succession before and after; this is called "flowing along. 3. The second explanation: pure and impure unmanifests—excluding those that are non-indicative and neutral—are designated as "pure and impure," while only those that are exclusively wholesome or unwholesome are so named.
4. The third explanation: [it is defined by] being derived from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*). This is intended to distinguish it from various types of acquisitions (*prāpti*).

Furthermore, because they are similar and continuous, it is said again that although the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derivatives (*upādāya-rūpa*) arise simultaneously and are similar and continuous, the latter are not derived from the primary elements because they do not possess the nature of matter (*rūpa*).

The *Vibhāṣā* states that "derivation" (*upādāya*) has the sense of "cause," meaning they act as the five kinds of causes, such as the cause of production (*janana-hetu*), and so forth, as will be explained in the following text. This clarifies the reason for establishing the designation.
It is said that by these eight explanations, although the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) is of the nature of bodily and vocal form-action (*rūpa-karman*),
it is called "unmanifest" because— unlike manifest bodily and vocal actions which are both of the nature of form—

it does not manifest itself so as to make others understand the goodness or evil within one's mind. Thus, the reason for establishing this name is that it does not manifest itself to make others understand.

Furthermore, because bodily and vocal informative actions (*vijñapti-karman*) manifest and cause others to understand the goodness or evil within one's own mind, they are called "informative" (*savijñapti*).
Thus, the *Karmasiddhiprakaraṇa* asks: "Why are they called 'informative'? It is because they can manifest the mind that initiates the action, causing others to know it.
To clarify this meaning, a verse says: "By externally manifesting bodily and vocal informatives, [one reveals] what was thought within the inner mind; it is like that..."
The fish dwelling in the deep waters stir the waves to reveal themselves; this "explanation" (śāstra) clarifies that this is the tenet of the Sautrāntika masters. The *Nyāyabindu* states:

"The explanation [indicates] that this is the intention of other masters," for the Master of the Sūtras (the author of the *Abhidharmakośa*) does not accept such a kind of unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*).
Briefly stated, unmanifest form is of two types: first, that which arises from bodily and vocal manifest karma.
The wholesome and unwholesome matter produced by the two [types of volition] and by meditative concentration is called "unmanifest" (avijñapti).

The preceding single verse correctly defines the characteristics of the unmanifest; from here on, the following two verses address the topic as it arises from the discussion, defining the primary elements (mahābhūta) that constitute its basis.
Within these, the first verse defines the four great elements in their substantial sense, while the second verse defines them in a conventional sense.
Regarding the name "Four Great Elements" (*mahābhūta*), there are three parts within the initial verse of the treatise: first, restating the preceding question; second, presenting the root verse;
and third, explaining the text of the root verse. Within the explanation of the verse, there are six sections: first, the explanation of the second line;

second, the explanation that the four elements are called "elements" (*dhātu*) because they can maintain their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) as well as derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*); third, the explanation that these four great elements are also called... [text fragment].
The primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are the basis for all other derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*), and thus they constitute their genus. As the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"The term 'genus' (*prakṛti*) and the term 'producer' (*janaka*) are merely different names. Below, it explains the term "great" (*mahat*) through three meanings: first, because its essence is vast;

second, because each atom (*paramāṇu*) among the ten types of derived matter is surrounded by the four primary elements; and third, because each atom of the four primary elements [is likewise so constituted].

First, because there is no necessity for the other ten derived forms (*upādāya-rūpa*) to exist in every location, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are appropriately termed "great" due to the vastness of their substance.

Second, within the dense aggregations where earth and the other elements predominate, their form and appearance are "great"; thus, at the time of the world's initial formation, the element of earth predominates and fills the world, and the form and appearance of the earth are great.
Subsequently, when the three calamities arise, within the dense aggregations where water, fire, or wind predominate, the forms of water, fire, and wind [are likewise great].

Regarding the statement that "the characteristic is great because it gives rise to various great functional activities": within the world, all great functional activities of construction and creation arise from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
First is the greatness of essence (*svabhāva-mahattva*), second is the greatness of characteristic (*lakṣaṇa-mahattva*), and last is the greatness of function (*kāritra-mahattva*).

The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "Furthermore, in this context, because the two terms 'great' (*mahat*) and 'element' (*dhātu*) are both present, only the four [elements] are established; [other entities] are excluded."

Space possesses magnitude but lacks the meaning of being a "seed" (*bīja*) and the designation of being "productive" (*janaka*); therefore, derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*) and other conditioned non-material phenomena are not seeds.
As previously stated, the two meanings of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are mutually inconsistent;

thus, if even one [of these two] is lacking, they cannot produce or cease, nor can they bring about the remaining derived matter. Therefore, the primary elements are... [only those possessing both characteristics].
Regarding the *Vibhāṣā* on "neither increasing nor decreasing," they state: if there were decrease, there would be no capacity [for increase];

if there were increase, it would be useless—just as a bed has four legs. This explains the third phrase. "Growth" (*vṛddhi*) refers to the blowing forth of things so that they flourish, or the blowing forth of water so that it flows and extends;
thus the five functional activities are established. Since this is so, the fourth phrase can be understood according to the text.

In the *Ṣaṭpādābhidharma-śāstra* (Six-Legged Treatise) and the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*, as well as in the Sūtras, a question is raised: "What is called the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*)? The answer states:
"It is the nature of lightness and movement. Because lightness and movement are concordant and similar, it is said that "lightness" refers to "movement.

Furthermore, because the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* and the Sūtras also state that the nature of lightness is a derived form (*upādāya-rūpa*), it follows that the wind element [is likewise a derived form].

Motion is its intrinsic nature; however, when the preceding sūtras and śāstras answer that "lightness and so forth are the nature of motion," they cite the lightness of the derived (bhautika) matter to reveal the moving substance of the primary element (bhūta).
Thus, the sūtras and śāstras also state that lightness constitutes the wind-element (*vāyu-dhātu*), yet in reality, lightness is a derived fruit.
Among the seven case-endings (*vibhakti*), this refers to the second case, the accusative (*karman*), which is why it is called "lightness."

This is because it is the function [of wind]. Regarding its seventh transformation, the *Commentary on the Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (Shel zhengli lun shu), in explaining the fourth fascicle of the *Nyāyabindu*, states:
"Because motion in relation to the three qualities such as solidity is most difficult to discern, the light effect is cited to reveal the cause of wind.
Although all four great elements are light causes, this statement is made because [lightness] is predominant [in wind]; although fire is also predominant, it is not definitive."

Furthermore, because *samādhi* (concentration) and lightness (*laghu*) are similar in their mutual dependence on motion (*calatva*), the treatise and the sūtra state that lightness and so forth are of the nature of motion.

From here below is the second verse, which distinguishes the four great elements as provisional designations (*prajñapti*). Within this passage there are three parts: first, the inquiry into their origination;

second, the presentation of the root verse; and third, the explanation of the root verse. Within the latter, there are two sections: first, the individual explanation of the root verse, which may be understood according to the text; second, [the summary].
Why is this aggregate [of form] explained below in general as having eleven types of "form" (*rūpa*)? In the text, the initial question asks:
"Are these eleven types of form—from the eye as the first to the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) as the last—called 'form'? Below, the answer provides two explanations:

the first states that it is called "form" because it undergoes transformation and decay (*rūpyate*); the second states that it is called "form" because it offers resistance (*pratighāta*). Regarding this:

In the first section, there are eight parts: (1) establishing the thesis that it is called "form" (*rūpa*) because it undergoes transformation and decay; (2) citing a sūtra as proof, beginning with "As the Blessed One said...";
(3) asking who is capable of causing transformation and decay; (4) answering that it is by contact with the hand and so forth;

(5) further explaining that transformation and decay means being susceptible to affliction and destruction; (6) citing a sūtra as proof of this affliction and destruction, beginning with "Therefore, in the *Arthavargīya*..."; (7) [the seventh part]; (8) [the eighth part].
Question: Furthermore, how is it that form (*rūpa*) is afflicted and destroyed by desire? Answer: Because it arises through being disturbed, afflicted, and transformed by desire.

Regarding the second [section] of the text, there are seven points: First, the Sarvāstivāda establishes their thesis, stating that some say it is called "form" because it is subject to transformation and obstruction (*rūpaṇa*).
Second, the Master raises an objection: If that were so, then atoms (*paramāṇu*) should not be called "form," as they lack transformation and obstruction. Third, the Sarvāstivāda...

Vasubandhu rescues this difficulty by saying that it is not so; there is not a single atom (*paramāṇu*) that dwells in isolation. It is because atoms aggregate and abide together that the meaning of "changeable and obstructive" (*rūpaṇa*) is established.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "There is no single atom that exists alone in the present, for they abide in accumulation;

thus the meaning of changeability and obstruction is established. Some say that there are indeed atoms that exist in isolation, and only then do they become changeable and obstructive, yet they do not produce consciousness. Fifth.
Since consciousness depends on the accumulation of conditions, it is like the established theory of atoms (*paramāṇu*):

although atoms have no spatial dimensions and no mutual contact, they are nonetheless admitted to possess the functions of resistance (*sapratigha*), opposition (*sāvaraṇa*), and obstruction (*pratibandha*). One should know that the meaning of "transformation and resistance" (*rūpaṇa*) is likewise.

[The opponent] objects: if the meaning of transformation and resistance can be established when a multitude of present atoms are gathered, how could it be established when those atoms disperse upon encountering unconditioned atoms?

It is not called "form" [in the past or future]. The Sarvāstivādins offer this defense: "This [past and future form] also existed as having the capacity for resistance (varṇa-pratighāta) at one time, and it belongs to the same category as that which is presently existing.
For example, when firewood is currently being burned, it can still be called 'firewood';

even wood that has not yet been burned or has already been burned is called 'firewood' because it belongs to the category of firewood. Sixth, the Master [Vasubandhu] again raises an objection regarding the ten types of material form that have existed in the past...

When there is an aggregation, the meaning of "obstruction and change" can be established; however, for non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), this is not the case because atoms do not aggregate across the three time periods.
Consequently, all non-informative matter would fail to be designated as "matter" (*rūpa*).
Regarding this sixth objection, the third section of the seventh chapter below contains the successive defenses offered by three Vaibhāṣika masters.
The Master then provides three distinct explanations. Regarding the first, there are two parts. First, the Vaibhāṣika masters offer a defense by means of both doctrine and analogy, stating:

"Because manifest form (*vijñapti-rūpa*) possesses resistance and changeability, the non-manifest (*avijñapti*) follows suit; thus, it too receives the name 'form,' just as when a tree moves, its shadow also moves accordingly.
Second, the Master refutes this interpretation, asserting that it is not so. He first refutes their claim that non-manifest form is not ultimate [matter].
Since the subtle [unmanifest] lacks resistance and obstruction, how can it receive the name "matter" (rūpa) by following that [manifest action]?
If the unmanifest receives the name "matter" by following the manifest, then the unmanifest should likewise be composed of atoms, characterized by resistance and obstruction, and visible.
Next, he refutes the analogy: if the unmanifest receives the name "matter" by following the manifest, it would be like a shadow that follows when a tree moves.

If that which moves were to perish along with the manifest action (*vijñapti*), then the non-manifest (*avijñapti*) would necessarily perish as well; for just as when a tree perishes, its shadow must necessarily perish.
If the shadow perished along with it, one could say that the shadow moves following the tree.

Since the non-manifest does not perish along with the manifest, how can the non-manifest be designated by the name "matter derived from the manifest" (*rūpa-anupātta*)? The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "Some explain that because manifest matter possesses transformation and resistance (*pratighāta*), [the non-manifest]..."

To claim that it also receives the name "matter" (rūpa) by following [the mind] is illogical; matter that evolves in accordance with the mind does not arise from informative action (vijñapti), and thus it would not be matter.
Next, the second Vaibhāṣika master’s defense is explained. Within this passage, there are five parts: first, the statement of that master’s defense;

second, the explanation by another Vaibhāṣika master regarding the sixth difficulty mentioned above; and [the point that] because its basis, the primary elements (mahābhūta), possess resistance and transformation, non-informative action (avijñapti-karma) is indeed matter.

Furthermore, both the "matter" (rūpa) and the "unmanifest" (avijñapti)—whether in a state of concentration or distraction—are dependent upon the primary elements (mahābhūta). The two masters raise an objection:

"If that is so, since the five sense organs (*indriya*) upon which they depend possess resistance (*sapratigha*), the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, should also be termed 'matter'. That teacher offers this defense: "This objection is not equivalent.
When the unmanifest arises depending on the primary elements, it arises directly from them; however, [the case of the sense organs] is not the same," says Kātyāyanīputra.

The *Pratyaya-varga* (Chapter on Conditions) states that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) act as causes for derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*). The *Abhinava-vibhāṣā-śāstra* explains that the four great elements function as the five causes—namely, the cause of production (*janana-hetu*) and so forth—for derived matter;
since all such causes are subsumed under the category of causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the *Abhinava-vibhāṣā-śāstra* asserts that there are ten causes that constitute causal conditions:

the five causes beginning with the associated cause (*samprayukta-hetu*) and the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), and the five causes beginning with the cause of production (*janana-hetu*) and the supporting cause (*niśraya-hetu*). For example:

A shadow arises in direct dependence on a tree, and light is produced in direct dependence on a jewel; however, when the five consciousnesses, such as visual consciousness, depend upon the eye and so forth, it is not like that.
They do not arise through such direct dependence, for the five sense organs serve only as the "efficient cause" (*kāraṇa-hetu*)—acting as a superior, auxiliary condition for their arising.

Thus, the five consciousnesses do not undergo transformation according to their remote dependence [on the organs], which possess the quality of resistance (*sapratigha*). Fourth, the Master [Vasubandhu] first refutes this analogy.

The statements that "the shadow depends on the tree" and "the light depends on the jewel" do not accord with the tenets of the *Vibhāṣā*. According to the school of the *Vibhāṣā*, the eight subtle particles (*aṇu*) are inseparable;
the subtle particles of visible color (*varṇa*) such as shadow and light each depend upon their own respective four great elements (*mahābhūta*) within those shadows and lights.
How, then, can it be said that the shadow depends on the tree or the light depends on the jewel? Next, [the text] refutes the conventional designation of these phenomena.
Even if you grant that your shadow and light depend upon the tree and the jewel, the unmanifest color (*avijñapti-rūpa*) is not like those shadows and lights depending on the tree and the jewel;

for according to the Vaibhāṣika school, although the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) upon which it depends have ceased, the unmanifest color continues to arise in a constant succession and does not perish along with them.
If the unmanifest color were the same as the shadow and light depending on the tree and the jewel, then it would perish when the tree and the jewel perish.

If [the unmanifest] were to cease following the cessation of the shadow and light, it would follow that the unmanifest ceases when the four great elements cease, and thus there would be no continuity.

For these five reasons, what was stated above does not resolve the objection. Next, the third point—the Vaibhāṣika master’s renewed defense against the objection that the five consciousnesses should also be called "matter" (rūpa) because they follow the sense organs—is presented;
this section contains three parts, the first of which describes the third Vaibhāṣika master.
The Master separately explains the objection regarding the five consciousnesses mentioned above: "The supports of the five consciousnesses, such as visual consciousness, are not fixed;
they may be characterized by resistance (*sapratigha*), namely the simultaneous sense organs such as the eye, or they may lack resistance, namely the immediately preceding ceased mind (*manas*).

However, the support of the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) is not like this, as it relies solely on that which possesses resistance. This second point summarizes the previous objection; therefore, the preceding citation concerning the five consciousnesses [serves as the basis for this argument].

It is difficult to establish that [the three fetters] are not uniform; the fundamental tenet that "matter" (*rūpa*) is defined by resistance (*pratighāta*) is thus logically established. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"Furthermore, it is illogical for the six consciousnesses to be of one nature or one category, nor could they be both matter and non-matter.

Since there is no such thing as 'unmanifest' (*avijñapti*) that does not arise based on matter, its basis must possess resistance; therefore, the unmanifest that depends upon it is also established as matter."

Regarding the term "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*): just as the names and concepts for "ox" or "peacock" are established based on minor classifications [of their physical forms], they do not lack differentiation; thus, one should not raise an objection against this.
The explanation states that in the West, the water buffalo is called "earth-sleeper" (*bhūmiśaya*) and the peacock is called "earth-caller" (*bhūmiruta*).
Just as a water buffalo cannot sleep unless it is in the water, yet must come out onto dry land to sleep—whereas [the peacock] remains in the water.

The middle [category] is also called "earth-dwellers" (*bhūmi-śāyin*); this name is established based on their youth, for when peacocks fly they cannot cry out, but only when on the ground can they cry—thus they are called "earth-callers" (*bhūmi-kūjita*).
This name is also established based on their youth. According to the Sarvāstivāda school, there are four types of phenomena that are not subject to resistance (*apratigha*):
first, atoms (*paramāṇu*); second, past matter (*atīta-rūpa*); third, future matter (*anāgata-rūpa*); and fourth, [unmanifest matter].

That which is called "unmanifest form" (*avijñapti-rūpa*) and yet is designated as "subject to transformation and resistance" (*rūpaṇā*) is also a name derived by taking a small portion from the ten types of aggregated matter in the present.
The above was the fourth section, consisting of three verses, which analyzed unmanifest form; hereafter begins the fifth section, which [analyzes] the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
The mutual inclusion of the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*) can be understood from the text as it stands.
Above, five and a half verses specifically clarify the mutual inclusion of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and the bases and elements;

hereafter, secondly, one and a half verses specifically clarify the mutual inclusion of the three aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations (*vedanā-, saṃjñā-, and saṃskāraskandha*), and the bases and elements. Within this section, there are three parts.

First, the connection between the preceding and following sections; second, the citation of the root verse; third, the commentary on the text of the root verse. Within this commentary, there are four parts:

first, the commentary on the first phrase regarding the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), which refers to the three feelings—the experience of suffering, pleasure, and so forth—and the three types of contact that lead to the understanding of pleasure and the other feelings.

Second, the commentary on the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) and below, which explains the second phrase as it appears in the text. Third, the commentary on the third phrase, beginning with "Excluding what has already been mentioned," and so forth.

Within this passage there are six points. First, the direct explanation of the verse: excluding the previously mentioned three aggregates of form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), and perception (*saṃjñā*), as well as the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna*) mentioned later in the verse, all remaining forty-four mental factors (*caitasika*) and fourteen formations dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*)—these fifty-eight dharmas are termed the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
Second, reconciling with the Sūtras: although the Sūtras state that the six types of volition (*cetanā*) constitute the aggregate of formations, [this verse] explains it more extensively.

Because these three are preeminent, they are specifically mentioned; therefore, the Buddha, in the *Sūtra on the Lower Fetters*, specifically mentions that "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*) refers to the act of conditioning.
If this were not the case, the Sautrāntika master would be subject to a counter-objection from the Sarvāstivāda, as found in the *Nyāyānusāra*:

there are certain Sautrāntika dissenters who, apart from the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), establish only three mental factors—namely, sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*). Thus, he now presents a counter-objection.

If one does not speak in terms of the "predominant" [factors], then the remaining forty-four mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) and the fourteen dissociated factors (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) would not be included within the aggregates (*skandha*).

Consequently, they would not be comprised within the Truths of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and Origination (*samudaya-satya*). If they were not comprised within the Truths of Suffering and Origination, they could not constitute the Truth of Suffering;

it should be understood that the Truth of Origination must be abandoned. Otherwise, there would be no one capable of attaining the fruit of Arhatship. (Five citations from sūtras prove the universal knowledge.)

Regarding abandonment, as the World-Honored One has said: "If, with respect to even a single contaminated resultant dharma, one has not used the path of non-obstruction to reach it and has not used the path of liberation to realize it, I say that one cannot bring an end to suffering or attain the fruit of Arhatship;

because the meaning of the contaminated cause has not been severed by the path of non-obstruction and has not been extinguished by the path of liberation, it is likewise in all six cases. Therefore...

It must certainly be concluded below that although there are six textual passages, they are combined to explain the third line; the four [points] therein are what has been explained above, while the remaining three lines can be understood from the subsequent explanation.

Thus far, the second section—consisting of one and a half verses—clarifies the inclusion of the three aggregates (skandhas) of feeling, perception, and formations, as well as their relationship to the bases (āyatana) and elements (dhātu).

From here below is the third section, consisting of two verses that specifically clarify the inclusion of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) within the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*).

Within the first verse, there are three parts: first, concluding the preceding section and introducing the subsequent one; second, presenting the root verse, wherein the first line correctly identifies the aggregate of consciousness and the following three lines clarify its inclusion within the bases and elements;
third, explaining the text of the verse, which has three sub-sections, the first of which explains the initial [line].
The Master [Xuanzang], about to explain this passage, first cites the third fascicle of the *Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā* (Treatise on Right Reasoning), which states:

"Consciousness (*vijñāna*) means 'to cognize' (*upalabdhi*)," which signifies the general apprehension of the characteristics of an object. Each consciousness generally apprehends the respective characteristics of its own particular object;
that is to say, although many objects such as visible forms may appear before the eye-consciousness, it only apprehends visible form and does not apprehend sound and so forth. It only apprehends...
Blue and so forth do not mean that blue and so forth are [the object]; nor are they the agreeable or disagreeable, the male or female, the human or stump, the acquisition or loss, and so on.
Just as the eye-consciousness, with respect to its own object, grasps only the general characteristic (*nimitta*), so too should the other consciousnesses be understood accordingly.
The commentary explains: "Just as when the eye-consciousness takes as its object the intrinsic nature and characteristic of blue, it [relates] to the eye..."
When an image of blue appears upon consciousness, this very appearance is termed the "aspect" (*ākāra*). However, this aspect has no separate ontological substance;

it is subsumed within the aggregates, elements, and bases according to the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*). That is to say, when it appears upon the aggregate of consciousness, it is subsumed within the aggregate of consciousness;

when it appears upon sensation, perception, and so forth, it is subsumed within the aggregates of sensation, perception, and so forth. The same applies to the elements and bases. It is not, however, the object of cognition (*ālambana*).

Regarding the inclusion by way of conditions (*pratyaya-saṃgraha*): this corresponds to the "objective part" (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the Mahāyāna. If the objective part of the Mahāyāna resembles form (*rūpa*), it is included within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*);

if it resembles feeling, perception, and so forth, it is included within the aggregates of feeling, perception, and so on. The same applies to the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*). They are categorized according to the nature of what they resemble.

Furthermore, the aggregates, elements, and bases are also included among the "object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*). As for "consciousness," which means "to cognize," it refers to the mere general grasping of an object.

The meaning of "the aspect of the image of the object-field" (*dhātu-pratibimba-nimitta*) distinguishes it from feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and so forth, by specifically taking up the aspect of the object.

This means that each of the six consciousnesses individually and separately takes as its object the six sense-fields; the collective grasping of the images of those respective sixfold objects is called "discernment" (*vijñapti*).

Each [consciousness] is distinct and separately discerns the images of the six sense-fields—this is the meaning of "discernment. It is the meaning of collectively grasping one's own respective object-field. That is to say:

Although many objects such as the six sense-fields (ṣaḍviṣaya) are present before it, that eye-consciousness (cakṣurvijñāna) perceives only visible form (rūpa) and does not perceive the other four fields such as sound;
this distinguishes it from the four consciousnesses beginning with the ear-consciousness, which perceive only the twenty types of visible form such as blue and yellow.

This meaning does not imply that the name "blue" is what is distinguished; rather, it means that while the eye-consciousness perceives the object blue, it also perceives the name "blue," each being distinct.

Regarding the object (*artha*), if it is like the category of "feeling" (*vedanā-skandha*), one grasps the general characteristic of blue as a whole while separately grasping its specific aspects—such as being disagreeable, agreeable, or neutral—which are objects of mental ideation (*saṃjñā*).

In the category of "ideation," one grasps the general meaning of blue as a whole while separately grasping specific characteristics such as male, female, a tree stump, and so forth. In the category of "volition" (*cetanā*), one grasps the general characteristic of blue as a whole while separately grasping specific characteristics such as gain and loss;
thus, these all possess both general and specific interpretations. Consciousness (*vijñāna*), however, is not like this; it only grasps the general characteristic of blue and so forth.
It does not grasp the distinct characteristics apprehended by feelings such as the agreeable or disagreeable;
it does not grasp the distinct characteristics apprehended by perceptions such as "man" or "tree stump"; nor does it grasp the distinct characteristics apprehended by thoughts such as gain or loss.
Just as that visual consciousness grasps only the general characteristics, such as blue and so forth, within its respective object, so too should the other consciousnesses be understood accordingly.

Regarding the question of whether the mental factors such as perception (*saṃjñā*) and feeling (*vedanā*) have a collective or individual nature, if one says there are two types of understanding—collective and individual—how can it be that they lack two distinct entities?
Why does the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* state that there is no determination of duality? The answer is: while there are two functions, there is no duality of entity.

"No determination of duality" means there is no entity that constitutes a dual determination. In the present text, the phrase "each and every distinct discernment" refers to the six respective objects of the sensory realms.

The aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is defined by its specific etymological analysis as follows: it takes the individual objects as its conditions and grasps their respective images; when these images appear, each is clearly cognized.

Because it performs the function of "cognizing" (*vijñapti*), it is called the aggregate of consciousness. Furthermore, this is differentiated into the six groups of consciousness (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna-kāya*), which are easy to understand.

One should know that the following [section] explains the remaining three phrases, which are likewise easy to understand. Thirdly, the section beginning with "Thus, these ten... provides a general summary.
The five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements are mutually identical.

The preceding line of verse correctly identifies the mutual identity of the aggregates, bases, and elements; the latter half of the line states that the six groups of consciousness are designated as "mind.
Within this passage, there are four parts: first, it restates the six consciousnesses as distinct phenomena from the mind.

Answer: There is no other distinct dharma. Third, within this very absence of a distinct dharma, it is consistent with the root verse because the six consciousness-bodies, having ceased immediately prior, serve as the *manas*;
thus, there is no distinct dharma. Fourth, the explanation of the root verse can be understood according to the text.

In the text establishing the eighteen *dhātus* from the latter half of the verse, there are three parts: first, the preceding section as the question; second, the presentation of the verse itself as the answer;

and third, the commentary on the text of the verse. Within the commentary, there are three sections: first, the commentary on the verse itself: "It should be understood that these six bases (*āśraya*), which are the six faculties (*indriya*);

the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) which depend upon them (*āśrita*); and the six objects (*viṣaya*) which are their objective supports—each consisting of six, constitute the eighteen *dhātus*. Second, "If that is so," and so forth.

The objection that the three [conditions] are not so is incorrect; the following commentary explains that because the remaining afflictions (*kleśa*) that moisten rebirth are absent, the subsequent consciousness does not arise.
Thus concludes the third section, which consists of two verses specifically clarifying the inclusion of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) within one another.

Below this, the fourth section consists of one verse that subsumes all phenomena (*dharma*) under one aggregate, base, and element. Within this passage, there are three parts; first, the restatement [of the subject].

Regarding the previous question, the subsequent section may also be divided into three parts: first, the individual questions; second, the summary question; and third, the response by citing the verse.

Third, the explanation of the main text of the verse contains four sections. The first is the explanation of the second line [of the verse]: "One should know that the aggregate of form comprises eleven [bases]; the mind-base (*manāyatana*) comprises all mental factors;
and the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) comprises forty-six mental concomitants, fourteen non-associated formations, and the three unconditioned phenomena. This is the general summary.

1. To encompass all phenomena exhaustively, the first phrase is explained as follows: "Third, regarding the various bases (*āyatana*), from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), one encompasses oneself and not others;
this explains the remaining two phrases. 4. "If, regarding the various bases, from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one encompasses others."
From here below, the fifth section consists of one verse-line explaining the two [sets of] bases—eye, ear, and nose—and the two elements within a single textual passage.
First, it restates that the bases of eye, ear, and nose each have two [types], and that the eighteen elements in substance are not twenty-one.

This objection is irrational; below, the root verse is cited as the answer. Within this, the first two lines directly explain the preceding objection; both the verse and its commentary are easily understood. The subsequent [lines] follow.
The two lines explain that the eye, ear, and nose each have two locations. Within the text, there are three parts: first, citing the preceding section as a question;
second, providing the root verse as the answer; and third, explaining the text of the root verse. Within this third part, there are five sections: first, recounting the ancient explanations;

second, the Master’s refutation of the ancient explanation with the words "This explanation is not correct" and so forth; third, the ancient masters’ question to the Master with the words "If that were so," and so forth; fourth... [text truncated].

"Generating consciousness" begins the Master’s exposition of the current explanation of the five [aggregates]. "Therefore, the three faculties" concludes that each of the three faculties has two locations, as can be understood from the text.

Below this, the sixth section consists of one verse explaining the meaning of the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and bases (āyatana). Within this passage, there are three parts; first, it concludes the preceding discussion.

Question: Regarding the latter two [stanzas], the root verses are cited as the answer, and there are three explanations of the meaning of those verses. Within this section, there are four parts. First is the explanation of the meaning of "aggregate" (*skandha*).

This contains four sub-sections. First is the direct explanation of the meaning of the root verse: that the sense of a collection or combination of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) is the meaning of "aggregate.

Second, under the heading "As stated in the Sūtra," there is an introduction of scriptural evidence from five perspectives to demonstrate that the term "aggregate" explains the meaning of "collection": (1) the three time periods; (2) ... [the remaining items follow].

1. Internal and external; 2. the three coarse and the four subtle; 3. the four superior and inferior; 4. near and distant; 5. the three fetters—by means of this sutra, the meaning of "aggregation" (*rāśi*) is established. 4.
Within this sutra, the following explains the interpretations of two masters regarding the five gates of scriptural exegesis. First, the explanation of the Vaibhāṣika master:
within this sutra, the passage on "the impermanent having ceased," etc., explains that the form (*rūpa*) of the three time periods can be understood. Next, by means of the three... [text ends]

The explanation of the meaning regarding the internal and external begins first with the gateway of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). One's own five sense organs and the six objects of the five senses are called "internal" forms;

all other forms—those belonging to the bodies of others and those not included among sentient beings (insentient matter)—are called "external. Next, the internal and external are distinguished by means of the twelve bases (*āyatana*):
the forms of one's own and others' five sense organs are called "internal," while the six objects of one's own and others' [senses] as well as insentient matter are called "external."

Because they are external, it is said that, when distinguished by way of their bases (*āyatana*), there is one set of four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) for internal mindfulness of objects (*smṛtyupasthāna*) in relation to internal bases, and another set of four alternatives for external mindfulness of objects in relation to external bases; this can be understood through reflection.

Next, the two subsequent meanings explain the gate of the coarse and the subtle; therein, first, the ten material [bases] are called "coarse" because they possess resistance (*sapratigha*), whereas the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) does not.

Regarding the subtle, it is explained next by means of the relative nature of the ten material elements (*daśa-rūpa*) to define the coarse and the subtle; thus, it is said that "sometimes [the distinction] is by the power of relativity.

For example, a peach is called "coarse" in relation to a jujube, while it is called "subtle" in relation to a melon. If one were to object that this difficulty is invalid because there is no distinct entity for relative coarseness and subtlety, that is not so;
for the objects of comparison differ. Just as a peach is considered coarse in relation to that jujube, it has never been considered coarse in relation to a melon.

To consider the gourd as fine in relation to something else, while that very same thing was never considered coarse [in relation to it], is like the relationship between father and son; likewise, suffering, origination, and denial are established through mutual dependence.
To explain the categories of "with resistance" (*sapratigha*) and "without resistance" (*apratigha*) by combining them with this principle of mutual dependence is an error.

Next, the explanation of the categories of superior-inferior and distant-near is easily understood. Following this, the remaining four aggregates are explained by analogy; therefore, it says "up to the aggregate of consciousness."

The same applies to the middle [category]. Just as there is a distinction between the coarse and the subtle within a single category, the four aggregates are all non-obstructive (*apratigha*); therefore, they cannot be described as "coarse" by virtue of being obstructive. Regarding these four aggregates:

those based on the five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*) are called "coarse," while those based on the mental faculty (*manas*) are called "subtle. Alternatively, they may be distinguished according to the realms (*bhūmi*):
the four aggregates of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are called "coarse," and the four aggregates of the first dhyāna stage are called "subtle," and so on, up to the formless [realm].

The same applies to all locations regarding the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; such is the explanation of the Vaibhāṣika masters. Regarding the meaning of the fetters and attachments, the person [who follows this] next describes the interpretation of the teacher Dharmatrāta:

the five objects grasped by the five faculties are called coarse matter (*audārika-rūpa*); the remaining five objects grasped by the mental faculty (*manas*), as well as the unmanifest (*avijñapti*), are called subtle matter (*sūkṣma-rūpa*).
Those that are undesirable are twenty-one types and are called inferior matter (*hīna-rūpa*); those that are desirable are two types.

The eleventh is called "superior form" (*viśiṣṭa-rūpa*), which refers to form-objects (*rūpāyatana*) that are not in the range of vision; alternatively, eleven types of form are called "distant form" (*dūra-rūpa*), while those in the range of vision are called "near form" (*antika-rūpa*).
Regarding the three time periods—past and so forth—and the categories of internal and external, these are evident from their respective names.

The same applies to the four aggregates beginning with feeling (*vedanā*). Furthermore, according to the power of their basis: that which depends on one's own body is called "near," while that which depends on another's body is called "distant."

The coarse and subtle aspects are as previously explained in the *Vibhāṣā*. Although there are four textual passages, they are combined to form the first explanation: that "aggregate" (*skandha*) means a "collection" (*rāśi*).
Below this is the second explanation: that "aggregate" means a "gate for the arising" (*āyadvāra*), which refers to the six sense organs, the six objects, and the mind and mental factors.
The meaning of "place of growth" (*āyatana*) is the meaning of "location"; thus, the etymological explanation is clear.

From here on, the third section explains the verse’s statement that "the lineage (*gotra*) is the meaning of the realm (*dhātu*). This passage contains nine parts: first, the teaching of the Dharma explaining that the lineage of all phenomena is the meaning of the realm;
second, the illustration through analogy, beginning with "Just as in a single mountain... and so forth; third, [the illustration] "In this way, within a single body... and so forth.
4. Below, the dharma of the example is raised; here, "lineage" (*gotra*) is explained again as having the meaning of the root of birth.
Just as parents are the root of the physical body's birth, they are called the "lineage. 5. Question: In this way, of what are the eyes and so forth the root of birth? 6. Answer:
It refers to their own kind, namely the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), which is the root of birth. 7. Objection: If that were so, there would be no...
1. It is because [the *dhātu*] should not be called a "sphere" (*dhātu*) since it does not arise from a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) as its basis;
2. it is because the eight [factors]—mind and mental states—are produced by their own kind as the basis for the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*); 3.

it is because other masters state that while "sphere" (*dhātu*) has the meaning of "kind" (*jāti*) or "type," although there are nine textual instances, they are combined into this third explanation, which defines "sphere" (*dhātu*) as the meaning of "lineage" (*gotra*).
From here below, in the fourth section consisting of questions and answers for detailed analysis, there are two parts. First, the Sautrāntika critique of the Sarvāstivāda:

If it is said that the meaning of "aggregate" (*skandha*) is the sense of a "collection," then an aggregate would necessarily consist of many real entities accumulated together to form a collection, just like a "collection of sounds" or a "conventional self.
Second, the explanation of this critique by the three Vaibhāṣika masters; herein is the explanation of the first master.
This objection is not valid, because a single, ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*) is also designated as an aggregate (*skandha*). Next, the Sautrāntika critique is set forth:

"If that were so, one should not say that the meaning of 'aggregate' is the meaning of 'collection,' for a single, substantial entity does not possess the quality of being a collection. The *Nyāyānusāra* states:

"If the meaning of 'aggregate' is explained by the sense of 'collection,' then the aggregate would not be real, because a collection is a conceptual construct (*prajñapti*). This objection is therefore invalid.
Because the term "meaning" (*artha*) is established based on a collection (*rāśi*), the collection itself is not the meaning; rather, the meaning is a particularity of a real entity (*dravya*).
Since the collection is not a real entity, this explanation reveals that the Sūtra possesses a profound purport.

Just as when one speaks of a "collection," apart from the basis of that collection, no separate, substantially existent entity of a collection can be found, so too, when one speaks of a "self," one should not seek a real self existing separately outside of the aggregates (*skandha*) such as form (*rūpa*).
The self is conventionally designated within the continuity of the aggregates (*skandha*) because it is like a worldly collection;
it does not exist as a substantial reality. Furthermore, a single atom is subsumed within the three times and so forth; when analyzed by wisdom, it is reduced to a mere aggregate.

Although the aggregate is indeed a collection, it exists as a real entity, and the same applies to other phenomena. Therefore, the aggregates are not merely conventional designations. Moreover, [the designation of "self"] also arises with respect to each individual distinct phenomenon.

Because they are taught as aggregates (*skandha*), they are certainly not merely conventional designations; for example, co-arising sensation is called the "aggregate of sensation" (*vedanā-skandha*) and perception is called the "aggregate of perception" (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
Other teachers explain it according to the Sūtra: because they arise in combination at all times, the meaning of an "aggregate" is established even though the individual factors are distinct.
A second Vaibhāṣika master says that the meaning of an aggregate is the sense of being able to bear the heavy burden of the fruit (*phala-bhāra*), according to worldly usage in the West.
The shoulder is called a *skandha* because it is a place where things are gathered. Regarding the third Vaibhāṣika interpretation, there are eight points in the commentary:
first, it describes that interpretation by stating that the meaning of "being divisible" is the meaning of *skandha*. Thus, there is a worldly expression:
"Lend me three coins; I will pay you back threefold. If one says, "Lend me three *skandhas*, I will give them back to you," [it would be understood accordingly].
1. Therefore, it is known that "part" (*bhāga*) is the meaning of "aggregate" (*skandha*); this interpretation deviates from the Sūtra. 2. Below, the Master [Vasubandhu] refutes [this view]. 3.

If it is argued that this Sūtra [supports the view], the Master below restates the objection and refutes it. 4. Therefore, that Sūtra says...; the Master cites the Sūtra and briefly explains it as "a single collection" (*rāśi*) to clarify the intent of the previous refutation.
5. He concludes: "Therefore, like a collection, an aggregate is necessarily a conceptual existence" (*prajñaptisat*). 6. The Vaibhāṣika masters [respond].

The opponent counters the proponent: "If that is so, you must admit that the ten material bases (*daśa rūpāyatanāni*) are also conventionally existent (*prajñaptisat*), because the atoms (*paramāṇu*) of the eye and so forth must accumulate to a great extent to constitute a sense-faculty (*indriya*) or a source of production (*āyatana*). The proponent replies: "This objection is unreasonable.
Within the accumulation of many faculties and objects, every single atom possesses causal efficacy (*hetu-vṛtti*). Therefore, each individual atom is both produced and productive."

Just as a single strand of hair cannot restrain an elephant, but only when many strands are gathered together can they restrain it—and when these many strands restrain the elephant, each individual strand possesses the power to restrain the elephant—so too it is with the *paramāṇu* (extreme atom) as a source of production (*janmamukha*).

Since the meaning of "aggregate" (*skandha*) is the sense of being "gathered," a plurality of *paramāṇus* is required to constitute an aggregate; a single *paramāṇu* cannot be called an aggregate. Therefore, [the objection] is not tenable.

By analogy with the aggregates (*skandha*), the same applies to the bases (*āyatana*). If it were not the case that each individual atom possesses causal efficacy, then when the six sense faculties and their six objects cooperate to produce consciousness, since they would individually lack causal efficacy, one should not establish them as distinct bases.

Consequently, there would be no distinction between the twelve bases; rather, since the faculties and objects arise together to produce consciousness, there would only be a single causal efficacy belonging to the combination, and thus there should only be six bases.
Because the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) arise together to produce consciousness, which possesses causal efficacy, they are divided into twelve bases (*āyatana*).

Thus, it is known that the collection of atoms (*paramāṇu-saṃcaya*) of the eye and so forth produces consciousness; each individual atom possesses causal efficacy, and each individual atom is itself a base (*āyatana*).

This is the position of the Master [Vasubandhu] as he recounts the doctrine of the *Vibhāṣā*. However, the masters of the *Abhidharma-ṣaṭpāda* state in the *Vibhāṣā* as follows: [they maintain that only the collection of atoms constitutes a base].

If one does not conceptually analyze form as a collective designation of aggregates (*skandha*), it is said that an atom (*paramāṇu*) constitutes a single constituent element (*dhātu*), a single base (*āyatana*), and a single aggregate;
this is because elements and bases are not accumulations, and thus a single atom is a partial instance of a collective designation of an aggregate.

If, however, one does conceptually analyze form as a collective designation of aggregates, it is said that an atom is a single constituent element, a single base, and a single aggregate—just as a forest is a composite whole consisting of many trees.
Because it is divided, a tree is a "whole" (sāvayava) and its parts are the "parts" (avayava); because it is a single part, an atom (*paramāṇu*) is likewise related to an aggregate (*skandha*).
Furthermore, the aggregate is a conventional "whole," for it possesses many atoms as its parts, while the atom is a real "part," being a single part of the conventional aggregate.

Therefore, when they say that an atom is called "one aggregate," this should be understood as a metaphorical designation of a "whole aggregate" applied to the atom's parts, just as [the term "tree"] is used when a tree is burned.
Just as when a small portion of cloth or thread is burned, one speaks metaphorically of "burning the cloth" by saying, "I am burning the cloth.
The preceding half-line of the verse explained the meaning of the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu); the latter half-line explains the reason for these three categories.

Within this passage, there are three parts: first, the question regarding the threefold teaching; second, the response provided in verse; and third, the explanation of the verse’s main text. Within the latter, there are [three further points].

Second, first, the general presentation: because there are three grades of those to be converted by this school, the World-Honored One taught the three categories (*skandha*, *dhātu*, and *āyatana*). Second, the detailed explanation:
