regarding sentient beings who are deluded about the mind-mental factors (*caitta*) and collectively grasp at a self—there are some sentient beings who are not confused about form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*);
they know that the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is composed of various parts, yet they say there are six aggregates which are not real entities, being merely confused about the mind.

The "dharma-sphere" (dharmāyatana) refers to the experience of pleasure and pain, the differentiation of distinct characteristics, and the capacity to produce both good and evil—all of which are functionally attributed to a self and collectively grasped as "I.
To refute this grasping, the five aggregates (pañcaskandha) are taught to open up the mental factors (caitta).

As for form (rūpa), it is not opened up because fools are not deluded regarding it; they simply grasp form as the self, thinking that seeing forms, hearing sounds, and so forth, are all [the functions of the self].
I have taught the twelve bases (*āyatana*) and divided form (*rūpa*) into ten bases in order to destroy this foolish attachment.

By teaching the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), I have shown that they are not deluded; by teaching the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*) and the sense-base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), I have revealed that form is a composite of many parts and is not a self.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who are deluded regarding form and mind, such as those who think, "I see form," "I hear sound," and so forth.
Other categories such as visible forms and sounds are all of the nature of "one" (the mind); it is to refute this attachment that the eighteen elements (*dhātus*) are taught.

By expanding the mind into seven and the forms into ten, one does not become confused regarding mental phenomena and so forth; thus, the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), the faculties (*indriyas*), the three feelings, and the three [realms] are established in their totality, as can be understood from the text.

From here below, the seventh section contains one verse that explains the reason for establishing the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) as a distinct category. In this passage, first, the question is raised:

"For what reason did the Blessed One state that the remaining forty-four mental factors are collectively placed within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), while separately dividing feeling and perception (*saṃjñā*) into two distinct aggregates?

Second, the root verse provides the answer. Third, the commentary on the verse follows; within this commentary, there are four parts, the first of which explains the "root of dispute" (*vivāda-mūla*). Regarding the root of dispute:

There are two types: namely, the conflict arising from attachment to the five sensual desires (*pañca-kāma-guṇa*) which gives rise to the affliction of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and the conflict arising from attachment to various views (*dṛṣṭi*) which gives rise to the affliction of views.
These two divisions of affliction—craving and views—have the two mental factors of feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) as their respective predominant causes.
By the power of relishing feelings, one becomes greedily attached to the five sensual desires, giving rise to the affliction of craving; by the power of distorted perceptions...
Therefore, by being greedily attached to various views, one gives rise to the afflictions and disputes of the "view-division" (dṛṣṭi-bhāga).

Second, regarding the phrase "the phenomena of birth and death" (*saṃsāra-dharma*), the explanation of the causes of birth and death can be understood [from the following]. Third, "by these two causes" explains the two subsequent lines [of the verse].

Because the reasons for the sequential order of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) will be explained in this verse and in the subsequent verses, it should be known that four [categories] are established separately.
The reasons for the sequential order of the five aggregates will be explained in the two subsequent verses.
From here on, the eighth verse and a half explain why the aggregates do not include unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).

In this passage, first there is the question, second the citation of the verse as the answer, and third the explanation of the verse itself. Within the explanation of the verse, there are three parts; the first explains that unconditioned phenomena cannot [be included].
It is said that within the aggregates such as form (*rūpa*), [unconditioned phenomena] do not correspond with the five meanings of form and so forth;

that is to say, their essence does not possess the meaning of "form" as being subject to change and resistance, and so on up to the meaning of "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) as being the act of discerning. Furthermore, they cannot be designated as a sixth aggregate because they do not correspond with the meaning of a "collection.
Unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) do not possess the five categories of temporal divisions—past and so forth—in the same manner as form and the other aggregates.

One may briefly designate a single aggregate as the "unconditioned aggregate. Furthermore, the second master says that the term "appropriation-aggregate" (*upādāna-skandha*) is used to reveal the basis for both defilement and purification;
this is because the term "aggregate" (*skandha*) reveals both defiled and purified bases, as aggregates encompass both the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*).
Since the unconditioned possesses neither of these two meanings, it is not established as an aggregate. A third master further states: "Just as when a jar is broken, it is no longer a jar..."

Regarding the statement that "the cessation of these aggregates (skandha-nirodha) should not be an aggregate," the Master [Vasubandhu] refutes this, saying: "In the case of the bases (āyatana) and elements (dhātu), this would likewise result in a logical error;

for the cessation of the bases and elements would become unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), and thus it should not be included within the bases or the elements. The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "The Sūtra-master raises an objection, saying:

'In the case of the bases and elements, this would likewise result in a logical error; that is, the cessation of the bases and elements would not be a base or an element,' which contradicts your own established tenet in its entirety."

Regarding the gateway of the aggregates (*skandha*), sentient beings conceive of a self; however, at the stage of entering the remainderless state (*anupadhiśeṣa*), all aggregates cease instantaneously.

This is not the case for the bases and elements (*āyatana* and *dhātu*), because they do not arise in their entirety. It is only the arising of the aggregates that is metaphorically designated as "birth.

If the cessation of the aggregates were also established as the aggregates, then even after one has entered *parinirvāṇa*, the remaining aggregates would have to persist. Sentient beings fear that the aggregates involve many faults and afflictions; therefore, they ought to have no [fear] regarding *nirvāṇa*.

The notion of "peace" (*śānta-saṃjñā*) does not apply to the sphere of the non-locus (*apratiṣṭhāna-dhātu*), because it is entirely full of faults; furthermore, since the sphere of the locus still persists in other states, one should not use that as an analogy to establish this [fault].

The intended meaning of the term "cessation" (*nirodha*) here is not to indicate the emptiness of annihilation (*uccheda-śūnyatā*), for the essence of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is not annihilation.

Therefore, the intended meaning of the term "cessation" here is to indicate that when all characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*) are entirely absent in a certain place, it is called the "cessation of the aggregates" (*skandha-nirodha*). This is the third [point].

The meaning of "aggregate" (*skandha*) refers to a "heap" (*rāśi*); it cannot be named as "cessation" (*nirodha*), "gate" (*mukha*), or "lineage" (*gotra*), for such meanings do not exist therein either, and thus they should not be cited as analogies.

Following this, the ninth section consists of one and a half verses that distinguish the sequence of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*); within this, the first half-verse is as follows:

The verse clarifies the sequence of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). In the prose commentary, there are three parts: first, concluding the preceding section and introducing the subsequent one; second, presenting the root verse; third, explaining the root verse. Within this explanation, there are six sections.

First, it explains that the sequence is established according to coarseness (*audārikatva*): because form (*rūpa*) possesses resistance (*sapratigha*), it is the coarsest among the aggregates and is therefore taught first.
Among the four formless aggregates, feeling (*vedanā*) alone is coarse because its mode of activity (*ākāra*) is what the world refers to when speaking of "my hand" and so forth.

Painful speech is not uttered. Among the two aggregates of *saṃskāra* (formations) and *vijñāna* (consciousness), the aggregate of *saṃjñā* (perception) is the coarsest, because perceptions such as "male" and "female" are first cognized;
the *saṃskāra* aggregate is coarser than *vijñāna*, because afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion easily take on distinct modes of activity (*ākāra*) that are easy to cognize;

and *vijñāna* is the most subtle, because its mode of grasping the general characteristics of objects is difficult to cognize. Second, from "beginningless time" onwards, [the text] explains the "concomitance" (*anuvartin*).
The sequence of defilement establishes this order; the preceding three—form, feeling, and perception—are all defiled consciousnesses, while the rest of the text is intelligible.

Alternatively, form is established first according to the sequence of the "receptacle and its contents" as explained below: just as worldly food and drink must be placed within a receptacle, form is like the receptacle that comes first;
since there must be a receptacle for the food and drink to be placed in, feeling corresponds to the food and drink and is thus established second.
Food and drink cannot be presented alone; they must necessarily be accompanied by pickles and side dishes (*sūpa*). Since these serve as adjuncts to flavor, they constitute the third [analogy].
Furthermore, even when there are edible items, one requires a cook to prepare and season them; thus, the conduct [of the mind] is like the fourth [analogy], the cook.

When these four are prepared, there must necessarily be someone to consume them; therefore, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is likened to the fifth [analogy], the eater. These four explanations follow the respective realms (*dhātu*).

Established as a separate sequence: in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the characteristics of the five sublime sensual pleasures (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*) are clearly perceived;

in the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the characteristics of feeling (*vedanā*) are clearly perceived through cultivation; in the three formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) of the formless realm, the characteristics of perception (*saṃjñā*)—such as the perception of the "infinite space"—are clearly perceived through cultivation;
and in the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), the characteristics of volition (*cetanā*) that project an eighty-thousand-eon lifespan are clearly perceived. These four are [the first four].

Regarding the four stations of consciousness (*vijñāna-sthiti*), consciousness dwells within them, with consciousness itself as the fifth; this reveals their sequence to be like that of a field and seed in the world.
The four stations of consciousness are like the field, and consciousness is like the seed. Because there are five fetters (*saṃyojana*), the sequence of the aggregates (*skandha*) is thus.

Since the subsequent [aggregates] are established based on the preceding ones, it is by virtue of these four principles of sequence and cause that feeling (*vedanā*) is established separately from the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
The two aggregates of feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are considered coarse among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) because they are coarse in their nature;

this is the "gate of coarseness and subtlety. They give rise to defilement; this is the "gate of the arising of faults. Feeling is like food, and perception is like condiments that enhance the flavor; this is the "gate of the vessel and its contents. Furthermore, they are predominant within the two realms;
this is the "gate of the distinction between the realms. For these four reasons, the preceding verse establishes feeling and perception as separate aggregates.

Below this, there is a single verse that explains the sequence of the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*). Within the first verse, which introduces the section on the bases and elements, it should first be explained that the sequence of the six faculties (*indriya*) is established;
from this, the sequence of the six objects and the six consciousnesses can be understood.

Second, the root verse is presented. Third, the root verse is explained. Within this explanation, there are four parts; first, the initial phrase is explained regarding the six faculties. [The text continues with the commentary on the specific faculties.]
The first five [faculties], such as the eye, apprehend only present objects; therefore, they are mentioned first. The object of the mind (manas) is indeterminate:

it may belong to the three time periods, or to unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta), or it may apprehend only one, two, three, or four [of these categories]. Because these are hidden, they are mentioned last.

Regarding the second interpretation of the second phrase, which states that the "four objects" consist only of derived matter (upādāya-rūpa): the word "previous" from the first phrase flows over here to this second phrase; thus, in the second phrase, it should be stated as follows:
Among the five objects, the first four are exclusively derived matter; because they are manifest, they are mentioned first. The object of the body is indeterminate:
it may take the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) as its object, or it may take the seven kinds of derived matter, or it may take both the primary and derived elements together.
Because it is subtle, it is mentioned last. Regarding the third phrase, "the rest": this refers to the aforementioned four objects, according to their respective [characteristics].
Because their functions are far-reaching, swift, and clear, they are mentioned first. Among the preceding four [faculties], the two faculties of eye and ear perceive objects at a distance;
therefore, they are mentioned before the two faculties of nose and tongue. Between the eye and the ear, the eye’s function is more distant than the ear’s, and thus it is mentioned first.

For example, one can see mountains from afar with the eye, whereas one cannot hear sounds from such a distance with the ear. Furthermore, the function of the eye is swifter than that of the ear; the eye sees first, while the ear hears later.

Because one hears the sound of a bell or drum only after striking it, and because the two faculties of the nose and tongue both perceive their objects through contact that is not distant, the nose is mentioned first due to its greater speed and clarity.
For instance, when facing various fragrant foods and drinks, the nose perceives the fragrance first while the tongue tastes the flavor later;
since the fragrance is perceived first, it is more rapid. Furthermore, the eight subtle elements are inseparable, and within these subtle flavors, the fragrance is likewise predominant.
Because the nose is clear regarding fragrance, it first perceives subtle fragrances; because it does not perceive tastes or odors, the fourth [of the four] explanations is not applicable.

Alternatively, the order of the faculties is explained according to their respective locations within the body, from top to bottom: the support of the eye, consisting of the four types of sensory matter (*catvāraḥ spraṣṭavya-dhātavaḥ*), occupies the highest position;
next are the ear, nose, and tongue; and the body faculty mostly resides below them. The mental faculty (*manas*) has no fixed location.
Because it abides therein, the sixth *āyatana*—which arises based upon the five sense-faculties—is the mental faculty (*manas*); therefore, it is said to be mentioned last.
Below this, the tenth section consists of one verse explaining the general and specific names of the *āyatanas*; in the text, the initial question asks: "For what reason are there ten..."

All bases (*āyatana*) are subsumed within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), yet why is the general name "base of form" (*rūpāyatana*) established for only one type, while the other nine are given distinct names?

Furthermore, the essence of all twelve bases is *dharma*; why is the general name "base of phenomena" (*dharmāyatana*) established for only one type, while the other eleven bases are given distinct names?
Second, the presentation of the root verse; third, the explanation of the root verse. Within the text, there are eight sections; first is the explanation of the term "for the sake of distinction."

In order to bring about an understanding of the various distinctions between the five objects (*viṣaya*) and the five faculties (*indriya*) as being both objects and subjects, ten distinct bases (*āyatana*) are established within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) according to their specific characteristics;
they are not collectively designated as a single "form realm" (*rūpadhātu*).

Furthermore, if there were no specific designations for the nine [bases] such as the eye and so forth, yet their substance were still form, then by establishing a name based on their commonality, it would be called the "form realm."

This single form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is distinguished by the nine names beginning with "eye"; while the nine types beginning with the eye are established with names based on their individual characteristics, the single form realm alone receives its designation from a general perspective.
Although the general name is unique and does not apply to the other nine, it is nonetheless a specific name for those very [nine] when the general term is applied.
Thus, the names of the ten bases (*daśāyatana*) are all established as distinct; this is the second explanation of their preeminence. Furthermore, regarding the various tens...

Regarding "form within the form realm" (*rūpa-rūpadhātu*), it is established as a name based on its preeminence among the general category of forms for three reasons: first, because it possesses resistance (*sapratigha*), such that it undergoes transformation and disintegration when touched by hands and other objects;
second, because it is visible (*sanidarśana*), such that it can be pointed out as being here or there;
and third, because in the world, this alone among the ten bases—such as the eye—is conventionally referred to as "form. It is for these three reasons [that it is so designated].
5. Because its meaning is most preeminent, it is established as the general name "four. Furthermore, in order to distinguish it from the other eleven bases, the single "dharma-dhātu" is established;

it is not the case that all eleven are called "dharma," just as was explained previously regarding "form" (*rūpa*). Although a general designation is applied, one should know that it is actually a specific name.
As for why "most preeminent" (*parama*) is not mentioned [as a synonym], it is because "preeminent" (*adhipati*) already implies this. Furthermore, it explains how many dharmas are subsumed. And...
Because this *dharmadhātu* encompasses many dharmas, such as the sixty-four types of perceptions (*saṃjñā*) and so forth, it should be given the general name "Dharma" based on its numerousness;
thus, according to the *Mahāvyutpatti*, it is explained through seven ways as the "predominant dharma. Furthermore, the "predominant dharma" refers to *nirvāṇa*;

since this is subsumed within this *dharmadhātu*, it is named after its excellence and uniquely designated as the "Dharma-sphere" (*dharmadhātu*). Eighthly, other masters state [the following], which is now cited for clarification:
The *Mātṛkā-vyākhyā* can be understood according to the text.

From here below, the eleventh section contains four verses that subsume the distinct aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*). Among these, the first verse subsumes the *dharma-skandha* of the sūtras;
the second verse distinguishes the measure of the *dharma-skandha*; and the third verse subsumes other [teachings] from within the sūtras.

Regarding the fourth verse of the [section on] the aggregates, bases, and elements (*skandha-āyatana-dhātu*), which gives rise to further discussion from the treatise itself, there is an explanation of the *Āgama* concerning the essential nature and characteristics of the six elements among the sixty-two elements.
Within the first verse, there are five parts: first, the citation and explanation of the remaining names of aggregates, bases, and elements;

second, the statement that these names arise from conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) and are thus called "conceptualization"; third, the question as to whether these very aggregates, bases, and elements are subsumed [within themselves]; fourth... [and so forth].

3. Are they apart from these aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu)? Answer: They are all subsumed within these aggregates, bases, and elements; this should be understood accordingly. 4.

To briefly distinguish the inclusion [of other categories], because various names for aggregates appear in other sūtras, the root verse is cited to include them. 5. Regarding the explanation of the root verse, there are two masters' views according to the *Vibhāṣā*.
The first master says that the Buddha’s teaching has speech as its essence; he asserts that all aggregates of dharma (dharma-skandha) are...
The second master asserts that the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) subsumes all [dharmas].
He states that what is called the "Dharma-aggregate" (*dharmaskandha*) in the Buddha's teaching has as its essence the mental formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).

Since ancient times, various masters following the Sarvāstivāda have maintained that the nature of the body of the teaching is either sound-voice, or names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and syllables (*vyañjana*), or else the grasping of sound-voice, names, phrases, and syllables. Now, according to the new [school]...

The *Vibhāṣā* masters who provide the critical evaluation (the *pūrvapakṣa*) maintain that the essence [of the Buddha’s teaching] consists solely of sound; therefore, the new translation of the *Vibhāṣā* states: "Question:
What constitutes the essence of such Buddhist teachings? Is it vocal action (*vāg-karman*), or is it names (*nāman*) and so forth?

If it were vocal action, how would one reconcile this with what is said later? What dharma is designated by the term 'Buddhist teaching'—is it the collection of names (*nāma-kāya*), the collection of phrases (*pada-kāya*), and so on?"

Furthermore, how is it to be reconciled with what is stated in the *gāthās* regarding the sequence of phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*), the sequence of arrangement, the sequence of distribution, and the sequence of conjunction?

If one intends for the verse (*śloka*) to be the cause of the composition, then "text" (*vyañjana*) is simply the syllable (*akṣara*). If the verse proceeds based on the name (*nāman*), then the composer relies upon it.
If [the verse] were identical to the name and so forth, how would one reconcile this with what is stated here? And what is meant by "Buddha-speech"? Even down to... [the question continues].
Vocal intimation is what is called "Buddha-teaching" (*buddhavacana*). One should respond by stating that its substance (*dravya*) is vocal action (*vākkarman*).

Regarding the subsequent explanations, how should they be reconciled? What dharma is designated by the term "Buddha-teaching"? It refers to the collection of names (*nāmakāya*), the collection of phrases (*padakāya*), and the collection of phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*), as well as their sequential conjunction.
The answer is that the subsequent text is intended to reveal the function of the Buddha-teaching; it does not seek to disclose the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the Buddha-teaching itself.

Question: How should one reconcile the statement in the *Gāthā* that the function of the Buddha’s teaching consists of the sequential arrangement and combination of sets of names (*nāma-kāya*), phrases (*pada-kāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*)?
Answer: There are those that operate upon names and those that operate upon meanings. Here, we shall first cite those that operate upon names;
some say that the essence of the Buddha’s teaching consists of names and so forth. Question: How then should one reconcile this with what is stated in the present text?
Question: What is meant by "Buddha-teaching" (*buddha-vacana*)? Answer: It refers to speech and even vocal intimation (*vāg-vijñapti*). Why is it so stated?

It is said thus because they function as successive causes (*pāramparyahetu*). For example, just as a son and grandson are born in succession based on one another, so too does speech give rise to names (*nāman*), and names manifest meaning (*artha*).

This is what is being stated. The essence of this is vocal action (*vāk-karma*), for it is that which is spoken by the Buddha’s intention and heard by others. Question: For what reason [is it called Buddha-teaching]?

Question: Is it the case that the Teaching consists solely of vocal intimation (*vijñapti*) and not non-intimation (*avijñapti*)? Answer: It is called the "Buddha's Teaching" because it produces correct understanding in others; since the production of correct understanding in others occurs solely by means of intimation, [it is so designated].

Furthermore, it is said that the Buddha's Teaching is apprehended by the auditory consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*). Since the auditory consciousness can cognize the Buddha’s vocal intimation but cannot cognize non-intimation, [non-intimation] is not the Buddha's Teaching.

Moreover, it is said that the Buddha's Teaching is apprehended by two types of consciousness: the Buddha’s vocal intimation is apprehended by the auditory consciousness, and [the non-intimation] is apprehended by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Furthermore, because the two types of consciousness can cognize manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*) but cannot cognize non-manifest action (*avijñapti*), the latter is not the Buddha’s teaching.

Moreover, it is said that the World-Honored One sought the words of manifest action for three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) until they were now fully accomplished; it was not non-manifest action.

From here below is the second verse, which analyzes the extent of the *Dharmaskandha*. In this passage, first there is the question, followed by the response given in verse, and finally the commentary on the root verse, which has three interpretations.

According to the first master’s interpretation, he states that each of the eighty thousand *dharmaskandhas* is equal in extent to the *Dharmaskandhapāda*, one of the six *pādas* of the Abhidharma composed by Mahāmaudgalyāyana, which contains six thousand verses; that is to say, those...

Each of the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma (*dharmaskandha*) consists of six thousand stanzas, as explained in the *Dharmaskandhapāda* among the Six Treatises on Abhidharma (*ṣaṭpādābhidharma*).

Thus, the Tathāgata’s eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma comprise eighty-four thousand times six thousand stanzas; however, here, based on the total number, they are simply referred to as "eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma.
A second master states that [the term] refers to the words that express the aggregates, bases, elements (*skandhāyatana-dhātu*), and so forth, according to their specific meanings.

Since the number of distinct dharma-gates that are the referents (*vācya*) is eighty-four thousand, there are likewise eighty-four thousand aggregates of dharmas (*dharmaskandha*) that serve as the designators (*vācaka*).
Now, in this text, the referents are briefly enumerated as follows:

(1) the five aggregates (*skandha*), (2) the twelve bases (*āyatana*), (3) the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), (4) the forty-two dependent originations (*pratītyasamutpāda*), (5) the four truths (*satya*), (6) the four nutriments (*āhāra*), (7) the four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), and (8) the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
1. The four immeasurables; 2. The four formless attainments; 3. The eighteen liberations; 4. The eleven and eight bases of mastery; 5. The ten spheres of totality; 6.
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; 7. The six supernormal powers; 8. The knowledge of the cessation of outflows; 9. The knowledge resulting from prayer; 10.
The four types of analytical knowledge, and all other eighty-four thousand dharma-gates that are explained—these constitute the first [category].
Because the teaching that expresses [the Dharma] is called a single "Dharma-skandha," there are eighty-four thousand Dharma-skandhas in total.
According to the third proponent, the one who speaks according to reality, sentient beings to be converted possess eighty thousand distinct types of conduct, such as greed and hatred;
in order to counteract those eighty thousand types of conduct, the Blessed One proclaimed eighty-four thousand Dharma-skandhas as the counteractive practices. Thus it is said.
The eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma (dharmaskandha) taught by that Blessed One are all subsumed within two of these five aggregates.

This is because the first teacher [Vasumitra] maintains they are subsumed in the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), while the second teacher [Dharmatrāta] maintains they are subsumed in the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha); since these two teachers speak collectively, it is said they are subsumed in two aggregates.

However, according to the opinion of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*’s commentator (the *Vaibhāṣika*), because verbal action (*vākkarman*) is their intrinsic nature, they are subsumed solely in the aggregate of form; furthermore, their essence is also that of teaching (*deśanā*).

The function of verbal action (*vākkarman*) consists of names, phrases, and phonemes; this is because they are explained as the union of essence and function, and because they are subsumed within two aggregates.
The *Vibhāṣā* states that one should explain it thus: "Verbal action is its essence. [Objection: How should the subsequent statement be reconciled?

What dharma is called "Buddha-teaching" (*buddhaśāsana*)? [Answer: It refers to the sets of names, phrases, and phonemes (*nāmakāya-padakāya-vyañjanakāya*). [Response: The subsequent text is intended to clarify the functional activity of the Buddha-teaching.

In order to reveal the essential nature of the Buddha’s teaching, from this point onward is the third section, which summarizes the remaining aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu). Within this, first the categories that summarize the remaining aggregates, bases, and elements are presented;

then the root verses are cited; and finally, the commentary on those root verses follows. This commentary consists of three parts. First, the summary of alternative names for the aggregates; within this [section]...

First, the explanation of the first three phrases; second, the explanation of the fourth phrase as it appears in this treatise; third, regarding the five aggregates such as morality (*śīla*) taught in various sūtras:

therein, the aggregate of morality is subsumed within this aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), while the remaining four aggregates are subsumed within this aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

According to the *Vibhāṣā*, the morality associated with the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*) constitutes the body of morality (*śīla-kāya*); the no-more-learning [states] of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and signlessness (*animitta*) are [the body of concentration].

This is the number of liberations associated with the concentration of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the knowledge of the destruction [of the outflows] (*kṣayajñāna*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), and the right view of one beyond training;

this is the body of liberation of one beyond training. Question: What is the distinction between the body of wisdom (*prajñākāya*) and the body of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśanakāya*)? Answer:

The knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of its origin in one beyond training constitute the body of wisdom, because these two knowledges take bound phenomena as their object. The knowledge of the path and the knowledge of cessation in one beyond training are... [the body of the knowledge and vision of liberation].
The body of knowledge and vision of liberation (vimukti-jñāna-darśana-kāya) takes as its object the unconditioned dharma of non-binding.

Furthermore, the bodies of concentration and wisdom regarding the knowledge of suffering, origination, and cessation in one beyond training (aśaikṣa)—these three knowledges—take liberation as their object, but do not take the knowledge of the outflow-free (anāsrava) that takes liberation as its object.

The knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna) is the body of knowledge and vision of liberation; it takes liberation as its object and also takes the knowledge of the outflow-free that takes liberation as its object. There are two kinds of liberation.
The conditioned [factors] are the objects of the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of origination; the unconditioned is the object of the knowledge of cessation.

The knowledge of the path is the body of liberation-knowledge-and-vision (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana-kāya*), because it takes the three knowledges as its object through the path. The aggregate of morality (*śīla-skandha*) exists in six stages; the remaining aggregates exist in nine stages.

According to Kātyāyanīputra, there are two distinct meanings. Regarding the first meaning: what is the aggregate of the wisdom of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-prajñā-skandha*)? Answer: It is the wisdom of one beyond training.

The discernment of phenomena through investigation, which is associated with reflection, consists of various observations and analytical distinctions; this is called the aggregate of wisdom of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-jñāna-kāya*).

What is the aggregate of liberation and knowledge and vision of one beyond training? It is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*). According to a second interpretation:

furthermore, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, and the knowledge of the path constitute the aggregate of wisdom of one beyond training; the knowledge of cessation constitutes the aggregate of liberation of one beyond training.

Regarding the *Vimuktimārga-śāstra* (The Treatise on the Body of Liberation through Knowledge and Vision), it explains that, in the first sense, the wisdom of the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) constitutes the body of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*), while the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) constitute the body of liberation through knowledge and vision (*vimukti-jñānadarśana-skandha*), because exhaustion and non-arising reside within the body of liberation.

In the second sense, the knowledges of suffering, origin, and the path constitute the body of wisdom, because they do not take the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as their object; thus, the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) is [the body of liberation].
The body of knowledge and vision of liberation (vimukti-jñāna-darśana-kāya) is so called because its liberation is conditioned by the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
Above, the various names for the aggregates (skandha) were subsumed; now follows the second section, which subsumes the various names for the bases (āyatana).

Within this, first the ten totalities (kṛtsnāyatana) are subsumed; second, the eight spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana); third, the four formless spheres of mastery, as can be understood from the text; and fifth, the five [perfections].
In the ninth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama*, the section on the "Bases of Liberation" (*Vimuktyāyatana*) also states:
"What are the five dharmas that are difficult to understand? They are the five liberating entries (*pañca vimokṣamukhāni*). What are the five?

If a bhikṣu hears the Buddha preach the Dharma, or hears a fellow practitioner of the holy life (*brahmacārin*) speak, or hears a teacher or elder speak, he contemplates, examines, and discerns the meaning of the Dharma, whereby his mind attains joy; having attained joy..."
Having attained this, he gains love for the Dharma; having gained love for the Dharma, his body and mind become tranquil;
with body and mind tranquil, he attains meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); having attained meditative concentration, he attains knowledge in accordance with reality—this is the first liberation.
Entering into this, the bhikṣu hears the Dharma with joy, receives and upholds it, recites it with joy, and likewise preaches it to others with joy.
Reflecting and discerning, one likewise rejoices; attaining concentration regarding the Dharma is also like this.
The six types of inclusion [of sentient beings]—the two abodes of non-perception and neither-perception-nor-non-perception—can be understood according to the text.

Furthermore, in the third section on the inclusion of alternative names for the "Many Realms" (*Bahudhātuka*), the *Cittavarga* (Chapter on Mind), the forty-seventh sutra of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, the tenth *Bahudhātuka Sūtra*, it asks: "How does a bhikṣu know the realms?"
The Blessed One replied: "Ānanda, if there is a bhikkhu who perceives the eighteen elements—the eye element up to the mental-object element;
the earth element, water element, fire element, wind element, space element, and consciousness element; the desire element, ill-will element, and cruelty element;
the non-desire element, non-ill-will element, and non-cruelty element; the pleasure element, pain element, joy element, grief element, equanimity element, and ignorance element."
The element of awakening, the element of perception, the element of formations, the element of consciousness; the realm of desire, the realm of form, the realm of formlessness;
the realm of form, the realm of formlessness, the realm of cessation; the past realm, the future realm, the present realm; the sublime realm, the non-sublime realm, the intermediate realm;
the wholesome realm, the unwholesome realm, the indeterminate realm; the realm of the learner, the realm of the non-learner, the realm of neither-learner-nor-non-learner; the realm with outflows.
Regarding the realms: there are the uncontaminated realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*), the conditioned realm (*saṃskṛta-dhātu*), and the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛta-dhātu*).
As cited in the sūtras, there are six types of three, three types of two, two types of one, and four types of four; when eighteen realms are further added, there are sixty-two.
From here below, the fourth section consists of one verse that introduces a further discussion based on the preceding argument;
it explains the essential characteristics of the six elements (*dhātu*) as taught in the *Āgama* sūtras. This section contains five parts. First is the question:

regarding the six elements mentioned in that *Āgama*—of which four have already been explained and two, space (*ākāśa*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), have not yet had their characteristics explained—is that which is called "space" simply the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) entity known as empty space?
1. Is every element (*dhātu*) that is a consciousness—whether with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*)—called the "consciousness-element" (*vijñāna-dhātu*)?

2. Answer: No. 3. Question: Why is this so? 4. Response: It is answered by citing a verse (*kārikā*). 5. Explanation of the verse’s root text, which contains five parts: first, the explanation of the first line;

second, the explanation of the second line, beginning with "In this way," etc. Within this section, there is first a question and then an answer. According to the tradition of the *Vibhāṣā*, the apertures and interstices are themselves light (*āloka*).

Since darkness is not distinct from light, and since the two manifest colors of light and darkness can be perceived within apertures and gaps, it is said that the space-element (*ākāśa-dhātu*) has light and darkness as its essence.
One should know that this essence is not separate from day and night: daytime has luminosity as its essence, while nighttime has the color of darkness as its essence.
These very lights and darks are called "color adjacent to *āgama*. According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, *āgama* refers to doorways, windows, mouths, and nostrils.
Because it is an accumulation of coarse matter that is extremely capable of acting as an obstruction, it is called *āgha*. In its original language, *āgha* means "extreme obstruction.

This space-element (*ākāśadhātu*) consists of subtle light and darkness; because it is adjacent to that coarse matter of *āgha*, the color of the space-element is called "color adjacent to *āgha*" (*āghasāmantaka-rūpa*).
A second school of the *Vibhāṣā* masters asserts that *āgha* is itself space.
The element (*dhātu*) is that which is adjacent to matter; this space consists of the matter of light and darkness. It is obstructed by other things but does not obstruct others.
Because it does not obstruct others within this light and darkness, it is called "agha-matter. The original term is *agha*, which means "unobstructed" (*an-āvaraṇa*);
thus, it is "unobstructed matter" (*agha-anāvaraṇa-rūpa*). Since it is adjacent to other obstructive matters such as doors and windows, it is therefore called "adjacent" (*pratyāsanna*).
The former master, Ghoṣaka, explains that *āgha* refers to extremely obstructive matter (*paramāgha-rūpa*), which is the "neighboring" (*sāmantaka*) of the space-element (*ākāśa-dhātu*).

This [space-element] is the "neighbor" (*sāmantaka*) of *āgha*. Therefore, it is called "matter neighboring *āgha*" (*āghasāmantaka-rūpa*). This master explains that *āgha* is the "neighboring" (*sāmantaka*) matter;

because *āgha* can neighbor other obstructive matter, it is called "matter neighboring *āgha*" (*āghasāmantaka-rūpa*). Third, regarding all contaminated (*sāsrava*) matter, the following provides the explanation.
Regarding the third line, the fourth [verse] asks: "Why is it not stated that the various untainted consciousnesses (*anāsravavijñāna*) constitute the element of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*)?
The text first poses this question and then answers it with a verse: "Because these six elements are admitted to be the basis for the birth of all sentient beings;
thus, these six elements extend from the initial mind of rebirth-linking (*pratisandhikṣaṇa*) until the final mind at the end of life."
Because it is always able to sustain birth, the various untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas are not like this; they sever birth and therefore do not take up the untainted consciousness.

Among those six elements, the first four are included within the eighteen [elements], specifically within the element of contact (*spraṣṭavya-dhātu*). The fifth, the space element (*ākāśa-dhātu*), consists of light and darkness, which are colors (*rūpa*); thus, it is included within the element of form (*rūpa-dhātu*) among these eighteen elements. The six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) and the eighteen [elements] are as previously stated.

The first four elements are subsumed within the element of contact among these eighteen elements. The fifth, the space element—consisting of light and darkness as color—is subsumed within the element of form among these eighteen elements.
The sixth consciousness-element (ṣaṣṭhavijñānadhātu), which is included within the [eighteen] elements, is subsumed under the seven mind-elements (saptacittadhātu) among these eighteen elements.
As for the remaining fifty-six elements mentioned in other Āgamas, they are all, as appropriate, subsumed within these same eighteen elements.
Commentary on the Abhidharmakośa-śāstra, Fascicle One;
Commentary on the Root Text of the Abhidharmakośa-śāstra, Number Two;
Composed by the Śramaṇa Shentai of the Great Ci’en Monastery.
Section One, Part Two: The Analysis of the Elements (*Dhātu-vibhaṅga*).

Within the main body of the "Analysis of the Elements," the preceding twenty-five verses have generally elucidated the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*)—both with and without outflows (*sāsrava* and *anāsrava*).
Hereafter, nineteen verses provide a detailed classification of the eighteen elements through various categories. Among these:

The initial verse has three sections: first, the section on the visible and the invisible; second, the section on the resistant and the non-resistant; and third, the section on the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
In the text, the first part restates the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) from the preceding discussion and poses questions regarding these three sections;

next, the verse provides the answers, wherein the first line answers the section on the visible and the invisible, the second line answers the section on the resistant and the non-resistant, and the third line answers [the section on the three natures].
Following the section on the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), there are eleven parts in the commentary on the main verses of the text. First, regarding the explanation of the initial phrase:
among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the element of form (*rūpadhātu*) is "visible" (*sanidarśana*) because it can be demonstrated as being distinct from this or that.
Following this principle, it is said that the remaining seventeen elements are "invisible. As stated in the fourth fascicle of the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*: "Why is this called 'visible'? Because...
There are two reasons why it is "visible" (*sanidarśana*): first, because this form is necessarily accompanied by vision;
it is called visible because the form arises simultaneously with the eye, just as one who has a companion is said to be "accompanied. Second, because this form can be pointed out;

it is called visible because it can be indicated as being "here" or "there," just as an object of perception (*ālambana*) can be pointed out. Some say that this form [is visible] within its own sphere and so forth.
Because there are forms that can be manifested, it is called "visible" (*sanidarśana*), as it can be pointed out like this or that;

for this reason, it cannot be said that sound possesses an echo and so forth, as these would otherwise entail being visible, yet they do not arise simultaneously. Since this definition has been stated, the meaning that the other elements (*dhātu*) are "invisible" (*anidarśana*) is established by implication.
In this present passage, however, the second sense alone is used for the explanation, because it can be pointed out as being "this" or "that."

Because the eye faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) possesses the function of seeing, form (*rūpa*) is said to be "visible" (*sanidarśana*). This is like saying that because the mind (*citta*) has an object of cognition (*ālambana*), the mind is said to be "possessing an object.
The traditional rendering as "visible" (*dṛśya*) or "invisible" (*adṛśya*) is erroneous.

Regarding the second phrase of the verse, the first part concludes the preceding two points—that [the five faculties] are comprised solely within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). The statement that "ten elements (*dhātu*) are resistant" (*sapratigha*) explains the meaning of "obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*) as the primary definition.

The root verse states that there are three types; this section further explains these three extensively. First, it presents the number; fourth, it lists the names of the three types of resistance (*sapratigha*):

first, resistance as obstruction (*āvaraṇapratigha*); second, resistance as the objective field (*viṣayapratigha*); and third, resistance as the cognitive object (*ālambanapratigha*). Fifth, it distinguishes the characteristics of the three types of resistance.
Resistance as obstruction refers to the ten material elements (*rūpadhātu*) as its substance, such as when a hand obstructs a hand, or a stone [obstructs another].
"Obstruction by stone" refers to when either a stone or a hand mutually obstructs one another.

"Obstruction regarding the objective field" (*viṣaya-pratighāta*) refers to the five sense faculties (*indriya*), the seven mental elements (*dhātu*) in their entirety, and a portion of the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*); that is, a small part of twelve elements.

It refers to those factors that have a preceding object which are obstructed by that object within the spheres of form and so forth. Below, the treatise is cited as proof, such as that composed by Mahākātyāyanīputra.
The *Śarīra-pudgala-viniścaya-śāstra* contains two sets of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), which can be understood according to the text.
The *piśāca*—referred to as *viśada* in older translations—is the most eminent among the ghosts (*preta*). The *śiśumāra* has a form like that of an elephant;

in older translations of the *sūtras* and *vinayas*, it is sometimes called *śiśumāra* or *śiśumara*, which are merely phonetic shifts of the Sanskrit term. It is translated as "the fish that kills its offspring."
The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states that it is the crocodile (*nakra*), over twenty feet long, with four legs resembling those of a *tad* (crocodile). Its teeth are extremely sharp;
if birds or deer enter the water, its bite severs them at the waist. Regarding the "obstruction by object" (*ālambanapratighāta*) specific to the land of Guangzhou:

this refers to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) being obstructed by their own respective objects of perception (*ālambana*). Section Six: Distinguishing the Two Types of Obstruction. Text.

In the first part of the middle section, it is asked: "What is the distinction between resistance through the object-field (*viṣayapratighāta*) and resistance through the objective referent (*ālambanapratighāta*)? Next, it is answered:

"If, with respect to a certain object-dharma, these five faculties possess the functional capacity to apprehend that object, that object-dharma is said to be the 'object-field' (*gocara*) of these five faculties.
As for the mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*), they grasp their respective objective referents as having substantial existence and give rise to them."
That which serves as the condition for the mind and mental factors is called the "object-condition" (*ālambana*).

The intent of this question is to clarify that while the sense-faculties (*indriya*) are defined by their resistance (*pratighāta*) toward their respective objects, the faculties themselves are said to be "resistant with respect to their spheres," whereas the mind and mental factors are said to be "resistant with respect to their objects. What, then, is the distinction between these two types of resistance?

The answer below states: the five faculties and the five objects each possess their own distinct substance and arise through their own respective continuities; they do not [arise] solely because of the objects.

The five sense faculties (*pañcendriya*) arise together with their essential nature; their capacity to apprehend objects arises by virtue of those objects, and they do not arise when the object is absent.

Therefore, the five faculties are said to be "obstructed" (*sapratigha*) with respect to their objects in terms of this functional capacity. The mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitasika dharma*) also possess distinct natures that differ from their objects;
however, because the essence of the mind and mental factors cannot arise independently, they necessarily arise dependent upon an object and do not arise when the object is absent.

Because the substance of the mind and mental factors cannot arise with respect to their objective referents (*ālambana*), they are termed "obstructed by the object" (*ālambanapratighāta*) based on the substance of the mind and mental factors.
Regarding the distinction between "obstruction of the sphere" (*viṣayapratighāta*) and "obstruction of the object" (*ālambanapratighāta*) within the mind and mental factors:

it is called "obstruction of the sphere" with reference to the function of obstruction, and it is called "obstruction of the object" with reference to the obstructed nature of the phenomenon itself. This is the first part of the sevenfold explanation of the meaning of the term "possessing obstruction" (*sapratigha*).

Question: Why are the five faculties, such as the eye, said to possess "resistance" (*sapratigha*) when they function with respect to their own objects, and when the mind and mental factors function with respect to their objects?

Answer: Because these five faculties and the mind and mental factors do not proceed toward other objects or other focal points once they have transcended their own respective domains and focal points.
It is like a person whose eyes behold a southern wall; [the visual faculty] does not proceed beyond that wall.

One sees only the northern side of the southern wall and not its southern side; thus, the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) is said to be obstructed by the color-form (*rūpa*) on the northern side of the southern wall.
Alternatively, "obstructed" (*āvṛta*) has the meaning of "conjunction" (*saṃnipāta*);

that is, the five faculties—such as the eye—and the five consciousnesses function in conjunction with their respective objects and conditions. Therefore, they are obstructed by their own objective spheres of perception and cannot transcend them.

Because it arises from its own objective domain (*ālambana*), it is called "obstructed by the objective domain" (*viṣayālambanapratighāta*). The two sets of fourfold propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) cited previously from the *Prakaraṇapāda* can be understood here according to this intended meaning.
The *Nyāyapraveśa* states: "Only the ten elements (*dhātu*) subsumed within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) possess resistance (*sapratigha*);

'resistance' (*pratigha*) has the sense of obstruction. Because these [elements] obstruct that [object], they are called 'possessing resistance. Furthermore, there are three kinds of this [resistance]: resistance regarding the objective domain (*viṣaya-pratighāta*)," and so forth.
Because of the distinction between conditions and obstacles, there is "resistance regarding the object" (*viṣayapratighāta*).

This refers to the sense faculties such as the eye, as well as the mind and mental factors—those phenomena that possess objects—which, when encountering objects such as visible forms, are obstructed; thus they receive the name "possessing resistance. The *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* states:
"There is an eye that has resistance in water but not on land... and so forth, up to what should be said. The intended meaning of that treatise is that there is an eye [that functions] in water...

When the mind and its objects meet and are obstructed, this is called "resistance" (*sapratigha*) with respect to the objective field (*ālambana*). This does not mean that there is resistance in the sense of being physically impeded on dry land;

rather, it refers to the fact that mental states (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitasika*) are obstructed when they encounter their own respective objects, thereby receiving the name "possessing resistance. Furthermore, what is the difference between "objective field" (*viṣaya*) and "object of cognition" (*ālambana*)?

If a certain dharma has efficacy toward another dharma, then that [latter] dharma is said to have the former as its objective field (*viṣaya*), just as a person [is said to have a place as his field].
That which possesses superior efficacy is said to be the objective sphere (*viṣaya*) of the self; the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) arise by grasping that [sphere].
It is called the "object-condition" (*ālambana*) in relation to the mind and so forth. One should know this. Herein, the term "resistance" (*pratigha*) distinguishes the specific from the general;
although the three types of resistance were explained above in a general sense, one should know that in this verse it refers specifically to "obstructive resistance" (*āvaraṇa-pratigha*).
Therefore, the second line simply states that the ten material elements are "with resistance" (*sapratigha*) because they mutually obstruct one another and are subject to external obstruction;
thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* says: "Resistance (*pratigha*) has the sense of obstruction (*āvaraṇa*); because these have that obstruction, they are called 'with resistance'.

Consequently, by implication from this verse, the meaning of the ten material elements being "with resistance" applies analogously to the remaining eight elements, which are "without resistance" (*apratigha*). As for the nine... [if/then].

Regarding the "resistance of the objective sphere" (*viṣayapratighāta*), the following fourfold analysis distinguishes the three types of resistance. Within this context, one should formulate four propositions by contrasting the objective sphere with obstruction (*āvaraṇa*).

Specifically, the seven mental elements (*cittadhātu*) in their entirety and a portion of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*)—namely, those factors associated with mind (*cittasaṃprayukta-dharma*)—constitute "resistance of the objective sphere" because they are capable of apprehending objects; however, because they do not possess the nature of atoms (*paramāṇu*), they are not "resistance through obstruction."

This is the first clause; the remaining clauses are easily understood. Next, by correlating *viṣayapratighāta* (obstruction regarding the object-field) with *ālambanapratighāta* (obstruction regarding the cognitive object), only two clauses are formed.
According to the *Vibhāṣā*, if one asks about the broad in terms of the narrow, one answers according to the latter clause (*paścātpādaka*);

if one asks about the narrow in terms of the broad, one answers according to the former clause (*pūrvapādaka*). If there is mutual breadth and narrowness, they are analyzed through fourfold classification (*catuṣkoṭi*). Regarding those that are narrow and similar, the answer is as follows:

Thus, in the present text, "resistance by way of objective field" (*viṣayapratighāta*) is broad, encompassing all five sense faculties, whereas "resistance by way of object" (*ālambanapratighāta*) applies only to the mind and mental factors;

because the former is broad and the latter is narrow, one should answer according to the latter clause. That is to say: whatever is resistance by way of object is necessarily resistance by way of objective field;
however, there are things that are resistance by way of objective field but are not resistance by way of object—namely, the five [faculties] such as the eye.

The sense bases (*indriya*) have resistance through obstruction (*pratighāta-pratigha*), which belongs exclusively to matter; the objects (*ālambana*) have resistance through being an object (*ālambana-pratigha*), which belongs exclusively to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
Because their natures are distinct, there is no need to differentiate them further.

Herein, the Venerable [Śrīlāta] cites the statement of the Venerable Kumāralāta—known as "The Youth"—who was a teacher of the Sautrāntika school, to prove the meaning of resistance and non-resistance: "It is like a person looking with their eyes."
When [a mind] is directed toward the north wall from the south, it arises in the location of the south wall; because another [mind] directed toward the north wall obstructs it, it does not arise.

One should know that this constitutes "resistance" (*sapratigha*), while its opposite is "non-resistance" (*apratigha*). Although this is an explanation according to the Sautrāntika school, it does not contradict the meaning of the Sarvāstivāda;
therefore, it is stated that "this is what is accepted. (11) Regarding the explanation of the two final lines of the verse, the text first concludes the preceding section.

Next, regarding this object of focus, I shall provide a formal explanation of the root verse. Among the ten types of "resistant" (*sapratigha*) phenomena mentioned here, with the exception of visible form (*rūpa*) and sound (*śabda*), the remaining eight are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

This refers to the five material sense faculties and the objects of odor, taste, and tangibility; they are called "indeterminate" because their nature cannot be designated as either wholesome (*kuśala*) or unwholesome (*akuśala*).
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "Phenomena that are subject to praise or censure can be designated as being in the black or white [categories]."

In this chapter, those which are designated as "determinate" (*vyākṛta*) are so called because they are not subsumed under either of the two categories [wholesome or unwholesome] and their nature is not indistinct;

these are termed "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*) phenomena. Other masters claim that they are called indeterminate because they cannot be designated as having a ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*). The Master refutes this, saying:

"If that were so, the untainted (*anāsrava*) would be exclusively indeterminate. The remaining ten elements (*dhātu*)—namely, the seven mind-elements (*citta-dhātu*)—pertain to all three categories, such as the wholesome and so forth.

That which is associated with the five self-natures of wholesomeness, such as non-attachment, is wholesome; that which is associated with the five self-natures of unwholesomeness, such as attachment, is called unwholesome;

the remainder is called indeterminate. Within the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), if there is that which is wholesome by way of the five self-natures of non-attachment and so forth, or associated with the wholesome factors such as pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), or the two meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*), the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), acquisitions (*prāpti*), non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), and origination (*samutthāna*), or cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*), it is preeminent as wholesome.

In terms of meaning, all that is wholesome is designated as "wholesome. Thus, these five—greed and so forth—are unwholesome by their very nature (*svabhāva-akuśala*); lack of faith (*āśraddhya*) and the others are unwholesome through association (*samprayoga-akuśala*);

the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the acquisition (*prāpti*), the non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), and the motivating factors (*samutthāna*) are unwholesome by designation (*nāman-akuśala*). All else is designated as "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*).

As for the spheres of form (*rūpa-dhātu*) and sound (*śabda-dhātu*), if they are produced by the power of a wholesome or unwholesome mind, such as vocal intimation (*vāg-vijñapti-karma*), they are wholesome or unwholesome.

The remainder are termed indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). From here on, the next verse concerns the fourth gate: the distinction between those bound and those unbound. In the text, first the preceding section is concluded and the subsequent question is posed;

next, the verse is cited as the answer; finally, the root verse is explained. "Bound" (*baddha*) means being attached to, which carries the sense of being fettered. That which is bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is fully endowed with ten [factors].
Regarding the fourteen types [of dharmas] bound to the eight form-realms, excluding the objects of odor and taste as well as the consciousnesses of nose and tongue:

the Sarvāstivādins establish their thesis by excluding odor, taste, and so forth, on the grounds that these possess the nature of substantial food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*). The Master [Vasubandhu] raises an objection:

"If that is so because odor and taste have the nature of substantial food, and they are absent there, then the tangible realm (*spraṣṭavya-dhātu*), which also has the nature of substantial food, should likewise be absent there. The Sarvāstivādins respond: "That... [is not the case].
The four masters raise an objection: "If that were so, then odors and tastes would likewise [not exist in the form realm], as they too are not of the nature of edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*).
The Sarvāstivādins offer this defense: "Odors and tastes have no separate function apart from being food;
therefore, they do not exist in the form realm. However, tangibles do have functions other than being edible food, such as the five sense organs (*indriya*), clothing, and so forth."

Therefore, there are those in the form realm; furthermore, other Vaibhāṣika masters say that while abiding in this desire realm, one manifests meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) based on those dhyānas, and gives rise to the supernormal powers of sight and hearing to see and hear forms and sounds of the higher realms.

When entering dhyāna, the touch of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-spraṣṭavya*) arises; for this reason, these three—form, sound, and touch—are born together with that dhyāna and continue to accompany it as it arises there.
6. [The opponent argues: "Since odors and tastes do not exist there [in the form realm], those two [faculties] do not arise. The Master [Vasubandhu] objects:

"In that case, the nose and tongue faculties would not exist there either, because their objects—odors and tastes—are absent and thus they would have no function. 7. [The Sarvāstivādin] replies: "That is not so; the two faculties do have a function there.
The tongue faculty has the function of initiating speech, and the nose faculty has the function of adorning the body. 8. The Master pursues [the argument]: "If it is for the sake of adornment..."
The body and the arising of speech require only two bases: the physical matter (*rūpa*) and the tangible object (*spraṣṭavya*).

Regarding the nine types of *Sarvāstivādins*, it is explained that just as there is no male organ (*puruṣendriya*) in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there is likewise no base for it; since the two organs do not exist in the form realm, their bases also do not exist.
The Master [Vasubandhu] pursues this point: the base for the male organ could indeed be absent, because it serves no purpose in the form realm. As for the nose...
The tongue-base has the functions of producing speech and adorning the body; therefore, even apart from the sense-organ, there should be eleven [bases].

The Sarvāstivādins defend this by saying that although the organ serves no purpose [in those realms], it still arises—just as the organs arise for one destined to die in the womb despite the lack of utility.
What prevents the nose and tongue from arising in the Form Realm, even though they serve no purpose there? They may indeed arise. Thus, there are twelve.
The Master of the Treatise rebukes [the opponent]: Although there is no purpose for the roots of karma that yield fixed retribution for certain death in the womb, they are not without a cause.
As for the nose and tongue in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), from what cause do those faculties arise? (13) The Sarvāstivāda replies:

Regarding the nose and tongue, there is the cause of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), which gives rise to a distinguished karma; this karma is precisely the cause of the nose and tongue faculties. (14) The Master of the Treatise raises an objection:

If that were so, since craving for the objects of smell and taste is fixed upon their respective faculties, those who are free from craving for the objects of smell and taste would lack the motivating craving for karma;

thus, they should not possess the two faculties of nose and tongue. If you argue that even though they lack craving for the objects of those faculties, they nonetheless possess the two faculties of nose and tongue, then it should likewise follow that those who are free from craving for the object of the male faculty, or you must admit that the male faculty exists [in them] as well.
Regarding the claim that the male organ (*puruṣendriya*) does not arise because it is ugly, the Master of Treatises (*śāstrakāra*) refutes this defense by stating:
"If you say it does not arise because of its ugliness," [the opponent replies: "Sixteenthly, the Master of Treatises objects:

'If it were as you say, how could the Blessed One’s horse-hoof-shaped organ (*aśvakośagata-vasti-guhya*), which is concealed and adorned with a hundred merits (*śatapuṇya-lakṣaṇa*), be considered ugly, given that it is above it a floral pattern most lovely and delightful? Furthermore...
The objection is this: it is not the case that the sense organs arise only when they have a purposeful function. If there were the power of a cause, they would arise even if they served no purpose;

for instance, the sense organs arise in those who are certain to die in the womb. Furthermore, although the male organ is considered ugly in such cases, if one grants the existence of a cause, the male organ should still arise there.
Moreover, the karma for craving the organs does not exist in those [beings], nor does the karma for craving the nose or tongue exist in them.
There should not be seventeen [faculties], for the Sarvāstivādins raise an objection: "If the nose and tongue faculties do not exist there, it would further contradict the Sūtra.
The Sūtra states that those beings are without deficiency and that their faculties are not diminished. The Master of the Treatise explains the Sūtra by raising a further objection:

"According to that [Sūtra], one should say that the five faculties, such as the eye, are present; why then is it said they are not diminished? What contradiction is there if they are not present? [The Sarvāstivādins reply: "If they are not present..."
If one were to subtract the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*) from those who possess all the material faculties (*rūpīndriya*), there would then be nineteen; this is what is said.

The reason for establishing the two faculties of nose and tongue in the lower realms is that the Master [Vasubandhu] accepts them, whereas the male faculty is not established because it does not exist there. Thus, there are twenty.

Having concluded the discussion on the material realm, the fourteen points of our own school (*svamata*) are established. Next, the fourth line of the verse is explained: the last three [faculties] belong to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
This can be understood according to the text.
Below this, there is one verse-line concerning the fifth gate, the distinction between the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*), which can be understood according to the text.
Below that, there is one and a half verse-lines concerning the gate of having applied thought and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*); therein, the first two lines provide the formal analysis.

The subsequent single verse arises from the preceding discussion. Regarding the first part of the text: first, the previous section is concluded and a question is posed; next, the verse is cited as the answer; finally, the verse itself is explained.
Within that explanation, the first line is clear and requires no further commentary. Next, the following three lines explain the second line of the verse.

These "last three" refer to the fact that among the six sense organs (*indriya*), the six objects (*viṣaya*), and the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*)—namely, mind (*manas*), phenomena (*dharma*), mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the six faculties, six objects, and six consciousnesses—they each occupy the final position within their respective groups.

Thereafter, all three realms are common to three categories: (1) the element of the mind-base (*manāyatana*), (2) the element of the mental-consciousness-base (*manovijñānāyatana*), and (3) the associated element of dharmas (*dharmadhātu*), excluding *vitarka* and *vicāra*.
These two elements in their entirety and a small portion of the third exist with both *vitarka* and *vicāra* in the desire realm and the first dhyāna;

they are without *vitarka* but with *vicāra* alone in the intermediate dhyāna; and from the second dhyāna upwards, up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), they are without both *vitarka* and *vicāra*.

That which is without vicāra (sustained thought) within the three realms—namely, the dharmadhātu (dharma-realm), non-associated matter, and unconditioned phenomena, as well as vicāra itself in the intermediate dhyāna—is likewise included in the third category:
that which is without both vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra.

From here on, the question is raised: Just as in the desire realm and the first dhyāna there is at all times "vitarka" (applied thought), why is it said that there is "no vitarka, only vicāra" (sustained thought)?
Since there is no second vitarka, it is said there is no vitarka; however, because it is associated with vicāra, it is called "with vicāra.

This could indeed be included in the second category [of the fourfold classification]. But since *vicāra* within the desire realm and the first dhyāna is not subsumed under the three grades [of vitarka], what should it be named? Next...
Answer: This should be called "without investigation (avicāra) and with only examination (savitarka)," which is subsumed under the fourth category.
Because there is no second investigation arising simultaneously, it is called "without investigation"; because it is associated only with examination, it is said to be "with examination.

Since this exhaustively includes all phenomena, it is stated that the stage of "with examination and with investigation" (savitarkasavicārā bhūmiḥ) consists of four categories of phenomena, as can be understood from the text. Next, the second category is explained.
In the remaining ten material realms (*rūpadhātu*), both vitarka and vicāra are absent, because they are dissociated from vitarka and vicāra.
Following this, the next verse introduces a further discussion arising from the preceding argument. First, it restates the prior question:

"If the five groups of consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāya*) possess vitarka and vicāra, how is it that the Sūtra says the five consciousnesses are non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*)? Next, it presents the verse as an answer, followed by an explanation of the verse's meaning.

According to the tradition of the *Vibhāṣā*, there are three types of conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Although the five groups of sensory consciousness possess the first type, which is intrinsic conceptualization (*svabhāva-vikalpa*), they are said to be "without conceptualization" because they lack the other two types.
This is like calling a one-legged horse "legless. The essence of intrinsic conceptualization is exclusively vitarka (initial mental application), as will be explained later in the text.

The other two types of conceptualization follow their respective order: [the second is] discursive wisdom (*prajñā*) on the level of the mental consciousness, and [the third is] the various [mental factors] on the level of the mental consciousness.
Mindfulness (*smṛti*) is its essence. "Distracted" refers to wisdom associated with non-concentrated mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*);

this wisdom capable of deliberating upon phenomena is called "deliberative discrimination" (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*). Wisdom within concentration is non-discriminative; therefore, it cannot discriminate or deliberate upon phenomena.

Whether in a state of concentration or distraction, all instances of mindfulness associated with mental consciousness are able to recollect past objects and so forth; thus, they are termed [recollection].

The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, fascicle four, states: "Discursive wisdom (*vitarka*) associated with the distracted mental consciousness is called 'discriminative conceptualization' (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*), because within meditative concentration one cannot conceptually determine an object.

Since the wisdom within concentration does not function by conceptually determining the focal object as 'it is thus' or 'it is so,' herein one excludes that which is concentrated and takes up that which is distracted. If...

If one defines it as the various mindfulnesses associated with the distracted mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), they are called "discrimination by recollection" (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*), because their functions of clear recollection and the apprehension of the object are equal.

Although the five sensory consciousnesses are associated with wisdom (*prajñā*) and mindfulness, their functions of discernment and recollection are subtle; therefore, only the mental consciousness is taken [as the basis for this discrimination].

As for "discrimination," because its mode of activity is investigative, *vitarka* (applied thought) is said to be its essential nature (*svabhāva*). It is distinguished from the partial aspects of discernment and clear recollection.
Because it resembles *vitarka* (applied thought), the term "discrimination" (*vikalpa*) also applies to wisdom (*prajñā*) and mindfulness (*smṛti*).

By means of these three modes of activity, they are held together and cause the mind to engage with its object with clarity, which differs from the state of having already apprehended the object; thus, by excluding the arising of such [past] activities, the term "discrimination" does not apply to *saṃjñā* (perception).
Furthermore, because it cannot seal or maintain an object that has not yet been apprehended, the term "discrimination" does not apply to superior exegesis (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*).

Regarding "conception" (*saṃjñā*): when one has not yet ascertained an object such as a male or female, one is able to perform a discerning analysis and give rise to an interpretative understanding, thinking, "This is a man," or "This is a woman.
However, regarding objects that have already been ascertained, such discernment is unnecessary;

therefore, even with respect to ascertained objects, "conception" is excluded, because a discerning analytical process cannot arise there. Thus, the term "discrimination" (*vikalpa*) does not apply to "conception."

If [the former] can confirm and maintain an object already understood but cannot confirm and maintain an object not yet understood, it is called "discrimination" (vikalpa) because its application is not universal;
whereas the three types of discrimination apply universally to both objects already understood and those not yet understood, and thus differ from these two.
However, these two [types of discrimination] frequently involve a small degree of discernment and confirmation regarding objects both not yet understood and already understood.
