Question: Now one should investigate that just as all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) differ in their essential nature and characteristics, their arising is likewise distinct and diverse.
Do they arise together? Are there dharmas that necessarily arise together? There are two answers: first, there are those that necessarily arise together;

second, a general enumeration of all dharmas briefly comprises five categories; fourth, [this excludes] the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) because it does not arise. This is not discussed here. Now, first we shall distinguish the necessary co-arising of form (*rūpa*).
Below, twenty-seven verses clarify the three groups of phenomena (*dharmaskandha*), of which the first one is as follows:
In the verse explaining the co-arising of the material aggregate (*rūpa-piṇḍa*), first the thesis is stated, next the root verse is presented, and finally the text of the verse is explained.
Within this explanation there are sixteen sections. First, the initial two lines are explained:

among the material aggregates, that which is most subtle is designated by the name "atom-aggregate" (*paramāṇu-piṇḍa*) to show that nothing more subtle than this exists; this occurs in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) when it arises without sound or sense-faculties.
Regarding the eight substances—mountains, rivers, the earth, and so forth—that arise simultaneously, how is it that not even one of them fails to be present?

What are these eight substances? They are the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the four derived forms (*upādāyarūpa*): visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility. [The phrase] "without sound and with sense-faculties" explains the latter two lines.

In those atomic clusters (*paramāṇu-saṃghāta*) that are without sound but possess sense-faculties, these simultaneously arising substances are either nine or ten. Specifically, a cluster possessing the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) consists of nine substances.

When eight things arise together, they are as previously described, with the body as the ninth. In other cases, such as the collection of the four sense organs (the eyes, etc.), ten things arise together;
these nine things are as previously described, with one additional thing—the eye, ear, nose, or tongue—added, because these four sense organs are never dissociated from the body organ (*kāyendriya*).

In the case of a collection of four atoms, ten things arise together; when these four organs are considered in relation to one another, their locations are distinct, and their sensations (*vedanā*) are each separate.

Therefore, they do not mutually increase one another. The preceding text is identical to the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* (Zaxin lun), which states that one should know that the atoms (*paramāṇu*) of the four sense organs consist of ten types;
the body organ consists of nine, and the remaining eight are as previously mentioned. Dharma-teachers and others rely on this as the correct interpretation.

However, in the *Vibhāṣā*, there are two masters who provide explanations. The first master says: "In all cases, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are never separated from color and sound throughout the entire desire realm."
The second master says that not all of the four great elements necessarily possess visible form and sound, and that not all matter in the desire realm necessarily possesses odor and taste.
Master Nianfa, relying on the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, judges that the interpretations of these two masters from the *Mahāvibhāṣā* are both incorrect;
it is only when the views of the two masters are combined that they constitute the correct doctrine. The first master says that all [four great elements]... [all four great elements].

The claim that "the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are necessarily not separated from form (*rūpa*), and all form in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is necessarily not separated from odor (*gandha*) and taste (*rasa*)" is the correct interpretation.

The claim that "the four great elements are necessarily not separated from sound (*śabda*)" is not the correct interpretation. A second master says: "It is not necessarily the case that the four great elements possess sound;

this is the correct interpretation. It is not necessarily the case that they possess sound, nor is it necessarily the case that all form in the desire realm possesses odor and taste. This is the [correct] meaning.
If one were to follow the correct principle (nyāya), it should be stated that all four great elements (mahābhūta) are necessarily not separated from form (rūpa) but need not possess sound (śabda);

and that all matter (rūpa) in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) is necessarily not separated from odor (gandha) and taste (rasa). To claim that this is the correct principle according to the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* is a grave error.
Kātyāyanīputra asked: "Who possesses the possession of sound? He replied: "Those in the desire realm and the form realm. Furthermore, the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* states: [as cited above].

Because there are eighteen elements among the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñi-sattva*), we know that the first master of the *Vibhāṣā* maintains the correct position that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are never separated from visible form (*rūpa*) and sound (*śabda*), and that all matter (*rūpa*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is never separated from odor (*gandha*) and taste (*rasa*). Therefore, the present treatise states:
"If sound arises within any of the aforementioned aggregates, it increases by nine, ten, or eleven respectively, because the sphere of sound (*śabdāyatana*) exists."
It is said that sound does not arise independently of the sense faculties; rather, it is asserted that it arises with the appropriated great elements (*mahābhūta*) as its cause.
However, the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* and the verses of this treatise do not mention sound because sound arises only when the great elements strike one another.

Thus, this treatise adds it specifically, whereas the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* omits it for brevity. As the tenth fascicle of the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "In the absence of sound, eight things arise together without the sense faculties."

If sound produced in this way were the ninth category [of derived matter] yet was not explicitly mentioned, it is because its production is shown to result from the mutual impact of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), and is not like form (*rūpa*) and so forth, which exist at all times.

As for the question of how sound within the internal body arises—given that it is not produced by the mutual impact of the primary elements—the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (Treatise on the Correct Theory) answers:
"Because within the internal body, it is constantly struck and activated by external wind. Thus it is produced. Therefore, [the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*] does not mention it.
It is asked: "Regarding manifest form (*vijñapti-rūpa*), it exists within the desire realm and the first dhyāna, but it cannot be said to exist in higher stages.

Now, since manifest speech (*vāk-vijñapti*) no longer exists there, how can there be the sense-sphere of sound (*śabda-āyatana*)? The answer is: Sound is produced with external primary elements (*mahābhūta*) as its cause; since this does not preclude external matter (*rūpa*), there is no fault.
Furthermore, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Chengshi lun), in refuting the Sarvāstivādins, states that some proponents of the treatises say that the four primary elements strike against one another.

The claim that sound exists because contact is uniform is incorrect; therefore, we know that within the bodies of sentient beings, there is always mutual contact and obstruction by the external four great elements (*mahābhūta*), and thus sound is constantly present.
Consequently, in the realms of desire and form, sound is established as a factor, and for non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*), it constitutes ten bases (*āyatana*).

Question: If it is said that sound exists because there is constant contact within the body, why does the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* state: [...]* *Note: The final sentence is truncated in the source text.*

The *Yunxian* (Cloud Manifestation) states that [the great elements] arise because the great elements strike one another, and not because they exist at all times like [other] forms (*rūpa*) and so forth.
In response to this, it is said that external great elements constantly obstruct internal great elements; therefore, it is stated that "they arise because the great elements strike one another.

This is explained separately because the four objects (*viṣaya*), such as form and so forth, do not exist eternally by virtue of constant mutual striking, but rather exist spontaneously. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 90, says: "Body, form, sound, and touch..."

Regarding the question of whether one who possesses the elements (*dhātu*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) necessarily possesses those of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*):
it may be so for the elements of body, visible form, and tangibility. But how is it with the element of sound (*śabdadhātu*)?

It is always possessed [in these realms]. Some say: "Because the great elements (*mahābhūta*) are constantly present in sentient beings within the desire and form realms, they must always produce sound. Criticism: This is not so.
One should state this: if the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) necessarily always produce sound, by which great elements is that produced sound created?

If it were created by those very same [elements], then many resistant forms (*sapratigha-rūpa*) would be produced from a single set of four great elements. If one says it is created by other [elements], then other sets of four great elements would also necessarily produce sound;
thus, through such a succession, there would be the fault of infinite regress. One should therefore state: [it is] produced in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Within the bodies of sentient beings in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), many of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) exist within a single body;

those that strike against one another produce sound, while those that do not strike one another give rise to no sound. Although the element of sound (*śabdadhātu*) must necessarily exist within a single body, it is not the case that sound is produced throughout all parts of the body.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 127, asks: "Do the four great elements [of one instance]..."
Regarding the question of whether one primary element (mahābhūta) produces many derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) atoms, this should be stated as follows:
One set of the four primary elements produces only one atom of derived matter. Some say it produces many; however, the critique states that the former explanation is superior.
[The Sautrāntikas] ask: If the four primary elements arise inseparably within various aggregates, why is it that only one of them is perceived?
Regarding the other four [elements] within that aggregate, the Master [Vasubandhu] sets forth the Sautrāntika response:

Within that aggregate of the four great elements, one clearly acquires that whose functional power (*śakti*) is predominant; the substantial bodies of the other three great elements are not non-existent.
For example, when a needle-point and a tally-stick touch together and are bound into a single bundle, although both touch the body, it is only the needle’s functional power that is strong.
One perceives the needle-point but does not perceive the counting-stick;

likewise, when salt flavor is mixed with flour, if a person tastes it, the power of the salt prevails so that one perceives only the salt flavor, yet the substance of the flour is not non-existent. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, fascicle five, states:

"Now one should investigate whether, within an aggregate of matter consisting of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), [the elements] exist as substance (*svabhāva*) or as function (*vṛtti*). For what reason, then, is such an exhortation made?"
In order to investigate and eliminate this unreal fault, the Master of the Sūtras (Sthiramati) states in his own treatise:
"This is a fault belonging to that school"; by "that school," he refers to the Vaibhāṣikas, who say:

"Although all primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are equally present in their essence within any given aggregate, there may be cases where the activity of one is particularly predominant, just as it is with the mind and mental factors."
Regarding the salt taste within the lump that was perceived, it is uncertain what the intended meaning of this passage in the Sūtra is: does it definitively refer to the Vaibhāṣikas?
If one claims it refers to the great masters who excellently explain the Abhidharma, they do not hold such a view;

for they maintain that the primary elements (mahābhūtas) predominate by way of their essential nature, such that within the various material aggregates of stone, water, flame, and wind, the characteristics of solidity, moisture, heat, and motion respectively prevail.

If it were because each aggregate (*rāśi*) predominantly perceives one [quality], then since the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are equal in substance within each aggregate, it would not be the case that only one is perceived therein.

Furthermore, the names "earth" and so forth would be established merely according to worldly convention; thus, there would be no actual cause for them, as they would be mere verbal designations like empty space.

Since all material aggregates are identical in their shape and color, if one holds that the substances such as solidity are equal and without distinction, what could be the cause [for the differentiation]?

If one claims that distinct perceptions, such as "this is the earth," arise based on their functional utility (*kāritra*), this is logically untenable. This is because there is no difference between functional utility and the entity's own nature (*svabhāva*).

If functional utility were real, it would result in an increase in the entity's substance; since utility is identical to the entity, it is the entity itself that increases. If functional utility were unreal, it would likewise result in an increase in the entity's substance, for it is not different from the entity.
Thus, there is no case where an unreal utility increases while remaining distinct from the entity. By this, the [opponent's] position regarding the mind is refuted.

Regarding the analogy of salt within the aggregate of mental factors (*caitta*): because the function of salt—such as its capacity for taste—is identical to its substance, it is said that the substance and function increase together when described in general terms.
Nevertheless, there are distinctions: because the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) possess resistance and can be accumulated, their spatial differentiation is clearly discernible.
Sensations (*vedanā*) and the other [mental factors] lack resistance and cannot be accumulated; they are distinguished as being more or less intense solely through the difference in their functions.
Because they differ in this way, the substance (*dravya*) of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) can be accumulated; thus, in terms of their substance, they are said to increase.

As for the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), they are said to increase in terms of the differentiation of their functional activity (*kāritra*). Is it not the case that material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) are also seen to increase in terms of their function?

For example, vinegar mixed with water, a potent medicine mixed with poison, or salt mixed with water—although these two categories are similar in kind, their functions differ. How then can you say that matter is described only in terms of its substance?
This increase is not contradictory because, although the atoms of vinegar and water that come into contact are equal in number, their tastes differ;

the atoms of the taste of vinegar are more numerous, while the atoms of the taste of water are fewer, and thus the taste of vinegar prevails. Furthermore, this is due to the increase in substance, for within various aggregates, the substance of those things possessing taste and so forth becomes more predominant.
This refers to the principle of causal origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) regarding the distinction between the predominance of function, as seen in cases such as potent medicine and poison.
Therefore, their nature is such that, although few, they are able to subdue many; it is not the case that a distinct function arises from a different nature.
Thus, to insist on the increase of function is a false conception. The Sautrāntikas ask again:
How is it known that within each individual aggregate there are also the other three great elements? The Sarvāstivādins answer: Because within each individual great element-aggregate...

Because water performs the function of cohesion, fire of maturation, wind of growth, and earth of support—since these are the functions of the four great elements—it is known that all four great elements are present [in every substance].

Other masters say that because when solidity and so forth are perceived, there are immediately the characteristics of fluidity and so forth, it is known that water and the other elements already exist within solidity and the rest.

Furthermore, just as within a mass of water, due to extreme cold, the characteristic of warmth arises even though it is not separate [from the water], so too [the other elements exist within one another].
There are cases where the function of cold increases, such as when water within clouds produces lightning through the impact of cold; lightning is, in fact, the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*).
It is also like when a person makes lime by burning stone, and after the stone has cooled, water is poured over it, whereupon fire immediately emerges.
Furthermore, because there are degrees of intensity in the functions of sensation (*vedanā*) and sound, one perceives only the superior sensation while failing to perceive the inferior one.
When a sound is heard, one hears only the superior sound and not the inferior one;
other masters say that within this single great aggregate, there remain three other great seeds whose functional capacities exist but whose substantial characteristics have not yet manifested.
Therefore, the Sūtra says that within the original aggregate there are various *dhātus*, where *dhātu* refers to the seed. The Sautrāntikas ask: how is it known that [seeds] exist within the wind?
8. Although visible color (varṇa) exists, it cannot be perceived [here]. This is because I know it only through the authority of the scriptures; it cannot be known through logical inference.
Alternatively, since fragrance can be apprehended when combined with wind, and since fragrance is never dissociated from visible color, one may also infer that visible color exists [there].
9. By analogy, regarding the realm of form (rūpadhātu): as stated in the previous fascicle, fragrance and taste do not exist in the realm of form.
Therefore, among those [derived elements], when sound is absent, there are six, seven, or eight; when sound is present, there are seven, eight, or nine arising together.

This can be understood by analogy, which is why the verse does not state it separately. An outsider asks: "Does the term 'entity' (*vastu*) in this verse refer to the substance (*dravya*) itself, or does it refer to the twelve bases (*āyatana*)?
The Master replies by counter-interrogating the outsider: "If that were so, what fault would there be? The outsider says: "There would be eleven."
If one were to claim that a person exists apart from these [aggregates], there would be faults in both cases.

If one speaks in terms of their substance (dravya), then numbers such as eight, nine, or ten would result in a discrepancy between the greater and the lesser, because every collection of atoms (paramāṇu) necessarily possesses dimensions such as length and so forth, since many atoms must gather together.

Furthermore, among the tangibles, either heavy or light touch must necessarily be present, and likewise, either smooth or rough touch must be present. In some places, there is cold; in others, hunger.
Due to thirst, there are eight [qualities]; among these, by adding length, heaviness, smoothness, cold, and hunger, they become thirteen kinds; with nine [qualities], they become fourteen;
with ten, they become fifteen. Thus, what was said regarding "eight, nine, or ten" would have the fault of being too few or too many.

However, if one speaks according to the twelve bases (*āyatana*), then saying "eight, nine, or ten" and so forth would be excessive, because the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are already subsumed within the base of the tangible (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*).

Eight should be explained as four, nine should be explained as five, and ten should be explained as six; thus, what was said regarding eight, nine, ten, and so forth, would have the fault of being excessive.
One should know that the Master of the Treatise explains both cases as being without fault:

it should be understood that the "entities" (*vastu*) mentioned in this verse refer in one part to the substantial entities (*dravya*), namely the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) which serve as the basis, and in another part to the twelve bases (*āyatana*).
This refers to the fourteen external derived forms (*upādāya-rūpa*) consisting of the five sense organs (*indriya*) and the four objects (*viṣaya*). An outsider asks:

"If that is so, the entities of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) should become numerous. Just as among the eight entities, the four derived forms each depend on their own distinct set of the four primary elements, there would be four derived forms and four sets of four primary elements, totaling sixteen; thus, they would amount to twenty. Why, then, do you speak of only eight or nine?"
Regarding the statement that there should be twenty-four items, it should actually be stated that there are twenty-eight. Fifteenth, the Master of the Treatise explains:

It should be understood that herein, the categories are explained based on their essential types (*tattva-jāti*). Since the fourfold, fivefold, and sixfold sets of great elements (*mahābhūta*) do not differ in their fundamental nature, they are not enumerated separately.
The *Nyāyabindu* states: "If one were to claim that the term 'item' (*vastu*) refers to the essential nature (*tattva*) or the locus (*sthāna*), it would be either too few or too many."
There is no fault in this, because it is explained through the distinctions between the basis (*āśraya*), the supported (*āśrita*), the substance (*dravya*), and the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

That is to say, if it is explained in terms of the substance of the basis, or if it is explained in terms of the locus of the supported, or even if it is explained solely in terms of the substance, there is still no fault.

This is because it is stated therein that they arise simultaneously with the primary color; therefore, the substance of shape-color (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*) and so forth does not exist determinately apart from light.

Since [the primary elements] do not exist within [derived matter] such as light and so forth, they exist only as a locus (*āśraya*). However, in order to refute various denials, the great elements (*mahābhūta*) are explained separately.
Regarding these various denials: some deny that there is a distinct nature (*svabhāva*) for derived matter produced by the great elements;

others deny that there is a distinct body of derived matter within the sense-base of tangibility (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*); and still others deny that all aggregates (*saṃghāta*) consist of [all four] elements.

Whether one claims [the primary elements] possess all [characteristics] or else slanders them by saying their number is indeterminate and distinct from the great elements (*mahābhūta*), these slanders are all eliminated.

If it is argued that because each great element produces its own distinct derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*), there would consequently be many [derived matters], this reasoning is incorrect, for it is spoken of in terms of categories (*jāti*).
The commentary explains: there are three interpretations here; the first, concerning the basis of substance (*dravya*) and the basis of location (*sthāna*), is the same as in the *Abhidharmakośa*.
The second [category] refers exclusively to the substance of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

This is because it is stated that among the substances of the four great elements, those which definitely produce the four faculties (*indriya*) necessarily arise simultaneously with the great elements that produce them; thus, they are said to be of ten or eleven kinds.
This is like the substance of long and short shapes and so forth, which do not necessarily possess color or light within all instances of the four great elements.
In light and other such phenomena, there is only the luminosity of visible color (*varṇa-rūpa*), and thus no derived shapes (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*) such as length and so forth.

Now, regarding the statement that within the collection of primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that constitute the sense organs, ten types of matter and so forth necessarily arise together: the third [section] explains that this refers either solely to the locus (*āyatana*).

This is because the locus alone is capable of refuting many misconceptions; therefore, the Master [Vasubandhu] separately discusses the sixteen [factors] including the primary elements outside of the locus, thereby rebuking the opponent.
Why should one make such distinctions regarding speech? Speech arises according to desire; its frequency and quantity are indeterminate, following whatever one wishes.
One should reflect upon the meaning: why is much speech necessary?
From here below, twelve verses distinguish the collection of mind;

therein, the first five verses distinguish the five universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), the next four verses distinguish the number of times the five categories of mind arise, the following two verses distinguish the specific mental concomitants (*caitasika*), and the final verse distinguishes the various names for these mental concomitants. Within the first five verses, there is first...

The four-line verse distinguishes the simultaneous arising of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). In the commentary, first the preceding section is concluded and the subsequent section introduced;
next, the root verse is cited; finally, the root verse is explained. Within the explanation of the root verse, the first line is explained: mind and mental factors necessarily arise together.

Just as one who possesses mastery is called "self" (*ātman*), and that self must have something over which it exercises mastery, so too the mind exercises mastery [over its concomitants]; therefore, it is not like that which is not mind.
Because the king [the mind] has sovereignty, that which necessarily arises in dependence upon it is called a "mental factor" (*caitta*). Next, the second phrase is explained:
"all formations" (*saṃskāra*) refers to all conditioned things comprised within the three aggregates. The term "necessarily co-arising" from the preceding phrase flows over into this second phrase;
it means that when the two aggregates of matter and mind arise, they must necessarily be accompanied by the four characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*).

Because they arise together, it is said that "conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) possess characteristics (lakṣaṇa). Regarding the phrase "or acquisition (prāpti)": among conditioned phenomena, only those pertaining to sentient beings arise simultaneously with acquisition;
other non-sentient phenomena do not, as this is not fixed. Thus, it is said "or by reason of clarity" because the mind arises together with its objects;
this applies equally to both conditioned phenomena and their characteristics. The intention is to clarify that the mind also arises together with characteristics or acquisitions.

Next, there are two lines that cite the number five for the primary mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) to explain the verse. First, citing the mental factors and noting they reside in five categories, this cites the number to explain the first line.
Second, "What are the five? and so forth, which provides a question-and-answer format to list the names of the five categories and explain the second line.
Third, "Ground" (*bhūmi*) refers to the sphere of activity; this is a general explanation of the meaning of the number and the name. "Ground" refers to the locus...

Regarding the "basis for activity" (*caritrapada*): just as the earth in the world is the basis for the activities of people, if this mind-king (*cittarāja*) is the basis for the activity of those mental factors (*caitta*), then this mind-king is said to be the "ground" (*bhūmi*) for those mental factors.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, fascicle ten, states: "If this is that which can serve as the sphere of activity for those mental factors, then this dharma is said to be the ground for those dharmas."
Next, there is one verse that analyzes the universal mental factors (mahābhūmika-dharma). Within this text, there are four parts. First, it explains the meaning of the term "universal" (mahābhūmika):
the ten factors, beginning with perception (saṃjñā), are called "great dharmas" because the mind-king (citta-rāja) serves as the ground (bhūmi) for these ten great dharmas;

since the name is derived from the result, the mind-king itself is designated as the "universal ground. Regarding the analysis of the meaning of the universal ground, if these ten dharmas serve as the mind-king...

All those factors that can be termed "great" among the conditioned—namely, the ten factors beginning with sensation (*vedanā*) and conception (*saṃjñā*)—are called the "universal mental factors" (*mahābhūmikadharma*).

They are called "great" because these great factors are always present in all states of mind, whereas other mental factors are not. The *Nyāyapraveśa* (Treatise on Correct Reasoning) states: "The 'ground' (*bhūmi*) is the mind;

because they are the ground for the great factors, they are called the 'universal ground' (*mahābhūmika*). Among these, any factor that belongs to the universal ground is called a 'universal mental factor'."

This means that these factors are universally associated with all categories of mind; for this reason, they are not among the "universal mental factors" (*mahābhūmika-dharma*), because they arise together with the mind.
There are four parts to this section: (1) the statement of the two questions regarding what those universal mental factors are;

(2) the answer provided by a verse; (3) the explanation of the verse's text, which consists of three sub-sections; and (4) the initial explanation of the fourth line, according to which the *Mahāvibhāṣā* tradition states that there are ten such factors.

In every moment of mind, these factors are universally present; however, since ancient times, various masters have established different systems regarding the "universal mental factors" (*mahābhūmika*).
For instance, the masters of the *Abhidharmakośa* establish them according to five criteria: first, they must pervade all levels; second, they must pervade all six consciousnesses;

third, they must pervade all three natures; fourth, they must pervade both the outflowing and non-outflowing states; and fifth, they must arise simultaneously with the primary mind. The remaining thirty-six factors do not possess these five characteristics.

It is not established as such for doctrinal reasons. Although the Tripiṭaka Master Chang-er (Long-ear) possessed the eight supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), he did not establish them as universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*).

Dharma Master Hefu possessed nine meanings [for their establishment], yet he too did not establish them as universal mental factors. Now, according to the *Abhidharmakośa*, they are established based on only one meaning:

namely, that they pervade all states of mind. The other thirty-six [mental factors] do not pervade all states of mind; therefore, they are not established [as universal]. Second, within this [context]...

The following explains the names and meanings of the ten dharmas mentioned in the three preceding phrases. Among these, seven dharmas are easily understood. As for *prajñā* (wisdom), it refers to that which is capable of discerning phenomena (*dharma*).
According to the tenets of this treatise, seeking [the truth] is called *darśana* (view); decisive resolution is called *jñāna* (knowledge); and discernment is called *prajñā* (wisdom).

As for *manasikāra* (attention), it refers to that which causes the mind to be awakened; the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* calls this *smṛti* (mindfulness), whereas here it is termed *manasikāra*. It is correct [to use the latter].
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*, fascicle eleven, states: "That which causes the mind to move toward an object is called the characteristic of attention (*manaskāra*). Question:

If it were only that which moves the mind toward an object [that constitutes attention], then the other mental factors (*caitta*) would be unable to take an object. Answer: This objection is irrational.
Because all mental factors function in dependence upon the mind, when the mind itself is moved, the movement of the others is also established; therefore, there is no lack of mental factors.
That which cannot take as its object a past mind-king (*citta-rāja*) is like a person who is asleep and lacks awareness;
because of *manasikāra* (attention), it causes the mind-king not to sleep, which is called "arousing. *Adhimokṣa* (resolute conviction) refers to that which can confirm an object;
the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* calls it "liberation" (*vimukti*), while here it is called "resolute conviction. It is the liberation regarding an object and the confirmation that it must be so.
This is called "resolute understanding" (*adhimukti*). It is a matter of great difficulty to know the collection of minds, for all mental states are formless;

thus, their distinct characteristics are subtle and minute. It is already difficult to discern them through sequential analysis as they arise one after another in succession, let alone when ten factors coexist simultaneously in a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).
Even with the physical sense organ of sight perceiving a hundred flavors in various medicinal herbs, it is still difficult to grasp the distinctions between those hundred flavors.
How much more so for formless phenomena (*ārūpya-dharma*), which are apprehended solely by mental discernment (*buddhi*)? Thus have the four fetters been explained.
Next, one verse distinguishes the ten wholesome ground factors (*kuśala-mahābhūmika*). In this passage, the meaning of the term "ground" (*bhūmi*) is first explained:

the ten factors beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) are called "great wholesome factors" (*mahā-kuśala-dharma*); because they serve as the ground for the mental sovereign (*citta-rāja*), they are termed "great wholesome" from the perspective of their result.

Regarding this explanation of the name "ground": if dharmas such as faith (*śraddhā*) belong to the great wholesome ground, they are termed "great wholesome ground factors" (*kuśalamahābhūmika*) by virtue of their capacity [to arise] together with it.
That is to say, ten dharmas are called "great wholesome" because they are always present in all wholesome minds; this also serves to distinguish them from the mind-king (*citta-rāja*).
Second, the question: What are those ten dharmas? Third, the answer provided by verse: As the Master of the Treatise (*śāstrakāra*) establishes [them], they possess five characteristics.

Establishing the Great Grounds (mahābhūmika): 1. They pervade the three realms; 2. They function through the six consciousnesses; 3. They include both the out-flowing (*sāsrava*) and non-out-flowing (*anāsrava*);

4. They are all-inclusive; 5. They are exclusively wholesome (*kuśala*). The present verse explains only one of these meanings—namely, that they "pervade only the wholesome mind. This term "only" serves to exclude those factors common to the Great Grounds (*mahābhūmika*) that are not restricted to the wholesome.

Although the Great Grounds pervade the wholesome mind, they are not exclusively wholesome because they also function within the three natures (wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate). Therefore, the phrase "pervading the wholesome mind" excludes those [other factors].
Twenty-six: The Enumeration of Factors Not Pervasive of Wholesome Minds. This is the fourth explanation within the body of the verse.

First, it explains that these factors—such as faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth—are pervasive only of wholesome minds. Second, it cites "faith" for explanation: first, it explains it as that which clarifies and purifies the mind;

second, it explains it as the present acceptance and conviction regarding the Four Truths, the Three Jewels, and the relationship between karma and its results as presented in the fundamental treatises. Third, it cites [the term] again.

The Sautrāntikas raise an objection regarding the frequent establishment of *praśrabdhi* (pliancy) as being the mind’s serviceability (*cittakarmaṇyatā*). They ask: "Is there not also a sūtra that speaks of bodily pliancy (*kāyapraśrabdhi*)? The Sarvāstivādins explain: "It is not that such a teaching does not exist;

however, this [bodily pliancy] is like bodily sensation (*kāyikī vedanā*), which is called 'bodily' because it relies upon the physical sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*). One should understand that its essence is actually mental. The same applies to the pliancy associated with the five sensory consciousnesses. [Reference: *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Chapter 6, Verse 49. The Sautrāntika critique appears in the commentary on this verse.

The Sarvāstivāda response is found in the subsequent prose. The mention of the "five consciousnesses" refers to the pliancy associated with the five sensory perceptions. The term "four sūtras" likely refers to specific scriptural citations used by the Sarvāstivādins to support their position.

The [Vaibhāṣika] school objects: "If there were a factor of mental pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) associated with the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), how could these five consciousnesses—which do not arise simultaneously with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)—be established as the limb of enlightenment consisting of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*)? The Sarvāstivāda explanation should be understood as follows:

In the sūtras, this "pliancy of the body" refers to the tactile sensation of lightness (*laghu-spraṣṭavya*) among the seven types of derived tangible objects (*bhautika-spraṣṭavya*). It causes the body to become buoyant and uplifted.

The state of serviceability (*karmanyatā*) arises simultaneously with the untainted mental consciousness (*anāsrava-manovijñāna*). Regarding the six schools of the Sūtra-piṭaka, they raise an objection:

since the essence of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and light contact (*laghu-spraṣṭavya*) is a contaminated material phenomenon (*sāsrava-rūpa-dharma*), how can it be said that this constitutes the awakening-factor of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-sambodhyaṅga*)?
The Sarvāstivādins explain that there is no fault because it is conducive to the awakening-factors; for the material pliancy of light contact can induce the awakening-factors through the body.

Because the mind is pliant (*praśrabdhi*), [the factor of] *samādhi* is established. **Question:** (Sautrāntika) Is it not also seen that other factors are described as being "conducive" (*anuloma*) or "associated with" (*sahagata*) [a particular state], such that they are spoken of in accordance with that?
**Answer:** (Sarvāstivāda) Yes; there are such scriptural statements. For example, the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "Joy (*prīti*) and the factors associated with joy are called the *prītisambodhyaṅga*.

Hatred (*vyāpāda*) and the factors associated with, co-arising with, or being its own-nature cause (*svabhāva-hetu*) or pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) for hatred are called the hindrance of ill-will (*vyāpādāvaraṇa*), and so forth. Thus, according to the *Nyāya*, it is established.
The eleventh fascicle of the *Śāstra* states: "Some say that since 'bodily pliancy' (*kāya-praśrabdhi*) is mentioned here, it is not the case that only mental factors are termed 'pliancy.
This statement is unreasonable, for [if it were so], feelings (*vedanā*) and other factors would also have to be described in this same way.

However, the various feelings associated with the five consciousnesses are termed 'bodily feelings' (*kāyikī vedanā*). Some further state that even if there were an entity of pliancy that was not mental..."
However, since what is discussed here are mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), it should not be said that [the body] is a limb of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*).

Rather, because the pliancy of the body (*kāya-praśrabdhi*) can induce the pliancy of the mind (*citta-praśrabdhi*), which is the essence of the limbs of awakening, it is also called a limb of awakening.

Furthermore, in other passages, hatred (*dveṣa*) and the causes of hatred are called the hindrance of ill-will (*vyāpāda-nīvaraṇa*); likewise, although both insight (*vipaśyanā*) and diligence (*vīrya*) are called the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*), even though that [diligence] is...
Because it arises from reflection and diligence, and is neither hatred nor wisdom, yet accords with them, it also receives their names; this case should be understood in the same way.
Regarding the five explanations of equanimity (*upekṣā*): first, the Sarvāstivādins establish their tenet that the nature of mental equality and the nature of non-arousal are called equanimity.
Second, the Sautrāntikas ask: how can one speak of the presence of both attention (*manasikāra*) and the nature of arousal within a single moment of mind?
The Sarvāstivādins explain: "Does it not state previously that the characteristics of all minds and mental factors are so subtle as to be difficult to discern?
How can this be contradictory? The Sautrāntikas respond: "Even if a phenomenon is capable of being discerned, it may still be known through careful investigation and deliberation.
Yet, among these, the mental factor of equanimity (*upekṣā*) is the most difficult to discern; how then can [your claim] be contradictory?"

5. The Sarvāstivāda explanation: "They arise together because they are not contradictory.
