It is not the case that there is no *sabhāgatā* at all, for if there were none, the aforementioned cognitions, understandings, and verbal expressions would be impossible. Therefore, the existence of *sabhāgatā* is proven by logical necessity. Furthermore, the *sabhāgatā* of sentient beings is distinct from the *sabhāgatā* of phenomena, because the former pertains to the continuity of consciousness and the latter pertains to the nature of the dharmas themselves. Thus, the *sabhāgatā* of sentient beings exists as a real entity (*dravya-sat*). This concludes the explanation of *sabhāgatā*. Next, we shall explain the *jīvitendriya* (life-faculty). The life-faculty is the support for the warmth and consciousness of sentient beings; it is the cause that maintains the continuity of the aggregates. It is a subtle force that sustains the body and prevents it from decaying. It is not the same as the physical heat (*ūṣman*), for even when the heat is absent—as in the case of an embryo in the womb—the life-faculty still persists. Nor is it the same as consciousness, for even when consciousness is suspended—as in the state of *nirodhasamāpatti*—the life-faculty continues to function. Therefore, the life-faculty is a distinct dharma that acts as the basis for the maintenance of the body and the continuity of the aggregates. It is said to be "subtle" because it is not perceived by the senses and its activity is difficult to discern. It is "the support" because it serves as the foundation for the persistence of warmth and consciousness. It is "the cause of maintenance" because it prevents the aggregates from disintegrating. This life-faculty exists in all sentient beings, whether they are in the desire, form, or formless realms. In the desire and form realms, it is associated with the five aggregates; in the formless realm, it is associated with the four aggregates. It ceases only at the moment of death. Thus, the life-faculty is established as a real entity that sustains the life-force of sentient beings. This concludes the explanation of the life-faculty. Next, we shall explain the *nikāyasabhāga* (group-homogeneity). The group-homogeneity is the cause that establishes the similarity among sentient beings belonging to the same class, such as humans, gods, or animals. It is what causes those born into the same realm to have similar bodies, faculties, and modes of behavior. It is not the same as the *sabhāgatā* previously discussed, for while *sabhāgatā* refers to the general homogeneity of all phenomena, *nikāyasabhāga* specifically refers to the homogeneity of sentient beings within a particular category. It is a subtle force that ensures that those born as humans share common characteristics, such as a similar physical stature and sensory capacities, distinguishing them from other classes of beings. It is said to be "establishing similarity" because it is the primary factor that makes members of a group appear alike. It is "the cause" because it is the underlying condition for the manifestation of these similarities. This *nikāyasabhāga* exists only in sentient beings and not in insentient objects. It is abandoned at the moment of death and acquired at the moment of birth. It is not eternal, for it changes with the state of the sentient being. Thus, the *nikāyasabhāga* is established as a real entity that accounts for the shared characteristics of sentient beings within a specific class. This concludes the explanation of the group-homogeneity. Next, we shall explain the *vijñapti* (informative action). Informative action is the movement of body and speech that manifests intention. It is of two types: bodily informative action and vocal informative action. Bodily informative action consists of the physical movements of the body, such as walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, which inform others of one's intentions. Vocal informative action consists of the utterances of speech, such as words, phrases, and syllables, which inform others of one's thoughts. Both types of informative action are based on the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of earth, water, fire, and wind, and they manifest through the transformation of these elements. They are called "informative" because they communicate the internal intention to others. They are "action" because they are the performance of an act. Informative action is impermanent and ceases moment by moment, yet it produces a result through the power of the intention that initiated it. It is not the same as non-informative action (*avijñapti*), for while informative action is visible and audible, non-informative action is invisible and inaudible, existing as a subtle force that continues to produce results even after the initial movement has ceased. Thus, informative action is established as a real entity that serves as the medium for expressing intention through body and speech. This concludes the explanation of informative action. Next, we shall explain non-informative action. Non-informative action is a subtle force that continues to produce results even after the initial movement of body or speech has ceased. It is produced by informative action or by a formal vow (*samādāna*). It is not visible or audible, but it exists as a latent potentiality that persists until it is abandoned. It is called "non-informative" because it does not communicate intention to others in the way that informative action does. It is "action" because it is a result of an act that continues to exert influence. Non-informative action is of two types: that produced by informative action and that produced by a vow. The former occurs when one performs a physical or verbal act that is subsequently followed by a non-informative force, such as the merit or demerit generated by a good or evil deed. The latter occurs when one takes a vow, such as the precepts of a lay follower (*upāsaka*) or a monk (*bhikṣu*), and thereafter possesses a continuous force that maintains the restraint even when not actively performing the prescribed actions. Non-informative action is impermanent and ceases when the conditions for its production are exhausted or when it is explicitly abandoned. Thus, non-informative action is established as a real entity that accounts for the continuity of karmic results beyond the moment of the initial act. This concludes the explanation of non-informative action. Next

The first case refers to one who dies in the human realm and is reborn again in the human realm; such a person undergoes death and birth, yet does not relinquish nor acquire a new human *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneity).
The second case refers to one who enters the state of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) at the moment of doing so;

they relinquish the *nikāya-sabhāga* of an ordinary worldling (*pṛthagjana*) and acquire the *nikāya-sabhāga* of a noble one (*ārya*). The third case refers to one who dies in the human realm and is reborn elsewhere.

The realms of the gods and so forth involve death and birth; this constitutes the relinquishing of the human *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous class) and the obtaining of the *nikāya-sabhāga* of the realms of the gods and so forth.
The fourth alternative refers to cases other than those previously described.
Although there have been five textual passages above, they are combined as the first section, which sets forth the Sarvāstivāda school’s position. Hereafter begins the second section of the treatise.

The Master [Vasubandhu], representing the Sautrāntika school, rebukes the Sarvāstivāda. First, the rebuke: If there were a separate, substantial entity called "the homogeneity of ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjanatva-sabhāgatā*), what would be the purpose of separately establishing "the nature of an ordinary being" (*pṛthagjanatva*)?
It is not the case that apart from the homogeneity of persons, there exists a separate "human nature. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"When one who possesses the homogeneity of ordinary beings enters the state of transcending birth, they relinquish the homogeneity of sentient beings; when they enter *nirvāṇa*, they relinquish it."
Is this nature of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) the same as the commonality of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana-sabhāgatā*)? This cannot be so, because their functions differ.
That is to say, the cause for the mutual similarity of their physical forms, activities, and inclinations is called "commonality" (*sabhāgatā*).

However, that which is the cause of being an ordinary person—characterized by its opposition to the attainment of the Noble Path—is called "the nature of being an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjanatva*). At the moment one enters the state of certainty (*niyāma*), [one abandons] the commonality of ordinary persons as well.

Regarding the abandonment [of the state of being an ordinary person], one also attains the "nature of an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjanatva*); yet, while it is abandoned, there is no explicit explanation.

This is because the "homogeneity of an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjana-sabhāgatā*) and the "nature of an ordinary person" perform different functions; therefore, the "nature of an ordinary person" is established separately from the "homogeneity of an ordinary person.

Furthermore, since humans do not perform functions distinct from those of the "homogeneity of humans," the "nature of a human" (*manuṣyatva*) is not established separately from the "homogeneity of humans. These are the two criticisms.

It is not something perceived by worldly direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because it is not a form (*rūpa*); nor can it be discerned by inferential cognition (*anumāna*), because it serves no practical purpose.

Although worldly people do not discern that there exists a distinct substantial entity called "homogeneity of sentient beings" (*sattva-sabhāgatā*) apart from form and mind, they nonetheless apply the cognition and verbal expression "sentient being" to them without distinction, as they all equally possess the nature of a sentient being.

Therefore, even if it possesses a substantial entity (*dravya*), what use would it be? The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "How is it known that the homogeneous character (*sabhāgatā*) has utility, since it is not material (*arūpin*)?

It is because it can produce things of a non-substantial nature; this is like knowing that past karma exists by seeing its subsequent fruit, or as practitioners know their present destinies through contemplation.

This explains that one knows there was previously performed karma by seeing the fruit obtained in the present, and likewise, practitioners know their current course of existence through direct observation.
Question: Since the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) is non-material (*arūpa*), it cannot be said to be perceived;

how then is it known to have the function of producing similar categories of sentient beings that are mutually comparable? Answer: It is known by seeing its common fruit and thereby inferring the existence of its homogeneous cause.
For example, by seeing the fruit obtained from present karma, one infers the existence of the karma performed in a previous life as its cause.
If there is indeed a functional discerning wisdom (*buddhi*) by which one infers [its existence], how can it be said that "it cannot be discerned by discerning wisdom,

as it has no separate function"? Furthermore, since the various Arhats and others of the Sarvāstivāda school, who practice meditative concentration and contemplation, know it through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),
how can it be said that "it is not perceived by worldly direct perception, because it is not a material form (*rūpa*)"?
Those in the world with distracted minds do not cultivate the gates of contemplation; they know the five commonalities (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of form and so forth through direct perception (*pramāṇa*).

Although these are not known through the cultivation of contemplation regarding form, those who practice contemplation know them through a concentrated mind. Because those in the world with distracted minds do not cultivate contemplative practice, they do not specifically discern the existence of the "sentient-being commonality" (*sattva-sabhāga*);
nevertheless, regarding sentient beings, they perceive no difference in their effects. Thus, it is known [that such a commonality exists].
Since these are all the functional activities of the essence of the *sabhāgatā*, how can you say, "Even if the essence exists, what use would it be?

This is the third objection. Furthermore, for what reason do you not allow that there is a *sabhāgatā* among insentient things—such as (1) rice, (2) barley, (3) beans, (4) gold, (5) iron, (6) mango trees, and (7) *panasa* trees—which likewise possess mutual similarity within their own respective classes?

It is like the color and shape of a mature *āmra* fruit, which resembles that of a wood-apple (*kapittha*); from beginning to end, their colors are so similar that it is difficult to discern whether they are raw or ripe.
The *Parnaśa* tree produces extremely large fruits, as big as winter melons and very sweet in taste. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* objects:

"Why do you not also allow that the *āmra* and other such trees are established as the five destinies (*pañca-gati*), and that mung beans and the like are established as the four modes of birth (*catasro yonayaḥ*)?"
Furthermore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, never taught that there is a "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*) for insentient things; rather, I interpret it as follows:
first, because grasses and the like lack mutual functional activity or shared intentions, the World-Honored One did not state that they possess a distinct homogeneity.
Second, [the production of such things] necessarily depends upon sentient beings, for it arises only through their presence.
Because they cause plants and trees to resemble one another, only sentient beings are said to possess "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*). There are three types:

first, that which is obtained as a result of maturation (*vipāka*) in the present through the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) of past karma; second, that which is obtained in the present through diligent effort in the present as a result of outflow (*niṣyanda*);

and third, [the homogeneity of] those two types of things, such as grass and trees, which lacks both of these causes, and therefore lacks homogeneity. It is precisely for this reason [that only sentient beings possess it].
Regarding the statement that there are real entities (*dravya*), four objections are raised:

furthermore, since the various *sabhāgatās* (homogeneities) differ from one another, how could they give rise to a cognition and designation (*prajñapti*) of non-difference without yet another *sabhāgatā*? The *Nyāyabindu* offers this defense:

because all *sabhāgatās* serve as the cause for things being similar within their respective classes, they themselves function as the cause for the cognition and designation of mutual similarity among those of the same class.

Just as the eye, ear, and so forth are established as having the nature of matter (*rūpatva*) by being derived from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), even though those primary elements themselves lack derivation from other primary elements;
and just as the "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*) is established as having that same nature even though it lacks homogeneity; so too, [the opponent's objection] must be addressed.

Furthermore, this would clearly establish what the Vaiśeṣikas maintain: their school asserts the existence of a category called "universal" (*sāmānya-pada-artha*), which constitutes the universal commonality across all phenomena.

It is said that verbal cognition (*śabda-jñāna*) arises from this; furthermore, they insist that there exists a category (*padārtha*) of "similarity and difference" (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*), and that it is from this category of similarity and difference that verbal cognition of similarity and difference arises.
The commentary explains: "The non-Buddhists have a treatise called *Vaiśeṣika*.
In the old scriptures, Paramārtha calls them *Vaiśeṣika*; Master Kumārajīva calls them *Vaiśeṣika*—the term is a corruption. [It should be] *Vaiśeṣika*."

The Master [Vasubandhu] here calls this the *Vaiśeṣika* (Excellence School). Some say there are six categories (*padārtha*): first, substance (*dravya*); second, quality (*guṇa*); third, action (*karman*); fourth, generality (*sāmānya*); fifth, particularity (*viśeṣa*);

and sixth, inherence (*samavāya*). There are nine kinds of substances, namely: earth, water, fire, wind, space, time, direction, self (*ātman*), and mind (*manas*). Furthermore, there are eighteen kinds [of qualities], namely:
color, sound, odor, taste, touch, number, measure, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, "this-ness," "that-ness," intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, and aversion.
The karma of functional power (*prabhāva-karma*) is of six kinds: namely, lifting, lowering, contracting, extending, moving, and the cognition of similarity and difference.

Regarding similarity and difference, there is the cognition of similarity and difference based on direct and inverse causes; for example, because a cow possesses the characteristics of a cow, it causes the cognition of a cow to arise with respect to all cows of its own class as being similar to one another and different from horses.

When the cognition takes a cow as its object, the cognition of "cow" arises identically regarding all cows; when a cow moves away, that cognition is "direct" (*anuloma*), while [the cognition] regarding all horses is "inverse" (*pratiloma*).
One cannot produce the cognition of a cow from the cognition of a horse; this very cognition would thus contradict your Sarvāstivāda tenet that there exists a distinct *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity).
How does this differ from the category of *anyatva* (difference) held by these non-Buddhists?

Some claim that when a cognition exists and a cognition arises based upon it, this is what is meant by "possessing a cognition" (*sajñāna*), which is precisely the meaning of *mahāsāmānya* (the Great Universal). They maintain that there is a single *mahāsattā* (Great Being), and this entity is eternal.
Abiding causes all phenomena to exist; if phenomena are associated with this [quality of] abiding, they thereby attain existence.

You maintain that there is no distinction [between this and] the "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*), so how does it differ from the meaning of this term "existence"? Conjunction (*saṃyoga*) refers to the effect being within the cause;
by virtue of this category of conjunction, cause and effect are brought together. Among the six categories (*padārtha*) in the text, two...

I challenge you on the meaning of these terms: if you, as a disciple of the Buddha, establish these two kinds of *sāmānya* (homogeneity), you should clarify that what you have set forth is actually the position held by the Vaiśeṣikas—those who are disciples of external paths.
That school maintains the existence of a fifth category (*padārtha*), called the category of "universal" (*sāmānyapadārtha*), which causes all phenomena to exist;
it is from this universal that the verbal cognition and the conceptual knowledge [of "existence"] arise. You, O Sarvāstivādin...
To establish many instances of "undifferentiated commonality" (*aviśeṣa-sabhāgatā*) is precisely the fifth category (*padārtha*) of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

They further maintain a fourth category, "commonality-and-difference" (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*), which causes the class of cows to be identical [to one another] and different from the class of horses; it is from this that the verbal cognition of "commonality-and-difference" arises.
Since your proposed "differentiated commonality" (*viśeṣa-sabhāgatā*) is equivalent to the non-Buddhists' category of "commonality-and-difference," your [position]...
If one were to establish two kinds of *sabhāgatā*, it would effectively manifest the tenets held by the Vaiśeṣikas.
Although there have been five objections above, they are combined here as the second point, wherein the Master [Vasubandhu] recounts the Sautrāntika critique of the Sarvāstivādins.

From here below is the third section: the Sarvāstivādins’ defense against the five objections. Since [the first four objections] are identical to those raised against the non-Buddhists (tīrthika), they only defend against the fifth objection.

The Vaibhāṣika masters offer this defense: their adherence to the existence of the category of "existence" (astitva-pada-artha) and the category of "sameness-and-difference" (sāmānya-viśeṣa-pada-artha) is not the same as the meaning of "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā).
They assert that the category of existence is a single, eternal entity that exists within multiple things.

[The opponent] attempts to turn this argument around, claiming that all phenomena possess a self, and that there are no distinctions among their shared characteristics (*sabhāgatā*), such that each and every sentient being possesses its own distinct [self] that arises and ceases moment by moment, its nature being impermanent. How could this be the same as their own tenet?

For them, the category of "sameness and difference" (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*)—just like the category of "sameness and difference" in a cow—is a single dharma whose nature is eternal, existing within the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) across many cows.
To overturn the [opponent's] position, [the author] states that the universals (*sāmānya*) of "cow" and so forth are distinct from those of "horse" and so on;

furthermore, I maintain that these specific universals (*sabhāgatā*) exist individually within each cow, possessing their own nature and being impermanent moment by moment. How could this be the same as the tenets of the Vaibhāṣikas? The Vaibhāṣika masters offer a further defense, saying:
"Moreover, whether it is established through external [evidence] or not established through external [evidence], this *sabhāgatā* must necessarily be a real entity (*dravya*)."
Because it is stated in the sūtras; as the Blessed One said: "If one returns here, one obtains the human homogeneity (*manuṣyasabhāgatā*)," and so forth at length.

The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "If the Vaiśeṣikas maintain that the referents of these two phrases are a single entity that is momentary, impermanent, and without support, even if they were to concede this, there would be no great fault. However, this is not maintained by those who are not Vaiśeṣikas."
Because the sense faculties, such as the eye, are capable of engaging with objects such as visible forms, the Śākyaputrīyas abandon such a view and instead formulate a different interpretation;
therefore, that objection is merely partisan speech and should not be accepted by those seeking correct reasoning.
Although the Sautrāntikas have this position, they do not state that there exists a separate real entity called "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā). The Vaibhāṣika masters ask: [Why is this so?]
If that is so, what is this "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*) that you have described? The Sautrāntikas reply:

It is simply the designation "human homogeneity" and so forth applied to those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of a similar type when they arise—just as there is a "homogeneity" of rice and so forth.
The Master [Vasubandhu], the author of the *Abhidharmakośa*, critiques this Sautrāntika position, stating it is not well-said because it contradicts our Sarvāstivāda school.

The three verses from this point onward distinguish the maturation (*vipāka*) of the non-conceptual state (*asaṃjñika*). In the text, there are two parts: first, the initial section concludes the preceding discussion and poses the question;
second, the verse is cited as the answer, followed by an explanation of the verse’s meaning. Within the explanation, there are two sections. First, the two lines are explained:

"If one is born in the Heaven of Vast Results (*Bṛhatphala*) or among the gods of the non-conceptual state (*asaṃjñisattva*), [there occurs] a non-material, non-mental dharma of maturation which causes future minds and mental factors to cease. This is called...
Non-conception (*asaṃjñika*) is a real entity (*dravya*) because it can obstruct future mind and mental factors, causing them not to arise for a time;
thus, the opinion of many ancient masters—that one attains non-conception at the point where past mind and mental factors have ceased—is incorrect.
Just as non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) obstructs future phenomena, so too does this present fruition (*vipāka*) of non-conception obstruct future phenomena.

Because it prevents future minds and mental factors from arising for a time, the state of non-conception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) obstructs future minds—just as a dam or embankment holds back rivers and streams.
This explains the third phrase. Is this dharma exclusively a fruition result (*vipākaphala*)?
If so, whose fruition result is it? The answer is: it is the fruition result of the meditative attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*). (*Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*)
It is said that this dharma is exclusively the maturation (*vipāka*) induced by the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
This is because within the heaven of non-conceiving sentient beings, both non-conception and form are solely the maturation induced by that attainment of non-conception;

therefore, this attainment lacks the power to project the group-homogeneity (*nikāya-sabhāga*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), for the group-homogeneity and the life-faculty exist only where there is mind.
Because it is the fruit of the fourth dhyāna, the remaining aggregates in that state are a common *vipāka*. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* asks:

"What is the retribution received for the attainment of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*)? It answers: Some say that one receives the non-conceptual state (*asaṃjñika*), as well as the material body, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), and the physical location;

this is the fourth interpretation, which holds that the retribution of having a mind is received. The retribution of the other aggregates is a collective grasping-retribution (*upādāna-vipāka*). Others, however, say...

Regarding the state of non-conceptualization (asaṃjñi-samāpatti), it receives only the retribution of non-conceptuality; the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) and the basis of the body (āśraya) constitute the fourth explanation for the retribution of having consciousness, while the remaining aggregates (skandhas) are the common retribution.

Furthermore, there are those who say that in the state of non-conceptualization one receives the retribution of non-conceptuality, the life-faculty constitutes the fourth explanation for the retribution of having consciousness, and the remaining aggregates are the common retribution.
Furthermore, there are those who say that in the state of non-conceptualization one receives [the retribution of] non-...

Regarding the thought that the remaining aggregates (*skandha*) are a shared retribution, there are those who say that even during a state of mindlessness (*acittaka*), one experiences the fourth explanation;

and that during a state of having a mind (*sacittaka*), one also experiences the retribution of having a mind, while during a state of mindlessness, one experiences the retribution of mindlessness. Question:

How is it that during a state of mindlessness one also experiences the fourth explanation, and during a state of having a mind one also experiences the retribution of mindlessness? Answer: If that were so, what [fault] would there be?

Just as when one experiences the retribution of form, one also experiences non-form retribution; and when one knows that one is experiencing non-form retribution, one also experiences form retribution.

The Venerable Śamathadeva said: "The retribution of the attainment of non-conception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) results in obtaining non-conception, the acquisition of a physical basis, and the acquisition of mind.

It results in the acquisition of form and the life-faculty (jīvitendriya). Other formations dissociated from mind (cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra), as well as mind and mental factors (citta-caitasika-dharma), are not [the retribution of this attainment]."

The *Bao-ping* (Commentary on the Refutation) says: One should not make such a statement. To speak thus [is incorrect], for the wholesome state of non-conceptual absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) cannot create the basis for receiving a body.
Why? Because it is not karma. It is karma that can create the basis for receiving a body and can obtain the retribution of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).

The retribution obtained from non-conceptual absorption consists of the state of being without perception (*asaṃjñika*), and all other remaining factors are likewise the fruits of its retribution. The commentary explains: "If one relies upon..."
Among the eleven positions presented by the *Vibhāṣā* masters, the *Vibhāṣā* school’s own assessment (the *pūrvapakṣa*) adopts the second position.

Now, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* asks whose maturation (*vipāka*) it is, and answers that it is the maturation of the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), which accords with the statement of the second master in the *Vibhāṣā* as upheld by the *Vibhāṣā* school.

Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states that both the [attainment of] non-perception and the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*) are exclusively the maturations induced by the attainment of non-perception, which is likewise consistent with the *Vibhāṣā*.
The first master’s explanation is not that which was retained by the *Vibhāṣā* commentators. Question: Where do the sentient beings of the non-conceptual realm (*asaṃjñi-sattva*) reside?
Answer: They reside in the Vast Fruit (*Bṛhatphala*). That is to say, within the Vast Fruit Heaven there is a high and superior pavilion;

from the Vast Fruit devas looking down toward the seawater, it is a certain number of *yojanas*, and from the top of the pavilion looking up, it is likewise that same number of *yojanas*, just as in the case of the intermediate [space].

Just as the height from the abode of the Brahmā King to the birth of the Brahmā-purohita Heaven is a certain number of yojanas downward, so too is the distance from there upward to the top of the Brahmā King’s palace; one may analyze the text according to this specific meaning.

1. Above, first, the presentation of the essential nature of the retribution of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*). 2. Second, this dharma [is explained] downwardly; the five fruits are differentiated as being the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*). 3.
Third, regarding the difficulty concerning the fruit of maturation, below is presented the essential nature of the cause of the maturation of non-conception.

4. Fourth, as for where the sentient beings of non-conception dwell, below is the determination of their place of residence. 5. Fifth, as for whether they are always without conception, below is the determination of their existence from beginning to end.

Regarding the passage on "perception in the intermediate state of non-perception," the initial question asks whether those [beings] during the five hundred eons are perpetually without perception or if they do possess perception.

The answer is that for much of the time between birth and the moment before death, they possess perception. The Master Satyasiddhi says it may be like the duration of the *śastra-kalpa* (the age of weapons), during which they possess perception for a long time.
Nevertheless, they are called "beings of the Heaven of Non-Perception" because, from the time those sentient beings are born until shortly before their death...

During the intermediate five hundred great eons (*mahākalpa*), the perception of long duration does not arise; this is termed "the realm of non-perception" (*asaṃjñisattva*) from the perspective of its predominant state.
To cite a sūtra as proof: when those beings are about to die, because perception arises, they pass away from that place.
Then, when sentient beings are about to die, it is like waking from a long sleep, where perception arises once again. Sixth, following their death there, this explains their decline.

Regarding their place of rebirth: having passed away from that Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*), they will necessarily be born in the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) and not in any other of the three meditative realms (*dhyāna*).

This is because the power of the previously cultivated non-conceptual absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*)—which serves as the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*)—has been exhausted; and when the retribution is spent and life ends, they are unable to further cultivate the four dhyānas there.
Thus, they are not born in the four dhyānas, just as an arrow shot into the sky falls to the ground once its momentum is spent; they are born in the Desire Realm.
Because it is like the earth, one will necessarily be born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

If sentient beings are destined to be born in those five destinies of the desire realm, they must possess a determinate karma to be experienced in a subsequent life (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya-karman*) within whichever of the five destinies of the desire realm is applicable;

the meaning of being born into these five destinies is as explained previously. Accordingly, for those who are to be born in Uttarakuru, there must necessarily follow birth in the six heavens of the desire realm.
In the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 154, it is asked: "When one is born into the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*), how many faculties (*indriya*) cease?

The answer is: "Eight; namely, the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, life, mind, and equanimity faculties. Question: From what state does this [being] arise when born into the Heaven of Non-conception? Answer:

This refers to arising from the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) of the Heaven of Non-conception, which is born into the existence of the Heaven of Non-conception. Question: At that time, do faith and the other [faculties] also exist? Answer: Yes.

Question: When the faculties (*indriya*) are present and ceasing, why is this not mentioned? Answer: This passage should have been stated as follows: "Either eight or thirteen [faculties are involved];
among these, if there is a final indeterminate mind, there are eight; if it is wholesome, there are thirteen.

That it is not stated in this way should be understood to mean that the meaning here is incomplete (*sāvaśeṣa*). Some explain that herein [the author] relies solely upon both the state of cessation and the state of arising.

This [position] asserts that the five faculties, such as faith and so forth, exist only at the stage of cessation (*nirodha*) and not at the stage of arising (*utpāda*); therefore, it does not state to which realm the minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) that cease are bound.

[Question: To which realm are the faculties that manifest present? [Answer: Eight, as previously stated. [Question: To which realm are the minds and mental factors that manifest present? [Answer: They belong to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).

Since death and birth necessarily involve the arising of a mind belonging to the same level (*bhūmi*), when one passes away from the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*), [the faculties of the realm of form manifest].
How many faculties cease? Answer: Eight, as previously explained. What kind of fettered mind and mental factors cease? Answer: Those fettered to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).

How many faculties are present? Answer: Either eight, nine, or ten. Regarding the formless [faculties], there are eight: the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, life, mind, and equanimity faculties. With one sexual organ, there are nine, adding either the male or female faculty.
With both sexual organs, there are ten, adding both the male and female faculties. To what are these fettered? [They are fettered to the realm of form.]

Question: When the mind and mental factors manifest, how do they answer [to the state of being] bound to the desire realm? By this, it is proven that one who passes away from the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*) is necessarily reborn in the desire realm.
Question: Where exactly is one reborn? Answer: Some say one is reborn in hell; some say one is reborn in the evil destinies (*apāya*).

Those who speak thus say that one is necessarily reborn in the desire realm, though the specific location is not fixed: one may be reborn in the evil destinies, or among the gods, or as a human. Question: Why?

Therefore, one who passes away from the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*) is necessarily reborn in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). The answer is: it is due to the power of the volition of maturation (*vipākacitta*).
This is because, according to the specific power possessed by the volition of maturation, only such a maturation is caused to arise.

Other masters say that when the lifespan of non-conception is exhausted, the karma for lifespan in other realms does not increase; that is to say, while the karma for the lifespan of non-conception was previously increasing, now—
Having exhausted the life-span karma of other realms and because it was not previously increased, one passes away from there and is necessarily reborn in the desire realm. Question:

Since they have also previously given rise to the three lower types of intention, why do these not induce the fruit of that life-span? Answer: Although they have previously given rise to the three lower types of intention, these were not firmly adhered to;
therefore, they do not induce that life-span. It is only because of firm attachment to the fourth type of intention that it induces [the life-span].
Regarding that lifespan, some say that although he previously gave rise to the lower three intentions, these were not what he sought;
he sought only the fourth intention. Others say that although he previously gave rise to the lower three intentions, they were merely like paths traversed rather than the destination;
the fourth intention is the true destination, unlike those traversed paths. Therefore, it cites his lifespan as evidence.

It is taught that when one performs karma to be experienced in the next birth (*upapadyavedanīya*) in the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*), by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), one also performs karma to be experienced in a subsequent birth (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Just as when one performs karma to be experienced in the next birth in Uttarakuru, by the very nature of things, one also performs karma to be experienced in a subsequent birth among the devas of the desire realm.
Some say that the desire realm is the place to which all sentient beings who fall [from higher realms] return.

This refers to sentient beings who, through the power of karma and the power of cultivation, proceed to the form and formless realms; when that karma is exhausted, they fall back into the desire realm.
It is like the great earth, which is the place of retreat to which all flying birds return.

That is to say, when flying birds soar into the void by the power of their wings, once the strength of those wings is exhausted, they fall back to the earth. This applies to sentient beings as well, including those in the realm of non-perception.
Having remained for five *kalpas* in the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*), like one awakened from deep sleep, they are unable to grasp any further karmic maturation (*vipāka*).

They then follow toward the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), just as a person sleeping at the top of a tree, leaning against a branch, suddenly wakes up after a long time and—forgetting how to grasp it—falls to the ground.
It is the same with them; some say that those who seek non-conception regard the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) as the ultimate truth.

They maintain that the maturation of that [attainment] is *nirvāṇa*, and so forth, up to being born among those gods; this adherence follows them until later, when they are about to die from the realm of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*).
At that time, seeing the signs of their future rebirth, they think: "There is certainly no *nirvāṇa*. If it truly existed, I would have already realized it;
why then do these signs of rebirth appear before me now? Thus, by slandering *nirvāṇa* and the Noble Ones, [they fall into error].
Because of this path, one passes away from that state and is born within the miserable realms (durgati). The Venerable Ghosaka also stated:

"Because they slander nirvāṇa and the noble ones (ārya), upon the end of their life there, they will certainly be born in the miserable realms. Question: What is the difference between the attainment of non-conception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) and the state of non-conception (asaṃjñika)?
Answer: Their difference lies in their names; this is called the attainment of non-conception, and this is called the state of non-conception. Furthermore...
Next, the fruit of this non-ideation absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is the state of non-ideation (*asaṃjñika*).

Furthermore, the non-ideation absorption is a dharma of maturation (*vipāka-dharma*), while the state of non-ideation is the maturation itself. Furthermore, the non-ideation absorption is wholesome (*kuśala*), whereas the state of non-ideation is neutral (*avyākṛta*).

Furthermore, the non-ideation absorption is meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), whereas the state of non-ideation is birth (*upapatti*). Furthermore, the non-ideation absorption involves the effort of preparatory application (*prayoga-prayāsa*).

The state of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*) arises from mental attention (*manasikāra*), whereas the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) does not arise through the effort of preparatory application (*prayoga*).

Furthermore, the attainment of non-perception is accessible both here [in the desire realm] and there [in the form realm], and it can manifest in either place; however, the state of non-perception exists only there [in the form realm], and it manifests only there.

Moreover, the attainment of non-perception is acquired through preparatory application, whereas the state of non-perception is acquired by birth (*upapatti-lābhika*). This is what is called "non-perception."

Regarding the distinction between the states of perception and non-perception, when asked where the Heaven of Non-perception (asaṃjñisattva) is included, the masters from outside [of Kaśmīra] say that it is a separate ninth within the fourth sphere of mind (manāyatana).
The masters of Kaśmīra, however, state that it is included within the Heaven of Vast Fruit (bṛhatphala).
Nevertheless, because it is a superior state of tranquility, it is established as a distinct name, just as a forest retreat (araṇya) near a village is designated separately.
What is the physical size of those dwelling in that heaven? Answer: five hundred *yojanas*.
What is their lifespan? Answer: five hundred *kalpas*. In what posture do they abide? Some say they sit cross-legged like the Śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas;
others say they sit squatting with heels tucked in like the Brāhmaṇas. As for such explanations, it is according to the posture in which they previously entered this meditative absorption.

The Master [Vasubandhu] then asks: "If one remains in that state of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñika*) for five hundred eons by means of such deportment (*īryāpatha*), should it be said that there is perception when those non-conceptualizing beings are born, or is there no perception?
This is explained at length. Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed? Answer: It is intended to refute the doctrines of other schools and to clarify our own position.
That is to say, some assert that non-conceptualizing beings possess neither mental perception (*citta*) nor mental factors (*caitta*) at the time of birth or at the time of death.
To refute that intention and demonstrate that when those sentient beings are born and when they die, they both possess mental consciousness (*cittanimitta*) and are not without mental consciousness,
because there is death and birth; or alternatively, to refute the claim of some who say that non-percipient sentient beings possess mind at birth but lack mind at death,
[this is taught] to show that at the time of death they also possess mental consciousness and are not without mental consciousness, because there is the passing away of life.

Alternatively, there are those who say that although beings in the state of non-perception possess mind both at the time of birth and at the time of death, it is only a single moment [of mind] and not a lack of continuity.
To refute their view, it is shown that when they are born, a long period has already passed since their birth and the mind continues in succession until later they become non-perceptive;
then, emerging from the state of non-perception, they possess mind for a long duration before finally relinquishing their life. Therefore, it is stated thus.
Is there any instance where the mind exists for only two moments—namely, at the time of conception (*pratisaṃdhi*) and at the time of death? One should answer: no.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka says there is, namely, in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*).

Is there any instance where the mind at conception serves as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for the arising of the mind at death? One should answer: no. The Venerable Ghoṣaka says there is, namely, in the same case.
Is there any place in the Heaven of Non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva*) where the mind at rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi-citta*) arises for the death-mind (*cyuti-citta*) by way of the four conditions?

One should say no. The Venerable Ghoṣaka says there is; that is, he maintains that it is precisely in the Heaven of Non-perception. It is for the purpose of refuting such views that this treatise was composed. Regarding the nature of the non-perceptive state:
when one is born there, should one be said to have perception (*saṃjñin*) or to be without perception (*asaṃjñin*)? One should say that one has perception. This...
This immediately refutes the view that those born in the Heaven of Non-perception (asaṃjñisattva) are without mind at the time of birth, as the Blessed One said:
"When those sentient beings arise from perception, they pass away from that place. At the time of passing away from there, is it to be said that their perception ceases or does not cease?
The answer is: it should be said that it ceases. This, then, refutes the view that those in the Heaven of Non-perception are without mind at the time of death.
Question: In what state should it be said that their perception ceases? Answer: It should be said that it ceases while remaining in that very state.
This [response] refutes the view that non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*) do not possess even a single moment of mind at the time of death or birth.

Question: Regarding non-percipient beings, is the preceding mind more frequent or the subsequent mind? Answer: Some say the preceding mind is more frequent, not the subsequent, because... [the latter has not yet arisen].

When entering the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), because the force of the continuity of maturation (*vipāka-saṃtati*) is extremely powerful, one remains with a mind for a long time before entering that state;
having emerged from non-conception, because the force of the continuity of maturation has weakened, one possesses a mind for only a short time and then immediately passes away.
Some say that the subsequent mind is more [numerous] than the preceding minds, because at the time he had not yet entered the state of non-conception...
Because their minds are so intense and keen in their eager pursuit of non-conception (*asaṃjñā*), they enter the state of non-conception while still possessing a mind for only a short time;

yet, having emerged from non-conception, because they no longer have anything to pursue with eagerness, they remain with a mind for a long time before finally relinquishing their life. Regarding this explanation, it is not fixed:
sometimes the former period is long and the latter short, and sometimes the former is short and the latter long, as there are differences according to the specific inclinations of those individuals.

Regarding that perception (*saṃjñā*), should it be said to be wholesome (*kuśala*) or indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)? Answer: It is either wholesome or indeterminate. Regarding that perception, how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) increase in association with it?
Answer: [The number of] outflow-tainted objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). Regarding how many fetters (*saṃyojana*) bind it? Answer: Six.

As for "that perception," it refers to the perception of the cessation of perceptions (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha-saṃjñā*). That which is wholesome or indeterminate: the wholesome refers to innate wholesomeness (*upapatti-labdha-kuśala*); the indeterminate refers to the obscured-indeterminate (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).

Regarding the "indeterminate" (avyākṛta) or "unobscured-indeterminate" (anivṛtāvyākṛta) [defilements] that have the out-flowing (sāsrava) dharmas of the form realm as their object—namely, the latent tendencies (anuśaya) of the fourth mental consciousness that take out-flowing dharmas as their object—one asks:
Why do the latent tendencies that take the out-flow-free (anāsrava) dharmas as their object not increase in accordance with those perceptions? Answer:

Because they conceive of non-perception (asaṃjñi) as nirvāṇa and the Heaven of Non-Perception (asaṃjñisattva-deva) as the true path; thus, from being born there until passing away from there, they regard it solely as such.
This grasping again follows and turns toward the true path of cessation, not slandering it as non-existent;
therefore, at that time, the untainted object does not give rise to the six fetters of bondage—excluding anger, envy, and stinginess—with the remaining fetters continuing to operate. Question:

Is the emergence of the perception of non-perception abandoned by the five categories [of afflictions], or is it abandoned only through cultivation? If so, what is the fault? If it were abandoned by the five [categories], then regarding the ten gates...

How should one explain the following passage? "If one says that past dharmas arise as the equal-and-immediate condition for two minds, and if they are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), how then should this text be explained?

Furthermore, regarding the statement: "In that [past], the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) which have the contaminated (*sāsrava*) objects of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) as their objective support increase," some say this applies to all five types of abandonment.
How should the explanations given in the *Daśamukha-śāstra* (The Ten Gates) be reconciled? The answer is found in that text.
One should say that past dharmas serve as the equal-and-immediate condition for the arising of six types of minds—namely, five from the form realm and one from the formless realm.

What is the intention behind not making such a statement? It should be understood that the text speaks with reference to the mind emerging from the two mindless absorptions (*acittaka-samāpatti*), and does not speak of the mindless attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*). Why is this? Because the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) for the two mindless absorptions...
It arises through mental attention (*manasikāra*) and is without perception (*asaṃjñin*); it is not otherwise. Other masters say that it is abandoned solely by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

How should one interpret what is stated in this text? Answer: This text states that those perceptions (*saṃjñā*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are equally subject to the increase of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned by cultivation;

yet, why does it not make this specific assertion? One should know that within this context, it ought to be explained as follows: [the text implies that while they are indeed so, the specific phrasing serves to exclude other categories].

When those who possess such a state pass away, their minds pertain to all five categories; it is not merely that they speak of the mind of non-perception [as the one at death], because the mind at the moment of death is preceded by its own retinue.
Regarding this, the critique states: It should be understood that the former explanation is superior, as there is no other principle to exclude the other types of mind.
The following three stanzas distinguish the two meditative attainments without mind (*acittaka-samāpatti*).

Within this, the first stanza specifically explains the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the next one and a half stanzas specifically explain the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), and the final two lines provide a general differentiation between the two attainments.

Regarding the first section, there are five parts: (1) concluding the preceding discussion and posing a question regarding the names of the two attainments; (2) answering the question regarding the names of the two attainments; [and so forth].

A separate question asks: what are the characteristics of the initial non-ideational absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*)? Fourth, the verse is cited in response. Fifth, the text of the verse is explained.

Within this section, there are seven parts. First, the first line is explained as previously stated: there is a maturation (*vipāka*) phenomenon called "non-ideation" (*asaṃjñin*), which is capable of causing the cessation of mind and mental factors;
it is thus named "non-ideation. Furthermore, there is another distinct wholesome phenomenon that is neither form nor mind, which is capable of causing [the cessation] of future [states].

The cessation of mind and mental factors is called the essence of the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*). Next, its name is explained: because those who have attained it are "non-conceptualizing persons," it is called the "attainment of non-conception.
This name is derived from both the person and the essence; alternatively, because this meditative state can cause conception to cease, it is called the "attainment of non-conception.
This name is applied to the phenomenon based on its function and its essence. The word "thus" (*iti*) in the verse indicates that this attainment alone is capable of ceasing mind and mental factors.

Because the maturation (*vipāka*) of the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñi*) is the same, it is explained by analogy; however, such categories as wholesome (*kuśala*) and neutral (*avyākṛta*) dharmas are not the same. First interpretation: Regarding the intent of the latter [verse], one asks:

"In which stage does this meditative attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) exist? Answer: It is said that the latter attainment exists precisely in the fourth dhyāna, and not in the others.
Second interpretation: Regarding the verse's inquiry into liberation, one asks: "For what purpose is the meditative attainment of non-conception cultivated? Answer: It is said...

Seeking true liberation, they cling to the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), holding it to be true liberation; thus, in order to realize that true liberation, they cultivate the attainment of non-perception.

Regarding the four explanations in the verse: since the previously mentioned "retribution of non-perception" (*asaṃjñi-vedanīya-vipāka*) is of a neutral nature (*avyākṛta*) as it is a maturation (*vipāka*), this need not be stated further, as it is established by itself.
Now, the attainment of non-perception is exclusively wholesome (*kuśala*); therefore, it is capable of summoning [the state of] non-perception.

Question: Regarding the five aggregates of the gods of the Ābhāsvara Heaven, which are the maturation (*vipāka*) of karma, according to the five explanations, they are exclusively "to-be-experienced-in-the-next-birth" (*upapadya-vedanīya*).

Question: Since these are of a wholesome nature (*kuśala-dharmatva*), to what type of experience do they correspond? Answer: They correspond exclusively to being experienced in the next birth; they are not "to-be-experienced-in-this-life" (*dṛṣṭadharma-vedanīya*), "to-be-experienced-in-a-later-life" (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya*), or "indeterminate" (*aniyata-vedanīya*). Why is this so?

Because one who has attained this concentration may also enter the state of "right-nature-departure-from-arising" (*samyaktva-niyāma*), and once having entered it, there is absolutely no possibility of its arising again in the present life.

It is established that the designation "attainment of non-percipient beings" (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is spoken of in terms of its actual manifestation (*samudācāra*), and not in terms of its possession (*prāpti*).
Furthermore, it is accepted that this attainment is accessible to both those outside of this Dharma and to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), but not to noble ones (*ārya*).

Regarding the six types of explanations, it is also accepted that this attainment is obtained only by ordinary worldlings and not by noble ones, because noble ones regard the attainment of non-percipient beings as [they would view]... [the state of] hell.
Because one does not delight in entering a deep pit, the Noble One has no perverted mind regarding the phenomena of birth and death;

he knows that by practicing this concentration, one will certainly be reborn in the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*), where five hundred great eons will pass in vain, making it difficult to attain the Path or to emerge from it.
Furthermore, once rebirth there is completed, one will inevitably fall back and be born again in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*). Therefore, he regards this concentration as he would a deep pit.
Furthermore, one might cling to the retribution of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-vipāka*) as true liberation;

yet, regarding this state of non-conceptual absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), it is the perception of the Truth of the Path—that which leads to deliverance from birth and death—which causes one to cultivate this absorption.

This is because no noble being (*ārya*) clings to that which is tainted (*sāsrava*) and devoid of retribution as true liberation or *nirvāṇa*, nor do they cling to the tainted state of non-conceptual absorption as the true path of deliverance. Therefore, [this is not the case].

This concentration must certainly not be practiced by the seven classes of non-Buddhists or by any ordinary worldlings. If noble ones cultivate and attain this fourth mental absorption, they all obtain it;
for as with those who possess a mind, they likewise obtain the ability to go and come through beginningless birth and death.

As for the attainment of the mindless absorption (asaṃjñi-samāpatti), [the Buddha] did not answer, citing the general case to illustrate that others—ordinary worldlings—are even further removed from it than the noble ones.
When one attains the fourth dhyāna, one does not yet attain the state of non-conception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti), much less so for a noble one (ārya). Why is this?

Although that state of non-conception has been practiced throughout beginningless saṃsāra, because it is a state of mindlessness, it must be attained through the application of preparatory effort (*prayoga*).
Therefore, at the moment of its initial attainment, only one lifetime is acquired—namely, the present—as when one first attains a distinct [attainment].
Regarding the *vimukti-śīla* (liberation precepts) and so forth:

next, in the single verse that separately clarifies the characteristics of the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), there is first a question, followed by an answer given in verse, and finally an explanation within the body of that verse.
First, the initial phrase is explained as it can be understood from the text; second, [the phrase] "for the sake of dwelling in tranquility" refers to the prior state of non-conception (*asaṃjñin*).

1. This attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is preceded by the mental attention (*manasikāra*) of the perception of renunciation, seeking liberation through the fruit of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-phala*).
2. This attainment of cessation is preceded by the perception of cessation (*vyupaśama-saṃjñā*), seeking a dwelling in tranquility. 3. [Regarding the distinction:

The aforementioned attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) exists in the fourth dhyāna, whereas this attainment of cessation exists only at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). 4. [Regarding its nature: It is wholesome (*kuśala*); this is the same as the aforementioned attainments.

Its nature is exclusively wholesome and not indeterminate or defiled, because it takes a wholesome mind as its cause and motivation. Regarding the five explanations, the two types of feeling are indeterminate.

The aforementioned *asaṃjñi-samāpatti* (attainment of non-perception) is only conducive to feeling in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*), whereas this *nirodha-samāpatti* (attainment of cessation) is conducive to feeling in the next life, subsequent lives, or is indeterminate.

Question: What stage (*bhūmi*) and how many aggregates (*skandha*) are the retribution (*vipāka*) summoned by this attainment? Answer: It summons the retribution of the four aggregates of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). This is the sixth explanation.

The Noble One states that the attainment of non-ideation (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is attained only by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), whereas this attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is attained only by noble ones (*ārya*).

It is not possible for an ordinary being to produce it, because they fear its total annihilation; furthermore, it can only be produced through the power of the Noble Path (*ārya-mārga*), as one enters it with the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) of attaining *nirvāṇa* in this very life (*dṛṣṭadharma-nirvāṇa*).

The commentary explains: "One cultivates the attainment of non-ideation to cease the mind while possessing form, without fearing annihilation; one cultivates the attainment of cessation [to cease both mind and form]."

This meditative absorption (samāpatti) exists prior to the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñin*). Since form (*rūpa*) has already been extinguished previously, the mind is now extinguished as well; thus, both form and mind are absent.

With neither form nor mind present, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) has nothing upon which to rely. Ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) possess views, or have not yet severed the view of self (*ātman*); because they fear the annihilation of the self, they are unable to cultivate the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

Noble ones (*ārya*), however, have severed [wrong] views or do not fear the annihilation of the self, and therefore they cultivate the attainment of cessation. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states that this is not so.

Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who are able to give rise to the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) have not yet abandoned the obstacles to the attainment of cessation belonging to their own level;

therefore, they have not yet given rise to [the abandonment of] what is to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) regarding the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). Alternatively, they lack the capacity to ever give rise to it. It is not that ordinary beings can transcend what is to be abandoned by insight regarding the Peak of Existence.
Furthermore, as for the noble ones (*ārya*) who have attained the attainment of cessation, there is another explanation which states that by means of... [text fragment].

Because ordinary beings fear annihilation, while noble ones enter this state through their resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) in *nirvāṇa* in the present life, it is held that only noble ones attain it and not ordinary beings.
This [position] is unreasonable, because it is the same for the attainment of non-conceptual absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).

There is no difference between the two regarding the cessation of mind or the resolute conviction in *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, some here say that the fourth [attainment] consists of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
Because the coarse [states] still have a basis, one does not fear their cessation; yet that too is irrational.

One cultivates the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) for the sake of extinguishing the mind and with the thought of renunciation (*naiṣkramya-saṃjñā*) in order to seek liberation. To fear the extinction of the mind while cultivating the attainment of non-perception is not the correct principle.

Since one cultivates the attainment of non-perception with the thought of renunciation, one should likewise enter it through the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) that it is superior to *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, for them...

It is said that this is not the primary cause; the seven explanations [regarding] the attainment of this meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) through application (*prayoga*) are also as previously stated for the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñi*), which is not attained through the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya*).
Question: By what means is it attained? Answer: It is attained through application, and so forth, as can be understood.
The eighth explanation concerns the attainment [of cessation] upon becoming a Buddha. Question 1: Does the Blessed One also attain it through application? Answer 2: No. Question 3: How then?

Fourth, the verse states that at the time of attaining Buddhahood, one acquires [the fruits]; this means that when the Blessed Buddha attained the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), he acquired the state of a Buddha.

There is not a single dharma among these that is acquired through preparatory effort (*prayoga*). Question: Since the Blessed One had never previously arisen in the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), how could he, upon attaining the knowledge of exhaustion, become one liberated in both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*)?
Answer: Because he had already attained mastery over the arising of the attainment of cessation, just as before.

Regarding those that have already arisen, they are established as being attained through both [the path of seeing and the path of cultivation]. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "Does the Blessed One also attain it through preparatory effort (*prayoga*)?

No. Why? Because he attains it at the time of becoming a Buddha. It asks: "Is it not the case that even the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) is not called 'attained' at the time of becoming a Buddha?
How much more so the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), since all Bodhisattvas [attain] the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*)?"

Because the state of *samādhi* is called "attainment" (*prāpti*), and the moment the essence of that attainment arises is called "attaining," it should be said that at the time of attaining Buddhahood, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) manifests without the need for further application (*prayoga*).

This is because when one briefly gives rise to the desire [to manifest them], all perfections (*saṃpatti*) arise in accordance with that desire; it is not as if all the qualities present within the Buddha-body were newly attained at the moment of attaining Buddhahood.

How can it be said that the Tathāgata attains the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) at the moment he realizes the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), given that during his bodhisattva stage he was already eternally free from all defilements of affliction (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*) and thereby enabled the arising of the qualities within the Buddha-body?

For it is taught that all the qualities possessed by a Tathāgata are attained through freedom from defilement (*vairāgyalābhika*). That statement also contains an error; however, if one provides a general explanation according to the specific circumstances, it means that regarding—

To speak figuratively, it is like calling a distant sound "near," or because one will certainly attain Buddhahood at the time of the Vajropama-samādhi, it is also called "attaining Buddhahood without interval.
Furthermore, since one attains Buddhahood in the *kṣaṇika* (momentary) concentration, let us set this matter aside for now.

When the Blessed One had not yet arisen from his meditative absorption, how did he, upon attaining the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), achieve the supreme, perfect, and simultaneous liberation that is forever free from [defilements]?

Because of the definitive explanation and because of the non-accomplishment [of the state] through abandonment, one attains mastery over the arising and cessation of the meditative absorption (*nirodhasamāpatti*);
thus, like one who has already arisen [from it], one becomes "liberated in both ways" (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*). The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* master rebukes the author of the treatise, saying:

"Is it not the case that even at the moment of attaining Buddhahood, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) is not called 'attained,' let alone the meditative absorption of cessation? For all Bodhisattvas, while abiding in the Diamond-like Samādhi (*vajropamasamādhi*), manifest..."

Regarding the statement that "at the prior time, one is said to attain the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*)," this means that when the essence of the knowledge of exhaustion exists in the phase of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*), it is called the attainment of knowledge.
The *Miśraka-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* further states: "By the power of the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), one attains both conditioned and unconditioned fruits. Answer:

Regarding the attainment of the knowledge of exhaustion at the moment of becoming a Buddha, one should explain that the knowledge of exhaustion also manifests without depending on preparatory effort (*prayoga*); it arises momentarily through desire.
When joy manifests, all perfect virtues arise in accordance with that joy; therefore, the opponent below challenges the Master, asking:

"If the merits possessed within the Buddha’s body are attained at the moment of Buddhahood, how can you say that the attainment of the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is attained at the time of the Buddha’s knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*)?

This is because when Bodhisattvas abide in the Diamond-like Samādhi (*vajropamasamādhi*), through the power of the path of non-obstruction (*ānantaryamārga*), they are eternally free from all [defilements].
Because it is defiled by *upādāna*, the merits within the Buddha’s body arise while remaining in the state of the characteristic of birth (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*).

Thus, the *Samyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* states: "At the time of birth, there is liberation of mind. This is because that [text] asserts that all merits possessed by the Tathāgata are obtained through the departure from defilement (*vairāgya-prāpta*).
Consequently, what the author of that treatise says also contains an error. To provide a contextual interpretation for the sake of the author of that treatise, it is said:

Regarding the statement that one attains Buddhahood from a distance while in proximity to the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), or that one is called "attained to Buddhahood" because one necessarily becomes a Buddha at the time of the diamond-like concentration—let us set aside this matter for now.

When the Blessed One had not yet arisen from the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) but had attained the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), how did he become one liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*)?
[Answer: At the time he attained the knowledge of exhaustion, he became permanently detached from cessation.

Because it exhausts the obstacles to meditative absorption (*samāpatti-āvaraṇa*), it is called "attaining absorption. In reality, however, there is no such thing as "attainment" (*prāpti*). This is because when one attains the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), there is no "attainment" that exists prior to the dharma [of cessation] itself.
Furthermore, it is because one abandons the state of non-accomplishment (*aprāpti*). Question: The previous treatise states that "by attaining that dharma, one abandons its non-attainment.
Since the Buddha had not yet attained the attainment of cessation at the time of his *kṣayajñāna* (knowledge of exhaustion), how can it be said here that he "abandoned the absorption"?
Question: Must one necessarily achieve [this]? Answer: Master Xuanzang explains that there are two kinds of non-attainment (*asvatantrya*).

First, when one is a bodhisattva, there is the non-attainment of the arising of mastery; second, at the time of attaining Buddhahood, there is the non-attainment of the arising of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) mastery.
What is meant here by "attaining Buddhahood and abandoning non-attainment" refers to abandoning the non-attainment of the arising of meditative concentration mastery.

Because one has attained mastery over emerging from meditative absorption (*samāpatti-vyutthāna-vaśitā*) through having acquired its attainment (*prāpti*) since its accomplishment, one subsequently possesses the non-accomplishment (*aprāpti*) of that mastery.

When one later emerges from absorption, because there is an acquisition of the attainment of the absorption that was just emerged from, one abandons the non-accomplishment of mastery over emerging from absorption.

Furthermore, regarding other future absorptions that have not yet arisen, because there is no acquisition of their attainment, one abandons the non-accomplishment of mastery over emerging from those [future] absorptions.

Regarding the ninth explanation—that it is not among the preceding thirty-four moments of thought—among these, the Western masters (Pāścāttya) maintain that prior to his final birth, while still in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), the Bodhisattva first gave rise to this meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Why is this position of the Western masters not accepted here?
If one were to accept the position of the Western masters, it would accord with the reasoning of the Venerable Upagupta as stated in the *Lokasthānavibhāṣā* (formerly known as the *Upagupta-śāstra*).
The master Kūṭadanta composed a treatise titled the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (Treatise on the Foot of Reasoning), which states as follows:
"It should be said that the Tathāgata first enters the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and subsequently gives rise to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*).

The masters of Kaśmīra—formerly called Ji-bin, a corruption of the sound—state that it is not the case that he first enters the meditative attainment of cessation and only afterwards gives rise to the knowledge of exhaustion.
Why is this? It is because it is traditionally taught that a Bodhisattva attains enlightenment through thirty-four moments of thought (*cittakṣaṇa*).
In the *Abhisamaya*, there are sixteen moments, namely eight moments of receptivity (*kṣānti*) and eight moments of knowledge (*jñāna*).

When one is free from attachment to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), there are eighteen moments, namely nine paths of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) and nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). These eighteen, added to the previous sixteen, constitute the thirty-four. The first thirty...
Regarding the thirty-fourth section on the Noble Collection of the Threefold Practice, subsumed under the Jewel of the Buddha:

when all Bodhisattvas descend upon the Bodhi tree to subdue Māra, they have already attained freedom from craving in the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). Only then do they enter the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*);

it is no longer necessary for them to abandon the afflictions of the lower stages belonging to the Sphere of Nothingness through the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Within this interval, there is none.
Because it can accommodate dissimilar, non-percipient, and tainted states of mind, Bodhisattvas in the stage of training do not give rise to the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Regarding the "foreign masters" (*bahirdeśaka*): the country of Gandhāra lies to the west of Kaśmīra;
therefore, the "western śramaṇas" mentioned previously refers to those from outside Kaśmīra, which is why they are called "foreigners" here.

The various masters thus rebuked the Master of Kaśmīra: "If you maintain that after the mind of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), an intermediate mind of a different class—namely, the mind of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*)—arises and thereby one enters the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), what fault would there be? The Master of Kaśmīra replied:

"If that were so, there would be the fault of 'transgressing the mind' (*citta-vyutkrānti*). However, the Bodhisattvas do not transgress their own minds. This is the interpretation of the foreign masters (*bahirdeśaka*).
The Bodhisattva Ratna does not transgress his mind; yet it is not that he does not transgress the untainted noble path.
(1) The masters of Kaśmīr ask: If that is so, how is it that his mind does not transgress? (2) The foreign masters answer:

"As long as I have not attained the eternal exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*), I shall never loosen this [vow]," such as sitting cross-legged (*paryaṅka*) and so forth. (3–8) The Master of the Treatise critiques the former masters of Kaśmīr.
This is because it is taught as the tenet of our own school. Next, regarding the two lines below [the verse],
in the preceding section on the analysis of various categories, the initial summary of what preceded and the introduction of what follows—

due to the explanation of the definition of the cessation of extinction (*nirodhasamāpatti*) in relation to specific individuals— although there are many similarities and differences between the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), regarding that...

Within this, there is further discussion of similarities and differences; next, the verse text is cited, followed by the commentary on the verse. Within the explanatory text, there are eight sections:
first, the explanation of the phrase distinguishing the common characteristics of the two attainments (*samāpatti*). These two attainments both arise based upon the desire and form realms.

According to the Sthavira school, if one is in the form realm, one cannot cultivate the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*); since that [position] is now being cited and refuted, if there were otherwise...

If one were to concede that the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) arises based on the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*), it would contradict this passage from the *Kātyāyanīputra-śāstra*, which states:

"There may be sentient beings who possess the 'form-aggregate' (*rūpa-skandha*) yet do not possess the 'five aggregates of formations' (*pañca-saṃskāra-skandha*); these are sentient beings bound by the fetters of form.
