If translated according to its original phonetic transcription, it is rendered as "form-aggregate" (*xíng*, pronounced *háng*); if taken as "formations" (*saṃskāra*) as the primary sense, then for people of this land, it would mean "concomitant formations" (*hùgèng*).
Because the pronunciation is reversed, it is now read as *chán* (market stall). A *chán* refers to a market stall because it possesses its own shops and stalls; thus it is called a *chán*.
The three realms have forty abodes, which are like the shops and stalls of a market; therefore, they are called *chán*.

Sentient beings of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are called "sentient beings of the form-stall" (*rūpa-chán-sattva*). Alternatively, excluding those born in the Heaven of Non-ideation (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*), the remaining heavens of ideation are where they dwell.
A different type of mind and the untainted mind (anāsrava-citta) are called "dissimilar minds" (*visabhāga-citta*).

Because this person possesses both the aggregate of form and the aggregate of formations belonging to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), this existence consists of more than five aggregates. Second, if one enters the attainment of non-ideation (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*); third, if one enters the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*);

or fourth, if one is born in the heaven of non-ideation (*asaṃjñi-deva*) and has already attained entry into the retribution of non-ideation—these are said to be cases where there is form in this existence.
There are those that are not of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) among the five types of existence; this is based on the fundamental treatise of Kātyāyanīputra.

If one enters the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), it is known through realization that these two attainments both arise based upon the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm; this is called their "similar characteristic.

As for the "different characteristic," the following explains the second phrase, which contains distinct internal points. First, the Sarvāstivāda establishes its thesis: the attainment of non-conception [arises] in the desire and form realms.
Both realms can attain its initial arising because it has been attained previously since beginningless time;
however, the initial arising of the attainment of cessation occurs only among humans, as it has not been attained since beginningless time and arises through the power of the Buddha’s teaching.

Once it has first been cultivated and arisen among humans, it subsequently arises again after one has first regressed from it and been reborn in the form realm, relying upon a body in the form realm. Regarding this, the two masters of the Sautrāntika school ask:

Is there also falling back from the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)? One should say that there is. If one were not to fall back, it would contradict the *Udāyi-sūtra* (formerly known as the *Udāyin-sūtra*).
The Master of the Treatise (*śāstrakāra*) explains the meaning of this sūtra passage as follows:

The Buddha taught that for the gods of the "Mind-made" heaven (*manomayakāya*), the body is not formed by means of physical food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), but rather the body is mind-made solely through meditative concentration (*samādhi*). The Buddha taught this.
The attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*) in the realm of form exists only at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

One attains this cessation attainment only after having abandoned the Peak of Existence or the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). If one has attained this cessation attainment, there is necessarily no falling back from it.

How, then, could one remain in the Sphere of Nothingness or below? Regarding the four modes of existence (*catasra upapattayaḥ*) within the realms, the Bahuśrutīya school maintains that the fourth consciousness also [exists].

Regarding the attainment of the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), that school maintains: "Ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) who have attained the fourth dhyāna are still able to enter the mindless state;

however, noble ones (*ārya*) who have attained the fourth dhyāna do not enter the absorption of cessation. Based on the tenets of the Sthavira school, which hold that there is no falling back from the absorption of cessation, this does not contradict the Udāyin-sūtra;
thus, this position is also established. [However,] the Sarvāstivāda school refutes the existence of the absorption of cessation within the fourth dhyāna.

The definition of the "attainment of cessation" (nirodha-samāpatti) cannot be established [as you claim]. Why? Because it is stated in the *Sūtra on the Nine Successive Attainments* (*Navānupūrvavihāra-sūtra*).

Since the attainment of cessation is taught as the ninth only after the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*), and the eight attainments involving mind, we know that one enters the attainment of cessation only after the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
If the attainment of cessation were situated within the four dhyānas, it would follow from the fourth...
Since the dhyānas involve mental concentration that enters the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the attainment of cessation ought to be the fifth [member].

The six *Sthavira* schools rebuke the Sarvāstivādins, saying: "If this were necessarily the case, and if the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihāra*) were established based on the order of their arising, how could there be the definition of 'leaping' (*vyutkrāntaka*)?
For example, when one leaps from the first dhyāna to the second and enters the third dhyāna, [how would the sequence hold]? Regarding the third dhyāna...
It should be the second [attainment] that transcends from the third dhyāna into the sphere of infinite space; the sphere of infinite space should be the third. Answer:
The establishment of the nine successive concentrations (*anupūrvavihāra-samāpatti*) is based on the sequential order; thus, there is no definition of "transcending" [the stages].
The Sarvāstivāda commentary explains that while this concentration is described according to the sequence followed by a beginner, once mastery is attained, one may transcend [the stages] at will.
Proceeding further.
Although there have been seven textual passages above, they are combined to form the second explanation of the second phrase. Below this begins the third section, the "Analysis by Various Gates.
First, the fundamental tenet is presented, stating: "These two concentrations have many meanings; first, there are differences in their stages (*bhūmi*). Fourth.

Because their minds belong to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), non-Buddhists consider only suffering and pleasure to constitute the suffering of birth and death. Suffering exists in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), while pleasure exists in the third dhyāna;

thus, non-Buddhists do not establish the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) as being within the cycle of existence. Since the fourth dhyāna transcends the stages of both suffering and pleasure, they believe that one thereby emerges from birth and death.

However, because the perception of ideation (*saṃjñā*) still persists, they have not attained *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, they cultivate the attainment of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) to realize the *nirvāṇa* of non-ideation (*asaṃjñi-nirvāṇa*).

Because it is a state of absorption, the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) exists in the fourth dhyāna, while the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) exists at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:

"The aforementioned attainment of non-conception exists in the peripheral region of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), whereas this attainment of cessation exists in the peripheral region of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), because the body born there in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is drawn forth by the most supreme karma; therefore, it is so named."
It is called "the Peak of Existence" (*bhavāgra*) because it is either the summit or the limit of existence, just as the very top of a tree is called its "peak.

Why is it that this meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) exists only in this stage and not in the lower stages? It is because one can attain this sublime liberation only by turning away from all states of mind and severing even the final state of mind.
This liberation is established based on two conditions: first, [the turning away from all mental activity]; second, [the severance of the final state of mind].
First, because it is weary of and turns away from all minds; second, because the mind at its limit is temporarily severed.
If this meditative absorption existed in the lower stages, it would not be "weary of and turning away from all kinds of minds," because one has not yet become weary of the minds of the higher stages.

Nor could it be called "the severance of the mind at its limit," because the minds of the higher stages have not yet been severed. It should, therefore, be called "weary of and turning away from only a few."

1. Because they are distinguished by various mental states, they should also be called "intermediate" (*madhyāntika*); 2. because there is a difference in the two preparatory applications (*prayoga*), as the mental orientations (*manasikāra*) of renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*) and cessation (*vyupaśama*) precede them;
3. because there is a difference in the continuity of the three [marks], since the bodies arising in the continuities of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*) differ; 4.

because there is a difference in maturation (*vipāka*), since the maturation of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) takes the maturation of the mindless state (*asaṃjñi-vipāka*) as its fruit; 5. because there is a mental orientation regarding the experience of feeling (*vedanīya*).
Because it accords with two types of feeling—those that are definitely produced and those that are indefinite—the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:

"The aforementioned state of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) accords with feeling to be produced in the next life as well as with indefinite feeling; this differs from the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.

The *Kośa* previously stated that the former, the state of non-conception, accords only with feeling to be produced in the next life, whereas this state of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) accords with feeling to be produced in the next life, in subsequent lives, and with indefinite feeling. In the present text, it says it accords with the definite...

Regarding the phrase "because it gives rise to two types of feeling produced by meditative concentration" (*samāpatti-ja*): the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is conducive to the feeling produced by concentration, while the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is conducive to both the indefinite [feeling] and the two types of feeling produced by concentration—namely, those arising at birth and those arising subsequently.
Sixth, regarding its initial arising: it occurs within the two realms and among humans, because it first arises there.

That is to say, the attainment of non-conception can first arise in both the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "Some say it arises only in the lower three [realms]."

The mental faculty (*manāyatana*) enters the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), but it does not exist in the fourth dhyāna, lest the cause and its fruit be too closely proximate. Some say it also exists in the fourth dhyāna;

however, the mental faculty enters the attainment of non-conception [only] excluding those born in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*), because they have already been born there and are experiencing that fruit.

Regarding the initial arising of the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), it occurs only among humans; for it is only among humans that there are those who explain, those who interpret, and those who possess powerful faculties.
By the power of preparatory application (*prayoga*), one first attains it while among humans; subsequently, having first undergone retrogression, one is born into the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

It is only after taking rebirth in the body of the form realm that one again cultivates and gives rise to it. One cannot enter the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), because there is no physical basis (*āśraya*) for it.

The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) necessarily proceeds in dependence upon both matter and mind; if one were to enter the attainment of cessation in the formless realm, both matter and mind would be entirely absent.
The life-faculty must be severed; since the aggregates abide in mutual dependence upon one another, there is no sentient being who possesses only a single aggregate.
Furthermore, because the mind and mental factors are inseparable, there is likewise no sentient being who possesses only three aggregates.
Although there have been six sections above designated as the third [part], "The Analysis of Various Sections," from here on begins the fourth [part], "Explaining the Names of the Two Samādhis.

Within this text, it first asks: since the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of these two samādhis consists in the cessation of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), for what reason are they specifically called the "Non-ideation Samādhi" and the "Cessation Samādhi"?
Answer: Because during the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for these two samādhis, one feels only aversion toward and opposition to these [mental states].
Therefore, as for the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), it is understood that [the knowledge of] feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth is merely a designation. The commentary explains:

Prior to the attainment of the non-conceptual absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), non-Buddhists (*bāhya*) think that birth and death do not exceed [the realm of] suffering and pleasure; since the fourth dhyāna has already transcended suffering and pleasure, they believe they can emerge from birth and death.

However, because the perception of mental phenomena (*saṃjñā*) still exists, they have not realized *nirvāṇa*. This is because the non-Buddhists do not understand the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) and the other [subtle states].
Because it consists of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*), during the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) one provisionally cultivates the perception of aversion;

and at the time when that perception ceases, the remaining minds and mental factors—comprising the ten wholesome factors, the ten [neutral] factors, and the twenty-one factors associated with the mind-king (*citta-rāja*)—all cease simultaneously.

Thus, twenty-one non-material mental factors are attained, replacing the twenty-one [factors of the previous state]. In this location, there exists the essence of the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), which proceeds from its preparatory application.

Because it is designated by the name "practice of aversion" (*udvega-prayoga*), it is called the "attainment of non-perception" (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the "attainment of the cessation of sensation and perception" (*saṃjñā-vedita-nirodha-samāpatti*).

At the time of the preparatory application (*prayoga*), one cultivates the various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) through sensation and cultivates the formless attainments (*ārūpya*) through perception; because these two categories involve exhaustion within a single realm, during the preparatory application there is merely aversion toward sensation and perception.
When these perceptions cease, twenty-one factors (*dharma*) are simultaneously extinguished, whereby twenty-one non-material [factors] are attained.

The mental factors substitute for the twenty-one states of mind and mental concomitants; it is named "the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling" (*nirodha-samāpatti*) based on its preparatory application (*prayoga*) of aversion and reversal.

Just as with the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), which is named after its preparatory application—desiring simply to know the mind—and yet when the fundamental state is achieved, one also knows the mental concomitants such as feeling, so too it is with these two attainments. (Section Five: Explanation)

Regarding the method by which the mind arises when emerging from the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*): the initial question in the text asks, "Since the mind has been interrupted for a long duration during these two attainments, how can it arise again from the subsequent mind?
Next, the answer provided by various masters explains that the Vaibhāṣika school maintains the existence of the past;
thus, they assert that the preceding mind of the attainment serves as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for the subsequent mind of the attainment.
Regarding the mind that arises immediately after the state of meditative absorption, the Sautrāntikas who maintain the existence of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) say:
"Just as when one is born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), form has been severed for a long time—whether for twenty thousand eons or even eighty thousand—how can form arise again later?
When that form arises, it must necessarily arise from the seeds of form within the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), and not from past form. The same applies to emerging from meditative absorption.

The mind should likewise arise from within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), because within the body possessing the five sense faculties there are newly produced seeds that give rise to the mind emerging from concentration;
it does not arise from a past mind prior to the concentration. Therefore, the former masters of the Sautrāntika school all maintain that the sprouts of two dharmas constitute the seeds.
These two dharmas refer to the mental sovereign (*citta-rāja*) and the body possessing the five sense faculties. As for the third, it is Vasumitra.

In the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (the *Śāstraviniścaya*), translated as *Shiyou lun* (Treatise of Vasumitra), it is stated: "If one maintains that the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is like the two preceding schools [Vaibhāṣika and Sautrāntika] and holds that there is no mind or mental factors therein, this fault follows.
I maintain that the attainment of cessation exists because of a subtle mind, and because the mind upon emerging from meditative absorption arises from it;

thus, there is no error of 'arising without a cause'. 4. Guṇamati’s Refutation of Vasumitra’s Position. Guṇamati, translated as *Miaoyin* (Wondrous Sound), states that this [attainment of cessation] exists.

What has been stated is unreasonable. Why is this so? If, within this meditative absorption, there were the three factors—the sense faculties, objects, and consciousness—in combination, then contact (sparśa) would necessarily arise as a condition, and feeling (vedanā) and perception (saṃjñā) would necessarily follow;

since these are established by scripture and can be understood accordingly, the dharmas such as feeling and perception would also not cease within this absorption. How, then, could it be called the "absorption of the cessation of feeling and perception"?

From this point on, the refutation of the opponent's defense is set forth: If that were so, the Venerable Vasumitra would argue that just as the Sūtra says "conditioned by feeling arises craving," an Arhat possesses only feelings but does not give rise to craving;

contact (*sparśa*) should likewise be the case. However, it is not the case that all contact serves as a condition for feeling and so forth, because in the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), contact does not produce feeling.
Therefore, this analogy is invalid, as there is a distinction [between the cases]. The Sūtra itself provides a qualification, stating: [text continues]
If ordinary persons and those in training experience craving conditioned by the various feelings born of contact with ignorance,

there is no instance where such contact and the resulting feeling are distinguished from one another; for this reason, the Vaibhāṣika masters maintain that all mental states cease within the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

The preceding section, consisting solely of the two passages of question and answer, constitutes the fifth part, which explains the method for generating the mind within the two meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*).

From here on, the sixth part explains the meaning of the names; in this section, first the question is posed: "According to the Vaibhāṣika masters, if there is no mind at all, how can it be called 'meditative absorption' (*samādhi*)?
Next, the Vaibhāṣika masters reply: "This *samādhi* is translated as 'equilibrium' (*samatā-gamana*); because there is no mind, it is called 'mindless absorption' (*acittaka-samāpatti*)."
By the power [of this concentration], the four great elements are made equal;

at the time of entering meditative absorption, there are no ailments such as wind, phlegm, or heat, nor can other conditions damage the four great elements of the person who has entered absorption. Therefore, it is called "equilibrium.
Taking equilibrium as the cause and the equality of the four great elements as the result, it is named after its result and thus called "equilibrium. This refers to the state of mindless equilibrium.

It is called "attainment" (*samāpatti*) because one reaches it through the power of the mind, or because one reaches it in a state of equilibrium; thus it is called "meditative absorption" (*samādhi*).

This second explanation states that because the power of the mind prior to absorption has departed from sinking (*laya*) and agitation (*auddhatya*), one reaches this state of non-mental activity (*acittaka*);

therefore, it is named after its causal function. Whether it is "reaching in equilibrium" or "equilibrium upon reaching," this is the definition of absorption. Seventh, the analysis of the designation of absorption.
In this passage, the initial question asks whether these two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) are substantially existent (*dravyasat*) or nominally existent (*prajñaptisat*).
Subsequently, the Sarvāstivāda responds that they must be said to be substantially existent, because they are able to obstruct and prevent future minds from arising.

From here on, the masters of the Sautrāntika school refute the Sarvāstivāda and set forth their own tenets. There are Sautrāntikas who say that the reasoning proving the existence of time cannot be correct;
for by the power of concentration (*samādhi*), there is a preceding mind whose power is able to obstruct [subsequent states].

Therefore, it is said that the mind preceding the concentration and the minds that are to arise within the remaining state of concentration are contradictory in three ways regarding their arising. Because this preceding mind arises, the others are inferred accordingly.
In other meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), the mind should arise [only] temporarily; within the five faculties (*indriya*) of that absorption, there is also the seed of aversion toward the mind.
Furthermore, the capacity to prevent the manifestation of the active mind upon its seeds is metaphorically designated as "absorption.

Within the five faculties of that absorption, because the seed of aversion toward the mind opposes the manifestation of the active mind, it is called the "basis of the opposing mind" (*virodha-citta-āśraya*).

This meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is established as a designation for the state in which the preceding mind can induce the five faculties within the concentration, causing them to continue in opposition to the mental factors that depend upon them;
thus, it is merely the non-arising of the active mind upon the seeds of the mind regarding the five faculties. It has no separate substantial entity.
This is a provisional designation for the state of non-arising; there is no entry before the absorption and no emergence after it, as it exists neither before nor after.

Since all states are non-existent—there being nothing before, nothing after, and only a momentary existence in the middle—it is fundamentally non-existent, now existent, and having existed, returns to non-existence;

therefore, it is conventionally described as being subsumed under the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Alternatively, within the five sense-faculties, there is the seed of the mind of aversion which functions to prevent the mind from arising;
this is the seed of the mind of aversion within the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), which was induced by the preceding state of mind and exists within such a meditative absorption.

The function of preventing the mind from arising arises from the mental state preceding meditative concentration; because it follows from that preceding state, it is designated by the name "concentration" and is conventionally established as such.
The above explains the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*); one should know that the same applies to the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*). That is to say, by means of...
The mind immediately preceding meditative absorption arises in contradiction to the minds that ought to arise within the remaining states of absorption;
because this pre-absorption mind arises through aversion, it causes the minds that would otherwise arise in those remaining absorptions to temporarily cease.

Within the five sense faculties, when the seeds of the mind are prevented from arising by means of aversion, that state of temporary non-arising is conventionally designated as the "attainment of non-perception" (asaṃjñi-samāpatti).
There is no separate substantial entity; as stated in other passages, it is as previously explained regarding the attainment of cessation.
The Master [Vasubandhu] critiques this Sautrāntika teacher’s position, stating that it is not well-said because it contradicts our own school’s tenets.
In the latter half of this verse, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is analyzed. First, the preceding inquiry is summarized; next, the verse is cited as the response;

finally, the text of the verse is explained. Within this explanation, there are two parts: first, the explanation of the first line, wherein the essence of the life-faculty is identified as longevity (*āyus*), followed by a citation from the root text to provide scriptural evidence.
Second, the explanation of the second line: first, a question is raised regarding what further phenomenon is designated as "longevity," which is then addressed.
The verse answers: There is a distinct dharma capable of sustaining warmth and consciousness, which is called *āyus* (life-force).

Below, a scriptural passage is cited as proof: when one abandons this body, it becomes rigid; dying while lying face up is called "rigid" (*jiāng*), and dying while lying face down is called "prostrate" (*pù*).

According to what is taught in the sūtra, there exists a distinct dharma capable of sustaining warmth and consciousness, causing warmth and consciousness to continue abiding in succession; for this reason, it is called *āyus*.
1. First, the Sarvāstivāda establishes its thesis. 2. The Sautrāntika asks: "If that is so, by what dharma is this life-force (*jīvita*) sustained? 3. The Sarvāstivāda answers:
"It is precisely warmth (*uṣman*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) that, in turn, sustain this life-force. 4. The Sautrāntika objects:
"If these three dharmas mutually sustain one another and continue in succession, which dharma would be the first to perish? By virtue of which would one [of them] perish first?"
Therefore, when the other two [heat and consciousness] cease in accordance with it, if one of them were not to cease first, these two would have to be eternal and never subject to passing away.
(5) The Sarvāstivāda explanation being thus, the Sautrāntika raises this objection:

"If that is so, for what reason do you not admit that karma alone can sustain heat and consciousness, rather than requiring a separate life-faculty (*jīvita*)? (7) The Sarvāstivāda rebuts this on logical grounds: "That is not correct."
It should be so; however, it must not be the case that all consciousnesses remain in a state of constant maturation (*vipāka*) from beginning to end.

While it might be possible for heat (*uṣman*) to be constantly in a state of maturation, the Sautrāntikas counter-argue: "If that were so, one should say that karma sustains heat, and heat in turn sustains consciousness.

Why is this life-force (*jīvita*) necessary? The Sarvāstivādins counter-objection: "In that case, within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there would be nothing capable of sustaining [consciousness]."

Because that [state] lacks warmth (*uṣman*), the ten Sautrāntika masters explain the difficulty by saying that it must be stated that there is no consciousness in the form realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) capable of maintaining the karma-condition.
The Sarvāstivādins pursue this objection: "How can one follow mere sentiment and repeatedly formulate counter-arguments and so forth?

Furthermore, they point back to the previous explanation to refute what was said before. What is meant by the "previous explanation"? It says: "Let it not be the case that all consciousnesses, from beginning to end, are [identical]."

12. The Sarvāstivādins maintain that *vipāka* (maturation) is their fundamental tenet; therefore, one must certainly admit that there exists a distinct dharma capable of sustaining warmth and consciousness, which is called "life-force" (*jīvita*).
13. The Sautrāntikas state their own position: they do not say here that life-force does not exist at all;
rather, they say that the essence of life-force is not a separate, substantial entity. 14. The Sarvāstivādins ask: If that is so, what dharma is designated as "life-force"?

Regarding the essence [of life], the Sautrāntikas respond as follows: It is the force of momentum (*sthiti-śakti*) that sustains the provisional *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous class of beings) projected by karma within the three realms;
this momentum, which exists upon the provisional *nikāya-sabhāga*, is called the essence of life.

This is further illustrated by the momentum for the growth of stalks, branches, and leaves projected by a grain seed until its maturation, or like the momentum for flight projected by a released arrow. (16. The Sautrāntika Exposition on Causes)
Using the momentum of an arrow’s flight as an analogy for the duration of its continued existence, this leads from one discussion to another:

the exposition of the Vaiśeṣika heretics’ adherence to the self (*ātman*) as possessing nine qualities—namely, (1) cognition, (2) pleasure, (3) pain, (4) desire, (5) aversion, (6) effort, (7) merit (*dharma*), (8) demerit (*adharma*), and (9) motion (*saṃskāra*), also called "velocity. If this motion resides within [the self], it causes wisdom...
It is known that either the object of cognition moves with extreme rapidity, or the physical body moves with extreme rapidity.

In the case of an external arrow, it moves rapidly because it is conjoined with this quality of rapid motion. To explain this, the Vaiśeṣikas claim that there exists a quality called "rapidity" (*java*), which is a specific sub-type of the category of "attainment" (*prāpti*).
This quality arises upon external objects such as arrows, and by means of it, [the arrow] moves rapidly.
Because of the power of rapid motion, the arrow continues to travel without ceasing until it falls to the ground.

(17) The Master of the Treatise refutes this by arguing that since the essence of rapid motion is a single entity, and because non-material phenomena (*arūpadharma*) are unimpeded, the arrow would not exhibit the distinct states of initial speed, intermediate slowing, and final arrival at the ground across these three temporal stages; for if the velocity were one, such distinctions could not exist.
Furthermore, because the nature of rapid motion is unitary, it would follow that the arrow could never fall,
for its nature of velocity is unimpeded. If you, a Vaiśeṣika, claim that the arrow falls to the ground due to being obstructed by wind,
then it should either fall immediately upon being discharged, or else it should never fall at all, since the obstructing wind is present both before and after.

Because there is no distinct [entity] that reaches [the object], the eighteen [factors] are combined; however, according to our own school’s fundamental tenet, there exists a distinct real entity capable of sustaining warmth and consciousness, which is designated as the essence of life-force (*āyus*).
This is a well-stated position. Although the preceding text combines these eighteen [points] to form the second explanation of the second line of the verse.

Above, the first verse-line was explained in its initial interpretation, and the second verse-line was explained in two parts; these two texts together constitute the first explanation, which concludes the commentary on the root verses.

From here below is the second section, consisting of questions and answers, which analyzes death through a fourfold classification (*catuṣkoṭi*) contrasting death due to the exhaustion of lifespan with death due to the exhaustion of merit.
Within this text, the initial question asks: "Is it because the lifespan is exhausted that one dies, or is there another cause? He then cites the original source himself.

The *Śāstravibhāṣā* (Treatise on Exposition) answers by stating that the four propositions—such as "death due to the exhaustion of the life-span" and so forth—can be understood from the *Prajñaptiśāstra*. The Master of the Treatise (*Śāstrakāra*) says:

Furthermore, one must also say "due to the relinquishing of the formations of life (*āyusaṃskāra*)," just as when a Buddha or an Arhat enters *nirvāṇa* by relinquishing the life-span, it is not because of harm from self or others;

thus, it is subsumed under the fourth category. The Master of the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise on Correct Reasoning) says: It should not be stated again that it is "due to the relinquishing of the formations of life," for such is the meaning [of the *Śāstravibhāṣā*].

Since the first [case] is already subsumed within the initial phrase, the commentary explains: "Because one has transformed the karma of longevity into the karma of wealth, it is known that death in the first phrase occurs because the karma of longevity is exhausted.
The Master further analyzes the third phrase, stating: "Within the state where longevity is exhausted, the exhaustion of merit (puṇya) no longer possesses the capacity to prevent death;
therefore, when both are exhausted simultaneously, death occurs, and this is designated as 'exhaustion of both.'"
In the *Commentary on the Truth of Death*, there are two interpretations. According to the first person: if one dies when the karma of longevity is exhausted, that is natural;
since there is no principle of "double death," even when the karma of merit is exhausted, there must still be something capable of causing death. If this were so, there should not be a third case.

Furthermore, if one speaks only of death through the exhaustion of the karma of merit, what further capacity would there be for death when the karma of longevity is exhausted? One should likewise pose this question in reverse.
Since the definition of death as the exhaustion of both types of karma is identical, one could claim that death occurs when both are exhausted, thereby establishing it as a third category.

[The opponent] offers two interpretations of the preceding two cases to argue against this, asserting that since both types of karma are exhausted simultaneously, they cannot be categorized separately; therefore, a third case should not be established.

The passage beginning "At the time of simultaneous exhaustion" is the response: if the exhaustion of the two types of karma were partial, they would be established as the first two cases. However, since they are exhausted together, they constitute a single instance.

Because both [karmas] are exhausted simultaneously and not separately, they cannot be distinguished as one being capable and the other incapable; therefore, the exhaustion of these two together constitutes the third phrase.
Master Jiang interpreted the text directly: among the exhaustion of the two types of karma, the life-karma (*āyus-karman*) is the predominant direct cause that induces longevity;

thus, when the state of the exhaustion of life-karma is mentioned, it specifically refers to the point where life is exhausted and death can no longer occur. As for the exhaustion of merit (*puṇya-karman*)...

Death has no further functional capacity; however, at the moment when [life-force and death] coexist, there is the designation of "death. Because it is designated as "death" at the time of their simultaneous exhaustion, death is so called.
Third, following this, we shall interpret the original treatise (*śāstra*). First, citing the question and answer from the *Jñānaprasthāna*:

"Should this life-force be said to proceed in accordance with the continuity [of the aggregates], or does it remain for the duration of a single arising? This was the question and answer from the original *Piṭaka*.

Regarding the meaning of the phrase "what is the significance?", the two masters of the treatises explain it as follows: If the supporting body is subject to harm, then the life-force (*āyus*) is also harmed accordingly;
this is the second point, the sense that the life-force proceeds in accordance with the continuity [of the body]. If the supporting body is not subject to harm, it remains just as it arose;

this is called the second [type], which arises once and then persists. Third, the Vaibhāṣika masters provide an explanation, stating: "The first clarifies the presence of obstacles, while the latter..."
This is to clarify that there is no obstruction [to death], because there are those who die prematurely according to this definitive meaning. The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (vol. 151) states:
"Should it be said that lifespan proceeds in accordance with the continuity [of rebirth], or that it remains for the duration of a single birth? In response, it is said:

"Sentient beings of the desire realm who do not abide in the meditative attainments of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), as well as sentient beings of the form and formless realms, should be said to remain for the duration of a single birth. Question: [What is the meaning of this?]
Why was this treatise composed? It is answered: in order to refute the positions of other schools and to clarify our own doctrine.
Specifically, the Dārṣṭāntikas do not admit the existence of untimely death. Why is this so? As the Sūtra says: "When one's lifespan has ended, it cannot be saved.
From this, they know that there is no such thing as untimely death. To refute their view and to demonstrate that untimely death does exist, this treatise was composed.
Question: What is meant by "continuing in accordance with the succession" (*anubandha*)? Some explain that calamities and misfortunes (*vyasana*) are called "succession.

This refers to when one is born in the desire realm and does not abide in the meditative attainments of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), such that life-force continues to proceed in accordance with calamities and misfortunes. Why is this so?

Because if one’s life-force is not constant in its activity, not constant in its progression, not produced through volitional effort, not proceeding through volitional effort, and does not function at the proper time [of death], [then it is said to continue in accordance with the succession].
If one engages in improper conduct, does not practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*), consumes unwholesome food, is not reborn as a non-reborn being,
fails to preserve what is matured, cannot discern between what is appropriate and inappropriate, does not take medicine, does not follow the physician’s instructions,

does not avoid calamities, and indulges in various harmful amusements— for these reasons, one’s lifespan will be cut short prematurely. If, however, one always acts [properly] regarding the lifespan...

Constantly turning the process of receiving and acting as one receives, when practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and consuming appropriate food, one causes that which is raw to ripen and discards that which is already ripe.
Being able to examine with discernment what is suitable and what is unsuitable, one takes medicine according to the physician’s instructions;
by means of such practices, one avoids calamities and stays far from harmful amusements, so that one's life does not end prematurely. Some say this is called the "form-body" (*rūpakāya*).

It is called "continuity" (saṃtati) because when one is born in the desire realm and does not abide in the attainment of non-perception or the attainment of cessation, the life-force (āyus) continues to evolve in accordance with the physical body (rūpakāya).
Why is this? If the body is harmonious and peaceful, the life-force will not meet with premature death; if the body is damaged or impaired, the life-force will meet with an untimely end.
Some say that the continuity refers to another's body, meaning that when one is born in the desire realm and does not abide in the attainment of non-perception or... [the text here is truncated].
The full attainment of lifespan proceeds in accordance with the continuity of another's body. Why is this?
If there is another body that does not cause harm to one’s own life-span, then the lifespan will not be cut short; if it does cause harm, then the lifespan will be prematurely ended.
Question: What is meant by "abiding once arisen"? Answer: Having arisen in accordance with its causes, it continues in succession and does not follow the calamities [of destruction].

That which functions in opposition to one's own body or the bodies of others through harm refers to those born in the desire realm who currently abide in the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), as well as those born in the higher realms; in all these cases, their life-span does not function in accordance with external conditions. Question:

In the desire realm, there are also those who have not entered the two types of mental equipoise (*samādhi*) whose life-span likewise does not function in accordance with conditions. Why is this not mentioned? Answer: It should indeed be mentioned, but it is not mentioned because... [text ends]

One should know that this meaning is incomplete; some say that what is stated here as "determined" refers to the fact that when one abides in the two mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*), the life-force (*jīvita-saṃskāra*) is determined and does not follow conditions, whereas in other states it may follow conditions—and for this reason, [the others] are not mentioned.

Others say that although there are indeed other instances in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) where [life-force] does not follow conditions, they specifically mention these two attainments here in order to demonstrate their sovereign power (*prabhāva*).
As stated in the Sūtras, there are four types of acquired personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) obtained by sentient beings:
first, an acquired personal existence that can be harmed by oneself but not by another; second, an acquired personal existence that can be harmed by another but not by oneself;
third, an acquired personal existence that can be harmed both by oneself and by another; fourth, an acquired personal existence [that cannot be harmed by either].
The physical body is neither harmed by oneself nor harmed by others. How is it that the physical bodies obtained by sentient beings can be harmed by themselves but not by others?
It refers to the gods of the Desire Realm who forget their play (*krīḍā-pramoṣaka-deva*);

at times they delight in their own bodies and become attached to their play, but when the time passes and they become exhausted, they lose mindfulness and die. Furthermore, there are also the gods of the Desire Realm who are obsessed with mental pleasures (*manomaya-kāya-deva*) who, at times...
Furthermore, there is another class of beings—whether nāgas, garuḍas, pretas, humans, or others—who can cause their own death but cannot be killed by others.
How is it that the physical bodies obtained by sentient beings can be destroyed by others but not by themselves? It refers to those dwelling within an eggshell or a womb.
Among those in the hells, there are some whose faculties are not yet fully developed and whose faculties are not yet matured;
furthermore, there is another class—whether they be nāgas, garuḍas, pretas, humans, or others—who can be harmed by others but cannot harm themselves.

What is the nature of the physical body acquired by sentient beings that can be harmed both by themselves and by others? It refers to the bodies of various birds and beasts, or nāgas, or garuḍas, or pretas.

Furthermore, regarding those persons or others who might be subject to self-harm or harm by another: what is that acquired personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) which is neither subject to self-harm nor harm by another?

It refers to all those born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), all those dwelling in the hells, those abiding in the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), or the meditative concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*); as well as those in the stages of followers by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and followers by dharma (*dharmānusārin*), and the final [moments] of their practice.
There are bodhisattvas together with their mothers while dwelling in the womb; wheel-turning kings and the mothers of wheel-turning kings while dwelling in the womb;

royal seers, messengers of the Buddha, and those prophesied by the Buddha—such as the son of the householder Dhaññakaṭiya, the son of the householder Uttara, the son of the householder Daḷidda, and the weaver Suppiya at the time of his bondage.
The Blessed One stated that there are four types of acquired selfhood (*ātma-bhāva*): those prophesied by the Buddha Kakutsunda;
those *pudgalas* dwelling in their final existence who have not yet accomplished what was to be done; the inhabitants of Uttarakuru at the beginning of the eon;
and those such as the Naga kings Ailavila, Sushena, and Śyāma, as well as others of this class who do not kill—these are called the four types of acquired selfhood.
When it was said that there are sentient beings whose acquired selfhood is neither harmed by themselves nor harmed by others,
the Venerable Śāriputra rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence,
and addressed the Buddha, saying: "Blessed One, what are those sentient beings whose acquired selfhood is neither harmed by themselves nor harmed by others?"
The Buddha addressed Śāriputra: "Sentient beings in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) neither harm themselves nor are harmed by others.
[Question: Sentient beings of the lower realms also neither harm themselves nor are harmed by others; why then does he speak only of those in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
[Answer: By mentioning the latter, the former is revealed. Because he first established this principle, he spoke thus. There are places where the Blessed One mentions the latter to reveal the former.
In passages such as the one cited above, it should be understood that there are cases where the beginning is mentioned to indicate the end, as when it is said:

"Possessing the first *dhyāna*, which is separated from life, is unwholesome, possesses vitarka and vicāra, and consists of joy and bliss born of seclusion, he dwells having fully attained it. Similarly, there are cases where the end is mentioned to indicate the beginning;

where the conclusion is mentioned to indicate the start; where the emergence is mentioned to indicate the entry; and where the culmination is mentioned to indicate the preparatory stage (*prayoga*). It should be known that this principle applies in all such instances. Some teachers have stated: [text omitted].

The lower stages are indeterminate; therefore, it is not said [that they are fixed]. This is because the self-bodies obtained by sentient beings in the lower stages may be free from calamities and misfortunes, as in the case of those abiding in the attainment of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), or they may be subject to calamities and misfortunes, as in the case of the gods who forget through play (*krīḍā-pramoṣaka*) and others.

In the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), there are no calamities or misfortunes; for this reason, it is specifically stated that there are four [types of] intentions. Furthermore, these also exist within the three formless realms (*ārūpya*).

Just as in the desire realm there are matters such as the "forgetting of death" through play, which do not exist at all in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, it is therefore said specifically that [these exist there].
It is taught that sentient beings of the lower stages all possess the predominant power of afflictions;

if these manifest, they immediately meet with untimely death. Since this affliction does not exist in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, for this reason the World-Honored One [said only...]
Regarding that, the Venerable Dharmatrāta says: "In this context, 'harmed by oneself' refers to being harmed by the counteractive path (*pratipakṣa-mārga*) of its own level;
'harmed by another' refers to being harmed by the counteractive path of a higher level.

According to the first interpretation, its own substance is 'harmed by itself,' meaning it is harmed by the noble path (*ārya-mārga*) of its own level; it is 'harmed by another,' meaning [it is harmed] by the second [level]."
Regarding the mundane path at the limit of the sphere of mind (*manas-kṛtsna*) up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), its own nature is harmed by itself;

that is, it is harmed by the noble path of its own level. It is harmed by others—that is, by the mundane path at the limit of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
The nature of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is not harmed by itself, because there is no noble path on its own level; nor is it harmed by others, as it is unsurpassed.
Because it is a mundane path at the limit of the stages (*bhūmi*), it is said to be attained specifically in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*);
it is not merely that which is destroyed. The commentary explains: *Dhāki* is *Dhāki-rāja*, which is translated as "The One Who Obtains" (*Cāyaka*).
This person obtained [alms] by begging on the banks of the *Dhāki* River and thus received the name *Dhāki-rāja*. Regarding the river deity, if one speaks in the masculine gender, one says *Dhāki*.

If, within the woman's voice, she utters the name *Dhyānodbhavā-mātṛ*, which in this language means "Mother Born from Fire," because she was obtained from within fire, she is thus called "Born from Fire" (*Huochu*).
The old transcription *Shutiqie* is a corruption of the sound. Being born from within fire is as described in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
*Uttara* means "Superior" (*Shangsheng*), and *Dharmī* means "Possessing Dharma" (*Youfa*); she is a deity.

*Dāmiḷa* here means "taking" (*grahaṇa*); because this son of a householder obtained [it] by begging from the deity Dharmadatta, he is called the householder’s son Dāmiḷa, which here means "the householder’s son who takes from Dharmadatta.
*Yaśas* here means "fame" (*yaśas*), and *Jīvaka* here means "livelihood" (*jīvana*); thus, he is called the youth Jīvaka, meaning "the youth of livelihood."

As stated above, these five types of persons are all those prophesied by the Buddha to be free from the two harms; thus, according to the first three phrases of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, as explained in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, they are not harmed by either [of the two].
These are: (1) those in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm; (2) all sentient beings of the form and formless realms; (3) denizens of hell (*naraka*);

(4) inhabitants of the northern continent (*uttarakuru*); (5) those on the path of vision (*darśanamārga*); (6) those in the meditative concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*); and (7) those in the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

1. The eight classes of *dhyāna-samāpatti*; 2. the *asaṃjñi-samāpatti*; 3. the nine *rāja-ṛṣis*, meaning that in the past there were wheel-turning kings (*cakravartin*) who renounced their royal positions, practiced the path, and attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) as divine seers;
4. those sent by the Buddha; 5. those predicted by the Buddha—of these five persons: first, Dāmilī, translated here as "Possessor of the Dharma";
second, the son of the elder Udraka, translated here as "Superior One"; third, the son of the elder Śyāmaka... [and so forth].
*Kīla* here means "old" (or "worn out"); *Yaśas*, the son of an elder, means "fame"; *Kumāra* means "youth";
and *Jīvaka* means "one who sustains life," referring to the youth Jīvaka. These five individuals together constitute the eleventh prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) spoken by the Buddha;
thus, there is no contradiction with the account of the twelve [disciples] and the ten final-birth Bodhisattvas.
3. When a Bodhisattva’s mother carries the Bodhisattva in her womb; 4. When a Cakravartin’s mother carries a Cakravartin in her womb.

5. The Master of the Treatise (Śāstrin) raises an objection: If all sentient beings in the form and formless realms are equally incapable of being harmed, why does the Sūtra state only that those in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception are not harmed by themselves or others? 6. The Vaibhāṣika masters provide the explanation.

According to tradition, it is said that the remaining three formless attainments (*ārūpya*)—the essential natures acquired through the four types of mental application (*manasikāra*)—can be harmed by the noble path (*āryamārga*) of their own level, as well as by the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of higher levels;
however, for the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), neither of these two harms exists.
Therefore, it is said to be "neither [of those] harmed. The Master of the Treatise refutes this, stating that the Peak of Existence is also harmed by the noble path of other levels.
Those who are subject to being harmed by others should be called "harmable by others. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:

"Alternatively, excluding those in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), sentient beings born among the other formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*) are also like the gods of the 'Forgetfulness through Play' (*krīḍā-pramoṣaka*) and the 'Anger of Mind' (*manah-pradoṣa*) in the desire realm;
they can only harm themselves. This is because they too, by the power of giving rise to such types of afflictions (*kleśa*), pass away from that state, or [pass away] otherwise."

Regarding the self-substance obtained within the various mental states of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), it can be harmed by the noble path (*āryamārga*) of its own level, and it can also be harmed by the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of higher levels.
However, in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), neither of these two types of harm exists; therefore, it is said to be "neither harmed by both.
Furthermore, since that which is not the Peak of Existence is also harmed by the noble path of other levels, it should be called "harmed by others" (*parahata*) according to this explanation.

In principle, this should also apply; however, the present statement refers to the intention of others, because the term "other" (*para*) is also applied to higher stages (*ūrdhva-bhūmi*) in reference to superior matters.
Alternatively, it is only when one lacks mastery over something that it is termed "other"; since the higher stages possess mastery over the lower ones, they are not called "other.
Nevertheless, one should raise this objection here: if the Buddha’s intention was to speak of self and other...
If the severance of all afflictions on the stages of the path (*bhūmi*) were called "harming oneself and others," then one should not say that death occurs because of oneself or others;

for death exists due to the non-severance of afflictions, not because of their severance. Furthermore, this does not accord with the logic of the previous explanation, which states that those in the hells (*naraka*) and so forth are not harmed by themselves or others.
Yet, that Venerable One, regarding what was previously stated concerning "self... [the text here appears to be truncated].
Having already understood the meaning of "harming others," in order to clarify further points, he spoke again as follows: "Venerable sir, do those sentient beings pass away from that place?
Or do they not pass away? Śāriputra, if those sentient beings have not yet severed their afflictions (*kleśa*), they do indeed pass away;
if they have severed their afflictions, they attain parinirvāṇa right there. For what reason, Venerable sir..."
However, based on the final [interpretation] regarding the selfhood thus attained, one asks the Blessed One again:

"Because they lack both self-harm and harm to others, there is an act of *codanā* (reproving) directed toward them, which serves as a superior means for causing them to abandon their karma. Furthermore, it is asked:

"Those sentient beings... and so forth, at length. Regarding this, the Master of the Treatise (*śāstrakāra*) explains in his commentary that it should be stated thus: the latter is mentioned to reveal the former; therefore, it is said.
As for the notion that [the two types of killing] are not mutually exclusive, in reality, all sentient beings of the form and formless realms are not subject to both types of harm;

this is included in the lower category. The examples for this can be understood. Eighth, the opponent challenges the Master: "In the *Brahmapārisadya Sūtra*, the meaning of the analogy is expressed by the word 'like' (*yathā*);
it may be stated thus: by citing one, the remaining phenomena are revealed; by citing one, those of the same class are revealed. Therefore, this refutation [is invalid]."
The *Śrāmaṇyaphala-sūtra* and the *Upāli-sūtra* both state that the term "like" (*iva*) occurs wherever it is found; therefore, it cannot be compared to the *Brahmakāyika-sūtra*.

Regarding this, the Master [Vasubandhu] counters the opponent’s objection: if the term "like" were to occur only when the meaning is explicitly illustrative—that is, when it functions as a simile—then the term "like" should not occur in other sūtras where it is not used as a simile.
Yet, the term "like" does occur in other sūtras, such as those concerning the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), which state that they exist.
"Beings with form who differ in body and differ in perception, such as humans and a portion of the gods—this is the first station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).

This refers only to the actual entities themselves; thus, it says "such as humans and a portion of the gods," making it clear that this is not merely a metaphorical comparison. Furthermore, the word "such as" (*yathā*) is used here in the same sense.
From this point on, one and a half verses distinguish four types of conceptualization (*saṃjñā*). Within this, the first two lines distinguish the four great conceptualizations;

the next two lines distinguish the mutual relationship between the large and small aspects, showing that they do not lead to an infinite regress; and finally, there are two more lines distinguishing the producer, the produced, and that which is produced, demonstrating that these do not exist apart from various causes and conditions.
Regarding the first two lines, the text contains three parts: first, the conclusion of the preceding section and the introduction of the present topic.
Next, following the citation of the verse, the commentary on the text of the verse is presented. This section has three parts. First, the initial line is explained:
because these four kinds constitute the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), if a phenomenon possesses these four characteristics, it must be conditioned.

These four characteristics are able to function as the defining marks upon all phenomena; because they exist upon them, they are called "conditioned. [This does not apply] to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
Because it is the opposite of this and lacks the four characteristics, it is an unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharma.
(2) From here below, the second phrase is explained, which is easy to understand. (3) Regarding the reconciliation of the scriptural text: first, the scripture is cited and questioned:
"Does not the scripture state that there are three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned? Should not four be mentioned in this sutra? Yet only three are stated, and not [four]."

What is this? In response, there are three explanations. The first explanation is that "not being stated" refers to the characteristic of duration (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*). However, the Sūtra speaks of "duration" as a mental designation (*manojalpa*); it is not the characteristic of duration itself.

It is an alternative name for the characteristic of difference (*anyathātva-lakṣaṇa*). Because it is a different name for duration, it is called "duration-difference" (*sthity-anyathātva*). One should understand it in this way:

just as arising (*jāti*) is established separately [from birth], and cessation (*nirodha*) is given the separate name "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*), so too "difference" has the separate name "duration-difference. If...
The three characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) cause the conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) to flow through the three periods of time;
this Sūtra describes them as the three characteristics of the conditioned in order to inspire a sense of weary detachment and fear in sentient beings.

That is to say, those future formations are driven by the power of the characteristic of arising in the future, causing them to flow from the future into the present; the characteristic of arising possesses the functional power to produce existence in the future.
Regarding the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena (*dharma*), they do not yet possess their functional activity (*kāritra*) while the characterized phenomena remain in the future;

it is only when they reach the present and abide in the state of the characteristic's activity that they possess the collective functions such as receiving the fruit, which is termed the "arising-activity" (*utpāda-kāritra*) of the phenomena. Because this is called "arising," it is when the characterized phenomenon first reaches the present that the power and function of the characteristic of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*) cause the characterized phenomenon to abide.
It is only when the characterized phenomenon reaches the state of the characteristic of change (*anyathātva-lakṣaṇa*) that it is then designated [as having ceased].

When the characteristic of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*) functions, it causes the characterized phenomenon (*lakṣya-dharma*) to undergo decay and change through the power of the subsequent characteristic of change (*anyathātva-lakṣaṇa*).

However, as long as the power of the characterized phenomenon has not yet decayed, this does not occur; rather, it is only when the power of the characterized phenomenon reaches the point of the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) that the phenomenon undergoes decay and change by means of that power.

Following the function of the characteristic of change, the function of the characteristic of cessation arises and is able to cause the powers of all phenomena to be destroyed; yet, [this applies only] to the power of the characterized phenomenon.
The function has not yet ceased because the present dharmas possess the power of their activity; it is only when the characterized dharma reaches the past that it is called "ceased.
This is because its power and activity have ceased, though the substance of the dharma itself does not cease—this is the tenet of the Sarvāstivāda school.

In this passage, only the power and activity of the three characteristics are mentioned; specifically, regarding those future conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), there is the future characteristic of arising.

When that which is shifted by the power of the characteristic of change (*anyathātva-lakṣaṇa*) arises from the future and exerts its function, it is called "entering the present," because it is designated as "present" due to having functional utility.
Furthermore, when it is driven and compelled by the power of the characteristic of cessation (*anirodha-lakṣaṇa*) to flow from the present into the past,
the power of its function is made to decay by the power of the characteristic of change, and its [substantial] basis is made to cease by the power of the characteristic of cessation.

The power and function [of the characteristic of cessation] destroy [the dharma], following which its analogy is introduced. One should know that it is likewise with respect to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) among the three characteristics; by citing the dharma to correspond with the analogy, it can be understood.
Because [the characteristic of duration] abides within those conditioned phenomena, upholding and establishing them so as not to cause weariness, the Sūtra does not mention it.

A second explanation states: furthermore, because unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) possess their own intrinsic nature and characteristic, and because the characteristic of duration would be confused with them, the Sūtra does not mention it.

The third explanation states: "Some say that this 'abiding' (sthiti) is spoken of together with 'change' (anyathātva) and collectively termed 'the characteristic of abiding-and-change' (sthity-anyathātva-lakṣaṇa).
Therefore, the Sūtra says: 'There are three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned. Question: For what purpose does the Sūtra thus speak of them collectively? Answer:

The intention of the Sūtra is that 'abiding' is that which sentient beings are attached to; therefore, it is taught [collectively] in order to cause them to cultivate weariness toward and relinquish it."
He instructed them to speak thus: "Just as in the world, when a woman of dark complexion and a woman of auspicious appearance are together, they are never separated;
so too, in order to repel Kṛṣṇa (the Black One), one must also abandon Śrī (Auspiciousness). The old translation, which calls him "the deity of merit and darkness" (Guǒdé Hē'àn Tiān), is incorrect.
Furthermore, during the time of the Buddha in the West, he had two daughters: one was named Tianhe (Sky-Black), and wherever she went, there were inevitably calamities and misfortunes.
The second is named Śrī; wherever she goes, there is benefit. These two women always follow one another and do not part.
Fools in the West, out of greedy attachment to Śrī, surely bring about their own ruin through Kṛṣṇa.
Wise people, wishing to repel Kṛṣṇa, likewise abandon Śrī. Therefore, this is cited here as a metaphor.
Therefore, it is certain that there are four conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*).
Next, the following two lines distinguish between the great and small characteristics. Furthermore, at the beginning of the text, a question is raised:

"Since these four great characteristics—arising (*jāti*) and so forth—are themselves conditioned, they must themselves have another set of four characteristics, such as arising. Second, [the author] points out the fault [of this position]: "If there were further characteristics for these characteristics..."

Furthermore, if there were further characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), because those characteristics would themselves have further characteristics such as "arising of arising" (*jāti-jāti*). To this, the third response should state:

"The primary characteristics (*mahā-lakṣaṇa*) have further non-characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*), yet this is not an infinite regress. Why is this so? The following verse provides a dual explanation for these four primary characteristics:
because the primary characteristics possess "arising of arising" and so forth, they are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); for they [apply] to eight [conditioned phenomena] and one [phenomenon].
There is a functional capacity, yet it is not infinite. This is the fifth [section], explaining the actual text of the verse. Within this, there are two parts:

first, the explanation of the verse’s main body, which describes the Sarvāstivāda school; second, the Sautrāntika masters’ statement, which follows with a debate against the Sautrāntikas. Within the preceding section, there are again two parts: first, the explanation of the initial phrase.
This refers to what was previously stated regarding the four primary characteristics—arising, arising-of-arising, and so forth—which means the four secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇas).

Regarding the four great characteristics (*mahā-lakṣaṇa*), such as arising (*jāti*), there are three names: first, they are called "primary characteristics" (*mūla-lakṣaṇa*) because they correspond to the secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*); second, they are called "great characteristics" (*mahā-lakṣaṇa*) because they correspond to the minor characteristics;
third, they are called simply "arising, abiding, and ceasing" because they correspond to the arising-of-arising (*jāti-jāti*) and so forth.

Regarding the minor characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*), there are also three names: first, they are called "secondary characteristics" (*anulakṣaṇa*) because they follow the primary characteristics; second, they are called "minor characteristics" (*kṣudra-lakṣaṇa*) because they are smaller in form than the great characteristics; third, they are called [the third name]... Because "arising of arising" and so forth cause the great arising to arise, the first term "arising" refers to the function (*kāritra*), while the second term "arising" refers to the great arising.

Because their essential nature is characterized by arising and ceasing, there is birth at the initial stage and destruction at the final stage.

Thus, we know that from the very beginning, they are constantly perishing moment by moment; it is only due to differences in the speed of this falling away that temporal distinctions such as "slow" or "fast" occur.

The meaning that objects such as diamonds are transformations of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and arise and perish moment by moment is established because, when various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) such as diamonds arise in a continuous succession of similar moments, there is no significant difference when comparing the preceding and succeeding states.

Thus, although the essential natures (*dharmatā*) of the preceding and succeeding moments are distinct, they appear as a similar succession. To this, the opponent raises an objection: "If there were a difference between those preceding and succeeding moments..."
Therefore, it is called "change during duration" (*sthity-anyathātva*). This refers to: (1) the final momentary sound; (2) the very first moment;

and (3) the possession of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) at the time of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. Because there is only the preceding thought-moment and no subsequent succession, each succeeding moment arises from each preceding one;
this is called "duration. Furthermore, because there is a distinction between these preceding and succeeding moments, it is called "change during duration. All [of these] are not... [omitted].

Because [the characteristic of] arising has already been established, there should be no two characteristics of duration (*sthiti*) and change (*anyathātva*); thus, the four characteristics you have proposed would not be universally applicable to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
Next, in response to this, it is clarified that within the characteristic of change, one does not intend to designate duration as a characteristic of the conditioned.

What is the meaning of this? It means that duration is distinguished by way of change; therefore, it is said to be the "change of duration. Even in the case of sounds and so forth, where there is no further dharma in a subsequent moment, [the characteristic of change still applies].

Because it continues from the preceding thought-moment, sound, and so forth, it may also be termed "abiding. If there is abiding in a continuous succession of prior and posterior [moments], there must necessarily be a difference between the dharmas of the prior and posterior moments.
By establishing characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) in this way, there is no fault of non-pervasiveness.
However, regarding these moments, what the Blessed One briefly indicated as the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) in the sūtras is that conditioned phenomena exist in the future.
The non-existence of the present that now exists is called "arising" (*jāti*); once the present has existed and it returns to non-existence, this is called "cessation" (*nirodha*).

Furthermore, the continuous succession of preceding and succeeding moments is called "abiding" (*sthiti*). Because the essential nature (*dharmatā*) of the phenomenon differs when these preceding and succeeding moments are compared, this is called "alteration" (*anyathātva*).

In this context, what [reason] is there for asserting that arising and the others are distinct entities from the essential nature of the phenomenon? The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* asks: "Is it not the case that your own school previously had something to fear?"
Since it is not admitted that there are distinct entities such as "arising" and so forth, one now loses the memory of what one has established for oneself:
how can a conditioned phenomenon, which in a single moment has the four dharmas— arising, abiding, change, and cessation— as its nature, lack even a single dharma existing at once,
thereby falling into the error of being simultaneously arising, abiding, decaying, and perishing?
Sixth, the Sarvāstivādins criticize the Sautrāntikas for asserting that apart from the dharmas of matter and mind, there are no separate entities such as "birth" (*jāti*);
how can the characterized dharma itself be established as the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*)?
Seventh, the Sautrāntikas rely on four analogies and criticize the Sarvāstivādins regarding how [the latter] explain the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, such as the [lines on the] hands.

The characteristic is not different from the Great Being (mahāsattva) and so forth; the principle regarding these conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*) should likewise be understood as such.

Because they are not distinct from the characterized (*lakṣya*), and because they function as the relationship between the agent and the object (*kāraka-karma*) to a certain degree, it is difficult to comprehend the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), such as form (*rūpa*).

This remains so until one understands that "arising" is the prior non-existence becoming present, "ceasing" is the prior existence becoming subsequent non-existence, and "abiding" is the continuity of the preceding and succeeding moments both before and after.

Since the subsequent continuity and its specific differences have not yet been understood as having conditioned (saṃskṛta) essence, it is not the case that the nature of matter (*rūpa*) and so forth is itself the characteristic of being conditioned;
nor is there a real entity (*dravya*) called "arising" (*jāti*) existing apart from that nature of matter and so forth.
The Sarvāstivādins then rebuke the Sautrāntikas: "If arising and so forth were entities separate from the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of conditioned matter and so forth..."
Furthermore, what is illogical?
The nine Sautrāntikas raise a counter-objection: at the single moment of a phenomenon such as form (*rūpa*), it would simultaneously undergo arising, abiding, decay, and destruction;
for in your own school, you maintain that the four characteristics exist only as designations external to the substance of the phenomenon itself.
The objection raised by Daśabala is not valid, because although the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) exist simultaneously in substance, their functions (*kāritra*) occur at different times.

That is to say: the function of the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) resides in the future; when it has not yet reached the stage of arising, it is called "about to arise" (*utpitsu*); when the function of the characteristic of arising is active, it is called "presently arising" (*utpadyamāna*).

The characteristics of abiding (*sthiti*) and so forth have already passed, which is why it is called "already arisen" (*jāta*). Therefore, that which is "already arisen" in the present does not arise again. Thus, [the objection] is not [valid].

At the time of arising in the future, there is no activity of abiding, change, or cessation; rather, it is only when phenomena have already arisen and are currently present that the three functions of abiding and so forth occur.
This is because the functions of the other three characteristics do not exist at the time of the characteristic of arising in the future.

Although the essence of the four characteristics exists only as a conceptual construct (*prajñapti*), there is no contradiction because their functions occur sequentially. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "To maintain that there is no distinct arising apart from conditioned phenomena..."
Such faults as these cannot be remedied, because the principle of a distinction in functional capacity for a single dharma at a single time is untenable.
However, if one accepts that arising and so forth exist separately [from the entity], there is no such fault, because their functions differ just as their entities are distinct.

11. The Master of the Treatise, representing the Sautrāntika school, exhorts the Sarvāstivāda: You should first investigate whether the substantial entity (*dravya*) of future phenomena exists or does not exist;
only then can it be established whether that factor has utility or lack of utility at that stage.

Even if you grant that arising (*jāti*) possesses activity (*kāritra*) in the future, since that activity is present, how could it be considered "future"? You must explain how the activity of arising can exist in the future.
Regarding the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*), when it exists in the present, its activity has already ceased and is no longer functional;
