how then can it be established as being present? One should explain the characteristic of the present. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, fascicle fourteen, states: "Even if one were to grant that arising possesses activity in the future, how could it be established as future?
One should explain the characteristic of the future: when the dharma exists in the present, its activity of arising has already ceased; how [can it be future]?"

It should be stated that what is established as present possesses the characteristics of the present; this is not contradicted, because there is no [dharma] that is not present yet exerts an activity (*kāritra*).

How could it be that the future [dharma] which is about to arise does not have the capacity to produce all dharmas? This very capacity is its activity (*kāritra*), for it is through the movement [of arising] that one speaks of it.
O "Beloved of the Gods" (*devānāmpriya*), you do not understand that this is a functional capacity (*śakti*) and not merely an activity (*kāritra*); this point is not a matter for debate.
If a phenomenon can act as a cause to project and draw forth its own effect, it is termed "activity" (*kāritra*);

if it can act as a condition to assist and support a dissimilar category, this is called "efficacy" (*sāmarthya*). As previously established, all present phenomena are capable of acting as causes to project and draw forth their own effects;
however, not all present phenomena are capable of acting as conditions to assist and support dissimilar categories. For example, visual consciousness exists in the dark.
As for its functional capacity (*śakti*), that which is impaired by darkness cannot serve as a contributing condition to assist the arising of visual consciousness;

however, its activity (*kāritra*) is not damaged by darkness and is certainly capable of acting as a cause to project the future eye. Thus, there is a distinction between its activity and its functional capacity.
Furthermore, regarding the production of similar and continuous effects, the power of attraction and projection is termed "determinate" or "indeterminate."

"Activity" (*kāritra*) is also termed "efficacy" (*sāmarthya*). If, regarding the production of a fruit within a different continuum, something can merely act as a condition by supporting its arising, this is not "activity" but rather "efficacy.

Do you not argue that the three factors—the patience of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), light, and the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*)—are all capable of exercising activity in the future? O Beloved of Heaven, you now cling to the literal text!
Regarding the meaning of "delusion," our school explains that this is merely a conventional designation for "activity" (*kāritra*) based on the capacity of the proximate conditions;
for it is logically established that among the various conditions for the arising of phenomena, these constitute the most proximate conditions.

Thus, by excluding the function of the cause of duration (*sthiti-hetu*), the name "activity" is conventionally applied to this state, and such designations as "duration" and so forth should be understood accordingly. This applies to the stage of the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*).

Light also possesses superior functional power during its state of activity, and thus this name is provisionally established; however, in reality, it is not the case that only when drawing forth a fruit is it called "activity.

Having above refuted the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*), the following section refutes the remaining three characteristics; therefore, it is said that the three functions of abiding (*sthiti*) and so forth are all simultaneously manifest.
Within a single moment of the essence of a single dharma, there exist the characteristics of abiding (*sthiti*), decay (*jarā*), and destruction (*anityatā*).
At the time when the characteristic of abiding causes this dharma to abide, at that very same time, the characteristics of decay and destruction cause it to age and perish.

At that moment, is this dharma designated as "abiding," or is it designated as "decaying" or "perishing"? The Sarvāstivādins maintain that the functions of these three characteristics—abiding and the others—are distinct.
At that time, his statement would contradict the principle of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhanga*).

If the Sarvāstivādins say, "We define a single dharma as a 'moment' when the functions of all four characteristics have reached their completion while it exists between two points in time," we shall first refute the characteristic of duration (*sthiti*) individually. You must now explain:

for what reason does the characteristic of duration differ from cessation, such that when both characteristics are present at the same time, the characteristic of duration is able to cause the dharma to endure first?

You should now explain: for what reason do the two characteristics of duration (*sthiti*) and change-and-destruction (*anyathātva-vināśa*) coexist with arising (*utpāda*), yet duration alone is able to first abide in the dharma that is its locus, without itself changing or perishing?

If you say that the power of duration is strong and thus functions first, why does it later become weak such that it, along with the essential nature of the dharma itself, encounters decay and destruction through change and destruction? If you say that the characteristic of duration...
That which has already performed its function should not perform it again, just as that which has already been born cannot be born again; this may be granted.

Now, the function of "arising" (*jāti*) consists in drawing forth the factors to be produced and causing them to enter the present; once they have entered, they cannot be drawn forth again. It would follow that "abiding" (*sthiti*) should not be like this.
For the function of "abiding" consists in establishing the factors to be abided in so that they do not decay or perish; once they have abided, could they be made to abide again?

Because it abides in perpetual security, the function of the characteristic of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*) ought to arise; one cannot logically claim that it arises only once and then ceases to function again.
Furthermore, does the function of "false abiding" not cause things to exist momentarily before returning to non-existence, rather than arising constantly?

If you argue that "alteration" (*anyathātva*) and "destruction" (*vināśa*) act as obstructions, then since the power of alteration and destruction is stronger [than that of abiding], why do they not exercise their function earlier, while the function of abiding occurs later?

Above, the characteristic of duration (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*) was refuted individually; below, the two characteristics of change (*anyathātva*) and cessation (*vināśa*) are refuted collectively. Therefore it is said:
"Furthermore, when the function of duration has ceased, change and cessation—along with the primary dharma itself—naturally do not endure and immediately pass into the past.
Since change and cessation no longer exist, where would the primary dharma abide? Without these two characteristics, how could they exert their functional activity?"
Above, the critique was made in terms of location; now, to further critique it in terms of function, it is asked: "What further purpose is there for two functions?
Next, regarding the reason for the arising of the characteristic of duration (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*): once phenomena have arisen, they are maintained by duration so that they do not perish for a time.

Once the function of duration is relinquished, the phenomenon cannot remain and thus perishes naturally, thereby existing in the past. Therefore, the distinct function of cessation (*nirodha*) is the characteristic of duration.
Thereafter, there is nothing further to be done.
Above, the two characteristics of difference and cessation were refuted collectively; below, they are refuted individually. Since the text first refutes the characteristic of difference, it says:
"Furthermore, when a single dharma has arisen but not yet perished, it is called 'abiding'; when it has abided and is in the process of perishing, it is called 'cessation'."

This principle may indeed be granted; yet, even if one allows for difference, when subjected to rigorous analysis and examination regarding the substance of a single dharma, such difference logically cannot exist. Why is this so?

"Difference" refers to the mutual relationship between two dharmas—prior and posterior—in which their nature and characteristics undergo transformation. Since the subsequent dharma is not identical to the prior dharma, it can be said to be different.
This first establishes the logical principle of the characteristic of difference; therefore, the text speaks of "the son reciting and investigating."

The inquiry regarding the posterior dharma’s difference from the prior dharma is not established; this is an advance toward refutation. That the posterior dharma differs from the prior is not a single dharma;
this is a retrogressive inquiry. The final two lines conclude [the argument]: "Therefore, to establish difference within a single dharma ultimately does not succeed.
Master Zhendi’s original commentary states: "This verse also appears in the *Upadeśa* on the *Mahākātyāyanāvavāda-sūtra*, in the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*."
The phrasing and names of these [characteristics] differ due to superior causes and conditions; how could it be that the establishment of difference within a single dharma is ultimately not achieved?
Below, the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) is specifically refuted:

if, as the Sarvāstivādins and others maintain, cessation does not depend on external causes—as stated in the *Karma-pāda*—then even though other schools such as the Mahīśāsakas and Saṃmitīyas assert external causes and conditions for cessation, the characteristic of cessation would still [be untenable].
The dharma that is capable of extinguishing and the dharma that is to be extinguished are like fire burning objects; this serves as an analogy for the first point.

Although previously it was intended to show that abiding and extinction occur at different times, this explanation is made because of what was said: sentient beings are like those who take purgative medicine.

Although there are causes and conditions for taking the purgative, it cannot immediately produce its effect; one must wait for the deities to arrive before it can subsequently produce its beneficial effect below. If not... [text ends]
If all the devas could naturally achieve healing solely through the causal conditions of medicine, then those conditions should cease as soon as they have performed their function;
what need is there to separately postulate a "characteristic of cessation" (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*)?

Furthermore, the Sthaviras, the Saṃmitīyas, and others maintain that the mind and mental factors perish spontaneously at each moment (*kṣaṇika-svayaṃ-nirodha*) without depending on any external causes of cessation; thus, the functions of cessation and duration cannot exist sequentially.
Since that which abides perishes spontaneously at that very moment, it would follow that a single dharma both abides and perishes simultaneously within one and the same time;

this contradicts correct reasoning. Because the Master of the Twelve Treatises (Vasubandhu) adopts the Sautrāntika position, he explains the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*) in terms of a continuum (*saṃtāna*), which does not contradict correct reasoning and is well in accord with the sūtras.

The preceding two lines distinguish the four great characteristics (*mahālakṣaṇa*); the next two distinguish the great and small characteristics and further establish the characteristic of characteristics (*lakṣaṇalakṣaṇa*).

From here on, the final two lines distinguish the producer (*janaka*) and the produced (*janya*) of arising; [the text notes that] these do not exist apart from various causes and conditions. Within this section, the initial question asks:
"If arising (*jāti*) exists in the future and gives rise to the dharmas it produces, then since the characteristic of arising would exist upon all dharmas in the future, why..."

It does not arise all at once. Next, the verse is raised as a response; following this, the commentary on the verse explains the original text. First, it provides an initial explanation of the verse’s main body to resolve the preceding objection.

Second, the Sautrāntika objection is addressed: "If that were the case—that [arising] occurs without being distinct from other causal conditions—then for us Sautrāntikas, we do not see any functional capacity for arising apart from causal conditions.
Since there is no separate characteristic of arising, when the causes and conditions conjoin, all phenomena simply arise."
If [production] does not arise, what need is there for the characteristic of production (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*)? The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:

"Although the characteristic of production acts as a proximate cause arising simultaneously to produce all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) that are produced, it must necessarily depend upon a preceding cause of its own kind (*sva-jātīya-hetu*) and the assistance of other external conditions (*bāhya-pratyaya*) in their conjunction.
If this is so, we perceive only the causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) possessing the capacity for production; there is no separate characteristic of production."
This criticism is not valid. If one only admits that future dharmas arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions, this same criticism applies:

since the causes and conditions for future dharmas do not differ [from those of the present], why are they not produced all at once? Furthermore, if even when one among the causes and conditions is missing, the result still arises because it is "the remainder," then the result should also arise [in the absence of other factors].
Moreover, just as the visual faculty is projected by prior karma, even though it is separated [from its object], [the result would likewise follow].

Furthermore, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) should also be produced [independently], or else the eye-faculty should be produced solely through the power of the primary elements and not through prior karma;
or else, since the primary elements drawn forth by karma that produce the various eye-faculties never fail to be present at the time of their arising, when one arises, the others should also arise;
or else, the primary elements would have no efficacy with respect to the eye, for we do not see any primary elements of the eye apart from the preceding ones.

Since the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) arise individually, they would be rendered useless as causes for the subsequent arising of the eye, because the power of the primary elements—such as earth—to produce the eye and so forth is not observed to persist over time; indeed, such persistence is not even perceived.
Furthermore, the causal power of the primary elements should not be considered the cause for the arising of the eye and other faculties. Moreover, you maintain that there exists the seed of karma.
If the transformation of the continuum of the self were unimpeded, why could all karmic fruits not arise instantaneously?

If it is only when assisted by causes and conditions that the seeds of karma can produce [fruits], then one might ask: since the conditions alone should be able to produce them, what need is there for the seeds of karma?
For if the manifold conditions are absent, the fruit does not arise; yet, since it relies on the assistance of conditions, the seeds of karma are nonetheless not non-existent.
Although it relies on various conditions, how can you deny the characteristic of arising? The Sarvāstivādins explain: "How could all existing phenomena be known by you?

The four characteristics, such as arising, are subtle in their dharmic nature and extremely difficult to know. For example, although the four great elements that constitute the eye-faculty exist substantially, they cannot be perceived;
if the characteristic of arising did not exist, there would be no cognition of 'arising. This mind serves as proof for the dharma."

Furthermore, the sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī-vibhakti*), which denotes a possessive relationship, would be untenable; for instance, [expressions] such as "the arising of form" (*rūpasyotpādaḥ*) or "the arising of feeling" (*vedanāyā utpādaḥ*) would be improper, just as one should not say "the master of form" (*rūpasya svāmī*).
This same critique applies to everything from "non-arising" up to "non-ceasing," as appropriate to each case.

Regarding the four sūtras concerning the refutation of the result: if the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*) were non-existent, there should be a cognition of arising; if that were so, then... [the text continues].

Regarding the establishment of the realization of emptiness and selflessness, one should externally maintain that the nature of emptiness and selflessness exists as a reality. The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "Furthermore, another objection says:

'If the characteristic of impermanence were to exist as a distinct entity apart from the nature of impermanence, why would the characteristic of suffering not likewise exist as something distinct from suffering?
Such an analogical objection is invalid. If it is argued that the nature of impermanence exists because there is a basis for it in the characteristic of impermanence..."
Regarding this statement, an objection is raised: "The nature of suffering should also exist by virtue of a characteristic of suffering.
However, the nature of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) is impermanent; it ceases solely by taking cessation as its condition.

Just as the nature of conditioned phenomena is impermanent and must depend on the condition of arising to originate, so too, even if the nature of suffering were further to have a characteristic of suffering as its condition, what would that establish?"
Because the reasoning used in the analogy is thus unestablished, the objection regarding emptiness and selflessness is already refuted.

Furthermore, the characteristic of impermanence is also the essence of the characteristic of suffering, because it possesses no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), as stated in the Sūtras on suffering. Moreover, that [objection] should likewise encounter such a refutation:
if a produced phenomenon can only arise when there is a distinct causal condition for its production, then one must likewise admit a distinct [condition] for the phenomenon of suffering.

If suffering must wait for conditions to become suffering, or if the phenomena produced by it were to arise spontaneously even apart from their productive conditions—just as suffering and so forth do—then this would be the case.
Furthermore, as previously stated: what was stated?

It is that when, according to your position, something exists at a certain time, it necessarily depends on the generative function of other factors to come into being. In our school’s doctrine, however, because [the nature] exists at all times, phenomena possess an intrinsic nature (*dharmasvabhāva*).

If suffering, selflessness, and so forth did not depend on causes and conditions, they would necessarily possess the same nature as cessation; furthermore, cessation should be like arising in that it would require other factors.

Therefore, we know there exists a distinct factor capable of extinguishing internal causes, which—being separate from the phenomenon to be extinguished—is called the characteristic of impermanence (*anityatā-lakṣaṇa*).

If one argues that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) have no distinct cause for their extinction, then arising should likewise be the case; these two [arising and extinction] would exist without depending on causes, differing from the entity itself merely as distinct phenomena.
Alternatively, one should state the reason for the distinction between these two. The explanation is as follows:

there is another objection which says, "If the characteristic of impermanence (*anityatā-lakṣaṇa*) exists as a distinct entity apart from the three times and the five aggregates, why does the characteristic of suffering (*duḥkha-lakṣaṇa*) not likewise exist as a distinct entity apart from the three times?
The Master replies: "Such an objection based on analogy is logically invalid; I maintain that the nature of impermanence exists throughout the three times."

Because of the characteristic of impermanence (*anityatā-nimitta*), there is that upon which one can rely to formulate this objection: "The nature of suffering (*duḥkhatā*) should likewise exist by virtue of the characteristic of suffering (*duḥkha-nimitta*).

However, the intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*) of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) throughout the three periods of time is impermanent; yet, when they reach the present, they cease solely due to the condition of the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-nimitta*).
Consequently, their function of grasping an effect ceases and they enter the past, just as the intrinsic nature of future conditioned phenomena is non-existent.
It is always necessary to wait for the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*) as a condition for [a dharma] to arise and become present;

however, the impermanent nature (*anityatā*) of the three time periods does not depend on the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) to constitute that impermanent nature. Thus, the impermanence of the three time periods contradicts the intention of the Noble Ones (*ārya*).

Furthermore, even if there were another suffering (*duḥkha*) acting as a condition, what further use would it be? Therefore, the reasoning of the analogy you have cited is invalid, and by this, [your objection] is already refuted.

The objection that [the nature of] emptiness and selflessness would be untenable is also refuted by the fact that the nature of emptiness and selflessness is established not through the characteristics of emptiness and selflessness, but by virtue of the intrinsic nature of phenomena being empty and selfless.

Therefore, it cannot be objected: "If that were so, in order to establish the cognition of emptiness and selflessness, one would have to postulate a separate substantial entity (dravya) of emptiness and selflessness external to phenomena;
furthermore, since the nature of all phenomena across the three times does not persist eternally, when they are about to enter the present..."

Because the characteristic of arising arises from the characteristic of arising, the cognition of "arising" and the sixth grammatical case (the genitive) regarding the arising of form and so forth occur only in relation to the reality of phenomena;
they do not arise apart from the principle that all phenomena are eternally empty and selfless.

Since emptiness and selflessness do not depend on a characteristic of emptiness and selflessness external to the phenomena themselves, the cognition of emptiness and selflessness takes as its object only the principle of the emptiness and selflessness of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
It does not take as its object the emptiness and selflessness that exist outside of phenomena. Furthermore, the characteristic of impermanence and cessation is itself the characteristic of suffering;

because its essence is impermanent, it is suffering, as stated in the Sūtras and because it contradicts the intent of the Noble Ones. Thus, suffering pervades all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena, for the nature of suffering is ever-present and does not require a separate characteristic of suffering.

Above, the opponent raised an objection based on cessation; below this, the Master [Vasubandhu] counters with an objection based on the opposite, arising. Furthermore, that [opponent] should likewise encounter such an objection:

if a produced phenomenon requires separate conditions for its arising before it can arise, then one must admit that the three time periods contradict the intention of the Sage, or that a phenomenon of suffering would only become suffering after depending upon separate conditions for suffering; or else, the produced phenomenon [itself] should [arise without conditions].
Arising apart from conditions occurs spontaneously, just like the nature of suffering and so forth. Furthermore, it was previously stated; what was meant by that previous statement?

It is as you Sautrāntikas maintain: among conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), when something exists in the present, its capacity for the arising of a dharma as a conditioned phenomenon must necessarily depend on other conditions.
In our Sarvāstivāda school, however, all things exist throughout the three periods of time.

Therefore, if dharmas possessed an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that did not depend on causes and conditions, then suffering, emptiness, and selflessness would exist as an intrinsic nature at all times;

consequently, there would be no need to establish separately the characteristics of suffering, emptiness, and selflessness apart from the dharmas themselves. Furthermore, cessation (*nirodha*) would have to be like arising (*utpāda*), requiring other "characteristics of arising" for the dharma to cease.
Thus, we know that there exists a distinct capacity for cessation within the internal cause, which is separate from the dharma to be ceased; this is termed "non-existence" (*abhāva*).

If it is claimed that the characteristic of cessation is constant, then it would follow that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) likewise have no distinct cause for their arising, as these two characteristics—arising and cessation—are both distinct entities from the characterized substance (*lakṣya*), just like [the characteristics of] greatness and smallness are distinct from the magnitude they characterize. Alternatively, one must explain the reason for the distinction between these two:

whether they depend on a cause or do not depend on a cause. To establish the three [characteristics], etc., is like establishing the two [characteristics], etc., such as the magnitudes of large and small.

This object is different from that object; their names are distinct. When gathered together, they constitute conjunction (*saṃyoga*); when dispersed, they constitute disjunction (*vibhāga*). When an object is in another location, it is "that"; when in its own location, it is "this.

The above constitutes the category of quality (*guṇa*). The Vaiśeṣika school also establishes the categories of substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*). Substance is one; qualities are two; and actions are four.

There are five points of similarity and difference and six types of conjunction (*saṃprayoga*). When it is said here that "existence" (*sat*) and so forth constitute the category of existence (*sattā-padārtha*), this refers to the category of existence and includes the other three categories.
Because the category of existence causes all phenomena to possess an essential nature (*svabhāva*), the category of existence is termed "existence-nature" (*sattā*).

Based on these three [categories], a slight degree of conceptual understanding arises. You, Sarvāstivādins, should thus resemble the Vaiśeṣika outsiders regarding the category of reality (*dravya-padārtha*).

The followers of the Vaiśeṣika school maintain that there exist external entities such as "oneness" and so forth—like the distinct measures of large and small—which are separate from one another, or which exist apart from this or that, such as the categories (padārtha) of generality (sāmānya), particularity (viśeṣa), activity (karma), and inherence (samavāya).
Furthermore, they assert that the category of quality (guṇa) consists of twenty-one types, namely: color, odor, taste, tangibility, sound, dimension, and so forth.
Combination and separation, this and that, pleasure and pain, love and hatred, as well as effort, recollection, dharma, and adharma—these twenty-one categories consist of three types.
The five kinds beginning with color are the specific qualities (*viśeṣa-guṇa*) of the five great elements; the seven kinds beginning with number are the nine common qualities (*sāmānya-guṇa*);
and the nine kinds beginning with cognition are the specific qualities of the self (*ātman*). They establish nine categories of reality (*tattva-padārtha*), namely:
This means that [the opponent] raises an objection based on the seven common attributes—earth, water, fire, wind, space, time, and direction—as well as the "present" mentioned in the current text.

Furthermore, it is argued that in order to establish the sixth case (genitive) construction, such as "the aggregate-nature of form," there must be a distinct entity of an aggregate existing apart from form;
likewise, regarding the statement "the intrinsic nature of form," there is no intrinsic nature of form existing separately from form itself. This is the... [first point].
Since the sixfold transformation could not otherwise be established, birth and the other [characteristics] are merely conventional designations; there is no separate, substantial entity.
To understand that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) were previously non-existent in the future and now exist in the present, "birth" is conventionally designated.

Likewise, because these phenomena were previously non-existent and now exist, and because the category of the five aggregates (*skandha*) is vast and manifold, the sixth [aggregate] is spoken of to distinguish it from the remaining aggregates, based upon the five aggregates such as form (*rūpa*).

By rephrasing [the statement] as "the arising of the aggregate of form" (rūpaskandha) or "the arising of the aggregate of feeling" (vedanāskandha), it is indicated that this arising is exclusively the aggregate of form and not other aggregates such as feeling;
therefore, it is said that the arising of form applies to the other aggregates in the same manner.

This is analogous to how, in the world, one speaks of "the fragrance of sandalwood" to distinguish it from other fragrances such as olibanum, or "the substance of a pebble" to distinguish it from other substances such as common stones.
The arising of this form should also be understood in this way; likewise, the abiding and other characteristics of form should be understood accordingly. The Sarvāstivādins raise a counter-objection:

"If conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise apart from the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*), why do unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*)—such as space (*ākāśa*) and the three [other] unconditioned phenomena—not also arise?
The Sautrāntikas respond with a counter-reproach: "The designation 'arising' for conditioned phenomena is due to their existence after having previously been non-existent."
If the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is eternal by nature, how can one say it arises?

Furthermore, just as the expression "nature of things" (*dharmatā*) does not state that all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena possess arising, so too you must admit that not all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are subject to arising.

Moreover, according to your own school, although all conditioned phenomena equally possess the characteristic of arising, you nevertheless maintain that causes and conditions [act] upon conditioned form and mind.
The causal conditions for each phenomenon within its own class are distinct: the causal conditions for matter have the capacity to produce matter, but lack the capacity to produce mind;

the causal conditions for mind have the capacity to produce mind, but lack the capacity to produce matter. Likewise, the causal conditions for mental phenomena have the capacity to produce mind, but lack the capacity to produce matter.
Thus, you must admit that, according to my Sautrāntika school, all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are the same in this regard.

Regarding the characteristic of non-arising: although all arising conditioned phenomena possess the causal conditions of their own kind, when compared to those two dharmas [conditioned and unconditioned], one—the conditioned—possesses the function of arising, while the other—the unconditioned—lacks the function of arising.
Because the unconditioned lacks the causal conditions of its own kind, it cannot arise.
(7) The exposition in the *Vibhāṣā* regarding the underlying tenets of our own school can be understood according to the text.
The following two verses distinguish name (*nāman*), phrase (*pada*), and syllable (*vyañjana*). Within this, the first two lines distinguish the characteristics of name, phrase, and syllable;

the next two lines provide a classification of names, phrases, and syllables according to various categories; and the final line provides a general analysis of the *sabhāga* (homogeneous) and other factors.

Regarding the initial section, the first verse poses the preceding question, followed by the citation of the verse as the answer, after which the text explains the meaning of the verse. Within that explanation:
First, regarding the phrase "the word 'etcetera' (*ādi*)": "etcetera" includes the phrase and the *vyañjana-kāya* (phoneme-body). One should know that this is explained below.

Regarding the statement "here, name (*nāman*), flavor (*rasa*), and conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) are called 'that which is produced by conceptualization' (*saṃjñākṛta*)," it means that [the term] "deity" (*deva*) is a designation received from its cause.

Furthermore, it is explained that "name" is so called because it can give rise to conceptualization; thus, "name" is a designation received from its effect. This refers to the act of forming a conceptualization.
Therefore, it is called "perception" (*saṃjñā*). The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-śāstra* states: "Perception refers to the conceptualization and grasping of phenomena;

it is the perception produced by words conventionally established by common consensus, such as 'eye,' 'ear,' 'bottle,' 'clothing,' 'chariot,' and so forth. The commentary explains: "Perception refers to the conceptualization and grasping of the characteristics of phenomena;
it is the perception produced by words conventionally established by the multitude of people. Because words can produce perception, they are so named."

Conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) is the cause, and the arising of conceptualization is the name (*nāman*). The eyes, ears, and so forth are themselves what are called "eye," "ear," "vase," "garment," "chariot," "I," and so on.
According to that explanation, one should understand that here "name" refers to that which is produced by syllables (*akṣara*) as the cause for conceptualization;

from conceptualization, names such as "visible form," "sound," "odor," "taste," and "tangible object" arise. Because they are designated according to their causes, it is said: "as with the mention of visible form and sound."
Regarding the threefold explanation of the phrases concerning the perceptions of fragrance, flavor, and so forth: "phrase" (*pada*) means "to clarify.

It clarifies the ultimate meaning of a subject, such as the textual passages stating "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent" (*sarvasaṃskārā anityāḥ*). Alternatively, it refers to that which can distinguish [the following] three meanings: (1) function (*karman*), (2) quality (*guṇa*), and (3) time (*kāla*); it clarifies these three meanings through their corresponding distinctions.
This is what is called a "phrase" (*pada*). The old *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "A virtuous friend is encountered at one time."
This single phrase is cited to demonstrate its characteristics: "friend" refers to the person; "good" refers to the family's virtue; "at this time" refers to the timing;
and "encountering" refers to karmic function. These three together constitute one phrase as a "correspondence," while the various different phrases constitute "distinctions.
When the Buddha was a bodhisattva, he was a king named Śūrasoma, who spoke this verse for King Pradyota.
The causes and conditions are as explained in the separate record. Regarding the fourfold explanation of the script: "script" refers to characters such as *śa*, *a*, *i*, *ī*, and so forth.
These sounds are long in the former part and short in the latter. Foreigners often use compound characters as names; if one calls out "A," it has no referent or distinction, being merely a character.
Only when combined with other characters can it signify or distinguish meaning, such as in the word *ācārya*, which only becomes complete at the end.
When distinguishing that which expresses [meaning], at the time when [the components] have not yet been joined, one merely obtains what is called a "syllable" (*akṣara*).

In this context, a single syllable possesses that which it expresses, such as "form" (*rūpa*) or "sound" (*śabda*), and because it expresses [a meaning], it is termed a "name" (*nāman*); this does not mean that it is not also a "syllable. Furthermore, there are compound syllables that constitute a name;

for example, the words *lingqin* (apple) and *pípá* (loquat). If one calls out "lin" alone, it does not yet constitute a name; nor does calling out "pa" alone constitute a name. Only when they are joined together do they form [a name].
The name "A" merely has its own referent, and the "handle" (pa) likewise has its own referent; they are not like the sound "a-a," which has no referent whatsoever. Question:
Is it not the case that here the syllable "a" can point to the written strokes on paper, and thus it should also be the name for the written strokes on the paper? Answer:
It is not for the purpose of manifesting the written strokes on paper that one utters the word "a" with the mouth. Rather, it is called "a" within the mouth.
The phonemes and so forth are merely for the purpose of manifesting the various *a*-phonemes within the mouth;

the creation of the written form of the letter *a* on paper is intended to ensure that others, even though they do not hear me pronounce the *a*-phoneme from my mouth, may nevertheless understand it simply by seeing the written form of the letter *a* on paper.
Therefore, the written forms on paper are created [to represent] the various *a*-phonemes and so forth within the mouth.
This is not merely a matter of categorizing the names of characters written upon paper.

Regarding what is called "categorizing the scripts," for instance, there are twelve thousand five hundred characters in the seal script (zhuan) currently in use here; when classified, they reach as many as seventeen thousand characters.

As for the classification of scripts according to their original categories, the *Abhidharma-samuccaya-vyākhyā* and the *Buddhacarita* state that there are sixty-four types of distinct scripts from various lands.
The fifth section is the general explanation.
The preceding explanation of the chapter on "conception" (saṃjñā) involved only single names, phrases, and syllables;

it dealt only with names and not name-bodies (nāmakāya), only with words and not word-bodies (padakāya), and only with phrases and not phrase-bodies (vyañjanakāya). What is now called the "general explanation" refers precisely to these names.
Regarding the body [of names], the phrase-body, and the syllable-body, it is asked: what are called the "name-groups" (*nāmakāya*) and so forth? The answer is:

the collective designation of concepts (*saṃjñā*) and so forth is precisely what is meant by "name-groups" and so forth. As for the term "collective designation" (*samudāya-vyapadeśa*), it refers to the sense of a "conglomeration.

Within the sense of a conglomeration, the Sanskrit manuscript recites *ca-kāra* (the letter 'ca'). The letter 'ca' signifies the sense of a conglomeration; as stated in the preceding recitation, "totality" (*samasta*) means "conjoined" (*samyukta*).
Because it collects meanings, the term "total" (*saṃ*) is translated as "comprehensive. "Singing" (*ghoṣa*) refers to the meaning of "delimiting" (*pratiṣedha*).
This delimitation is the essential nature of the phoneme (*akṣara*), such as *k* in *ka-tva* and so forth; it is the condition for the phoneme, not the essential nature of the phoneme itself.

Within this general explanation, a "name-body" (*nāma-kāya*) refers to two names—such as "form," "sound," "odor," and so on—coming together as a pair. A "phrase-body" (*pada-kāya*) refers to [statements] such as "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent."

Regarding the two phrases "all phenomena are without self" (*sarvadharma-anātman*), the "bodies of phonemes, names, and sentences" (*vyañjana-nāma-pada-kāya*) refers to the collection of two or more syllables, such as *ka*, *kha*, or *ga*.
As for the term "phoneme" (*vyañjana*) mentioned above, it refers to individual characters, such as when one speaks of the characters *ai*, *a*, *i*, or *ī*;
because these are spoken of individually, they are single phonemes. However, [combinations] such as *ka-kha-ka-ga* or *artha* must necessarily [be considered as collections].
Because it is a collection of five syllables, it is a *vyañjana-kāya* (phoneme-group). According to the *Nyāyapraveśa*, "extensive phonemes" refers to that which is capable of manifesting;

because by means of this, that [name or phrase] is manifested. The commentary explains: "Phonemes" (*vyañjana*) refers to that which is capable of manifesting names and phrases, for it is by means of these phonemes that those names and phrases are manifested.
Other masters state that syllables such as *ai* and *i* are capable of manifesting.
Because they consist of names (*nāman*) and phrases (*pada*), they are called "syllables" (*vyañjana*).
The preceding section has explained the recitation of the root text; hereafter follows the analysis through questions and answers. Within this text, the master of the *Purāṇa-śālā* asks:

"Since these three [names, phrases, and syllables] have speech as their nature, and sound is their substance, being subsumed under the self-nature of form (*rūpa*), how can they be said to be [mental factors]?"
Regarding the two [categories] of formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*), the Sarvāstivādins reply: "These three do not have speech as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);
speech is sound, yet sound alone cannot convey meaning. The Master of the Three Treatises asks again: "How, then, does it cause [meaning] to be conveyed? The Sarvāstivādins reply again:
"Speech gives rise to names (*nāman*); names can manifest meaning; thus, they are able to cause [meaning] to be conveyed. The Master of the Sūtras [replies]:...
It is said that not only sounds are called "speech," but rather it is because meaning can be understood through these sounds that such vocalizations are designated as speech.
Regarding this, the Sarvāstivādins ask: "What kind of sound allows meaning to be understood?
The Sūtra Master answers: "It refers to that which the speaker, in relation to various meanings, has established together with the public as a definitive means of expression (*abhidhāna-pramāṇa*)."

Furthermore, for example, in ancient times, among the nine meanings, people collectively established a single word expressing fear as the definitive means of expression (*vācaka-pramāṇa*) for those nine meanings, as stated in the verse.

Those Sarvāstivādins who maintain that names are the expressers of meaning must also necessarily admit that such a name which expresses meaning is one that people have collectively established as the definitive means of expression; this applies whether it concerns the meaning of this sentence...

If [a name] can only be manifested by means of a conventionally established designation, then since its function is already manifested by sound alone, why must one gratuitously postulate that there exists a separate, real entity called "name"? Below this, first, two points are raised for critique:

furthermore, it is not yet understood how this name is produced by speech—is it like the non-Buddhists' position, where the name is eternal and is manifested by speech because an eternal name is thus revealed? Or is it like...?
The Sarvāstivādins claim that names (*nāman*) are impermanent because they arise from speech; thus, they are called "produced" (*utpanna*).
If, according to the Sarvāstivādins, names arise from speech, then since the nature of speech is sound, all sounds such as those of wind or bells should be able to produce names.

That is to say, the sound produced as a name possesses distinctions of rhythm and tone; these distinct sounds are capable of manifesting meaning—why then would one depend on a separate "name"? If [names] were to...
Regarding those who maintain that speech is manifestative: the nature of the sound of speech should be able to manifest names through all sounds such as those of wind-chimes and the like.

If it is argued that the sound which manifests a name possesses distinctions of rhythm and tone (*svara-viśeṣa*), then these distinct sounds are sufficient to manifest the meaning; why wait for a separate "name"? The *Nyāyabindu* states:

"The objection against the position that sound itself is the signifier (*vācaka*) is equally applicable. That is to say, if the substance of sound were itself capable of manifesting meaning, [it would follow that all sounds do so].
There is no sound whatsoever that cannot manifest [meaning]. If you claim that sounds possess distinctions in their capacity to manifest, then such distinctions must themselves be names;

therefore, your critical inquiry does not constitute a valid objection. Furthermore, it is impossible for various sounds to aggregate together, nor can a single phenomenon arise gradually part by part.

How then could the production of a "great" [sound] necessarily be brought about by speech? This is the third challenge. Moreover, since sounds cannot be accumulated and no dharma arises incrementally, how can it be established that [the cognition of meaning] necessarily arises from the utterance of words?
The Master himself provides a rebuttal, asking: "How can the final moment of a series of past manifest actions (vijñapti-kṣaṇa) produce non-manifest action (avijñapti)?
The Master further raises an objection: "If that were so, since the name would arise from the sound at the final stage, one should be able to understand the meaning by hearing only the final sound."
The preceding section refuted [the opponent's view] on the grounds that names can manifest meaning by focusing on how names arise from long sounds;
however, this was not a refutation of the fundamental tenet of the Sarvāstivādins. Below, their fundamental tenet is refuted:

if one holds the position that speech produces phonemes (*vyañjana*), phonemes in turn produce names, and names then manifest meaning, the following objection should apply: if speech produces names, then [speech] must consist of various moments of phonemes.
It is impossible for [the phonemes] to aggregate, nor is there a single dharma that arises part by part; this is the difficulty of the objection.
Furthermore, the argument that the name arises [from the speech-sound] is refuted by the same logic. Below, we shall explain how the speech-sound manifests the name through analogy with "arising":
just as various moments of sound cannot aggregate, nor can a single dharma arise part by part, how could a name be manifested by being produced from speech?
The rest of the text is identical to what precedes it. The *Nyāyabindu* states:

"Furthermore, the Master of the Sūtras (Sautrāntika) says that various momentary sounds cannot aggregate, nor can a single dharma arise gradually part by part; how then could its arising be said to be produced by speech? Moreover, he explains for himself:
'How can the final moment of manifest action, depending upon the past moments of manifest action, produce the unmanifest action?'"
Furthermore, one might raise this objection: "If that were so, since the name would only arise at the final moment of the sound, one should understand the meaning by hearing only that final sound.

If you maintain the position that speech produces the phoneme (*vyañjana*), the phoneme produces the name (*nāman*), and the name then reveals the meaning, the fault and difficulty in this case should be the same as previously stated;
for it is impossible for successive moments [of speech] to be accumulated, and thus the fault regarding speech revealing the name should be illustrated by the same example.
Furthermore, regarding the production of phonemes through speech—whether by manifestation or by generation—it is illogical for speech alone to constitute either a name (*nāman*) or a phrase (*pada*).

This objection contradicts your own established tenet, which asserts that the past and future lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); since the preceding and succeeding moments of sound cannot arise simultaneously, how could they form a phoneme or a name?
And if a name forms a phrase, how could it be so if only the final moment, supported by the successive transmission of each preceding moment, [is present]?
If [words] constitute a sentence only upon hearing the final one, it would follow that the meaning is realized only at the end;

furthermore, since there is no mutual assistance between what has passed and what is yet to come, how could they assist one another through constant recollection? Since there is no mutual assistance, the subsequent moments must be similar to the preceding ones, and thus the latter, like the first moment, should be unable to signify the meaning.
Therefore, hearing the final [word] should not lead to the realization of the meaning; hence, the mutual relationship between the preceding and succeeding [moments] as asserted by them is untenable.

The position that the phonemes themselves are the expressive agents of the meaning is not established, for in our own school, it is accepted that the three time-periods of speech exist and are not non-existent.

Although names and so forth are produced only at the final moment—depending on what precedes them—one cannot comprehend the meaning merely by hearing that [final sound], because the hearing is incomplete, unlike the previously established convention of names and so forth.
This is because the sūtras refer to the sound as the factor that brings about [the expression]. Thus, it is concluded.

The fact that one may achieve comprehension upon hearing even a single sound is due to the power of habitual practice; based on this, one infers the rest. Therefore, the Master of the Sūtra (Sthiramati) said:

"That [position] is refuted; it is not this second [explanation]. Furthermore, regarding the statement that "syllables (*vyañjana*) are distinct from words," those of clear wisdom who dwell in contemplative analysis hope to discern their characteristics;
thus, they know that there are no syllables existing apart from words.
The above clarifies that names arise from speech; this refutes [the opponent’s view] by examining their manifestation and production. Now follows the fourth category of critique:
furthermore, whether names are manifested or produced by speech, according to the previous analysis of how speech gives rise to names, both are irrational. The Master Paramārtha states:
"The preceding refutation of names existing within sound does not establish [the opponent's position]. The opponent says: "If it is not established that names exist within sound..."
Previously, it was established that names reside within their referents; now, we further refute the claim that names reside within their referents.

Since names must arise simultaneously with their referents—just as the characteristics of arising and so forth arise simultaneously with the state of existence—the fifth point refutes that position as follows:

Furthermore, if one maintains that names arise simultaneously with their referents like the characteristic of arising, then when a name exists in the present, its past and future referents would not yet exist. Moreover...
After parents have given birth to a child, they establish names for the child according to their own wishes.
How could it be said that the name of the child arises simultaneously with its birth and so forth? Furthermore, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) originally have no names;

since unconditioned phenomena lack the sense of "arising," names were never previously admitted for them. Since a name is established neither within sound nor within the meaning itself, [the claim that it arises simultaneously with the object] is untenable.
Therefore, one should know that there is no separate entity called "name" (nāma) apart from the sixth aggregate of consciousness.

However, when the Blessed One says that desire depends upon names and that a person constructs phrases, this means that when the meaning is expressed, the conventional measure established by the multitude is sound itself;
there is no name distinct from sound. It is the specific arrangement of these sounds as names that constitutes a verse (gāthā); it is in this sense that a verse is said to be spoken.
Based on the very sounds themselves, the name "verse" (gāthā) is applied; this is merely a specific arrangement of the names of sounds.

Since there is no separate entity apart from the sounds, the verse likewise has no separate entity apart from the sounds. If one were to maintain that there is a separate entity called a "verse" external to the sounds, it would be like a row of trees or a sequence of mental states:
just as a "row" is formed by many trees, yet there is nothing external to the trees [that constitutes the row]. This is the correct principle.

In the case of sequential mental states arising one after another, there is no separate sequence external to the minds themselves; the verse is likewise so, meaning that there is no separate verse external to the sounds.
Thus far, we have refuted the existence of a distinct name-entity apart from the vocal sounds; hereafter, in the seventh [section], the Sūtra Master provisionally grants this concession.

If one were to claim that there is a distinct textual entity (*vyañjana*) apart from sound (*ghoṣa*) in order to refute [the view] that names and phrases are self-sufficient, or if one were merely to adhere to the old position that there is a distinct textual entity apart from sound—taking the mere collection of these as the bases for names and so forth, and further asserting the existence of additional individual names, name-bases (*nāmakāya*), phrases, and phrase-bases (*padakāya*)—then all of these would become useless.
The *Nyāyānusāra* accepts the Master’s [Vasubandhu’s] words, stating: "Or, if... and so forth.

The old position that there exists a distinct entity called "text" (*vyañjana*), which is then collectively designated as "name-group" (*nāmakāya*) and so forth, and that further entities exist beyond these which are then designated as "name-body" (*nāma-kāya*) and so forth, is redundant and irrational.

This is because multiple phonemes do not occur simultaneously; since the principle of collective aggregation is thus untenable, it cannot be the case that meaning is not manifested in each individual phoneme.

Therefore, just as a tree or other great composite formations do not fail to produce a shadow based on them, yet that shadow arises as a conventional designation while its substance is not identical [to the source], so too these various texts have been collectively gathered from the past;
although those names and phrases arise based on what appears similar, their substance is like that appearance. This is a well-stated principle that is thoroughly established. If this is so, then...
It follows that all conventional phenomena (*prajñapti-dharma*) could be established as having a real intrinsic nature (*dravya-svabhāva*), which would lead to such an error. Why is this?

Because within a single syllable, there are two names. Since no conventional phenomenon is formed by gathering together a single real entity, the conventional and the name do not correspond in their referents.
If even a single syllable possesses a name, how can one know that this name is separate from the syllable?
Yet, there is this single syllable which, though known to lack a real referent, has no designated object of its own;

nevertheless, depending upon it as a condition, a distinct name arises, which alone is able to express meaning. However, because they are extremely similar, their distinct characteristics are difficult to discern, just as, for example, it was previously difficult to distinguish between the various shades of color.
The above constitutes the seventh section, in which the Sautrāntika school extensively refutes the Sarvāstivāda by means of various arguments.
Below this is the eighth section, in which [the author] sets forth the non-Vaibhāṣika position that name-groups (*nāmakāya*) and so forth are not distinct entities separate from the mind;

rather, they are real and subsumed within the aggregates (*skandha*), and not merely nominal designations. Why is this? Because not all phenomena can be fully comprehended through mere discursive investigation (*vitarka*).
Therefore, it is said that there are no separate, substantial entities for the "body of names" (*nāmakāya*) and so forth.

The *Nyāyānusāra* states, as explained in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, that names, phrases, and phonemes each have three types. The three types of names are: the name itself, the body of names, and the multiple bodies of names;
phrases and phonemes are likewise. A name has many positions: it may be produced by a single syllable, two syllables, or many syllables. Regarding those produced by a single syllable:
When one syllable is spoken, there can only be a name (*nāman*); when two syllables are spoken, there is a "name-body" (*nāmakāya*).
Some say that when three syllables are spoken, it is called a "multiple-name-body" (*bahunāmakāya*); others say that only when four syllables are spoken is it called a "multiple-body-name.
Regarding those who assert that a name arises from two syllables: only when two syllables are spoken can there be a name; when four syllables are spoken, [there are] four...
At that time, it is said that when six syllables are uttered, one refers to a "name-body" (*nāmakāya*);

or it is said that only when eight syllables are uttered does one refer to a "multiple name-body. Regarding the production of multiple syllables, as for those produced from three syllables, when three syllables are uttered, there can only be a "name" (*nāman*);
when six syllables are uttered, one refers to a "name-body," or it is said that... [when eight syllables are uttered, one refers to a multiple name-body].
When there are nine syllables, it is called a "multisyllabic body" (*nāmakāya*); or it is said that one must have twelve syllables for it to be called a multisyllabic body.
This serves as the gateway through which other names arise as name-bodies (*nāmakāya*) or multisyllabic bodies, as should be explained according to reason.

Sentences (*pada*) also have many levels: namely, intermediate sentences, initial sentences, final sentences, short sentences, and long sentences. If eight syllables arise, they constitute an intermediate sentence.
Because the middle line is neither long nor short, it is called the "middle-positioned" [line]. Thirty-two syllables produce the fourth line; thus, these four lines constitute a *śloka*.
Most prose and verse compositions in the sūtras and śāstras rely upon this structure. If six syllables or more are produced, it is named the first line;
if twenty-six syllables or fewer are produced, it is named the last line. If six syllables are omitted, it is named a short line.
Beyond twenty-six syllables, it is called a long verse (*gāthā*). Furthermore, based on the intermediate-length verse, three types of explanations are distinguished:
when eight syllables are spoken, it may simply be called a "verse" (*pada*); when sixteen syllables are spoken, it is then termed a "verse-body" (*padakāya*).
Alternatively, it is said that when twenty-four syllables are spoken, it is termed a "verse-body. Or again, it is said that only when thirty-two syllables are spoken is it termed [a verse-body].

Since a collection of many phrases (*padakāya*) consists of syllables (*vyañjana*), there is only one category [of phoneme]. When one speaks a single syllable, it can only be called a "phoneme" (*vyañjana*);
when one speaks two syllables, it is called a "collection of phonemes" (*vyañjanakāya*); or it is said that when one speaks three syllables, it is called a "collection of phonemes";
or it is said that only when one speaks four syllables is it called a "collection of phonemes. Based on this principle, one should state it as follows:
When one syllable (*akṣara*) is spoken, there is a name (*nāman*), but no name-body (*nāmakāya*); there is no phrase (*pada*) or phrase-body (*padakāya*), nor multiple phrase-bodies;

there is a phoneme (*vyañjana*), but no phoneme-body (*vyañjanakāya*) or multiple phoneme-bodies. When two syllables are spoken, there is a name and a name-body, but no phrases and so forth (i.e., no phrase-body or multiple phrase-bodies);
there is a phoneme and a phoneme-body, but no multiple phoneme-bodies. When four syllables are spoken, there is a name and so forth... [and so on].

When three syllables (*akṣara*) such as "non-existence" (*abhāva*) are spoken, there are the three categories of name (*nāman*), etc.; when there are phrases (*pada*) such as "existence," there is the phrase-body (*padakāya*) but not the multi-phrase-body (*anekapadakāya*).

When three syllables such as "existence" are spoken, there are the three categories of name, etc.; when there are phrases such as "existence," there is the phrase-body but not the multi-phrase-body. When three syllables such as "existence" are spoken, there are the three categories of name, etc.;

when sixteen syllables are spoken, there are the three categories of name, etc., the phrase, and the phrase-body, but not the multi-phrase-body. When thirty-two syllables are spoken, there are the name (*nāman*) and the phrase (*pada*).
The three [categories] each possess three types; taking these as the gateway, the rest should be explained according to reason.

The two preceding lines distinguish the characteristics of names (*nāman*) and phrases (*pada*); from the next two lines onward, there is a detailed analysis through various categories. Within this text, the initial inquiry consists of four parts: first, an inquiry regarding the realms of bondage (*dhātu-bandhana*);

second, an inquiry regarding sentient and non-sentient entities; third, an inquiry regarding matured (*vipāka*), nurtured (*aupacayika*), and outflowing (*naiṣyandika*) phenomena; and fourth, [an inquiry regarding] whether [these] things are exclusively...

The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is not discussed because it consists only of the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*) and so forth at the moment of realization. Fourth, regarding the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*), the verse is first cited as the answer, followed by an explanation of the text of that verse.

Within this section, there are four parts; the first explains the realms of bondage (*dhātu-bandhana*). This category of "name-body" (*nāma-kāya*) and so forth is bound only to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Some say it also extends to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), yet it cannot be definitively stated. The *Abhidharmakośa* (Old Translation) also says: [it is] also...
Some say that in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), there is only reliance upon mental reflection (manasikāra).

Master Zhenshi (the "True-Truth" Master) states that the Saṃmitīya school establishes the name "mental reflection" for the formless realm because it is not called "verbal expression. Thus it is said: "This cannot be expressed in words;
it manifests based on the mind of mental reflection. Therefore, it is said that there is only reliance upon mental reflection. (Old *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 1).
Question: Is a name associated with the location of the body, or is it associated with the location of speech? Answer: Some say that a name is associated with the location of speech.

Those who maintain that a name is associated with the location of speech hold that when one is born within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), speech belongs to the desire realm, the name belongs to the desire realm, and the person belongs to the desire realm;
yet the meaning expressed may belong to any of the three realms or be unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Bound to birth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one utters speech belonging to the first dhyāna stage;

this speech belongs to the first dhyāna stage, the person belongs to the first dhyāna stage, and the meaning spoken belongs either to the three realms or is unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*). Or, born within the first dhyāna, one utters speech belonging to the first dhyāna stage;
this speech belongs to the first dhyāna stage, the person belongs to the first dhyāna stage, and the meaning spoken belongs to the first dhyāna stage or is unconditioned.

Whether bound to the three realms or unbound, when one is born in the first dhyāna and utters speech belonging to the desire realm, that speech is named after the desire realm and its person belongs to the desire realm;

the meaning of what is spoken is as previously explained. When one utters speech of the first dhyāna level while in the second, third, or fourth dhyānas, that speech is named after the first dhyāna and its person belongs to the first dhyāna; it is spoken by those in the second, third, or fourth dhyānas.
The meaning is as previously explained regarding being born in the second, third, or fourth dhyānas while speaking the language of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
This speech belongs to the desire realm, and the name belongs to the desire realm; the person is in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna, yet the meaning spoken is as previously explained. Question:
Those who maintain that names follow the location of the speech—namely, that the name belongs to the realm (the first dhyāna)—do the other three dhyāna stages have names? Answer: Yes.
There may be those who say, "There is no further speaker. To this, the critique says: one should not speak thus.
As previously stated, it is good to have a speaker. Furthermore, the term "speaker" refers to the person and the location.

If one speaks in this way, referring to the person and the location, then when one is born within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and utters speech of the desire realm, that speech belongs to the desire realm and its name belongs to the desire realm.

A person is one spoken of in the sense of the desire realm, as previously explained; being born within the desire realm, they produce speech belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna, and that speech is named after the stage of the first dhyāna.
This person belongs to the desire realm; "the meaning spoken by the person" refers to the desire realm, as previously explained.

Being born within the first dhyāna, they produce speech belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna, and that speech is named after the first dhyāna. This person belongs to the first dhyāna; "the meaning spoken by the person" refers to the first dhyāna.
The meaning is as previously explained: one born in the first dhyāna who utters speech of the desire realm—this speech is of the desire realm, while the person is of the first dhyāna;
the meaning spoken by this person of the first dhyāna is as previously explained.

One born in the second, third, or fourth dhyānas who utters speech of the level of the first dhyāna—this speech is of the name of the first dhyāna, while the person belongs to that respective level; the meaning spoken by them is as previously explained.

It is said that when one is born in the second, third, or fourth dhyānas and utters speech belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), that speech is designated by the name of the desire realm because it is spoken by a person belonging to that [desire] level;

the meaning is as previously explained. Question: If it is stated that names follow the location of the person, then while there are names in the second, third, and fourth dhyāna levels, does the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) have names? Answer: Some say it has; others say it does not.

Furthermore, there are those who say that [a single moment of mind] exists but cannot be described. The critique states: one should not make such a claim. As was stated previously, it is better to say:
"A single moment of mind can produce a single utterance, but a single utterance cannot express a single syllable. Question: When one speaks of a "river," is this not a single syllable?
Answer: It is so; however, by that time, many *kṣaṇas* have already passed. In the world, a single moment of mind must give rise to a single [utterance].

Regarding the statement that "a single utterance, a single word, or even a single syllable is spoken only by the Buddha, the World-Honored One," this means his speech is swift and light, his voice is faultless, and his eloquence is supreme.

One interpretation explains: when one born in the desire realm produces speech of the first dhyāna, or when one born within the first dhyāna produces speech of the desire realm, and so forth—all such instances involve the production of speech through the power of another's mind.
Question: Why are all such productions called "conforming to the location of the speech"?
Question: Is "name" (nāma) bound to the desire realm and the first dhyāna, or does it exist in the remaining three dhyāna stages? Answer: Some say it does not;
the Sarvāstivādins maintain that because "name" consists solely of verbal expression, it does not exist in the upper three dhyānas as there is no further speaking.
However, the Saṃmitīyas calculate that although there is no verbal expression in the upper three dhyānas, "name" still exists there, though it cannot be expressed.
Because it is designated by the name "conceptualization" (*saṃjñā*), it exists; yet because it is not a verbal designation, it cannot be spoken of.
Since this is not the meaning of the Sarvāstivāda, the critique states: "One should not speak in this way. Regarding what was previously stated by the Sarvāstivādins:
if one asserts that names follow the person and the stage, then while names exist in the stages of the second, third, and fourth dhyānas, do they exist in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) or not?
The answer is: Some say that in the Sarvāstivāda school there is no such thing as an "ineffable" designation. Others say that it does exist but is ineffable;
the Saṃmitīya school maintains that there is a designation for "mental application" (*manasikāra*), and because it is not a verbal designation, it is ineffable.
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Old Kośa) also states that this applies to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), and that this which is ineffable is [designated] solely by means of mental application.
The commentary on the basis states: "One should not say [it is] as previously stated that it does not exist in the formless realm.

This is because the proponents of the correct view merely critique the absence in the formless realm and do not state that it exists in the three higher dhyānas; furthermore, this does not contradict the previous critique regarding the absence in the three higher dhyānas.

Second, both interpretations hold that it is comprised within sentient beings (*sattva-saṃgṛhīta*), and each is included in the category of sentient beings such as individual bodies (*eka-kāya*) and so forth. It is capable of...

If it were as the non-Buddhists and others claim—that names exist within the meaning and are manifested by speech—then the speaker would not establish that the name is what manifests the existence of the meaning.
[Regarding the three explanations: Name-bodies (*nāmakāya*) and so forth are exclusively *niṣyanda* (outflow) results, because they are interrupted and then resumed again;
they are not *vipāka* (maturation) results, and they are not material form (*rūpa*) consisting of atoms (*paramāṇu*).

Because the four types of "nurturing" (aupacayika) are of an indeterminate nature (avyākṛta), it is said: "Furthermore, they are comprised solely within the unobscured-indeterminate (anivṛtāvyākṛta) nature.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "Moreover, the three—name and so forth—are comprised solely within the unobscured-indeterminate nature.

Therefore, when one who has severed the roots of goodness speaks of wholesome dharmas, although they establish wholesome names and so forth, they do not establish wholesome dharmas; likewise, those free from desire and greed do not establish unwholesome [names and so forth]."

Since those beyond training (aśaikṣa) do not produce defiled states, and since names and so forth— which are capable of signifying— are not the dharmas that are signified, it is explained that names, phrases,
and syllables are neutral by nature (svabhāva-avyākṛta) and are not included among the four types of neutral states.
From this point on, one verse-line universally analyzes the remaining dissociated factors (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*). Within the text: first, the thesis is stated and established;

next, the verse is cited to provide the formal analysis; finally, the commentary explains the content of the verse. Regarding the first part, the commentary on the initial phrase "is likewise" (*tathā*) uses the category of "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*) as an analogy, following the same pattern as the "sets of names" (*nāmakāya*) and so forth.
It is: (1) pervasive of the desire and form realms; (2) pertaining to sentient beings; (3) a result of outflow (*niṣyanda*); and (4) non-obscured and neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).

The commentary on the second phrase, including the mention of the "formless realm" (*ārūpya*), clarifies that the *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) pertains not only to the desire and form realms but also extends to the formless realm;

furthermore, the mention of "maturation" (*vipāka*) clarifies that *sabhāgatā* is not merely of the nature of outflow (*niṣyanda*), as it also includes maturation. Regarding the Bodhisattva, it extends to both maturation and [other types].

The subsequent sutra passage indicates that this realm encompasses three categories and possesses two meanings. The *Samyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* states: "It consists of the substantial entity (*vastu*), the nurtured (*aupacayika*), the retributive (*vipāka*), and the momentary (*kṣaṇika*)."
Because they are nourished by their respective seeds, the *vipāka* (maturation) and so forth are called the five kinds (*pañca-jāti*).

Since "kind" (*jāti*) has the meaning of "category," the *Abhidharmakośa* now refers to the nourished (*aupacayika*), the matured (*vipāka*), and so on as the five categories of phenomena (*pañca-jātīya-dharma*). The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* asks: "What is maturation?

It refers to the generic similarity (*sabhāgatā*) of births in the destinies (*gati*) such as the hells and animals. What is "homogeneity" (*nikāyasabhāga*)? It refers to the realm (*dhātu*), stage (*bhūmi*), location (*sthāna*), lineage (*gotra*), and clan (*kula*).

Regarding the "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*) of those such as śramaṇas and brahmins, whether they be learners (*śaikṣa*) or non-learners (*aśaikṣa*), some masters state that among all types of homogeneity, that which is produced by the projection of prior karma is the "ripened" (*vipākaja*) homogeneity, while that which arises from present application (*prayoga*) is the "outflowing" (*naiṣyandika*) homogeneity.

Regarding the third category [of the threefold classification], acquisition (*prāpti*) and the various characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are common to all three; that is to say, there are those that are momentary (*kṣaṇika*), outflowing, and so forth.
Because it is not a matured fruit (*vipāka*), it is not a minute atom (*paramāṇu*); because it is not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is not a non-nourished entity. This explains the fourth phrase.

Non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) and the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) are exclusively outflowing (*naiṣyandika*). The word "exclusively" is used to clarify that they are not matured fruits and are not produced by karma.

They are not matured fruits because they do not coexist with the forbearance of suffering (*duḥkhe-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*). They are not momentary because they are not minute atoms; they are not nourished entities.

The five explanations regarding unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) have already been stated. As for the meanings not yet explained—such as the attainment of non-perception (*āsaṃjñika*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)—they are not explained here because they have already been analyzed in detail previously.
For what reason are "possession" (*prāpti*), "non-possession" (*aprāpti*), and so forth not mentioned?

Because they pertain exclusively to sentient beings (*sattva*), as has already been stated in the section on "what constitutes a sentient being. For what reason are the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) not mentioned as being included among both sentient and non-sentient entities? Because they are common to both.
The preceding text has already explained that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are accompanied by [these factors]; therefore, those not yet mentioned should be understood accordingly.
The *Vibhāṣā* (14) states: Question: Why is it called "name" (*nāman*)? Answer: "Name" means to conform to a name, to summon by a name, or to be joined with a name.
"Conforming" is like going toward what one intends to do; "name" is established for this purpose, just as one should be joined [with it].
That which follows the formation of verses and causes them to accord with their meaning is here called "name" (*nāman*), because it possesses three meanings.
Mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) possess the quality of following [the object] but lack the sense of "joining," and thus are not called "names.

Other non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), material phenomena (*rūpa*), and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) possess both the qualities of following and joining, yet lack the meaning of "name"; therefore, they are also not "names. Now, what is a "name-group" (*nāma-kāya*)?

Question: What is the meaning of these two names, “collection” (*saṃghāta*) and “body” (*kāya*)? Therefore, why is a single [name] not called a “name-body”? Answer: It is because “many” signifies a collection.

For example, one elephant or two elephants are not called a “multitude of elephants”; it is when many elephants are placed together that they are called a “multitude of elephants. The same applies to horses and so forth.
As for the “phrase-body” (*padakāya*), the “multitude of phrases,” and the “syllable-body” (*vyañjanakāya*), the “multitude of syllables”: [the same principle applies].
It is likewise in this regard: among these, there are names (*nāman*), name-bodies (*nāmakāya*), and multiple-name-bodies (*anekanāmakāya*).
There are those produced by a single syllable, those produced by two syllables, and those produced by many syllables. Among those produced by a single syllable, there is merely a name;
