among those produced by two syllables, there are both a name-body and multiple-name-bodies. Some maintain that these should be based on three [syllables].
Regarding the term "name" (*nāman*): some maintain that it arises based on four syllables or two syllables;

within these, the two-syllable [unit] is merely a "name," while the four-syllable [unit] is a "name-body" (*nāmakāya*) or a "multiple-name-body" (*bahunāmakāya*). Others maintain that it arises based on six syllables or eight syllables;
within these, the three-syllable [unit] is merely a "name," while the six-syllable [unit] is a "name-body" or a "multiple-name-body."
Regarding the "body" (*kāya*): some maintain it is based on nine syllables, while others maintain it is based on twelve syllables.
Within that which is designated by four syllables, there is merely a name; within eight syllables, there is a "name-body" (*nāmakāya*) and a "multiple-name-body" (*anekanāmakāya*).
Some maintain this is based on twelve syllables, while others maintain it is based on sixteen syllables. Taking this as the gateway, one should apply it to names consisting of many syllables.
Knowledge is also like this. Other masters say that within what is designated by a single syllable, when that single syllable is uttered once, there is merely a name;
when that same syllable is uttered a second time, there is a "name-body" (*nāmakāya*); and when that same syllable is uttered three or four times, there are multiple "name-bodies.
It should be understood that the same applies to what is designated by two syllables and so forth. What, then, is a "phrase-body" (*padakāya*)?
Answer: When various phrases fulfill meanings that were previously unfulfilled, their conjunction therein is called a "multitude of phrases" (*pada-kāya*).
To establish this meaning, a sūtra is cited as proof, as the Blessed One said: "Commit no evil; practice all that is good;
purify your own mind—this is the teaching of all Buddhas. In this way, each of these four phrases is able to fulfill a meaning that was previously unfulfilled within them.
"Combination" refers to a group of multiple phrases (*pada-kāya*). Thus, within each of these four lines, there are meanings not yet fully expressed;

the "combination" therein means that either individual syllables within each of the four lines are combined to manifest those unfulfilled meanings, or else the various lines are combined to manifest the meaning of a completed verse. This constitutes one [type of] group of multiple phrases.
Within a single line, there is both a thesis (*uddiṣṭa*) and an explanation (*nirdeśa*). "All evils" is the thesis; "do not commit them" is the explanation.

Likewise, "these Buddhas" is the thesis; "the teaching" is the explanation. Therefore, this verse contains four complete elements: first, the thesis; second, the explanation; third, the lines; and fourth, the verses.
If one speaks of "all evils," it is complete in terms of the thesis; [it is likewise complete] in terms of the explanation, the lines, and the verses.

If it is incomplete, it is further stated that the three types of names—the heading, the explanation, and the sentence—are complete; if the verse is incomplete, it is further stated that all virtues are [complete].

If, within the general verse, both the heading and the explanatory sentence are complete, yet within the specific lines only the heading is complete and not the rest, and so forth—even further stating "these Buddhas"—this refers to the completion of both the general heading and the explanatory sentence, whereas if only the specific line of the heading is complete and not the rest...
Others further explain that the teacher’s instruction is entirely complete within this verse; it is of medium length, neither too long nor too short.

They do not know that eight syllables constitute a *pada* (line) and thirty-two syllables constitute a *śloka* (verse). Most verses in the sūtras and śāstras follow this rule, and the calculation for transcription also follows this method.
Furthermore, from six syllables up to twenty-six syllables, all may constitute a *pada*; however, as for those of six syllables:
That which consists of twenty-six syllables is called the "first phrase. That which is reduced by six syllables is called the "known phrase.

That which exceeds twenty-six syllables is called the "long phrase. What is the "multitude of phonemes" (*vyañjana-kāya*)? It refers to the collection of all syllables; this is what is meant by the "multitude of phonemes.
To establish this meaning, a scriptural passage is cited as proof, as the Blessed One said: "Desire is the basis of verse," and furthermore—
This refers to the verse (*gāthā*) which depends upon names (*nāman*) and the composer of the verse. Herein, "desire" (*chanda*) means the longing, delight, and affection for composing a verse;

this desire serves as the basis for the verse. This desire is the cause for the collection and arising of the phrasing. As for "phrasing" (*vyañjana*), it is called phrasing because it skillfully manifests [the meaning];
it is simply the syllable (*akṣara*), for there is no shifting of conceptualization therein. This also clarifies that it is capable of [expressing] the manifest.
To clarify that the verse-text has syllables as its substance and that the verse depends upon names: the verse is a conventional existence established in dependence upon names;
it is also said to depend upon words and phrases for the sake of brevity. Here, "dependence" is like a forest depending upon trees.

Furthermore, the composer of the verse—who conceives [the content] rather than analytically investigating it—produces various gāthās; this is called the "composer. The verse depends upon the composer, just as a snake depends upon its hole.
Just as water depends on its source and milk depends on the udder, one should know that there are differences in their designations:
there are names (*nāman*), name-bodies (*nāmakāya*); phrases (*pada*), phrase-bodies (*padakāya*); and phonemes (*vyañjana*), phoneme-bodies (*vyañjanakāya*).
Among these, in a single syllable there is a name, but no name-body, no multiple name-bodies, no phrase, no phrase-body, and no phoneme-body.
The body has no multiple phrases; the body has characters, yet the body has no characters; the body has no multiple characters; within two characters there is a name, yet the body has no name;
the body has no multiple names; it has no phrases, yet the body has no phrases; the body has no multiple phrases; the body has characters, yet the body has characters;
the body has no multiple characters; within four characters there is a name, yet the body has no name; the body has multiple names; it has no phrases, yet the body has no phrases.
The body has no phrases; the body has phonemes, and the phoneme-body has many phonemes. Within eight syllables, there is a name, and the name-body has many names.
The body has phrases and no phrases; the body has no phrases; the body has phonemes, and the phoneme-body has many phonemes.
Within sixteen syllables, there is a name, and the name-body has many names; there are phrases and...
There is the phrase-body (*padakāya*) and no more than that; there is the phoneme (*vyañjana*) and the phoneme-body (*vyañjanakāya*), and there is more than that phoneme-body.

Within the thirty-two letters, there is the name (*nāman*) and the name-body (*nāmakāya*), and there is more than that name-body. There is the phrase (*pada*) and the phrase-body (*padakāya*), and there is more than that phrase-body.

There is the phoneme and the phoneme-body, and there is more than that phoneme-body. Taking this as the gateway, the extent of what is spoken regarding the various collections of letters is as follows:

One should understand this according to the principle [in the fifteenth fascicle]. If it is said that *Śikhin* is a name for that which possesses characteristics (*sa-nimitta*) and *Ajita* is a name for that which lacks characteristics (*a-nimitta*), the explanation is as follows:
"According to" (*anuvartate*) means that the name proceeds in accordance with the meaning it expresses;

because the name corresponds to that which is expressed, it is called "according to the name. This refers to establishing the name "ox-horse" for the meaning of "horse" within this context, just as one seeks the name "ox-horse."

Because oxen and horses respond [to the call], it is called "summoning" (*āhvāna*). Because the name follows the verse (*gāthā*) so that the verse may meet with its meaning, it is called "conjoining" (*saṃyojana*).

In this context, because the name is seen to have three meanings, it is termed a "name" (*nāman*). Since the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) proceed in accordance with their objects (*ālambana*), they are called "following the mind" (*anuvartaka*).
Because oxen and horses respond when sought, they are also called "summoned"; however, they do not follow the composition of the verse.
Because they do not turn [the mind] so as to cause the verse to coincide with its meaning, there is no sense of "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*).

Since names manifest the essence [of phenomena], and the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are not the essence manifested by names, the mind and mental factors are not called "names. Other dissociated factors (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), form (*rūpa*), and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are the meanings that are signified;

because they correspond with the signifiers (*vyañjana*), they are called "conjoined" (*sahita*), and because they coincide with the signifiers, they are called "associated" (*anugata*). However, [the mind and mental factors] lack these.

Because there is no object to be summoned, it is not called "summoning" (*āhvāna*). However, insofar as the mind and mental factors are the objects to be expressed (*abhidheya*), they meet with the expressive [words];

thus, there is also the sense of "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*). Now, based on the fact that the mind and mental factors do not constitute the substance of the verse, do not follow the movement of the verse's composition, and do not cause the verse to meet with its meaning, it is not called "conjunction. Question: In verses such as "Commit no evil," etc., there are only four [lines]. How can this be?
Question: Why is it said that a verse consists of eight characters per line and thirty-two characters per stanza?
Answer: According to this local dialect, four characters constitute a line; however, according to the original phonetics, there are eight characters.
In the original phonetics, it is *sarva* (meaning "all"), *pāpa* (meaning "evil"), *mā kārṣīḥ* (meaning "do not do"). Thus, it is eight characters.

The eight characters constitute the first phrase. Their original pronunciation is *Kuśala* (translated here as "wholesome," with the preceding characters flowing into this phrase), *Sūtrasampadā* (translated as "practice").
These eight characters constitute the second phrase. Their original pronunciation is *Etad* (translated as "this"), *Buddhānām śāsanam* (translated as "the teaching of all Buddhas").
These eight characters constitute the fourth phrase. *Śikhī* means "crest," referring to a flame.
Regarding "Fire with Flames" (Agni): if fire possesses flames, its flaming appearance constitutes the "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa), and this is named Agni; here, it is translated as "Fire.
If one speaks of fire directly [without flames], it is "without characteristic" (alakṣaṇa). That which is proven by the sensation of heat is known to be without characteristic.

Section Two, Part Four: The Chapter on the Analysis of the Faculties (*Indriya-vibhaṅga*).

Within this section, there are five parts: first, the summary of what preceded; second, the statement that the characteristics of arising have been explained above; third, the citation of the preceding text;

fourth, the inquiry into which phenomena constitute the causes and conditions herein; fifth, the twenty-five verses beginning with "Now, the causes are of six kinds," within which [the following is contained].

The first twelve stanzas distinguish the six causes; following these, the subsequent thirteen stanzas—beginning with "Next, regarding mind and mental factors"—specifically clarify the four conditions.

Within the initial twelve stanzas, the first six distinguish the characteristics of the six causes, while the subsequent six, beginning with "Next, the pervasive and the similar," provide various categorical analyses. Within the first six stanzas, the first stanza is as follows:

Following the enumeration of the names of the six causes, the next five verses distinguish the essential characteristics of these six causes. Regarding the first verse: first, it asks what the six are; second, it provides the answer in verse form.
Within this, the first three lines list the names of the six causes, and the fourth line concludes that there are only six types of causes.

Subsequently, the verse is explained, which consists of three parts: first, the categories of the six causes are presented; second, they are enumerated; [and third, their characteristics are analyzed].

Regarding the explanation of the names of the six causes: the first three lines [of the verse] consist of three pairs of dharmas according to various masters; the subsequent line explains the fourth [point].

Within the analysis of the characteristics of the six causes according to the five types of verses, the first line distinguishes the characteristics of the *kāraṇa-hetu* (efficient cause). In this section, first the question is posed: "What are the characteristics of the first, the *kāraṇa-hetu*?
Next, the verse is cited as the answer. Finally, the text of the verse is explained. This explanation contains three parts: first...
The commentary on the root verse distinguishes between the essence and characteristics of the two types of causes.
Although the remaining five types of causes are all capable of producing effects, they are also termed "efficient causes" (*kāraṇa-hetu*).

While these other five causes possess both general and specific names, they are designated by their specific names rather than their general one; however, the single efficient cause has no further specific designation.

It receives a distinct designation different from the other five causes; although it is designated by a general term, it is itself a specific name—just as "the sphere of form" (*rūpāyatana*) or "the realm of form" (*rūpadhātu*) are general terms that function as specific names.
This efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*) excludes only its own nature, for all phenomena serve as efficient causes.
It is called an "efficient cause" because it produces an effect by way of not obstructing its arising; it is so named according to its function.
This is the name. From here below begins the third section: the analysis through question and answer. Within this, there are three questions and answers. The first asks:

"Is it not the case that because one has not yet known the truth of the dharmas, the ninety-eight afflictions and other outflows (*āsrava*) would arise? [The answer is: By means of knowing the truth of the dharmas..."
By principle, the ninety-eight afflictions do not arise indiscriminately; furthermore, wisdom acts as an obstacle to the arising of outflows (*āsrava*).

Just as sunlight can obstruct the visual consciousness from perceiving the stars, so too does sunlight act as an obstacle to the arising of visual consciousness. How then can conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*)—excluding their own selves—be considered efficient causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*) for all phenomena?

Next, the answer regarding wisdom: *Note: The provided text contains a mix of Chinese characters and Sanskrit terminology (e.g., *āsrava*, *kāraṇa-hetu*). The translation aims to preserve the technical philosophical content while rendering it into fluent English.*

Furthermore, light arises from outflows (*āsrava*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), which truly act as obstructions. At that time, it should be understood that these various outflows do not arise when they are not functioning as conditions;
likewise, when visual consciousness perceives stars at night, cognition and sunlight do not arise together.

Since those [obstructions] abide without obstructing, that cognition and light serve as the *kāraṇa-hetu* (efficient cause) for these outflows and consciousness. This is the second question and answer.

In this case, the arising of that fruit can act as an obstacle to this cause, just as the light of wisdom does not act as an obstacle to the outflowing consciousness (āsrava-vijñāna) and may be established as its cause.

Just as a sovereign of a nation may tolerate his subjects without harming them, if the arising of that fruit absolutely lacks the capacity [to obstruct] this cause, how could it be considered a cause even if it does not act as an obstacle? To point to the matter at hand: for example—

Regarding nirvāṇa and dharmas that will not arise in the future, when strictly compared to all conditioned dharmas that are subject to arising—such as the aggregates of the formless realm for a sentient being in hell—although these [nirvāṇa and so forth] exist in a manner similar to non-existence (like a rabbit’s horn), they lack the functional capacity to act as an obstacle.
Next, the answer is given: although they lack the function of obstructing, [they serve as causes].
Because at the time the fruit arises there is likewise no obstruction, it also functions as a cause.

This is like a powerless king who, although lacking the capacity to cause harm, is still spoken of in the same way as a powerful king. One might say, "I am at peace because my sovereign, though unable to act, does not harm me.
In this context, it is explained that all causes capable of producing [an effect] are *kāraṇa-hetu* (efficient causes). The *Nyāyapraveśa* states: "It is not..."
Regarding that which possesses the power to obstruct yet does not obstruct, and that which lacks the power to obstruct and thus does not obstruct:

there is a slight difference between them during the state of non-obstruction, because both equally lack the superior function of being an obstacle. However, if one speaks in terms of their distinct superior capacities, it is not that they lack the power to produce [their effects];
for example, the eye and visible forms in relation to the production of visual consciousness, food in relation to the body, and seeds in relation to [their sprouts].
Regarding sprouts and so forth, a third party raises this objection: "Since all phenomena abide without obstruction, they should all be capable causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
For what reason do phenomena not arise simultaneously? When one person commits killing, why is it that other people are not obstructed [from doing the same]?
And for what reason do all people not become established in the karma of killing just like the killer? Next, he explains this objection: It is not so; it is merely because...

It is accepted that all phenomena are *kāraṇa-hetu* (efficient causes) because they are not obstructed; this is not because there is a direct causal efficacy (*sākṣāt-kāraṇa-bala*) in the production of every effect.
Therefore, not all phenomena arise simultaneously, nor do all persons possess the direct power to kill;

it is not the case that everyone becomes an agent of the karma of killing simply by being present, as is the case with the actual killer. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, fascicle fifteen, states: "Therefore, with respect to the *kāraṇa-hetu* in relation to its [effect]..."

A fruit that is about to arise is not only unobstructed, but also possesses the power to arise; however, because it lacks the immediate cause (*samanantarapratyaya*) and the motivating cause (*hetusamutthāna*), all phenomena cannot arise simultaneously.
This is not like the case where all those who kill necessarily incur the karma of killing. The explanation states:

Although all phenomena are unobstructed, they cannot arise simultaneously because they lack their respective immediate causes. Likewise, although all people may be present, they do not all incur the karma of killing because they lack the specific causes for such an act.
Because they arise from a [specific] mental state, it is not the case that all who kill necessarily complete the karmic act of killing.

Thus far, we have clarified that there are two kinds of causes: first, the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), which lacks the power to produce [an effect] but is established as such because it merely does not obstruct;
for example, *nirvāṇa* and future dharmas that do not arise are both universally regarded as efficient causes with respect to the arising of all conditioned phenomena.
There is a generative power, such as that of the eye and visible forms toward the arising of visual consciousness and so forth;
according to other teachers, all *kāraṇa-hetu* (efficient causes) possess this generative power regarding the arising of their effects. Question:

For instance, how can things such as *nirvāṇa* or future dharmas that do not arise be said to possess generative power with respect to an effect such as visual consciousness? Answer: The mental consciousness takes them as its objects.

When a wholesome mind characterized by views of arising, or an unwholesome mind characterized by false views, arises with *nirvāṇa* and so forth as its object, subsequently, wholesome or unwholesome visual consciousnesses arise in succession due to this consciousness acting as their indirect cause (*pāramparyahetu*).

Thus, those [objects] such as *nirvāṇa* possess the power to produce the arising of visual consciousness. In the same manner, other phenomena should be understood accordingly through this method of successive causality.

It is known that although there is a generative power in the future with respect to the present—since there exists a successive generative power—the future lacks the generative power to grasp or yield a fruit.
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "Past dharmas act as the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) for the other two time periods;
those dharmas of the two periods, in turn, are the dominant fruits (*adhipati-phala*) of the past. Future dharmas [act as the efficient cause] for..."
The remaining two time periods [past and future] function as efficient causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*) because they do not constitute obstacles;

however, since those dharmas of the two time periods are neither simultaneous with nor subsequent to [the present], they do not serve as dominant results (*adhipati-phala*) for the future, for a result must necessarily be appropriated by a cause.

Thus, only two causes [the efficient cause and the co-existent cause] are admitted to apply across all three time periods solely on the basis of non-obstruction. As for present dharmas, they function as efficient causes for the other two time periods, and those two...
In the world, only future dharmas are the present fruit; conditioned and unconditioned [dharmas] are the cause;

conditioned and unconditioned [dharmas] are neither cause nor fruit; unconditioned [dharmas] are neither cause nor fruit; conditioned [dharmas] are the cause but not the fruit. For this reason, it is said:
"The efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu) is for the most part not the sovereign fruit (adhipati-phala). Why? Because...
All phenomena can act as efficient causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*), and only conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are sovereign fruits (*adhipati-phala*).

Among these, the following seven phrases distinguish the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*); therein are three sections: first, three phrases that correctly define the characteristics of the co-existent cause;
second, three phrases that distinguish the mental concomitants (*citta-anuvartin-dharma*); and finally, one phrase that explains the meaning of being a mental concomitant. Regarding this:
In the initial section of the text, there are three parts: first, a summary of what precedes and an inquiry regarding what follows; second, the presentation of a verse as a response;

and third, within that [verse], the first line establishes the thesis—that those which exist simultaneously and act as mutual effects constitute simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*). Next, its essential nature is indicated in four ways: (1) the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) in relation to one another;

(2) the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and the characterized (*lakṣya*) in relation to one another; (3) the mind (*citta*) and the mental concomitants (*caitasika*) that follow it in relation to one another; and (4) subsequent sections.
In the commentary on the verses, first, the initial phrase is explained as a question; second, the subsequent two phrases are explained as follows:

"Just as the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are mutually *sahabhū-hetu* (coexistent causes) as explained in the *Mahā-vibhāṣā*, so too are these characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) with the characterized phenomena (*lakṣya*), and the mind (*citta*) with its concomitants (*cittānuvartin*), mutually causes for one another. This explains the third [point].

The third section concludes: "Thus, the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), by virtue of being mutually the fruit of one another, exhaustively encompasses all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) as appropriate for each category.
It is not the case that all phenomena [are co-existent causes] with their secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*). The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* asks:

"Is it not the case that the mind (*citta*) and its secondary characteristics are not mutually fruits of one another, yet the mind and its secondary characteristics do constitute a co-existent relationship?"
The relationship between the primary cause (*mahābhūta*) and its derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) should also be understood in this way. Why is it not the case that by this analogy they are equal?

Although the mind and its secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) do not stand in a reciprocal causal relationship with one another, there is nonetheless a fixed principle that they stand in a reciprocal causal relationship;
furthermore, since the secondary characteristics of the mind share a single fruit with the mind, the mind stands as their simultaneous cause (*sahabhūhetu*).

Because there is no such relationship between the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*), the primary elements are not simultaneous causes (*sahabhūhetu*) for that [derived matter]. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Old *Vibhāṣā*) states:

"Those who assert that the power of the four great elements is untainted (*anāsrava*) maintain that among the co-arising causes, the three great elements—earth, water, and wind—are the causes for the earth element; those who assert that the power of the four great elements is tainted maintain that..."
Regarding the "outflows" (*āsrava*): the earth element is a co-arising cause for the three other elements, and those three elements are co-arising causes for the earth element.
Why is this so? Because the earth element possesses both a manifold nature and a unitary nature;
that which is manifold is a co-arising cause for that which is unitary, and so on, up to the wind element, which is likewise. The assessment states: as it is...

This proponent asserts that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), whether they possess outflow (*sāsrava*) or are without outflow (*anāsrava*), serve as co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) for one another:

the earth element (*pṛthivī-mahābhūta*) acts as a co-existent cause for the other three great elements, and the three great elements act as co-existent causes for the earth element. Why is this? Because the earth element does not arise without depending upon the earth element, yet it arises from derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).
As the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "Just as the four great primary elements (*mahābhūtāni*), when viewed in relation to one another, serve as co-existent causes despite their existence..."
Regarding the increase and non-increase of substance: these three and one are mutually causes for one another;
yet, a self-substance should not depend upon itself, nor should it depend upon the substance of causes and conditions, nor should it depend upon the substance of its own kind.

Each of the great elements depends solely on the other three; only when the four great elements of different kinds aggregate can they possess the functional capacity to produce derived matter (*bhautika*).

The definition of the cause (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*) stated here is too narrow, because it should be said that all mental concomitants (*citta-anuvartin*) and all primary characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are mutually simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) for one another. Furthermore, it should not be said that they are only mutual results (*phala*);
for the simultaneous causes and their characteristics are not mutual results, nor are the simultaneous causes and their characteristics mutual results. [If that were so,] what would be the result?
Therefore, this should be further analyzed as the characteristic of being a cause.

From here on, the three lines distinguish the dharmas that follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*). In the text, first there is the question, next the verse is cited as the answer, and finally the verse is explained.

Within the explanation of the verse, first the mental factors (*caitta*) are explained; below the section on the two dhyānas, the two types of restraint (*saṃvara*) are explained. Third, "those dharmas" refers to those [dharmas].
In the verse-commentary on the three types of discipline (*saṃvara*) among the mental factors (*caitta*), there are five explanations of characteristics:
the four explanations of those [disciplines] and the characteristics of the arising and so forth of the mind and mental factors. Sixth, the section beginning with "Thus" explains the third phrase.
The *Nyāyānusāra* asks: "Why are their secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) not mentioned? It does not state the reason for this omission; it will be explained later.

Now, to analyze the subsequent section explaining the meaning of "the mind's concomitants" (*cittānuvartin*), the text first poses a question, then presents a verse as the answer, and finally provides an exposition of that verse.

Within this exposition, there is first an explanation of the ten causes mentioned briefly in the verse. [The first] is by way of time (*kāla*): it means that these aforementioned concomitant phenomena share the same time as the mind.

[The second] is by way of fruit (*phala*); [the third] is by way of being wholesome (*kuśala*) and so forth. Regarding "by way of time," it means that these aforementioned concomitant phenomena and the mind are identical.

"Arising, abiding, and ceasing, as well as falling into the same time period, by way of having the same fruit, etc. means that this [mental factor] has the same fruit, the same maturation (*vipāka*), and the same outflow (*niṣyanda*) as the mind;

one should know that here, the former set—arising, abiding, and ceasing—manifests the sense of "simultaneity," while the latter set—the same fruit, etc.—manifests the sense of "commonality," each being distinct.
"By way of being wholesome, etc. means that this is wholesome, etc., in the same manner as the mind.
Because they are equal in nature, these ten reasons are called the *Cittānuvartana-siddhi-śāstra*. It asks:
"Is it not the case that by merely stating 'arising, abiding, and ceasing,' one already knows that they also fall within the same period [of time]?

Although this is indeed known—that they fall within the same period—one has still not yet understood that these phenomena and the mind are not separated from one another in the past or the future. Or, perhaps it is to demonstrate all...

Because they are non-arising phenomena (*anutpattidharma*), it is further stated that they "fall within a single time period" (*ekādhvapatita*). If this were so, one might simply say they "fall within a single time period.

However, this would not necessarily cause one to know for certain that they fall within a single time period. Would it not be the case that outflow fruits (*niṣyandaphala*) and ripening fruits (*vipākaphala*) are also subsumed under the category of "one fruit"?
How then can outflow and ripening fruits be spoken of as "one" outside of the category of "one fruit"? Indeed, this is so; the term "one fruit" used here [refers to the ripening fruit].
If one asks: "Does this statement not also encompass the outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) and the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*), since it is stated that they are 'also' included?

Although they are indeed included, they are not what is being clarified here. Furthermore, there are four types of virile fruits (*puruṣakāra-phala*): those that arise simultaneously, those that arise immediately, those that arise after an interval, and those that do not arise at all.
This [text] specifically clarifies the fruit that is not simultaneous with its cause, in order to preclude the view that it must arise simultaneously with its cause.

Within the assemblage of conjunction (*sāmagrī*), there is the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*); because this assemblage of conjunction is established as the fruit, it is not itself its own fruit of human effort.
This demonstrates that within the fruit of human effort of those [factors] arising simultaneously with it, there is no sense of being a "single fruit.

Therefore, the outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) and the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*) are cited separately. The commentary asks: "Is it not the case that..."? The question is: "Is it not so? (i.e., *nanu na*).

If one merely says that arising, abiding, and ceasing occur within a single lifetime, does this not mean one knows they also fall within a single world-age? The meaning of the answer below is as follows:
"Arising" refers to the characteristic of future birth, while "abiding" and "ceasing" refer to the present.

Although one thus knows they fall within the characteristics of the future and the present, because one has not yet understood how these factors relate to the mind of the past, nor [the nature of] those factors other than the characteristic of arising...
Because they are likewise not separate from the future world, the phrase "belonging to one time" is stated separately outside of arising, abiding, and ceasing.
Alternatively, it is to demonstrate that those dharmas which do not arise in the future world also belong to the future world;
since these too are dharmas that follow the mind, the phrase "belonging to one time" must be stated separately outside of arising, abiding, and ceasing. As for what was previously called "arising":
These are dharmas that are subject to arising in the future; "abiding" and "ceasing" are dharmas of the present. Furthermore, it is asked:

If this were so, one should simply say that dharmas are subsumed within a single time-period (*adhvan*), as this would exhaustively encompass them. Why then must one speak of "arising," "abiding," and "ceasing"?

If it were not so—if one were to merely say they are subsumed within a single time-period—it would not cause others to understand their beginning and end, because [the entire process] would be known only as being collectively subsumed within a single time-period. Thus, [the distinction is necessary].
In the future world, there are many moments of dharmas that initially exist together in the future;
subsequently, one moment of dharma flows into the present or the past, while the remaining moments of dharma still remain in the future.
It is not because they are said to fall together into a single world that one must separately speak of the arising, abiding, and ceasing of a single [dharma]. If dharmas are identical...

Since the arising and ceasing of a single lifetime must be known by others to necessarily fall within the same world-period (*loka-āyu*), one must specifically state "the arising and ceasing of a single lifetime" to distinguish it from other periods.
Furthermore, since this distinction exists even within the same time-period, both terms must be stated together.

Again, it is asked: Are not the outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) and the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*) also subsumed under the category of "concomitant fruits" (*anuvartaka-phala*)? How then can there be only one?

[Question: Is it not the case that, apart from the [primary] fruit, one separately speaks of the outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) and the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*)? [Answer: The response below states generally that this is indeed so;
however, the mention here of "one fruit" is based on a specific explanation, referring only to the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*).

Furthermore, [the questioner asks: "Is it not the case that since this term 'one fruit' is used generally, it also includes the outflowing and ripening fruits? [Answer: Although it is indeed based on the general statement of "one fruit,"...

This also includes results of equal outflow (*niṣyanda*) and maturation (*vipāka*); however, this section clarifies only the specific case of a single result versus the general case of multiple results, which is not what is being explained here.

Regarding the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*), there are generally said to be four types: first, the associated and co-existent causes (*samprayukta-hetu* and *sahabhū-hetu*), which produce [the result] simultaneously;

second, the condition of immediate succession (*samanantara-pratyaya*), which produces it without interval; third, the field and husband (*kṣetra-pati*), which produce it after a lapse of time; and fourth, the fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*), which is non-arising. As it is said:

The following passage extensively analyzes the meaning of this section, intending to demonstrate that the *puruṣakāra-phala* (fruit of human effort) which exists simultaneously with its cause is not a phenomenon that serves as a mutual fruit;

rather, it must necessarily share a single common fruit. This intent is to refute the position that holds that the *puruṣakāra-phala* exists only within the composite aggregate produced by the simultaneous arising of the associated [mental factors] and the co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*). This [aggregate] is what is associated and co-existent.

Because within a composite aggregate, factors act as mutual effects—just as perception (*saṃjñā*) and feeling (*vedanā*) are results of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) for one another—yet perception, in relation to its own essence, is not a result of human effort for that very essence;
and because within a single co-arising composite aggregate there are both results of human effort and those that are not, it is necessary to exclude them.
Thus, having excluded [the possibility] that the associated and co-existent causes (*samprayukta-hetu* and *sahabhū-hetu*) within the same aggregate constitute results of human effort:
Because it is a fruit, it is shown that among the simultaneous, co-arising, and combined *puruṣakāra-phala* (fruits of human effort), there is no sense of a "single fruit.

Therefore, apart from the single fruit, the fruits of *niṣyanda* (outflow) and *vipāka* (maturation) are separately mentioned as being present at the same time. These fruits—namely, those that arise together (*samprayukta*), follow along (*anuvartin*), or are acquired simultaneously (*sahaprāpta*)—are of the nature of *niṣyanda* and *vipāka* fruits;
there is no need to exclude the *puruṣakāra-phala*, for even that can exclusively take what is immediately subsequent (*anantara*).

Regarding the "single fruition of human effort" (*puruṣakāra-phala*) of non-arising factors, it is also evident that the co-arising and concomitant aggregates attain this same single fruition of human effort without the need to exclude their own selves.
However, when discussing the fruition of human effort within a composite aggregate of associated and co-existent factors, one must exclude the self;
thus, there are cases where factors share the same fruition and cases where they do not share the same fruition, as is the case with feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) as fruits.
Feeling (*vedanā*) does not share a single fruit with perception (*saṃjñā*), because feeling, when considered in relation to its own self-nature, is not its own fruit.

Furthermore, perception serves as the fruit for feeling, yet perception does not share a single fruit with feeling, because perception, when considered in relation to its own self-nature, is not its own fruit. However, perception and feeling are mutually "concomitant" (*anuvartaka*) in their mutual relationship, and thus they are called fruits of one another;
this is because they do not share a single fruit [with each other], but rather arise together in a harmonious aggregate (*sāmagrī*).

Regarding the "single fruit" for those of middling capacity, this does not mean the sense of a single fruit [in general]. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that "one fruit" refers to the fruit of liberation (*vimukti-phala*).
The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* states that "one fruit" refers to... [text fragment].

From here below is the second section, which concerns the mental factors (*caitta*) that follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*). Regarding the relationship of these mental factors to the mind as causes, the text clarifies the scope of their application through the dharma of mindfulness (*smṛti*).
Specifically, from the second *dhyāna* upward, for the resultant mind and mental factors, there are eleven factors;

when combined with the eight great and small characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), they total ninety-nine. Alternatively, one may proceed by considering only the mind-king (*cittarāja*) and those factors common to its operation. This is what is included here.
Among those with causes, the minimum number of co-existent factors for a mind-king (*citta-rāja*) relative to its concomitant mental states (*cittānuparivartin-dharma*) is two:
in the case of an indeterminate mind from the second dhyāna upward, it acts as a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) for ninety-eight dharmas;

specifically, ten universal ground dharmas (*mahābhūmika*), their forty primary characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and the eight primary and four secondary characteristics of the mind, totaling fifty-eight dharmas. The remaining [dharmas] are included among the universal ground dharmas.

The forty secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) are not causes. If one considers the ninety-eight [factors] in relation to the fifty-eight [factors] of the mind-king (*cittarāja*), excluding the four secondary characteristics of the mind itself, the remaining fifty-four are co-existent causes (*sahabhūhetu*) for the mind; the other forty-four are not causes.

Regarding the nine factors—birth (*jāti*) and so forth—that arise upon the mind-king within the ninety-eight, fifty-eight are causes and forty are not causes. Among the ninety-eight [factors], [the secondary characteristics of the mental concomitants are not causes].
The fifty-five "births" (*jāti*) are causes, meaning they pervade the fourteen primary characteristics (*mūla-lakṣaṇa*), the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), and the three great characteristics;
the remaining forty-two are not causes, meaning they pervade the aforementioned forty minor characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) and the three minor characteristics of the mind-king.
As with the "great birth" (*mahā-jāti*) above the mind-king, the other three great characteristics are likewise. As with the four great characteristics above the mind-king, the others are also so.

The same applies to the forty major characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) mentioned above. If one considers a minor arising on the level of the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) in relation to the ninety-eight [major characteristics], it serves as a cause for only one major arising;

the other ninety-seven are not causes. If one considers the ninety-eight [characteristics] in relation to a minor arising, there are five causes—namely, the mind-king and the four major characteristics;
the remaining fifty-three are not causes. This is the same as in the case of a minor arising on the level of the mind-king.

The same applies to the other three minor characteristics (*anuvyañjana*). Just as the four minor characteristics on the primary mind-king (*citta-rāja*) extend upward to the forty [characteristics], so too do the minor characteristics on the mind extend upward.

Question: Since the minor characteristics on the mind do not characterize the mind-king itself, yet the major characteristics extending upward are similar [in their relation to the mind], why are the major characteristics extending upward the causes for the mind-king, whereas the four minor characteristics on the mind are not? The Dharma Master has already reflected upon this.

Previously, based on two reasons, it was distinguished that the [mental] factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*) are pervasive with respect to the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), because they possess both the causes of association (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) and co-existence (*sahabhū-hetu*).

Therefore, they are pervasive with respect to the higher [mental] factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*). This is not because they are the co-existent cause with respect to the mind-king; rather, it is because the higher *mahābhūmika-dharma* and the lower *parīttabhūmika-dharma* are both co-existent causes with respect to the mind-king.
Regarding the fact that the lower *parīttabhūmika-dharma* (such as *saṃjñā*) is not a co-existent cause with respect to the mind-king, the Dharma Master [Hui]yi says: "It is pervasive."

The forty major characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the superior [dharmas] possess the power to produce their corresponding characterized phenomena (*lakṣya*), and because they are equal [in this regard], they are considered causes with respect to the mind-king (*cittarāja*).

The minor characteristics of the superior [dharmas] possess inferior power to produce their corresponding characterized phenomena; because they are unequal, they are not considered causes with respect to the mind-king. The *Nyāyapravēśa* (Treatise on Right Reasoning) asks:

"Why are the secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) of the mind not co-existent causes (*sahabhūhetu*) of the mind? The answer is: "First, it is not by the power of those [secondary characteristics] that the mind [arises]."
1. Because they arise [simultaneously]; 2. because the two minds do not serve as mutual fruits for one another; 3. because they possess efficacy toward a single dharma; 4.
because they do not share the same fruit as the mind-king (*citta-rāja*); and 5.

because, within the aggregate, many parts are not their fruits—by virtue of these many stated reasons, according to their characteristics, they are not called "dharmas that follow the mind" (*cittānuvartaka*). If this is so, how then are they related to the mind?
It can serve as a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) for them because they arise and so forth in accordance with the various states of the mental sovereign (*citta-rāja*).
Should it not be the case that, just as with the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), the mind also takes them as its co-existent cause? The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* asks:

"Should it not be the case that, just as with the arising of the primary elements, the mind also takes them as its co-existent cause? This means that just as derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) is not [the cause], [the mind is likewise not].
The arising and so forth of the effects are not such that they do not serve as co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) for the primary elements (*mahābhūta*);

this case should be understood in the same way. Such an analogy, however, is logically inconsistent: while the reciprocal effects belong to one realm (*dhātu*), they are not necessarily of that same realm.

Furthermore, it is not the case that all derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) is subsumed within the reciprocal effects of the primary elements; it is possible for derived matter to exist without being the effect of all the primary elements.
Because they produce results such as arising (*jāti*), these are cited as examples of what is common (*sādhāraṇa*), just as was stated previously. What was stated previously? It was said:

"It is not by the power of those [characteristics] that the mind can arise. To explain this, he asks: "Is it not equal? This is a question asking: "Should it not be like the four characteristics—arising and so forth—that exist upon the four great elements (*mahābhūta*)?

Just as the four great elements equally obtain the result of derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), do the arising and other characteristics existing upon the great elements not likewise [apply] to the great elements themselves?"
The derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) and the primary elements (mahābhūta) share the same arising-characteristics (jāti-lakṣaṇa) and so forth as their co-existent causes (sahabhū-hetu).

Although the minor characteristics (anulakṣaṇa) of the primary elements do not share a common result with the mind-king (citta-rāja), the mind-king should nevertheless take those minor characteristics as its co-existent causes.
To point out the specific case below: it is not the case that derived matter and the primary elements do not have the same resultant dharmas, such as arising, as their single fruit.

The four primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that arise together with others are not non-coexistent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) for those other primary elements; likewise, these minor characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) should also be so.

Furthermore, although they share the same fruit as the mental sovereign (*citta-rāja*)—namely, the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) and so forth—they should likewise not fail to be coexistent causes for that mental sovereign.
How can it be said that because they do not share the same fruit as the mental sovereign, the minor characteristics are not [coexistent causes]?
"Is it a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) for the mind? To this, the answer below is: "It is so. The principle of the examples cited here is not uniform.

Within a single mental complex (*citta-kalāpa*), those dharmas that are mutually resultant (*anyonya-phala*) obtain a single fruit; however, the many subordinate characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) upon the mental king (*citta-rāja*) are not the single-fruit dharmas of that [mind].
Only the four major characteristics (*mahā-lakṣaṇa*) upon the mental king are the single-fruit dharmas of the minor characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*). This does not apply to all [other] factors.

Since derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) is subsumed under one of the mutual fruits among the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), how could it be that derived matter is not the fruit of the four characteristics—arising and so forth—of those primary elements?
However, as for its being a cause for the primary elements, this is analogous to the minor characteristics;
just as they differ from the mental sovereign (*citta-rāja*), even though they share a single fruit, the mind likewise takes the minor characteristics as its simultaneous cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
If you ask why it was stated previously that [the minor four characteristics] do not arise from the mind, the answer is as follows:

because the minor four characteristics are the co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) of the mind; however, since the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and the four characteristics based upon those primary elements arise through their mutual influence, the minor four characteristics do not arise simultaneously with the mental substance (*citta-rāja*) in the same manner as the primary elements.

Regarding this error, the second teacher asserts that there are only fourteen factors that serve as causes for the mind—namely, the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*), the four primary characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the mind, and the four secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) of those fourteen.
The remaining eighty-four factors are not causes. The Master [Vasubandhu], in the subsequent treatise, refutes this, saying: "This explanation is not correct. Why?
Because the claim that these fourteen factors are the causes contradicts what is stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*. As stated in the first... [of that treatise].
The ninth fascicle states: "There may be a *duḥkhasatya* that has the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as its cause, but does not serve as the cause for the view of a self-identity.
This refers to [those factors] in the future existence, excluding the future view of a self-identity and its associated factors, as well as their arising, duration, aging, and impermanence;
these are excluded because they constitute the second 'conjunction' category. All other defiled *duḥkhasatya*s are [the subject]."

The nature of the view of self-existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in future lives, its acquisition (*prāpti*), the four minor characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of that acquisition, as well as the associated factors (*saṃprayuktadharma*), the acquisition of those associated factors,

the four minor characteristics of those associated factors, their acquisitions, and the acquisitions of the remaining nine [defilements] of the lower category of future suffering— along with their associated, co-existent, and other acquisitions—
are the characteristics of the non-universal proclivities (*asarvatragakleśa*) abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin in the past and present.

The dharmas that are to be abandoned by the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-heya*), whose seeds are exhausted, including their simultaneous acquisitions (*sahabhū-prāpti*) and the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*),

as well as those dharmas of the three times to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*) and the path (*mārga-darśana-heya*) whose seeds are exhausted, and all defiled (*kliṣṭa*) dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),

are all subsumed under the first category of the remaining defiled truths of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). Regarding the second category, there may be certain truths of suffering which have the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) as their cause and are also [the cause] of...
The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is both a cause and that which was previously excluded;

furthermore, since the factors associated with the view of a self-identity—namely its birth, aging, duration, and impermanence—arise from the view of a self-identity and also serve as causes for it, they fall within the category of "simultaneous exclusion.

Thus, one should know that the forty great characteristics (*mahālakṣaṇa*) throughout the four stages of the great earth act as simultaneous causes (*sahabhūhetu*) for the mental sovereign (*cittarāja*). Others maintain there are only fourteen.

The Dharma is a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) for the mind; other masters state this in their verses. However, when the text opens the discussion on "various matters," it does not include the associated dharmas (*saṃprayukta-dharma*) in its verses.

Since all five schools include them in their verses—excepting the future [dharmas], the view of self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), and birth, aging, duration, and impermanence—it is known that the four great characteristics (*mahā-lakṣaṇa*) of the higher stages are included among those not excluded. Thus, they apply universally to the great stages.
The Vaibhāṣikas state that [the view of self] does not serve as a simultaneous cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) for the mind-king (*citta-rāja*).

They say that the text of the *Prakaraṇapāda* should have recited the verse as follows: "Excluding the future view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and its associated factors (*saṃprayukta-dharma*), [as well as their] arising, aging, duration, and impermanence.

If it did not include the phrase "and its associated factors," then the meaning would imply that [the view of self] serves as a simultaneous cause; therefore, the statement is an incomplete one (*sāvasesa*).
In the *Nyāyānusāra*, the second master states as follows: "We do not recite [the sūtras] nor their associated dharmas;

rather, we should only retain the treatises after having analyzed them according to their underlying principles. Therefore, this [objection] may undermine the definition of the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), or one must instead accept the explanation of the co-existent cause as it applies to the sixth consciousness.
This indicates that the intention of that second master lies in the mind.

Because the primary characteristics (*mahābhūtalakṣaṇa*) are separated by the secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjanalakṣaṇa*), they are not simultaneous causes (*sahabhūhetu*) with respect to the mind; thus we know that the secondary characteristics generally separate [the primary ones] from the great ground [of mental factors].

Therefore, with respect to the mind, they are not simultaneous causes. Even if the secondary characteristics of the great elements are separated by the secondary characteristics of the great ground, they still serve as simultaneous causes for the mind.
Likewise, although the minor characteristics upon the mind are separated by the major characteristics, they too should serve as simultaneous causes for the mind.
The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* masters explain that the primary mental factors (*caitasika*) are not co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) for the mind because they possess five characteristics;
conversely, the universal secondary characteristics (*mahābhūmika-nimitta*) are co-existent causes for the mind because they lack those five characteristics.

If one does not include the phrase "and their associated dharmas" [in the verse], it would contradict the five characteristics of the minor characteristics (*parīttabhūmika*). Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states that there are others.

The third master says that all members of a simultaneous assemblage are mutually *sahabhū-hetu* (co-existent causes) for one another, because within such an assemblage, if even one element is missing, the remaining factors will not arise. Among these various explanations, the first is the most correct.
Furthermore, within this co-arising assemblage, there is that which is the "transformer" (*pravartaka*) rather than the "concomitant" (*anuvartaka*), namely, this mind (*citta*).
The King has only those that are "concomitants" (anuvartaka), namely matter (rūpa) and the mind-dissociated factors (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra).

There are those that are both "active agents" (pravartaka) and "concomitants," namely the mental factors (caitasika-dharma), because they follow the mind and act as concomitants, while also acting as active agents for the mind-dissociated formations.
There are two types that are neither, namely the remaining characteristics (lakṣaṇa) and so forth, excluding the three aforementioned categories.
From here below is the third section, which distinguishes the universal and the restricted through the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).

Regarding the principle that "because something is a co-existent cause, it is necessarily a co-existent cause," the meaning is restricted. Alternatively, there may be things that are co-existent but do not function as a co-existent cause;

there are four such cases: first, the various secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) existing in relation to their primary dharmas; second, these various secondary characteristics being mutually related to one another; [and so forth].

1. The dharmas that follow the mind (cittānuvartin) and their secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇa) are mutually related to the mind in four ways. 2. These various secondary characteristics are mutually related to one another in six ways. 3.
The non-obstructive derived matter (avijñaptirūpa) produced by the mind and arising simultaneously with it is mutually related to other such matter in seven ways.

4. All co-arising derived matter and the primary elements (mahābhūta) are mutually related in eight ways. 5. All co-arising acquisitions (prāpti) and the factors acquired (prāpyadharma) are mutually related in nine ways.

When these eight pairs of dharmas, such as the "turning" and so forth, are examined in relation to one another, although they are called "coexistent," they do not constitute a cause by virtue of being a coexistent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
This is because they do not share a single fruit, a single maturation (*vipāka*), or a single uniform outflow (*niṣyanda*);

furthermore, the "attainer" and the "attained" are not necessarily simultaneous, as they may occur either before or after. Even if they arise simultaneously, because they are remote from one another, they are not a coexistent cause. — [The Sautrāntika School] states this in a single sutra.

Question: Although all the principles of cause and effect discussed above may be granted for the sake of argument according to your logic, we have never observed such simultaneous causes and effects within the worldly phenomena of seeds and sprouts, which are universally accepted as being established through a sequence of mutual production.
Therefore, you must now explain how there can be a commonality among the clusters of dharmas that arise simultaneously.

At that time, the two Sarvāstivādins replied: "Is it not clearly perceived that the lamp-flame and the lamp-light are simultaneous causes and effects, and that the sprout and its shadow are likewise simultaneous causes and effects?

The Sautrāntikas then countered this, providing a detailed analysis of whether [the cause and effect] are identical, as the Sarvāstivādins maintain regarding a three-inch lamp-flame being simultaneously the cause and the light within the room.
Is it like the Sautrāntika school’s view that, due to the causal conditions of the previous person’s effort, lamp, vessel, oil, and wick, at a later time both the flame and the light arise together?
Are both the later flame and the light the joint fruit of those preceding conditions?

It is like when the sun first rises in the east: its original existence arises from the earth, and the minute particles (paramāṇu) of the sprout arise together; thereafter, [the light] extends to the eastern limit.

If a minute particle to the west of the light-obstructing tooth obstructs the light while its own shadow appears there, yet a minute particle to the east of the tooth obstructs the light so that no shadow appears, while a minute particle to the west of the tooth’s shadow appears as a shadow without obstructing the light—how can it be said that this function of the shadow has the tooth as its cause?
(4) The Sarvāstivādins [hold] that there is no principle of simultaneous fruit according to the Sautrāntikas; such [a position] should not be so. Fruit...

Since phenomena necessarily exist or do not exist in accordance with their causes, those in the world who understand the principles of logic explain the characteristics of cause and effect as follows:
if a result exists or does not exist depending on whether its cause exists or does not exist, that which is invariably followed is the cause, and that which invariably follows is the effect.
Among all co-existent phenomena, every phenomenon is a cause for every other phenomenon, and every phenomenon is an effect of every other phenomenon.
If a phenomenon (*dharma*) were the cause and all phenomena were not its effect, it would be illogical for them to constitute cause and effect.

The Sautrāntika school rebuts this by asserting that even if simultaneous cause and effect were possible according to your reasoning, you must next explain how they can be said to be mutual causes of one another.
The Sarvāstivāda replies: "Precisely because of what was stated previously—since all things exist and do not exist in relation to one another—they are all [mutual causes]."
