The earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) frequently acts as a support for others, yet although many instances of the earth element arise simultaneously, they are not *sahabhū-hetu* (coexistent causes) for one another;

this is because derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) is not produced by the earth element itself. Furthermore, the eight subtle particles (*aṇu*) that constitute derived matter, though inseparable from one another, lack the power to support each other reciprocally;
thus, they are not *sahabhū-hetu*. This is the case whether one great element among the four is considered in relation to the other three, or two great elements are considered in relation to one.
When things look toward one another with power, they abide by mutually supporting each other, like the three staffs of the world;

in this way, the principle of cause and effect for simultaneously existing phenomena (*sahabhū-dharma*) is established. Now, the Sautrāntika school cites a refutation and says: "Regarding the so-called [nine] sūtras," etc.
The Sautrāntikas urge the Sarvāstivādins: "This should be considered: do these three staffs abide through the power of mutual dependence arising simultaneously? Or [is it otherwise]?
Is it because of the combined power of the causes and conditions—the accumulation of human effort from previous lives—that those three sticks arise and remain together?
Or is there also some other distinct substance within them, such as a cord, a hook, or the ground, that simultaneously connects and supports them so they remain?
The Sarvāstivādins answer: Among these four conditions for the three sticks, there is also another factor of the same kind and equal status.
The power of three staffs supporting one another as they arise together is a metaphor for the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
Second, the harmonious conjunction of the previously arisen three staffs as similar causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) so that [the structure] arises from those three staffs is the similar cause.

Third, other entities such as ropes, hooks, and the ground which maintain and support it are the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*). Therefore, just as the three staffs abide by mutually supporting one another, [so too do these causes].

The meaning of the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) is established by this: the non-Buddhist practitioners of the Western Regions (India) always carry three staffs with them for the purpose of securing their food vessels and other items.
They bind the three staffs together at their centers with a rope, set them upright on the ground, and place a hook upon them to hang their belongings from.
Nowadays, those who observe [this practice] simply place their food vessels [therein]. On the sixteenth day of the sixth month of the year Guihai, he was born.
This establishes the master who composed the *Jñānaprasthāna* [in the form of] a commentary on the *Śāstra*.
Above, the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) was clarified; next, one and a half verses distinguish the similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*). In the main text of this section, there are three parts:

first, a summary that concludes the preceding and introduces the subsequent question; second, the citation of the verse as the answer; third, the explanation of the verse itself. Regarding the first part, the initial phrase is explained as follows:
Wholesome five aggregates serve as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) for wholesome five aggregates when viewed reciprocally;
the same applies to defiled (*kliṣṭa*) aggregates for defiled ones, with no further divergent explanations. Regarding the neutral (*avyākṛta*) five aggregates, there are four differing views.
The *Vibhāṣā* states that some say the non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) five aggregates serve as reciprocal causes, while others say they do not.

The four neutral aggregates (*avyākṛta-skandha*) serve as causes for the non-obscured-neutral form aggregate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-rūpa-skandha*), yet the form aggregate does not serve as a cause for the non-obscured-neutral four aggregates.

Why? Because its nature is weak and inferior. Furthermore, some say that the non-obscured-neutral form aggregate serves as a cause for the non-obscured-neutral four aggregates, [but] the non-obscured-neutral...
The four aggregates do not act as causes for the non-obscured-neutral form aggregate. Why is this?
Because the four aggregates are superior dharmas, whereas the form aggregate is an inferior dharma; a superior dharma does not act as a cause for an inferior dharma.
Furthermore, some say that the four non-obscured-neutral aggregates do not act as causes for the non-obscured-neutral form aggregate, nor does the form aggregate [act as a cause for them].

Regarding [the unconditioned] acting as a cause for the four aggregates, the current *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* is likewise identical [to the *Mahāvibhāṣā*]. Although there are four theories in the *Vibhāṣā*, none provide a formal evaluation (*an-avadhāraṇa*).
Based on the *Kātyāyanīputra-sūtra*, the fourth teacher’s position is correct; thus, Kātyāyanīputra states: "The four great elements and the mind-base (*manāyatana*) are each predominant.

Since the four great elements are the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and the mind-base is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), it is known that the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) aggregate of form does not act as a cause for the four indeterminate [aggregates]."

Because it is said that the form-aggregate (*rūpa-skandha*) acts as a cause for the four mental aggregates (*nāma-skandha*), yet the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) conditioned roots do not act as causes for the indeterminate unconditioned roots, we know that the four indeterminate mental aggregates do not act as causes for the indeterminate form-aggregate.
Next, regarding the mutual relationship across ten time periods, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"Furthermore, some say that while material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) have similar causes, they likewise do not act as causes for similar phenomena."
Regarding that which acts as a cause by way of similarity: it acts as a cause for what is similar to this body, but does not act as a cause for what is similar to other bodies.
As for acting as a cause for what is similar to this body, it is like this body at the stage of the *kalala* acting as a similar cause for the *kalala*.
An example of acting as a dissimilar cause is as when the *kalala* acts as a cause for old age.
In this way, when this body is at the stage of *arbuda*, it acts as the cause for the *arbuda* stage and so forth, acting as the cause even until the stage of old age;

furthermore, it acts as the condition (*pratyaya*) for the *kalala* stage. Likewise, when this body is at the stage of old age, it acts as the cause for the stage of old age and as the condition for other stages, yet it is not the cause [for those others].
If one were to speak in this manner, then the initial *kalala* would be without a cause, and the final form would likewise be without a cause.
Thus, there would be no fruit; yet there are those who further claim that material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) act as similar causes for similar phenomena,
acting as causes both for similar phenomena within this very body and for similar phenomena in other bodies,
while similar phenomena in other bodies likewise act as causes for similar phenomena in this body, and the similar phenomena in this body also act as causes for similar phenomena in other bodies.
A dharma that acts as a cause at one time may act as a condition and not a cause at another time.

Likewise, when the aging of another body acts as a cause for the aging of this body, the aging of this body in turn acts as a cause for the aging of that other body; it acts as a cause at one time, but at another time it acts as a condition and not a cause.
Furthermore, some say that material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) possess similar causes and act as causes for similar dharmas.
It acts as a cause for dissimilar dharmas; it acts as a cause for this body and also acts as a cause for other bodies.
For example, the *kalala* of another body acts as a cause for the *kalala* of this body, and that *kalala* of this body acts as a cause up until the stage of old age;
likewise, the *kalala* of this body acts as a cause for the *kalala* of another body, and so on.
When the *ābudha* of another body at the time of old age acts as a cause for the *ābudha* of this body, continuing until the time of old age;

and when the *ābudha* of this body acts as a cause for the *ābudha* of another body, continuing until the time of old age—at the stage of the *kalala*, it acts as a condition (*pratyaya*) and not as a cause. When the [body] of another at the time of old age [acts for] this body...
At the time of aging, this body acts as the cause for the aging of other bodies; at the time of aging, it acts as the cause for others.

The commentary states: "One should state it thus: the ten stages of other bodies act as causes for the ten stages of this body, and the ten stages of this body act as causes for the ten stages of other bodies.
External phenomena should be understood to be stated accordingly. Now, in this case...
In the text, the commentators state that within this single continuum of existence, the initial stage of the *kalala* can act as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for all ten stages;
each of the nine subsequent stages, such as the *arbuda*, acts as a cause for the remaining stages by excluding its own predecessor.
When compared with other subsequent continua of the same type, each stage likewise serves as a cause for all ten subsequent stages. One should apply this same principle by analogy.
Grain, rice, and so forth act as causes for their own respective classes. Next, [the author] refutes the Dārṣṭāntika school:

if one does not admit that matter (*rūpa*) is a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for matter, then that position contradicts what is stated in the original treatise. The *Kātyāyanīputra-śāstra* states:

"Past primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are the causes, conditions, and bases for future primary elements. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* says: "The Dārṣṭāntikas maintain that material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) lack similarity."
Because of the power of conditions, that phenomenon arises. How so? It is like digging a pit one hundred cubits deep and bringing forth mud;
then, through rain from the heavens, exposure to the sun, and the blowing of the wind, grass immediately grows.

Thus, although this mud has never produced anything before, or like grass and trees growing upon a roof where nothing had ever grown before—this place likewise has never produced anything—it is inferred that these act as similar causes for one another. Question: If...
However, how is that passage to be reconciled? As it is said: "The past four great elements and the future four great elements have causes, conditions, and supporting factors.
To this, he replies: "I do not have such a sūtra. It was spoken as previously described for the purpose of making such a text known.
For this reason, it is not necessarily required to provide a reconciliation. If one insists on reconciling it, how should one reconcile it with that Vaiśeṣika [position]?

There are two kinds of conditions: those that are proximate and those that are remote; those that exist within this very body and those that exist in other bodies are called causes (*hetu*), while those that are remote and exist in other bodies are called conditions (*pratyaya*).
The Abhidharmikas state that material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) have similar causes (*sabhāga-hetu*).

Question: If such [similar causes] exist, how do you account for what is taught by the Dārṣṭāntikas? Answer: [The Dārṣṭāntikas say: "If there were [such a cause], it would contradict their own position."
Because there are seeds residing within those phenomena that have not yet obtained the conditions for the sprout to arise, they do not grow; however, once those conditions are obtained, they do grow.
For instance, regarding grass and trees growing upon a roof, they may arise after a bird has brought a seed in its beak or the wind has blown one there;
it is for this reason that material phenomena possess a similar cause.

In the second [section], explaining the text regarding one's own category (*sva-nikāya*) and level (*bhūmi*), there are five parts: first, the question as to whether all similar [dharmas] are homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) for similar dharmas;
second, the answer that this is not so; third, the inquiry as to why; fourth, the citation of a verse answering that they are [homogeneous causes] for their own category and other levels;
fifth, the restriction that they act as causes only for their own category and own level—the detailed explanation below is easily understood.

Third, regarding the explanation of the preceding section on "previous births": first, the thesis is stated; second, there are two questions—namely, why this specific stage within one's own school (*sva-nikāya-bhūmi*) is not universal;

third, the verse is cited as the answer. Specifically, four questions are raised concerning how it is known that [the cause] belongs to a previous birth. Fifth, the answer is given: because the *Mūla-śāstra* states so, just as the *Kātyāyanīputra-abhidharma-śāstra* (Jñānaprasthāna) says:
"What is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*)? It is the wholesome roots of a previous birth [that serve as the cause] for those of a subsequent..."

Because the produced roots of goodness and their associated dharmas serve as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) for one another within their own realm, they constitute a cause. The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: Question:
For what reason are the previously arisen roots of goodness not said to have associated dharmas [as their cause], while the subsequently arisen roots of goodness are said to have associated dharmas?
Answer: That which should have been stated but was not stated, one should know that this statement is incomplete (*sāvaśeṣa*). Furthermore, there is another explanation: ...

In order to stop [the misconception that] a śramaṇa might be similar to a dharma, he says this: wholesome roots act as a similar cause for wholesome actions, but wholesome factors associated with wholesome roots do not act as a similar cause for wholesome roots;

wholesome factors associated with wholesome roots act as a similar cause for wholesome factors associated with wholesome roots, but wholesome factors do not [act as a similar cause] for wholesome roots.

It is with this intention that he says: "of its own realm" means that the desire realm acts as a similar cause for the desire realm, and so on, up to the formless realm acting as a similar cause for the formless realm. There is no [similar cause] for what is non-existent.
Regarding the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), as it was explained for one's own realm and own stage (*svadhātu-svabhūmi*), so it is [for others].

Regarding "the past and so forth," the *Vibhāṣā* states: "Past wholesome roots act as similar causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) for future and present [wholesome roots], and past and present [wholesome roots] act as similar causes for future wholesome roots.
Question: Why is this treatise composed once again? Answer: To distinguish [the relationship] across different time periods (*adhvan*).

Regarding the statement that the sequence of words is not disordered, that treatise subsequently clarifies—based on the *Vibhāṣā*—that if there were a "homogeneous cause" (*sabhāga-hetu*) in the future, there would be two difficulties:
first, the original sūtra does not mention it; second, there is the difficulty of two minds acting as causes for one another in succession.
If such a cause did not exist, there would be six difficulties; thus the *Vibhāṣā* asks: "Does a similar cause exist in the future?"

If it were not the case that [the future] exists, why would it not be stated here—just as it is stated—that the past acts as a similar cause for the future and the present, and the past and present act as similar causes for the future; yet it does not state that the future acts as a similar cause for the future?
If it exists, how could two minds not be reciprocal causes for one another? If it does not exist, then this statement [is made].
Question: How is it that a phenomenon acts as a cause for another phenomenon, or at times does not act as a cause for that phenomenon?

Answer: No. Question: If this phenomenon acts as a cause for that phenomenon at one time and does not act as a cause at another time—if it acts as a cause when the phenomenon arises and does not act as a cause when it does not arise—why is this so?
If one asks how the statement "it is not so" would apply to those who do not exist, such as the Kāḷāmas, how is it to be reconciled with the teaching:

"What are the dharmas that are not causes of the mind? The answer is: the first untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) of a person who has attained right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*). [This applies also to] all other ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) who are certain to attain right determination;
their first untainted mind [is likewise not a cause]. Question: As for those who have not yet attained right determination, [how is this to be understood]? One...
If all untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*) are dharmas that do not serve as causes for other minds, why does the sūtra speak only of the "first" untainted mind?

If it were otherwise, it would contradict other statements in this same sūtra, such as: "The Truth of Suffering has either the power of vision as its cause, or does not have the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) as its cause," and so forth at length, including:
"The view of a self-identity serves as a cause [for itself], but does not [serve as a cause] for the view of a self-identity."

Regarding the cause as a producer (*janaka-hetu*): it consists of all defiled *duḥkha-satya* (the truth of suffering) other than the past and present latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) and their associated factors;
other than the past and present universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) and their associated factors;
and other than future views of a self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and their associated factors. This is what is meant by [the cause as a producer].
Regarding the question of whether the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) serves as a cause for itself, but not for another instance of the view of a self:

if it is asked why a future *satkāyadṛṣṭi* does not act as a cause for [another] future *satkāyadṛṣṭi*, [the answer is: because one excludes the future *satkāyadṛṣṭi* and those factors associated with the view of a self;
if these did not exist, how would the *Vijñānakāya-sūtra* be reconciled? As it says: "In past defiled visual consciousness, the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) also..."

Are those which are latent dispositions (anuśaya) also causes (hetu)? And are those which are causes also latent dispositions? One should formulate four permutations (catuṣkoṭi) extensively: 1. Those which are causes but are not made latent by latent dispositions:

these are the latent dispositions that exist prior to that mind, all those of one's own realm (svadhātu) that do not take it as an object, and those that have already been abandoned even if they were previously objects;

as well as those associated with the latent dispositions that are liberated from them. 2. Those which are made latent by latent dispositions but are not causes: these are the latent dispositions existing in that [mind]... [text fragment].

Regarding those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that follow after this mind, which are universal (*sarvatraga*) within their own realm, are uninterrupted, and are both causes and activators (*paryavasthāna*):
these are the latent dispositions present prior to this mind, which are universal within their own realm, uninterrupted, associated (*samprayukta*), and not yet liberated [from them];

they are neither causes nor activators. Regarding those latent dispositions that abide following this mind, which are universal within their own realm but are not objects of perception (*ālambana*): [they are as described above].
If one has already abandoned all pervasive latent tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) of other realms, then by analogy with the past, future, and present, they should likewise not be [abandoned].
One should formulate four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) for this. While the four propositions regarding the past and present may be acceptable, how can those regarding the future be reconciled?
If they do not exist, how can the *Prajñapti-śāstra* be reconciled? As it says: "All phenomena have four matters: first, the cause; second..."
If the three bases of the fruit and the four objects of focus did not exist, how could there be an effect without a cause?
Since there is no cause, there would be no fruit. One should answer thus: in the future world, there is no similar cause because it does not exist;
for this reason, it is not mentioned. Furthermore, there is no fault of two minds mutually serving as each other’s objects.
Next, [the author] addresses the six difficulties; regarding the first difficulty, there are eight parts. First, he cites the root scripture, where that master of the *Kātyāyanīputra-śāstra* asks:

"Regarding the two periods [past and future], the master Vasubandhu explains this based on the three causes—simultaneous (*sahabhū*), associated (*samprayukta*), and maturation (*vipāka*)—which are causes at all times and never non-causes.
Because he says this, there is no fault. Furthermore, there are three [points] concerning existence.
The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that dharmas in the stage of "presently arising" (*pratyutpanna-janman*) in the future are necessarily capable of proceeding toward the present;

thus, when they reach the phase of the characteristic of "abiding" (*sthiti*), they serve as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) for those [dharmas] yet to arise. Therefore, Kātyāyanīputra, relying on the final stage of "presently arising" in the future, gave this answer:
"There is no time when [a dharma] is not a cause. As the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "This refers to the time of the final arising."

The meaning of being a "universal similar cause" (*sarvatraga-sabhāga-hetu*) that is capable of producing [results] is such that, from this point onward, there is nothing that arises which does not take this dharma as its cause.
The four masters do not accept the Vaibhāṣika explanation;

their response to the objection is not a sound one, because a future dharma prior to the stage of actual arising is not yet in the stage of actual arising, and thus it cannot serve as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) until it finally reaches the state of arising.

If it is only at the final stage that it becomes established as a cause capable of acting as such, then there must be times when it is not a cause. Why, then, do you answer that there is no time when it is not a cause?
Furthermore, if you answer that there is no time when it is not a cause based on its final stage, then Kātyāyanīputra asked again:
"If a dharma serves as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for another dharma, is there ever a time when it is not its equal-and-immediate condition?"

Kātyāyanīputra replied: "When this dharma has not yet reached the present but has already arisen"—if one answers according to the explanation of the Vaibhāṣika masters based on the final stage of actual arising (*sajjanana-avasthā*), then regarding the condition of equal and immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*), one should likewise answer that there is no time when it is not such a condition.
Based on the final stage of actual arising, why then do you answer, "When this..."?

Although the dharma has not yet arisen when it has not reached [its state], the Vaibhāṣika masters further explain this through two perspectives, as they do in the section concerning the *samanantara-pratyaya* (immediately preceding condition).
Just as it is explained there, so too should it be understood regarding this cause:
when this dharma has not yet arisen because it has not reached [its state], at that time it is not a cause. This is stated in the context of the cause based on its excellence (*prakarṣa*).
In the subsequent stage of actual arising (*jāyamāna*), there is no moment that is not a cause; it should likewise be so regarding those conditions (*pratyaya*).
Relying on the final stage of actual arising, there is no moment that is not a condition; it should likewise be so regarding the seven non-causes (*ahetu*).
By composing the text in this manner, what merit is gained? It merely demonstrates that the master of the treatise, Kātyāyanīputra, was not skilled in composition.
Therefore, this answer was given. The Master of the Treatise (Vasubandhu) critiques this, stating:

"Thus, it should be known that the previous explanation based on the three causes—simultaneous (*sahabhū*), associated (*samprayukta*), and maturation (*vipāka*)—is correct. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, Volume 16, states:

"Is it not the case that when dharmas are in the process of arising, they are already able to eliminate all obstacles; in relation to those [dharmas] yet to arise, can they not be said to be 'prior'? The answer is: "Yes, they can."

The homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) is established based on the sequence of before and after, not at the very moment of arising. This is because once that moment has passed, it has already transcended the subsequent stage; furthermore, as with other future phenomena, it does not yet possess the function of acting as a cause.

It is explained that the "moment of arising" refers to the time when the activity (*kāritra*) of the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) operates upon the substance of the dharma (*dharmasvabhāva*).

However, since the substance of the dharma remains identical to its state when the activity of the characteristic of arising has not yet occurred—and thus lacks the function of grasping an effect (*phalagrahaṇa*)—it cannot be said [to be the homogeneous cause] at that point.

As for the preceding point, since other future dharmas that have not yet arisen possess the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*), one should formulate a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) as follows:

"A dharma at the moment of its actual arising has not yet transcended its subsequent state" (the thesis); "because it has not yet acquired the activity of grasping a fruit" (the reason); "like other future dharmas" (the example). Regarding this, other masters explain:

although this [inference] generally relies upon the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*’s discussion of the six causes (*ṣaḍ-hetu*), there is no fault [in its application]. As for the question: "Since the future..."
If there are no similar-class (*sabhāga*) or pervasive (*sarvatraga*) causes, how can it be said that there is never a time when they are not a cause?
[The answer is: Although they do not exist in the future, this intention refers to their capacity to act as a cause once they reach the present;
thus, there is never a time when they are not a cause. Furthermore, this future state must also be definitively established.
There are those who say that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are necessarily able to act as causes at the moment of their arising because they remove all obstacles;

based on this, it is said of them that there is no time when they are not a cause. The explanation is as follows: The former interpretation refers to the capacity of all future [phenomena] at all times to serve as causes for the present.

The latter statement, "there is no time when they are not a cause," refers to the fact that, according to the current interpretation, they are necessarily able to reach the state of manifestation as a cause only at the very moment of their arising.

Therefore, this differs from the previous explanation; however, the Master of the Sūtras’ (Sautrāntika) statement is not a sound interpretation, because a future dharma does not function as a non-homogeneous cause (*asabhāga-hetu*) prior to its stage of actual arising, but only becomes so subsequently. Such an objection has already been resolved:
since there is no "before" or "after" for a future dharma, the meaning of saying that it is never a non-cause throughout the three time periods is to show that there is no fourth temporal state.
Therefore, the *Nyāyānusāra* explains: "The Master of the Sūtras’ (Sautrāntika) critique has already been resolved as follows:

since the future does not possess [the distinction of] prior and posterior, how can it be said that 'in the stage of being presently arising, it is not a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) beforehand, but only becomes one afterwards'?
Furthermore, when considering the three time periods, there is no moment that is not a cause. As Kātyāyanīputra asked: "If a dharma serves as a cause for another dharma..."

Regarding the question, "Is it the case that at some time within the three periods [of past, present, and future], this dharma is not a cause for that [dharma]? that sutra answers: "There is no time within the three periods when it is not a cause.

This is because, with respect to the future at the very moment of arising (*utpāda-kṣaṇa*), it is certain to function as a cause. Thus, by speaking in terms of the three periods, the meaning is that there is no non-causality within them;
the intent is to show that there is no fourth period. How, then, can one claim that the stage prior to the moment of arising is not identical [to the state of being a cause]?

Regarding the objection based on analogy, it is not a sound explanation. The *Śāstra* states: "If that were so, the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) should be explained in the same way.

However, since the *Mūla-śāstra* does not permit this, the *Mūla-śāstra* says: "At the time when this dharma has not yet reached the state of having already arisen," which is explained as referring to the moment of its actual arising.
Since there is no time among the three periods [of past, present, and future] when it is not a cause, [the objection] regarding the equal-and-immediate...
The intervening conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*) should be explained in the same way as this cause; even at the moment of actual arising, there is no time when it is not a condition.

However, the *Mūla-śāstra* does not accept this. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (the *Kātyāyanīputra-śāstra*) states: "When this dharma has not yet reached the state of having already arisen, it is not an equal-and-immediate [condition].
It does not say, "When it has not yet reached the state of actually arising, it is not an equal-and-immediate [condition]. The treatise says: "There is no such fault. Why is that? Because...

The immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is established based on the power of "making way" (*avakāśa*), not during the actual stage of arising; it possesses the capacity to make way only when [the effect] has already arisen.
Once it has reached the state of having ceased, it is called "already made way. As for the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), it follows the principle of a seed:

while in the stage of arising, it abides within the state of being a seed; once the effect has arisen, it is already capable of grasping the fruit. Therefore, the cause is not of the same category [as the effect].

Regarding the explanation of the "immediately preceding condition" (*samanantara-pratyaya*), there is no such fault. Why is this? The immediately preceding condition refers to the power of the preceding [moment] to clear the way for the subsequent one.

While that future [moment] is in the state of being about to arise (*utpāda-avasthā*), it possesses the capacity for the preceding cause to clear the way for the subsequent effect. This requirement reaches the present moment; when it is in the phase of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*), it is called the time of having already arisen.

At that point, because the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*) exerts its power, there is the clearing of the way for the subsequent effect. Thus, it is stated in the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*.

Regarding the activity of the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), it is said that when those dharmas arise, if they have reached the past and have already ceased, they are termed "having opened the way" for the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).

Just as with the nature of a seed, which can directly produce what follows, while the seed itself abides in the state of being about to arise in the future, within the dharma that the seed directly produces, it must necessarily reach the present phase; once it has arisen, it is precisely then that it can grasp the subsequent fruit.
Therefore, regarding the discussion on the non-homogeneous *samanantarapratyaya* (immediately preceding condition), it is said that other masters explain:

"Immediately after [the cause] is about to arise (*anantaram utpadyamāna*), this homogeneous cause necessarily takes its own fruit as the immediately preceding condition; however, it is not certain that [this occurs] while [the cause] abides in a state already ceased, for it takes its own fruit only when [the cause] has reached that stage.
Thus, one cannot rely on the explanation given at the time of actual arising. The commentary explains: "Other masters explain 'immediately after' as referring to the future."
From the moment of arising until the present phase of duration, this similar cause (sabhāga-hetu) necessarily takes its own fruit;

therefore, it is said with respect to the time of arising that there is no period among the three times when it is not a simultaneous condition (sahabhū-pratyaya) or an immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya).

However, this is not fixed [in all cases], because in the case of the two mindless attainments (acittaka-samāpatti), the preceding mind takes its fruit only after the mind emerging from the attainment has reached the past state of cessation.
It cannot be said that [the cause] arises at the same time as the basis and the supported, nor can it be said that because they arise simultaneously, the cause is necessarily able to grasp the fruit.
Regarding the argument that the cause is not a similar-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), the *Vibhāṣā* explains this by means of two perspectives;
as it is stated there, so it should be here, and as it is stated here, so it should be there. However, the Sūtra Master (Sthiramati) states it in this manner.
What function does this passage serve? It serves solely to demonstrate that the author of the treatise was not unskilled in composition;

rather, it further reveals the author’s mastery of literary expression. This is because he is able to show that among various compositions, some have implicit meanings while others have explicit meanings.
Next, responding to the second objection, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "As that Kātyāyanīputra said, those dharmas which are not causes of the mind..."
When asked how this is explained in detail, the answer is: This teaching concerns the ultimate state.
For one who has not yet attained right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), all untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*) that have not yet arisen are non-causes of mind;
when right determination is attained, the initial untainted mind is a non-cause of mind, while all subsequent untainted minds are causes of mind.
Therefore, that sutra states that the first untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) is not a cause for further minds.

Furthermore, some say that this [sutra] does not speak of "similar causes" (*sabhāga-hetu*), but rather speaks of two kinds of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*): those who are able to attain nirvana and those who are unable to attain nirvana.
In this context, it refers to those unable to attain nirvana when it says they are "not a cause for further minds. Why is this?
Regarding the statement that there are those who do not attain *nirvāṇa*, the answer is: "As it has been said, one will certainly attain right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*);
however, one should know that there are also those who will not necessarily attain right determination. Thus, this teaching is well-explained as being definitive.

It means that for all phenomena whose nature is not to take the mind as their own-part cause (*svabhāga-hetu*), such as those who have not yet attained right determination, [this applies] to all future [states].
The exhaustion of all untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*) is not a phenomenon that takes mind as its own-part cause (*sva-bhāga-hetu*).

When one attains right penetration (*samyak-nirvedha*), only the initial untainted mind is a phenomenon that does not take mind as its cause; all subsequent untainted minds are phenomena that do take mind as their cause.
Therefore, that sutra speaks only of the initial untainted mind as being a phenomenon that does not take mind as its cause. Furthermore...
Some say that this passage does not speak of a "similar cause" (sabhāga-hetu), because it speaks of two kinds of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*):
those who can attain *nirvāṇa*, who possess the first untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) as the efficient cause (*niṣpādaka-hetu*) for *nirvāṇa*;

and those who cannot attain *nirvāṇa*, who lack the first untainted mind as a cause for *nirvāṇa* and are thus called "non-mind-causes. This is what is stated in this sutra regarding those who cannot [attain it].

Regarding those who attain *nirvāṇa*, the statement that it is "neither caused by the mind nor the non-mind" means that there is no initial [moment] where the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) mind acts as the cause for *nirvāṇa*.

How is it known that there are those who do not attain *nirvāṇa*? The answer is: according to what is taught in this sutra—that those who necessarily attain right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*)—by analogy one should know that there are also those who do not necessarily attain right determination. This is the meaning of this sutra.

In the first part of the middle section, the question is asked: "What are the dharmas that are not causes of the mind? In the answer, the attainment of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) is cited as being a cause of the mind;
by contrast, this implies that failing to attain right determination is not a cause for the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) and nirvana.

Next, in order to resolve the third objection, this passage is first explained by citing the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* (formerly known as the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*), Volume Nine, Chapter on the Thousandfold Objections (*Sahasra-praśna-varga*).
It states: Question: Regarding the view of a self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), are the four noble truths the cause of that view of a self, or is the view of a self the cause of the four noble truths?

Answer: There are two cases. The view of a self is not the cause of those [truths], nor are those [truths] the cause of the view of a self. These two are [mutually exclusive] within their own respective categories (*svabhāga*).
Regarding those that are causes of the truth of suffering or of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), but are not themselves caused by the view of a self-identity;

or those that are causes of the view of a self-identity and are themselves caused by the view of a self-identity; or those that are neither causes of the view of a self-identity nor are themselves caused by the view of a self-identity:

these refer to all [defilements] except for the proclivities (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*) in the past and present, as well as their associated factors.

Regarding the suffering truths associated with the proclivities (*anuśaya*), excluding those past and present universal proclivities abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*):
those proclivities are associated with the suffering truths, excluding the future suffering truths associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*).

Excluding the arising, abiding, and ceasing of that view of a self-identity, as well as the arising, abiding, and ceasing of what is associated with it—whatever other defiled suffering truths there may be, the view of a self-identity is their cause, and they are also [associated with] the view of a self-identity.
Regarding "seeing the cause": this refers to those aforementioned excluded phenomena which are the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), yet are not its cause;
and those which are also not the cause of the view of a self-identity, namely, the non-defiled *duḥkhasatya*. As it is with *duḥkhasatya*, so too should one understand *samudayasatya*.
It is said that for both types of *satkāyadṛṣṭi*, the two truths of cessation (*nirodhasatya*) and the path (*mārgasatya*) are not their causes, nor are they [the causes] of those [two truths].
Regarding the two types of discrimination concerning the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) with respect to the two truths of suffering and its origin, one should distinguish them as follows:

when the truth of suffering is considered in relation to the view of a self, there are three propositions. First: either the view of a self is the cause of that [suffering] while that [suffering] is not the cause of the view of a self; second:

either the view of a self is the cause of that [suffering] and that [suffering] is also the cause of the view of a self; third: either the view of a self is not the cause of that [suffering] and that [suffering] is also not the cause of the view of a self. The first...

Regarding the single phrase: "The view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is its cause, but it is not the cause of that [view]. Excluding the second combined category, all other defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*) are included.
This refers to the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) in the past and present;

these are not mentioned separately because they are associated with the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), such as arising and so forth, which are acquired according to their respective objects and characteristics. Furthermore, the past [proclivities] are excluded.

Presently, when one sees the origin (*samudaya*) and abandons the universal proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*), those proclivities and their associated suffering-truth (*duḥkha-satya*) [are abandoned]. Furthermore, regarding the future world, three phrases are excluded;
first, the suffering-truth associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) in the future is excluded.

This is because the factors associated with the grasping at self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*) are included among those to be excluded, whereas the view of a self-identity itself is not what is being excluded here. Second, that which arises above the view of a self-identity—namely, its arising, abiding, and ceasing—is also excluded.
Excluding those [factors] already mentioned, whatever other afflicted *duḥkhasatya* (truth of suffering) there may be constitutes the first category:

namely, all pervasive and non-pervasive proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudayadarśana-prahātavya*) in the past and present; the essence of the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in the future;

the minor four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of that view of a self-body and the minor four characteristics of the factors associated with it; and furthermore, the characteristic of the view of a self-body itself.

The acquisitions (*prāpti*) of factors such as the Equality of Dharma (*dharmasamatā*) and so forth; the future acquisitions and the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the great and small [attainments];

the acquisitions of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) associated with those nine underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*)—excluding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)—along with their future four characteristics;

the seeds to be abandoned by the vision of the Truths of Origination and Cessation and by the Path, as well as the seeds of defiled phenomena to be abandoned by the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); all such things as these do not all arise from [the same cause].
The arising of the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) does not act as a cause for that [subsequent] view of a self; this is subsumed under the first single clause.

Regarding the second clause—where the view of a self is both itself and a cause for that [subsequent] view of a self—it refers to those aforementioned excluded factors. These [two clauses] above comprise the first two of the five categories of defiled *duḥkhasatya*.

Regarding the third clause—the case where the view of a self is not a cause for that [subsequent one], nor is that [subsequent one] a cause for the view of a self—[it refers to the remaining factors].
The "cause" refers to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) which abandons all non-defiled *duḥkhasatya*. Just as with *duḥkhasatya*, three propositions (*trikoṭika*) should be formulated;

the same applies to *samudayasatya*. Since *duḥkha* and *samudaya* are a single entity spoken of in two ways—as cause and effect—within the truths of suffering and origin, there is no proposition stating that something is a cause for the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) but is not produced from it. This is what is restated in the present text.
If it is difficult [to maintain] that there is no similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) in the future, then why does the *Prakaraṇapāda* state in its first section:
"There may be a Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) that has the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as its cause, but is not the cause of the view of a self-identity"?
This statement is made as an objection regarding the future; it merely refers to the future in order to specify what is excluded—that is, excluding the view of a self-identity of the future and...
Regarding those other defiled truths of suffering outside of that associated truth of suffering, there is a second category:

certain truths of suffering which have the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their cause and also serve as the cause for the view of a self-identity—namely, those factors excluded from the first category.

If future [dharmas] lack a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*), for what reason is the view of a self-identity included among those excluded when considering the view of a self-identity in relation to itself?

Although [future dharmas] are not associated causes (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*), or retributive causes (*vipāka-hetu*), it is possible for the view of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) to arise from a view of self-identity, because it arises from past and present views of self-identity.
How, then, can it be said that [the future] acts as a cause for the view of self-identity? Therefore, one must know that there is a sequence of prior and posterior within the future;

thus, the prior view of self-identity in the future acts as a cause for the subsequent view of self-identity, and for this reason, it is included among those factors to be excluded [from being a cause].—The Master [Vasubandhu].

The commentary states: The text of that *Prakaraṇapāda* should merely state that the suffering truth (*duḥkhasatya*) associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in the future is excluded;
it should not say "and that," for if one were to mention the suffering associated with the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), it would fall within the category of what is excluded.

Since the view of a self-identity is not part of the category of what is excluded, this does not constitute a valid objection. Even if there were such a statement using the phrase "and that," it is because [the text] has not yet...
Regarding the point that there is no sense of "prior" or "subsequent" in their arising, one should know that this [opponent's] statement is incorrect. Question:

For what reason was it that among the previously mentioned co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*), other masters did not include the verse regarding the associated factors (*samprayukta-dharma*) as being the incorrect position? The Vaibhāṣika masters say: That text must necessarily have been composed with such a verse;

precisely because they did not include the words "and those associated factors," it constitutes the incorrect position. Thus, the verse should be recited as follows: [The verse would have included: "...and those associated factors. Because these words were not included, it is established as the incorrect position.

If the inclusion of the phrase "and its associated [factors]" is considered the correct meaning, then in this context of the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), does the verse and that phrase constitute the incorrect meaning, while the absence of the verse and that phrase constitutes the correct meaning?

Answer: In the *Prakaraṇapāda*, the original text states that within the future [dharmas] there are three categories, excluding the suffering truth (*duḥkha-satya*) associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in the future.
This is cited here to illustrate the characteristic of the grasping at self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*).
In the second clause, among those things excluded by the "entry into what accords with the Dharma" (*dharmāvatāra*), the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is not excluded;

this also cites the arising, abiding, and ceasing of the view of a self-identity, taking the great arising, abiding, and ceasing as included in what is excluded, while the view of a self-identity itself is not excluded.
In the third clause, the arising, abiding, and ceasing associated with that [view] are also cited, taking the great arising, abiding, and ceasing of the associated factors as included.
Having entered into the factors associated with what is to be abandoned, this constitutes the first phrase of the exclusion. Master Fen states:
"Other masters have erroneously recited the third phrase and those two characters, placing them within the first phrase;

they claim that 'future satkāyadṛṣṭi and its associated suffering-truth' are excluded. Thus, both positions raise difficulties regarding the exclusion of future satkāyadṛṣṭi and its [associates] within the first phrase."
Because it corresponds to the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), it is difficult [to establish] a similar cause (*sabhāgahetu*);
thus, the third line of the verse and its associated arising, abiding, and ceasing are not established as simultaneous causes (*sahabhūhetu*).

Therefore, the Vaibhāṣika masters previously stated regarding the simultaneous cause that the text must necessarily be recited with the third line and the arising, abiding, and ceasing of those associated factors, making fifty-four dharmas.

Regarding the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) and the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), the Vaibhāṣika masters state that in the first phrase of that passage, it should simply say "excluding the future *satkāyadṛṣṭi* associated with the truth of suffering";
there is no need to mention "and those [dharmas] which may exist" as it is stated there.

Furthermore, one should understand that such an interpretation is not the original intent; for the preceding text takes up the [view] and its associated dharmas, whereas the subsequent text takes up [the view] and [its objects].
There is no contradiction between those two passages.
Next, regarding the resolution of the fourth objection, the *Vibhāṣā* states: "As it is said in the *Vijñānakāya-sūtra*, how is this further to be reconciled? It answers:
"Just as four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) are established for the past, they should likewise be established for the present; for the future, three alternatives should be established. Or...

There are causes that are not driven by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), those that are driven by the underlying tendencies, and those that are neither causes nor driven by the underlying tendencies. Regarding those causes that are not driven by the underlying tendencies:

they are the underlying tendencies that have already been abandoned and are associated with that mind. Regarding those causes that are driven by the underlying tendencies: they are the underlying tendencies that are still unabandoned and associated with that mind.
Regarding those causes that are neither driven by the underlying tendencies: [they are] the causes that are neither associated with those underlying tendencies nor have they been abandoned.
Regarding the statement: "As with other conditions, one should speak of all pervasive [factors] in another realm that are caused by others or caused by those caused by others;

what is the intention behind not speaking thus? The answer is: It is because one wishes to manifest that there is the sense of priority and posteriority within the future world. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"The logic of the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) may be applicable to the past, but how can the four alternatives be established for the future? Some have asserted this.

Regarding that, one should establish three propositions concerning the future: excluding those [dharmas] that increase by following along (*anuśerate*) but cannot act as a cause, because they lack a subsequent [moment].
However, the statement that "the future is like the past" is intended to show that at the very moment of arising, it necessarily enters the present;

and in relation to other [dharmas] yet to arise, it can be established as "prior," while in contrast to these, others may be called "subsequent. Other masters explain this, saying: "This explains the future..."
Regarding the future, there are also four propositions. It is not said that the future exists after the mind, as this would be the same as the case of the past.

That is to say, there are similar-type (*sabhāga*) and universal (*sarvatraga*) latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) in the future world; these increase in accordance with a defiled eye-consciousness in the future that has already apprehended its object but has not yet been abandoned, though they do not act as causes.
Thus, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states: "In the desire realm, there are [latent dispositions] in the present and future that exist before and after."
According to the meaning, it is based on the stage of actual arising, as explained in the *Nyāyānusāra*.

Next, how does one resolve the fifth objection? Furthermore, how does one reconcile the *Prajñaptiśāstra*, which states that all phenomena are determined by four factors—namely, cause, fruit, support (*āśraya*), and object (*ālambana*)?
It should be understood that in that text, "cause" refers to the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*) and the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*).

Regarding those that possess the causal relationship of associated and ripening (*vipāka*), this refers to the basis of the dominant (*adhipati*), human effort (*puruṣakāra*), and ripening fruits, namely the six faculties such as the eye;

their objects are the six spheres such as visible form. Since the homogeneous (*sabhāga*) and pervasive (*sarvatraga*) causes and their corresponding outflow fruits (*niṣyanda-phala*) are not mentioned within the determination of cause and effect, there is no fault.
Next, regarding the text that addresses the sixth objection, there are eight sections. First is the question:

"If there is no homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) in the future, then how can it be said that the homogeneous cause exists? Second is the response: "There is no fault, because we admit [the existence of the cause];

the homogeneous cause is established in relation to the states of the past and present, not in relation to the intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*) of the entity itself; thus, the cause exists in the future."

Because its essence (*tattva*) is without before or after, it is not established [as having temporal sequence]. Rather, because the functional activity (*kāritra*)—arising from its own-cause (*svabhāva-hetu*) through to the present world and acting in concert—is characterized by before and after, it is able to produce a subsequent effect.
However, this refers only to effects belonging to prior and subsequent states, not to an effect of the essence itself.

If, according to the Sautrāntika masters, the past and future lack intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva*), such that what was originally non-existent in the future comes into existence in the present, and having existed in the present enters the past;

Returning [to the original point], there is nothing established; the essence of the dharma of cause and effect is that all are originally without cause yet possess cause, and originally without fruit yet possess fruit.
Third question: If the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) exists in the future, as does the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*), what fault would there be?
Fourth answer: If it existed in the future, the *Mūla-śāstra* should have stated so. However, the *Mūla-śāstra* merely says: "Such faults exist in relation to the Sūtra."

Regarding the two periods of the past and present in contrast to the future period, [the treatise] does not state that there is a future [cause] with respect to the future period. As for the five external opponents, they claim:
"The *Mūla-śāstra* states only that the homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) which are capable of grasping and yielding fruit exist in the past and present;

it does not state that there is a future [cause] because there is no cause that grasps or yields [fruit] in the future. Therefore, there is no fault. The Master of the Treatise refutes the external opponents' claim that such a principle does not exist.
It is logically impossible for a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) to project a concordant fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) in the future, because there is no sequence of before and after [in the future].
If a homogeneous cause existed in the future, it would entail the error that two minds could successively act as causes for one another;

furthermore, it would result in the fallacy that a single mind in the future could serve as a cause, and yet another single mind in the future could serve as its fruit, despite the fact that conditions for arising have not yet been met.

Because it arises upon meeting conditions, and because a dharma that has already arisen serves as the outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) for a dharma yet to arise, it is not now claimed that the nature of what has already arisen cannot be the outflow fruit of what is yet to arise. This is because past dharmas are not the fruits of present ones;
thus, one knows that a presently arisen dharma cannot be the outflow fruit of a future, unarisen dharma, lest there be a case where the fruit exists prior to its cause.
Furthermore, due to the fault of [the cause existing] later, there would be no homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) in the future world. This is established through seven layers of questioning: 1.

If that were so, the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) should likewise not exist in the future; otherwise, the retributive fruit (*vipāka-phala*) would have to exist prior to its cause or simultaneously with it.
2. Moreover, dharmas in the future world possess neither priority nor posteriority. 8. Response: There is no such fault, because the retributive cause and its fruit are dissimilar.

Therefore, it is said that if the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and its fruit were of the same nature and similar, then since there would be no sequence of before and after in the future, they would have to be mutual causes for one another.

Since they would be mutual causes, they would also have to be mutual fruits. Such a relationship of mutual causality and mutual fruition between preceding and succeeding moments contradicts the principle of homogeneous causes and fruits;
this is not the case with the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*), where wholesome or unwholesome causes produce a ripening fruit.
Because their natures are similar, although they are separated by temporal sequence, there is no fault of mutual causality between preceding and succeeding moments;
thus, the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) is established based on the sequential positions of the past and present, whereas it does not exist in the future.

As for the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*), it is established based on its causal function across the three periods of time—past, present, and future—in terms of its unwholesome or impure nature, such that it is not non-existent in the future. Thus far, the future has been explained.
In the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, the *Vibhāṣā*, and the *Nyāyānusāra*, there are six difficult points (*durguṇa*) that are sequentially reconciled.

This treatise [the *Abhidharmadīpa*] reconciles only four of these difficulties and does not briefly reconcile the second and fourth. Among the various masters, some maintain that future [dharmas] possess homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*).

The *Vibhāṣā* sets forth two faults against this; first, that the sūtra-text does not mention such a cause, and since this treatise also [does not mention it], [the objection stands]. As for the first [point]:
The treatise states: "If there were a future [moment], the root treatise should have spoken of two; for beyond this, there is also the fault that the two minds would act as causes for one another.
Since this fault also exists in the aforementioned treatise, it says: "If there were no sequence of before and after, they would mutually act as causes for one another.
The externalist reconciles these two faults in detail, as found in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.

The preceding section has explained the verses regarding the prior arising [of causes]. Now begins the fourth part, explaining that the paths exist across nine stages in succession. In this text, first, the previous point is restated as a question:
"When it was said that 'homogeneous causes (sabhāga-hetu) belong only to their own stage,' upon what basis was this definitely stated?

Second, the answer is given: "It was definitely stated based on the contaminated (sāsrava) paths. Third, the root verse is explained: "If uncontaminated (anāsrava) paths are considered in relation to one another, each and every one of them pertains to all nine stages."
Regarding the passage explaining that the five [moments] act as causes while only those that are equal or superior act as results, there are six sections in the text:

first, the presentation of the thesis that [the moments of patience] act as causes for only what is equal or superior, and not as causes for what is inferior, because they arise from preparatory effort (*prayoga*); second, the section beginning with "For instance," which explains how the [patience] acts as a cause for what is equal;

third, the section beginning with "Furthermore, this very patience," which explains how it acts as a cause for what is equal or superior; fourth, the section beginning with "Furthermore, all those already arisen in the path of seeing" [explains the same].

5. Regarding the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the sixth section below explains the causes of equality and superiority by means of the three paths, distinguishing between those of sharp and dull faculties.
First, the analysis through question and answer: Question: How can the paths of the higher stages be the cause for the lower stages, and why are they termed "equal" or "superior"?
Answer: This is due to the increase of the cause and due to the faculties; that is to say, it is by way of vision (*darśana*).

Regarding the three paths such as the Path of Seeing, because the causes of the lower stages increase further and further within the nine grades—beginning with the lowest-of-the-low and so forth—the Path of Seeing of a higher stage serves as the cause for the Path of Seeing of a lower stage;

The following explains the definition and meaning of the term "ripening cause" (*vipāka-hetu*). This section contains five parts: first, a general inquiry as to how the meaning of the ripening cause can be understood;
second, two successive interrogations challenging the status of being a cause of ripening; third, a response that incorporates both explanations, asking what fault there might be therein;
fourth, two successive counter-objections based on those two explanations; and fifth, a conclusion indicating that both explanations are valid.

The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (Treatise on the Correct Theory), as previously cited, states: "The retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) is either explained by the *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound) construction, as when the Sūtra says 'the eye born of maturation' (*vipākaja-cakṣus*);
or it is explained by the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound) construction, as when the Sūtra speaks of 'the maturation of karma. The commentary explains:

'Either the karma that has been performed, upon reaching the time of its fruition, transforms and becomes capable of maturing; this retributive cause is so named because it maintains the functional capacity of that karma which undergoes transformation and maturation.'"

This is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound), or as the Sūtra says, "the maturation of karma. Here, "karma" refers to the agent (*puruṣa*), while "maturation fruit" and so forth refer to the maturation of that karma;
thus, it is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound) called *upapada-samāsa* (compound based on a subordinate term), meaning "that which depends on karma," just as an object depends on a person.
Third, regarding the meaning of "maturation" (*vipāka*): the explanation of this term has three parts, the first of which is the question.

What is the meaning of *vipāka* (maturation)? Two masters of the *Vibhāṣā* explain it as follows: because the cause is wholesome or unwholesome while the fruit is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it matures as something of a different category;

this is the meaning of *vipāka*. That is to say, the maturation cause (*vipāka-hetu*) matures only as something of a different category, whereas the co-existent, associated, homogeneous, and pervasive causes mature only as things of the same category.
Since the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) includes both the same and different categories, it alone [is excluded from the definition].

Regarding this single term "vipāka-hetu" (ripening cause), the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "The Master of the Sūtras (*Sūtrāntika*) says that the Vaibhāṣikas explain it thus—that which ripens as a different kind [of result]...
and that only this one cause is called the ripening cause; all of this is unreasonable.
For the Vaibhāṣikas do not definitively state that everything obtained through the six causes is termed 'ripened' (*vipakva*). Even if one were to grant that point..."

There is no fault in calling this a "distinct fruit" (*visadṛśaphala*). The Master of the Three Treatises (*Sanlun-zhu*) explains that a matured fruit (*vipākaphala*) cannot be obtained from other causes;
it receives the name "matured" only when it possesses two characteristics: first, its substantial entity arises through the specific transformation within the continuity of its karma;
second, the matured fruit is subject to limitations regarding time according to the superior or inferior force of its cause. It is not [the case that it lacks these].

The resultant entity produced by those two causes—the co-existent (*sahabhū*) and the associated (*samprayukta*)—must arise only through the transformation and differentiation (*pariṇāma-viśeṣa*) of the causal stream over a long period of time;

for [these two causes] bestow their fruit at the very moment they grasp it. Thus, although they possess the temporal sequence corresponding to the superiority or inferiority of the cause, they lack the first criterion [of a cause].
Furthermore, the fruits of the three causes—the efficient (*kāraṇa*), the homogeneous (*sabhāga*), and the pervasive (*sarvatraga*)—likewise [arise through such transformation].
Because the cause has temporal limits while the fruit—arising repeatedly until the very end of saṃsāra—is limitless, one should speak in this way based on these two points:
that which ripens through transformation, whether as cause or fruit, is the meaning of *vipāka* (maturation).
It should not be understood merely as "ripening of a different class" (*anyajāti-vipāka*), as the Vaibhāṣikas do, for that would only serve to distinguish it from other causes.
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* states that "vipāka" (maturation) refers either to maturing apart from the cause or maturing differently from the cause; these two pertain to the fruit.
Alternatively, it refers to the karma performed undergoing transformation and becoming capable of maturing at the time the fruit is attained; this one pertains to the cause.

Although there are three textual passages above, they are combined here as the third explanation of the meaning of the term "vipāka. According to the *Nyāyānusāra*, there are three explanations: first, maturing apart from the cause.

1. Ripening (vipāka) is the maturation of two distinct causes; 2. these two belong to the category of fruit (phala); 3. or, when that which is produced reaches its time of transformation, it is able to ripen—this one belongs to the category of cause (hetu).
Regarding this treatise, there are two interpretations: first, the explanation of the Vaibhāṣikas, who state that ripening in a different class constitutes the meaning of "ripening" (vipāka);
second, the explanation of the Master [Vasubandhu], who states that the ripening through the transformation of either cause or fruit constitutes the meaning of "ripening" (vipāka).
The *Nyāyānusāra* and this treatise together provide five explanations.
