As for the claim by some masters that they "together produce a single retributive fruit," this is incorrect;

what is clarified here is that the factors which are simultaneous causes obtain one and the same fruit—namely, one fruit of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*) and one fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*). It is within this context that "maturation" is being clarified.

Because they are matured causes (*vipāka-hetu*), the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) is distinguished [from them]; however, since the maturation cause produces its maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*) necessarily without distinction, it is said that they "collectively produce a single fruit.

The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* asks: "Do all acquisitions (*prāpti*) undergo mutual transformation? It answers: "Acquisitions do not undergo mutual transformation even when they occupy the same locus of the body.

If karma occupies the locus of the body and undergoes mutual transformation, its retribution also undergoes mutual transformation; this applies to both the retribution-consciousness and the retribution-form."

The factors of enumeration (saṃskāra-dharma) consist of those dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra) and matter (rūpa). Regarding matter, there are the four bases (āyatana): visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility.
Regarding the mind and mental factors (citta-caitasika), there are the feelings of suffering, pleasure, and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure, as well as their associated phenomena.

Regarding the factors dissociated from mind, they include acquisition (prāpti), birth (jāti), duration (sthiti), and impermanence (anityatā). The treatise states that at times two aggregates (skandha) act together as a ripening cause (vipāka-hetu) to produce a single result.
Regarding the single fruit, it refers to wholesome and unwholesome bodily and vocal actions, as well as their arising and so forth. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, fascicle sixteen, states:
"This ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) is generally said to be of two types: first, that which can project (*ākṣepa*), and second, that which can fulfill (*paripūraṇa*).

Furthermore, the homogeneous group-characteristic (*nikāya-sabhāga*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) cannot be projected by non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) alone; they are not concomitant with the mind."
The two types of karma—bodily and vocal—certainly cannot project the life-force (*jīvitasaṃskāra*) and the group-homogeneity (*nikāyasabhāga*).

Were it otherwise, it would contradict the first Sūtra and the *Nyāyānusāra*, which state that these are projected by volition (*cetanā*) within an inferior realm. Therefore, it is said that the life-force and group-homogeneity of existence in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are induced solely by mental karma (*manaskarma*), not by bodily or vocal karma.
Furthermore, regarding the numerous atoms (*paramāṇu*) of manifest bodily and vocal karma produced by a single moment of mind, among them...
First, regarding the projection of the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*): it is illogical to claim that these lack such a capacity.
If one were to grant that they simultaneously produce a single fruit together, it would follow that they must be mutual simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*).

However, it is not accepted in our school’s tenets that resistant derived matter (*sapratigha-bhautika-rūpa*) acts as a simultaneous cause, because it is not produced by their mutual power, nor does it arise sequentially, one after another. Furthermore, it is not the case that each individual [atom] reaches its ultimate limit [in isolation].

The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the homogeneous character (*nikāyasabhāga*) are drawn forth subtly by a single moment of mind; they do not have distinct functions for separately projecting subsequent [moments], yet there is no fault in this.

It is not the case that there is also this fault regarding the completing karma (*pūrakakarma*), because within a single lifetime, each [karma] is able to individually grasp the fruits of the perfection of visible forms, odors, tastes, and so forth.
Based on this, the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) is also explained in the same way; it is essentially the manifold abstinence (*virati*).
Because they arise from a single mind, it is not admitted that they are mutual simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*).

If there were unresistant derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) that was not a simultaneous cause, the term "resistant" (*sapratigha*) would be rendered useless; for it is stated that all resistant derived matter is not a simultaneous cause.

Therefore, this statement is made to show that resistant derived matter is never a simultaneous cause, whereas unresistant derived matter can be a simultaneous cause. It cannot be equated with the former.
Bodily and vocal actions bound to the desire realm cannot project [a rebirth]; as stated in the *Prathama-sūtra*:
"If one cultivates, knows, or frequently practices killing, one is born in the hells," and so forth, at length. Furthermore, as stated in the *Prathama-śāstra*:
"Among these three types of unwholesome conduct, which offense is the greatest? It is that which increases [the defilements], namely, false speech."

This karma, which can take as its maturation (*vipāka*) a lifespan lasting for an eon within the Avīci hell, is definitively explained as the "projecting fruit" (*ākṣepaka-phala*) mentioned previously.
This explanation clarifies the volition (*cetanā*) that initiates it, because it is coarse and easy to understand; thus, there is no first fault regarding its characteristics.

At times, four aggregates (*skandha*) act as causes to collectively produce a single fruit, which is intelligible. In the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), at times, a single aggregate acts as the cause to collectively [produce a result].

Regarding the production of a single fruit: it is said that attaining the state of non-ideation (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and its associated factors, such as arising (*jāti*), cannot produce the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) or the homogeneous character of the group (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
Sometimes two aggregates act together as causes to produce a single fruit;

for instance, the wholesome manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*) of the first dhyāna and its associated factors, such as arising, likewise cannot produce the life-faculty or the homogeneous character of the group. The explanation of these passages is clear.

From here below is the fifth [section]: "There are actions that produce a small number of bases (*āyatana*); there are actions that produce only one dharma-base, namely the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)," and so forth.
The term "and so forth" includes the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). The *Mahāvibhāṣā* states: "There are actions that obtain one sense-base, namely the life-faculty within the dharma-base.

The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* also says: "There are actions whose retribution arises as a single base, namely the life-faculty. Neither of these mentions the body-base (*kāyāyatana*) being produced by a combination [of multiple faculties].
The locus of the body’s contact is the basis for these various bases (āyatana). If one obtains the locus of the body’s contact, one obtains eleven bases;

as the body-base (kāyāyatana) is the basis for five bases, if one obtains the body-base, one obtains six bases. If one brings about the sense-sphere of the mind (manāyatana), one necessarily brings about two spheres, namely, the mind and the mental-object (dharmāyatana).
The above constitutes the correct interpretation (*samyak-artha*). From here below, the first master’s incorrect interpretation (*asamyak-artha*) from the *Vibhāṣā* is clarified:
he asserts that the five sense objects are mutually distinct and that all four great elements (*mahābhūta*) cannot produce visible form or sound.

Furthermore, because not all matter in the desire realm necessarily possesses odor or fragrance, there exists karma-induced "smoothness" and so forth among the seven derived tangibles (*upādāya-spraṣṭavya*), which are capable of producing the great elements and the tangibles themselves.
The other four sense-bases (*āyatana*) included within the [tangible] base need not necessarily exist;

although they are not separate from the body-base (*kāyendriya*), as in the human realm where the body-base is produced by wholesome karma, yet the eye-contact base may be produced by unwholesome karma. Because it is produced by the same [karma] that produces the four [other] bases, it is said:

"If it produces the tangible base, one should know it is likewise," based on the analogy of producing two bases. The extent to which the others are produced can be understood; all of these pertain to the first [dhyāna].

The first teacher’s position is not the correct doctrine, as there is karma capable of producing [results] from five [elements] or fewer; this is because the second teacher’s position is the correct doctrine according to the *Vibhāṣā*.
Thus, the fifteenth fascicle of the *Vibhāṣā* states: "All that relies on these [elements] says that all four great elements can produce visible form and sound;
all visible forms, odors, and tastes in the desire realm are ultimately never separated from one another. At that time, if the eye-base is obtained as a karmic retribution..."
If one attains the seven bases—eye, body, visible form, odor, taste, tangible object, and mental phenomena—the case of the eye, ear, nose, and tongue bases is likewise.

If one attains the body base, one attains six bases: body, visible form, odor, taste, tangible object, and mental phenomena. If one attains the visible-form base, one attains five bases: visible form, odor, taste, tangible object, and mental phenomena;
as it is with the visible-form base, so it is with the odor, taste, and tangible-object bases. There is karmic retribution for the attainment of eight bases.

Regarding the nine bases, ten bases, and eleven bases, the text states that there is karma capable of inducing either five [bases]. If one obtains the base of form (*rūpāyatana*), one obtains five bases;
as it is with the base of form, so it is with the bases of odor, taste, and tangibility. As the *Abhidharmakośa* previously stated:

"Just as in humans, the substance of the two sexual organs is induced by wholesome karma, while the sense-bases of color, odor, taste, and tangibility are induced by unwholesome karma. Because of the eye, [the other bases] are induced.
Regarding the statement that at the time of [attaining] form and so forth, one does not obtain the body-base (kāyāyatana): "or six" means that if one obtains the body-base, one obtains six bases;
"or seven" means that if one obtains the eye-base (cakṣurāyatana), one obtains seven bases.
The above has explained, according to the power of karma, that the various bases (āyatana) experienced by beings are necessarily inseparable from one another.
From here on, the numbers eight, nine, ten, and so forth refer to indeterminate results. For instance, when one acquires the eye-base, one acquires seven bases;
adding the ear makes eight, adding the nose makes nine, adding the tongue makes ten, and adding the mind makes eleven. This is because karma may yield either few results or many results.
Therefore, as with external seeds, fruits may be few or many. Regarding those with few fruits, such as rice, barley, and the like, they possess two characteristics and are thus called "few-fruited":
first, each seed produces only one fruit; second, each pod contains only one seed.

Regarding those with many fruits, such as the lotus, the pomegranate, and the *nyagrodha* tree, they likewise possess two characteristics and are thus called "many-fruited": first, [each seed produces many fruits]; second, [each fruit contains many seeds].
Having been planted for many years, there are two [characteristics]: first, a single pod contains many seeds;

second, from the sixth point below, it clarifies that when considering time-periods (*adhvan*) and moments (*kṣaṇa*), the cause is small while the fruit is great. There is karma of one period with maturation in three periods:

for example, an action to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-vedanīya-karman*). A single moment in the present is the creation of one period, yet its fruit—the present retribution—has already fallen away and passed.
The past is the continuity of past maturation; the present is the category of present maturation; and the future is future maturation.

There is no single maturation in one lifetime that is collectively produced by karma from all three time periods, because karmas of the three time periods, when compared with one another, are not co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*).
Furthermore, since wholesome and unwholesome causes arise through mental attention (*manasikāra*), let there be no reduction of the fruit relative to the effort exerted in the cause.

Therefore, although the karma of marks and retribution (*lakṣaṇavipākakarma*) created by a Bodhisattva over a hundred kalpas may result in a single body, the atoms (*paramāṇu*) and moments (*kṣaṇa*) of the marks they induce are each distinct;
it is not that the karma of a hundred kalpas collectively produces a single fruit, because they do not function as co-existent causes (*sahabhūhetu*), and thus their inducements are individual.

Furthermore, the fact that the maturation (*vipāka*) of many moments of karma occurs within a single moment is of the same category as the previous explanation; this is as stated in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 2.

10. Furthermore, it is solely by virtue of unwholesome karma that draws one into a particular homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) that one is born in hell. Once born there, only unwholesome phenomena exist:

the maturation (*vipāka*) of matter (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), mental factors (*caitta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*). Regarding matter, there are nine bases (*āyatana*), excluding sound;

regarding mind and mental factors, there are the sensation of suffering (*duḥkha-vedanā*) along with its associated factors; and regarding formations dissociated from mind, there is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).

The faculties, the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*), and [the states of] birth, aging, duration, and impermanence arise solely through the power of unwholesome karma that projects a homogeneous class into the realms of animals or hungry ghosts.
Once born there, one experiences the maturation (*vipāka*) of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, consisting of matter, mind, mental factors, and formations dissociated from mind.
Regarding the maturation of unwholesome dharmas, it consists of nine bases—excluding sound—and of mind and mental factors.

Regarding painful feeling (*duḥkhā vedanā*) and its associated (*saṃprayukta*) and dissociated (*viprayukta*) factors: the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*), acquisition (*prāpti*), birth (*jāti*), aging (*jarā*), duration (*sthiti*), and impermanence (*anityatā*);

and the maturation (*vipāka*) of wholesome factors (*kuśala-dharma*), which consists of the four bases (*āyatana*)—namely, visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility—as well as mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*).
Regarding pleasant (*sukha*), joyful (*saumanasya*), and equanimous (*upekṣā*) feelings, along with their associated and dissociated factors: acquisition, birth, aging, duration, and impermanence.
Other masters maintain that among the wholesome dharmas, there is no resultant matter (*vipāka-rūpa*) in the realms of animals and hungry ghosts;
rather, there is only resultant mind, mental factors, and formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*). Question:

If this is so, why is it observed that beings in the realms of animals and hungry ghosts possess forms that are either beautiful or ugly? Answer: Their unwholesome karma may have wholesome karma as its concomitant (*parivāra*).
There are those who take unwholesome karma as their retinue, and those who take wholesome karma as their retinue.
Those whose retinue consists of wholesome karma possess exquisite physical forms because they have well-subdued the power of unwholesome, base, and evil forces.

Those whose retinue consists of unwholesome karma possess ugly physical forms because unwholesome factors increase that base and evil power. The commentary states: regarding wholesome karma in those realms of animals and hungry ghosts—
It is also not logically contradictory that it can induce resultant (*vipāka*) matter; therefore, one should know that the initial explanation is correct.

When one is born among humans or devas in the desire realm through karma that projects a homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) by means of wholesome [karma], having been so born, one experiences the resultant matter of both wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, as well as the resultant matter of the mind, mental factors, and formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
Among these, the resultant matter of wholesome dharmas consists of nine bases (*āyatana*).
Excluding sound, the mind and mental factors consist of the feelings of pleasure, joy, and equanimity, along with their associated phenomena and dissociated formations;
the life-faculty, the group-homogeneity, acquisition, birth, aging, duration, and impermanence; and the maturation-forms of unwholesome phenomena—these constitute four bases:
namely, visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility. The mind and mental factors consist of the feeling of pain and its associated phenomena and dissociated formations.

Regarding those who attain birth, aging, duration, and impermanence, other masters state that within the realms of humans and devas, unwholesome dharmas do not have resultant form (*rūpa*), but only have resultant mind, mental factors, and formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*). Question:
If this is so, why is it that we currently perceive in the realms of humans and devas forms that are either ugly or beautiful? Answer: That is because their wholesome karma, or perhaps...
Unwholesome karma may have wholesome karma as its retinue, or it may have unwholesome karma as its retinue.
If unwholesome karma has unwholesome karma as its retinue, one’s physical form is ugly because the power of beauty is suppressed by the unwholesome.

If wholesome karma has wholesome karma as its retinue, one’s physical form is exquisite because the power of beauty is augmented by the wholesome. The commentary states: "In this regard, it should be understood as follows."
The initial explanation is correct because it does not contradict reason. Question: Among humans, there are those who possess both sexual organs;
is this the maturation (*vipāka*) of unwholesome karma, or is it the maturation of wholesome karma? Some say that it is the maturation of unwholesome karma.
Other masters say that, according to the place and time, the arising of one organ [at a time] is the maturation of wholesome karma.
Regarding the claim that it is improper and out of place for a second set of sexual organs to arise, this is the maturation (*vipāka*) of unwholesome karma. The commentary states:

one should explain it thus. Those two sets of organs—the male and female faculties—are themselves the maturation of wholesome karma; however, the visible form, odor, taste, and tangible objects at that location are the maturation of unwholesome karma.
It is simply through the wholesome karma that projects the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) that one is born within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).

Once born there, one experiences only the maturation (*vipāka*) of wholesome dharmas: matter (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), mental factors (*caitasika dharma*), and formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).

Regarding matter, it consists of the seven bases excluding sound, odor, and taste. Regarding mind and mental factors, they consist of the sensations of pleasure, joy, and equanimity, along with their associated dharmas.

Regarding formations dissociated from mind, they consist solely of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the group-homogeneity (*nikāya-sabhāga*), the state of non-ideation (*āsaṃjñika*), acquisition (*prāpti*), birth (*jāti*), aging (*jarā*), duration (*sthiti*), and impermanence (*anityatā*).

Due to karma that leads to a homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*) induced by the wholesome, one is born in the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*). Having been born there, one experiences only the maturation (*vipāka*) of wholesome phenomena:

the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), as well as the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*). Regarding the mental factors, these are the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) and its associated factors;

regarding the formations dissociated from mind, they are the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the homogeneous class of beings, acquisition (*prāpti*), birth (*jāti*), aging (*jarā*), duration (*sthiti*), and impermanence (*anityatā*). Furthermore, there are those who maintain...
This explains that when one is born in the hells due to karma of a superior grade of unwholesomeness that projects a homogeneous life-span (*nikāya-sabhāga*), once born there,
one experiences only the maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of those superior unwholesome factors. Likewise,

when one is born among the animals due to karma of a middling grade of unwholesomeness that projects a homogeneous life-span, once born there, one experiences only the maturation fruit of those middling factors.
It is only by means of inferior unwholesome karma that draws one into a common destiny (*nikāya-sabhāga*) that one is born among the hungry ghosts;

once born there, one experiences only the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of those inferior dharmas. Other masters say that it is only by means of superior unwholesome karma that draws one into a common destiny that one is born in the hells;
once born there, one experiences the ripening fruits of both superior and medium unwholesome dharmas.

The matured fruits of the animal and hungry ghost realms are as previously explained. Alternatively, some say that one is born in hell solely by means of an intensely strong unwholesome karma that projects a common destiny (*nikāya-sabhāga*);
once born there, one experiences the ripened fruit of those three grades of unwholesome dharmas.
One is born in the animal realm solely by means of a middling grade of unwholesome karma that projects a common destiny; once born there...
Having already experienced the ripened fruits (*vipāka-phala*) of those two lower grades of dharmas within that realm, beings in the ghost realm (*preta-gati*) are as previously described.
Alternatively, some say that one is born in hell solely by means of a karma of superior-grade unwholesomeness (*akuśala*) that projects the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*);

once born there, one experiences the ripened fruits of all three grades of unwholesome dharmas. However, it is solely by means of a karma of middling-grade unwholesomeness that [the homogeneous class] is projected.
Having been born into the realm of animals, once born there, one experiences the maturation of the three grades of dharmas;

yet, it is solely by means of karma of an inferior grade that draws the commonality of existence (*nikāya-sabhāga*) that one is born into the realm of hungry ghosts, and having been born there, one experiences the maturation of the two grades—inferior and middling—of those dharmas.
Furthermore, some say it is solely by means of karma of a superior grade that draws the commonality of existence.
Having been born in the hells, once born there, one experiences the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of those three grades of unwholesome dharmas;

yet, it is by karma of middling-grade unwholesomeness that draws the commonality of existence (*nikāya-sabhāga*) that one is born into the animal realm, and having been born there, one experiences the ripened fruit of those three grades of dharmas;
yet, it is by karma of inferior-grade unwholesomeness that draws the commonality of existence that one is born within the realm of hungry ghosts.
Having been born there, one experiences the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of those three grades of unwholesome dharmas. The commentary states: It should be explained as follows:
there are three grades of unwholesome karma that project rebirth in the destiny of hell (*niraya-gati-sabhāga-karman*). Depending on which of these one type occurs, one is born in hell;
having been born there, one experiences, as appropriate, the ripening fruit of those three grades of unwholesome dharmas. There are thus three grades.
Unwholesome karma that leads to rebirth in the common lot of the animal realm arises in the animal realm by means of any one of its three types;
having been born there, one experiences the ripening fruit of those three grades of dharmas as appropriate.

Unwholesome karma that leads to rebirth in the common lot of the hungry ghost realm arises in the hungry ghost realm by means of any one of its three types; having been born there, one experiences... as appropriate.
Furthermore, regarding the maturation of the results of those three grades of dharmas that are to be experienced:

some say that one is born in the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations solely through karma of the superior grade of goodness within the realms that projects a homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*); having been born there, one experiences only the maturation of the results of those superior-grade dharmas.
One is born in the desire realm solely through karma of the middling grade of goodness that projects a homogeneous class of beings.
Once born in those five heavens, they experience only the maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of those medium-grade dharmas;

yet, because they were drawn into the human realm by a karma of inferior grade belonging to the desire realm that projects a homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*), once born there, they experience only the maturation fruit of those inferior-grade dharmas.
Regarding this, there are also five masters' views on maturation, and the meaning of the *pūrvapakṣa* (the critical evaluation) is the same as for the unwholesome [dharmas] mentioned previously.

Because it has already been explained, they are not recorded here in full. Furthermore, there are three grades of wholesome karma that project rebirth in the first dhyāna; these do not differ in their commonality of type (*nikāya-sabhāga*).

Depending on which grade arises, one is born in the first dhyāna. Once born there, one experiences the maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of those three grades of wholesome dharmas—which do not differ in their commonality of type—according to their respective conditions.
However, it is only by means of a low-grade wholesome karma that one projects rebirth in the second dhyāna.

Beings born into the Heaven of Limited Light (*Parīttābha*) through karma that produces the group-homogeneity (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of that realm, once born there, experience only the maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of those inferior wholesome dharmas;

yet, by means of medium-grade wholesome karma that draws forth the group-homogeneity of the second dhyāna, they are likewise born into the Heaven of Infinite Light (*Apramāṇābha*), where, once born, they experience only the maturation fruit of those medium-grade wholesome dharmas; and by means of superior-grade [wholesome karma]...
When one is born among the Ābhāsvara devas through karma that projects the group-homogeneity (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of the second dhyāna, having been born there,

one experiences only the maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of those superior wholesome dharmas. When one is born among the Parīttaśubha devas through karma that projects the group-homogeneity of the third dhyāna by means of inferior wholesome [karma],
having been born there, one experiences only the maturation fruit of those inferior wholesome dharmas.
If one is born among the Apramāṇaśubha devas by means of karma that induces the group-homogeneity (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of the third dhyāna through a medium-grade wholesome [action],
once born there, one experiences only the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of that medium-grade wholesome dharma.

If one is born among the Śubhakṛtsna devas by means of karma that induces the group-homogeneity of the third dhyāna through a superior-grade wholesome [action], once born there, one experiences only that superior-grade [fruit].

The maturation fruit of wholesome dharmas is as follows: by means of a weak-grade wholesome karma that projects the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of the fourth dhyāna, one is born in the Anabhraka heaven;
having been born there, one experiences only the maturation fruit of those weak-grade wholesome dharmas.
By means of a medium-grade wholesome karma that projects the homogeneous class of the fourth dhyāna, one is born in the Puṇyaprasava heaven; having been born there, one experiences only...

One experiences the ripening fruit of those medium-grade wholesome dharmas solely through the karma of superior-grade wholesome [dharmas] that projects the generic similarity (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of the Fourth Dhyāna, whereby one is born among the Bṛhatphala devas;
having been born there, one experiences only the ripening fruit of those superior-grade wholesome [dharmas].
One is born among the Avṛha devas solely through the karma of inferior-grade mixed cultivation of dhyāna that projects the generic similarity of the Fourth Dhyāna.
Once born there as a deva, he experiences only the ripening fruit of that inferior mixed cultivation of dhyāna;
however, by means of karma that draws forth the generic similarity (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of the fourth dhyāna through medium-grade mixed cultivation of dhyāna, he is born in the Atapa Heaven.
Once born there, he experiences only the ripening fruit of that medium-grade mixed cultivation of dhyāna; however, by means of the superior grade...
Having practiced the mixed cultivation of dhyāna, one brings about the karma for the group-homogeneity (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of the fourth dhyāna that leads to birth in the Sudṛśa Heaven;
once born there, one experiences only the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of those superior levels of mixed cultivation of dhyāna.

Furthermore, by means of the extremely superior level of mixed cultivation of dhyāna, one brings about the karma for the group-homogeneity of the fourth dhyāna that leads to birth in the Sudarśana Heaven; once born there—
One experiences only the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of those superior-superior (*adhimātra-adhimātra*) mixed meditations (*vyavakīrṇa-dhyāna*).
Because one has been drawn to the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of the fourth dhyāna by means of the most superior mixed meditation, one is born in the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
Having been born there, one experiences only the ripening fruit of those most superior mixed meditation dharmas; there are three grades of goodness that draw [this result].
In the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), there is no distinct category of homogeneous character (*nikāyasabhāga*); rather, it arises through the karma of a single grade.

Having been born in that sphere of infinite space, one experiences the ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*) of those three grades of wholesome dharmas as appropriate. There are three grades of ripened fruits for the three grades of wholesome [dharmas] that induce the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
In the sphere of infinite consciousness, there is no distinct category of homogeneous character; rather, it arises through the karma of a single grade.
Once one has been born in those edge-spheres (*āyatana*), one experiences the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) of those three grades of wholesome dharmas according to what is appropriate for that body;

there are three grades of projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*) for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). There is no distinct homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) [for the intermediate states].

Depending on which single grade [of karma] one is born into the sphere of nothingness, once born there, one experiences the ripening fruit of those three grades of wholesome dharmas according to what is appropriate for that state.

There are three grades of wholesome karma that lead to rebirth in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), which do not produce distinct types of homogeneous character (*nikāyasabhāga*).

Whichever single grade [of such karma] arises, one is born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; having been born there, one experiences the maturation (*vipāka*) of those three grades of wholesome karma as appropriate.
Question: Why is it that the three grades of wholesome karma of the first dhyāna do not produce distinct types of homogeneous character?
Question: Do the three grades of wholesome karma belonging to the upper three dhyānas produce distinct ripening fruits (*vipākaphala*)? Answer:
Within the first dhyāna, there are sentient beings who dwell free from confusion; this is not the case in the upper three dhyānas. Other masters say:

"In the first dhyāna, since there is still *vitarka* (applied thought), how could there not be the various groups of consciousness (*vijñānakāya*) and the arising of the body belonging to that own level?"
Regarding vocal informative action (*vāg-vijñapti-karman*), this does not exist in the three higher dhyānas; thus it is explained:

among unwholesome actions (*akuśala-karman*), according to the *Vibhajyavādins*, whichever single grade of unwholesome action causes one to be born in hell, it alone draws the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
Once born there, one experiences the specific retributions (*vipāka*) of those three grades according to their respective correspondences; such is the maturation (*vipāka*) of unwholesome dharmas.
Regarding the results, there are three grades of unwholesome karma that lead to the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*) and produce the three grades of homogeneous character (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
Depending on which single karma brings about birth in the realm of hungry ghosts, one receives only one grade of homogeneous character.

Once born there, according to what is appropriate, one fully experiences the distinct retributive results (*vipāka-phala*) of those three grades, thereby fulfilling them as they correspond. This is explained in contrast to the previous five [realms] and is subject to critical evaluation.
Because the categories differ, these are not the correct principles. Among the virtuous karmas (*kuśala-karma*), there are also five divergent theories, all of which are incorrect.

The commentator says: The commentary states that one should explain it thus: there are three grades of virtuous karma that project the homogeneous character (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of the gods of Paranirmita-vaśavartin.
Depending on whichever grade [of virtue] one is born into the realm of Paranirmita-vaśavartin, once born there, according to...

Regarding the maturation of those three grades of dharmas, there are three grades of results: wholesome karma that draws one into the commonality of existence (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of the five lower heavens is of three grades;
by whichever single grade it may be, one is born into the five lower heavens.

Once born there, one experiences the maturation of those three grades of dharmas as appropriate, which consist of three grades of wholesome karma that draw one into the commonality of existence of the human realm; by whichever single grade it may be, [one is drawn there].
Having been born among human beings, once born there, one experiences the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of those three grades of dharmas according to what is appropriate for each.
The explanation states that the meaning is as previously explained regarding unwholesome karma:

because the desire realm is an indeterminate stage (*aniyata-bhūmi*), within a single category of homogeneous existence (*nikāya-sabhāga*), one may experience the full ripened fruit of all three grades. This applies to the first dhyāna as well.

Although this is a stage of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmi*), because it is inhabited by a multitude of beings with individual owners who dwell in a state of commingling, and because the initial dhyāna is produced from a single category [of karma], one experiences only a single category of the collective resultant fruit (*nikāyasabhāga*) that draws forth the total retribution.
Once born there, one must experience the complete individual resultant fruits (*prātibhinnika-vipākaphala*) of those three categories as they correspond to their respective conditions;
for these are the maturation fruits (*vipākaphala*) of distinct wholesome dharmas, determined by the state of meditative concentration.
In the three heavens of the upper three dhyānas within the realm of form, there are distinct locations for the three grades of results produced by projecting and completing karma;
therefore, the first dhyāna and the formless realm are designated as "karma with no distinction" that receives "results with no distinction.
In the desire realm and the non-fixed stages, there is no such thing as "karma with no distinction" that receives results of three distinct grades; therefore, the desire realm is not so described.

In reality, there is no distinct karma; however, it is said that within a single category of homogeneous character (*nikāya-sabhāga*) in the desire realm, one may obtain the full retribution of three categories of matured results (*vipāka-phala*), which are likewise the results of no distinct karma.
From here below, the seventh [section] distinguishes the maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*) from its cause;

because there is an interval between them, it is said that the maturation fruit does not coexist with the karma, nor is it produced in the same moment as the karma is performed. Even if the karma is performed in the present, one does not experience the fruit in that very same moment;

rather, the karma must necessarily be separated by many moments before the fruit can attain its stage. Furthermore, it does not arise immediately [after the cause], due to the power of the subsequent moment’s condition of immediate succession (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

Because it is that which is projected, and because the maturation (vipāka) that produces fruits of a different category must depend on the time of the cause, undergoing transformation within a continuum before it can manifest its result.

The above has distinguished the characteristics of the six causes; hereafter, the two lines [of verse] concerning the classification of the three times are explained. In the text, the initial question is as follows:

These six causes are established as residing in which time-periods? Second, regarding the answer: although the definition of the time-periods in which the causes reside has already been stated, it has not yet been summarized in verse;

therefore, one should provide a verse to distinguish them. Third, the presentation of the root verses. Fourth, the explanation of the root verses. Within this, there are three parts: first, the explanation of the pervasive (*sarvatraga*) and homogeneous (*sabhāga*) causes, which concern two time-periods;

second, the explanation of the associated (*samprayukta*) and co-existent (*sahabhū*) causes, which concern all three time-periods; third, the three verses [of the root text]. Since these have already been presented...

The meaning of the *kāraṇahetu* (efficient cause) as it abides is, by logical extension, applicable to all three time periods and to that which is non-temporal; however, because it cannot be definitively assigned to a specific temporal division, it is not mentioned in the verse.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "It cannot be said to belong to a fixed time period; therefore, it is not mentioned in the verse."

The two lines following this distinguish the essence of the five fruits (*pañca-phala*). Within the text, there is first a summary that concludes the preceding section and introduces the subsequent one;

next, the root verse is cited; finally, the root verse is explained. In the explanation of the root verse, there are two parts: first, the explanation of the root verse itself; second, the debate with the Sautrāntika masters, beginning with the words "The Sautrāntika masters say.
Within the first part, there is first the explanation of the first line; second, the explanation of the second line, beginning with the words "If that were so," which contains ten sections.

Regarding the first two points of inquiry: the first point asks, "If it is granted that the unconditioned state of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is a fruit, then it must have a cause.
The second point further states, "Since these three unconditioned states are granted to be efficient causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*), they must also have fruits;
for only in relation to a conditioned fruit can these unconditioned states be said to function as causes. To these two points, the response is given by means of a verse.

Only conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) possess six causes and five fruits; unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) do not. Why is this so? Because the three types of unconditioned phenomena lack the six causes and lack the five fruits.
The claim in the old *Abhidharmakośa* that "unconditioned phenomena are neither of the six causes nor of the five fruits" is a great error.

This is because the three unconditioned phenomena are indeed *kāraṇa-hetu* (efficient causes); how can it be said that they are not of the six causes? [This applies specifically to] *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through deliberation).
1. Since the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is the fruit of liberation (*vimukti-phala*), how can it be said that it is not one of the five fruits? 2. Question:

For what reason do you not allow that the various paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) act as the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) for the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*)? 3. Answer: The efficient cause is established on the basis of not obstructing the arising [of a dharma].

Since the unconditioned has no arising, what function would the path perform toward it such that it could be called an "efficient cause"? 4. Further question: If that is so, whose fruit is it? Who is the possessor of this fruit?

Regarding the meaning: how is it that there are six types of "covering" (praticchādana)? The answer is: they refer to the fruit of the path. To whom does this fruit belong? It belongs to the one who has attained it through the power of the path. Why is it called a "fruit"?
Because the meaning of "fruit" is established by way of retribution and attainment through supernormal power; thus, it is the meaning of "fruit. Seventh question:

If this is so, then the fruit of the path should consist solely of "attainment" (prāpti), because the capacity of the path functions toward attainment and not toward analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha). Eighth answer: It is not so. The function of the path operates both toward attainment and toward analytical cessation.

Because there is a distinction in their functional capacity (*śakti*), [the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*] asks: (10) "How is there functional capacity regarding the Path of Attainment (*mārga-pratilambha*)?
(11) The answer is: "Because it is capable of producing [it]. (12) It asks: "How is there functional capacity regarding the Path of Cessation (*nirodha-mārga*)?

(13) The answer is: "Because it is capable of producing [it]. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "I maintain that this fruit does not arise from the six causes; rather, the six causes previously mentioned produce their respective categories."
Therefore, if this were so, one should evaluate whether this cause of attainment (*prāpti-hetu*) should be established as a seventh cause, distinct from the six previously mentioned.

For this general reason, although the Path (*mārga*) is not a cause for the arising of cessation, it can be said that analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is the fruit of the Path’s attainment.
Fifteenth question: Since all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) lack a sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*), how can they be said to be [causes]?

Regarding the "efficient cause" (*kāraṇa-hetu*), the answer is that all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are established as efficient causes because they do not act as obstructions to other conditioned phenomena at the stage of their arising;
however, they are said to be "without fruit" because, being beyond the categories of time, they lack the functional capacity to either grasp or bestow a fruit.
The preceding section was the commentary on the root verse. Below begins the second part, the treatise debating with the Sautrāntika school, which contains forty-six points.

First, the Sautrāntika master’s position is stated: unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are not causes, because no sūtra states that a cause is unconditioned, whereas there are sūtras stating that a cause is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Second, the Sarvāstivādin asks: "In which sūtra is it stated that causes are exclusively conditioned? Third...
The Sautrāntika replies: As stated in the sūtras, all causes and conditions that can produce form are impermanent, and so forth—referring to the four [conditions].

The Sarvāstivādin asks: If that were so, then unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) would also not serve as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the cognizing consciousnesses, because since they are objects capable of producing consciousness, they too should be impermanent. The Sautrāntika replies: [We] speak only of causes.

That which can produce consciousness is impermanent; therefore, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) cannot function as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), because it is not a cause and is permanent.

This is not a redundant explanation; for the Sūtra merely states that those six causes and conditions which can produce consciousness are all impermanent, but it does not state that all four conditions for consciousness are impermanent.
Thus, the objection is invalid. (The Sarvāstivāda school [holds this view].)

Thus, one does not negate the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) [as a cause], for although it is not a productive cause, it is an enabling cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) simply because it does not obstruct. The Sarvāstivādins object: Although there is no sūtra stating that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are acting causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*), nor is there any passage in the sūtras that excludes them from being causes, and you have not seen the countless sūtras that disappeared at the end of the millennium—how can you definitively judge that there is no sūtra stating this?
The Sautrāntikas ask: If unconditioned phenomena can indeed function as causes, then [what is the meaning of] the verse cited in the question? What is it that is being questioned?
The term "dharma" refers to disjunction (*visamyoga*). The Sarvāstivādins respond that this is precisely the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) mentioned in the root treatise.

The Sautrāntikas object: "Is it not the case that in the first fascicle, the question was 'What is analytical cessation? and the answer was 'It is disjunction'? Now you ask again, 'Which dharma is disjunction?
and answer once more, 'It is analytical cessation. Therefore, you ought to provide a distinct exposition of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) through a separate section."
12. The Sarvāstivāda replies: This dharma exists as a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) beyond verbal expression, and so forth. 13. The Sautrāntika master explains:

All three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) lack a real substantial entity; they do not exist as distinct real things like the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), such as form (*rūpa*) and feeling (*vedanā*), because these unconditioned phenomena are non-existent.
14. The Sarvāstivāda asks: If that is so, why are they called "empty"?
The fifteen [factors] beginning with space are merely non-contact; they are metaphorically designated as the seeds of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of emptiness.
Those that will arise in the future are called "arisen"; those in the present are the phase of arising; and those in the past are the phase of cessation.

Because the past moment of cessation is precisely the moment of arising for the subsequent moment—just as the lowering and raising of the two ends of a scale are simultaneous—it is said to have already arisen.

At the stage when the seeds of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) arise and cease, if there is no power of the antidotal wisdom (*pratipakṣa-prajñā*), then at the moment the preceding thought-moment of the latent disposition ceases,

it can conjoin with the characteristic of the subsequent thought-moment’s latent disposition as it arises in a continuous succession. However, if by means of the power of discerning wisdom that acts as its own specific antidote (*svabhāva-pratipakṣa*),

the characteristic of the cessation of the previously arisen latent disposition has already ceased at the stage when the seeds are extinguished, then the remaining subsequent thought-moments of the latent disposition will not arise again.

The continued arising [of future dharmas] is termed "cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). When, apart from the power of deliberation, other fruits do not arise again due to the deficiency of necessary conditions, this is termed "cessation not through deliberation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
For example, when a person who was destined to live for a hundred years dies prematurely at fifty, the remaining fifty years of their *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous class) do not arise;
because the conditions for the remaining aggregates are deficient, they do not arise—this is termed "cessation not through deliberation."
These three unconditioned phenomena are all not substantially existent. Sixteenth, other masters of the Sthavira school state:

at the time of the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*), by the power of wisdom, the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the three realms do not arise; this is called analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). This is the nirvāṇa with remainder.

Because the conditions for the latent dispositions of the three realms are subsequently absent, the suffering of the three realms does not arise; it is not by the power of wisdom that the [suffering] of the three realms is extinguished.
Because suffering arises from the three realms, the non-arising of suffering is termed "cessation not through deliberation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); this is *nirvāṇa without remainder*.

Seventeenth, the Sautrāntika masters state: At the time of the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), the power of analytical wisdom causes the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the three realms to no longer arise;
because the cause perishes, the effect is accordingly lost, and thus it also causes future suffering in the three realms not to arise. This occurs provided that wisdom does not sever the cause.
Because this cessation of the fruit would not be established, it is said that without the power of discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*), this cessation of suffering would not be established;

thus, the non-arising of the suffering of these three realms is *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, which is also subsumed under analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). (18) Regarding the Mahāsāṃghika school, some say:
"Once all phenomena have arisen in the present, they subsequently cease naturally even in the past; therefore, the cessation of past phenomena is not [due to discernment]."

20. The Sautrāntika masters raise this objection: "The essence of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) as it is conceived regarding past phenomena must be impermanent, because it did not exist prior to their cessation.
21. The Mahāsāṃghikas counter-argue: "Is it not the case that analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is preceded by analysis?
Therefore, since this cessation exists prior to and subsequent to [the object], it too must be impermanent. 22. The Sautrāntikas [respond].
The Vaibhāṣikas argue that since analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) does not exist prior to the act of analysis, it can only exist after analysis has occurred;

how then can they accuse the analytical cessation itself of being impermanent? Why is this so? Because it is not the case that analysis exists first and the non-arising of future dharmas exists only afterwards.
The Mahāsāṃghikas ask: "What [is the basis for this]? The Sautrāntikas answer: "All dharmas arise because of the convergence of various conditions (*pratyaya*)."

Because they lack intrinsic nature, the principle of non-arising is primordially quiescent; yet, when the various phenomena of the three realms are analyzed by noble wisdom, they should arise because the requisite conditions are complete.
At the moment they are analyzed by noble wisdom, the causes of the phenomena of the three realms vanish and their effects are lost, such that they never again arise.
This reveals the principle of non-arising; regarding this principle of non-arising and non-origination, analytical discernment is effective.

"Ability" refers to the fact that while previously the dharmas of the three realms had no obstacle to their arising, now when noble wisdom arises, it acts as an obstacle to the arising of the three realms, causing the arising of the three realms not to occur;
this manifests the principle of non-arising, which is not something newly created.
[Question: The Mahāsāṃghikas ask: If only the future non-arising is *nirvāṇa*, how should this passage be interpreted?

The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "If one cultivates the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) during the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), practices them during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and repeatedly cultivates them during the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), such that the suffering of the three periods of time is forever severed, this is precisely nirvāṇa.
This refers solely to the sense of non-arising in the future, not in the past or present.
How can this not be contradictory? The twenty-fifth Sautrāntika master replies: "Although this text exists, it does not contradict the meaning. This sūtra..."

The intended meaning is that because the afflictions (*kleśa*) directed toward past and present suffering are abandoned, the objects follow the mind and are thus designated as "the cessation of manifold sufferings.

As the Blessed One said: "You should abandon craving for form; when the object follows the mind, it is then called 'the abandonment of form,' which refers to the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), and 'the full knowledge of form,' which refers to the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
This is explained in detail up to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), and the same applies to the past and present.

The meaning of the abandonment of suffering (*duḥkha-prahāṇa*) should also be understood in this way. Even if there were other principles for abandoning the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three time periods, the interpretation of the meaning based on the preceding reasoning would not be contradictory.

This is because when future afflictions that take the three time periods as their objects are abandoned—since the future afflictions capable of taking them as objects are severed—the objects are said to be abandoned in accordance with the mind;
thus, it is stated that the past and present afflictions are abandoned. Alternatively, within this sūtra, there may be a distinct underlying intention regarding the past and present.
The afflictions that arise during one's lifetime are called past and present afflictions;

as explained in the context of the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) arising from the three realms, these afflictions arising during one's lifetime in both [past and present] periods act as the perfuming cause (*vāsanā-hetu*).

This is because they give rise to what are called future afflictions, thereby inducing the seeds of the perfumed (*bhāvya-bīja*) within the five sense-faculties (*indriya*) and so forth in the present continuum, which constitute their fruit.
Because the seeds that are perfumed have their fruits severed, those past and present afflictions that act as perfumers are also said to be severed.
This is like how, when the fruit of maturation (*vipāka*) is exhausted at the time of death, it is also said that "karma is exhausted.

When these past and present afflictions are severed, it is a severance in which both the fruit is lost and the cause has perished. As for the severance of future sufferings and all currently active (*samudācāra*) afflictions, it occurs by means of this seed.

If future suffering and all afflictions (*kleśa*) do not arise at all due to the absence of their causes, and if the fruit is lost because the cause has perished, this is called "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*).
Were it otherwise, past and present afflictions would cease of their own accord; what need would there be to speak of abandonment?
For one does not need to exert effort when afflictions have already ceased in the past or are currently ceasing in the present, in order to bring about their cessation. (20)
6. Sarvāstivāda Question: If unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) have no essence whatsoever, how can that which is non-existent be established as "equal" or "one" among them?
(27) Sautrāntika Answer: I do not say that the essence of all unconditioned phenomena is non-existent;
rather, they exist in the manner I describe. For example, it is said that this sound existed previously, before it arose.
The future does not exist as something that can be traversed, yet because it is spoken of as existing, the meaning of "existence" is established;

one should know that the same applies to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) when it is said to exist. It is merely said that the unconditioned exists; it is not said that the essence of the unconditioned exists.

Although the essence of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) does not exist, it can still be praised; therefore, the substantial reality of the afflictions and so forth is ultimately non-existent, which is called "separation" (*visamyoga*).

Among all three types of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), the unconditioned phenomenon of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)—which is the cessation of defilements—is the most excellent.
To cause those beings to be converted to give rise to deep joy, one should praise this as the foremost.
(28) The Sarvāstivāda asks: If unconditioned phenomena are merely non-existent (*abhāva*), then because they do not exist, [they cannot be causes].
29. The Sautrāntika’s Rebuttal: It should be called the Noble Truth of Cessation. Furthermore, what is the meaning of "Noble Truth"? 30. The Sarvāstivādin’s Further Inquiry:
How can the Truth of Cessation be established as the third Noble Truth if it does not exist? 31. The Sautrāntika’s Response:
After the noble one has seen the Origin [of suffering] without interval, they subsequently see the cessation of that [Origin]. And...
32. The Sarvāstivāda objection: Because one explains to others the principle that cessation is non-existent, the third [point] is established.

If the essence of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) were merely non-existence, then consciousnesses that take space as their object (*ākāśa-ālambana*) or take nirvāṇa as their object (*nirvāṇa-ālambana*) would have to arise by taking a non-existent object as their domain, which would mean the mind could arise with respect to what does not exist.
33. The Sautrāntika response: There is no fault even in taking a non-existent object as an object; this has already been explained.

34. In the next life, one should extensively contemplate and analyze [this]. According to the Sarvāstivāda, if it is admitted that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) exist as distinct substantial entities, what fault would there be?
35. The Sautrāntika challenges: Furthermore, what benefit would there be [in such an admission]?
36. The Sarvāstivāda replies: To admit this is to fully embrace the tenets of the *Vibhāṣā*; this is what is called a "benefit. 37. The Sautrāntika [continues].
If there were a protective deity to guard [the doctrine], one would know for certain that he himself would surely protect the Vaibhāṣika school; why then do you need to protect it?

However, to assert that [unconditioned phenomena] exist substantially is to clarify their false conceptualization as being identical to that of the non-Buddhists; this is what is called a "fault. Why is this so?

Because these unconditioned phenomena are not substantially existent in the way that the five objects, such as form and so forth, can be known through the direct perception (*pramāṇa*) of the five consciousnesses. Can they be known...?

Furthermore, mental factors such as feeling (*vedanā*) cannot be known by the valid cognition of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), nor can they be apprehended through useful [perception] like the eyes or ears, nor through inference (*anumāna*).

Moreover, if unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) were to exist as external entities distinct from greed, hatred, and so forth, how could one establish the use of the sixth case—the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī-vibhakti*)—to express possession, as in "the cessation of that greed and so forth"? This is because cessation is not [ontologically distinct] from the phenomena of greed and so forth.

Because these two—conditioned and unconditioned—are mutually related yet not in a cause-and-effect relationship, according to our Sautrāntika school, we merely negate the arising of those things such as greed;
thus, the sixth case (ṣaṣṭhī-vibhakti) expressing a possessive relation can be established. This is because the non-arising of that thing, greed, is designated as "cessation" (nirodha).
Regarding this, the Sarvāstivādins maintain that although cessation exists as a distinct entity external to greed and the like, it nonetheless possesses a substantial nature.
When the acquisition (*prāpti*) of those [defilements] such as greed is severed, one then attains this analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);

thus, it can be said that this analytical cessation belongs to those defilements such as greed. (39) The Sautrāntika objects: For what reason is this analytical cessation definitively attributed to these afflictions?
It is only when the acquisition of the afflictions is severed that one is said to attain this cessation. (40) The Sarvāstivāda cites a sūtra to object to the sūtra [of the opponent].
As the Sūtra states: "How is it that a bhikṣu attains *parinirvāṇa* in the present life? The Sautrāntika school answers:

Therefore, because the seeds of the antidote exist within the basis—the body consisting of the five sense faculties—one is said to have attained *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore...
There are authoritative enumerations that can demonstrate that nirvāṇa has "non-existence" alone as its intrinsic nature; for instance, a sūtra states:
"The total and remainderless abandonment of all suffering... is called nirvāṇa," and so forth, with many such names as explained at length in the *Catuhsatyashāstra*.
Furthermore, the Sarvāstivādins rebuke the Sautrāntikas, saying: "Why do you not accept the statement that [nirvāṇa] is 'non-arising'?"
Because this unconditioned state of analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) causes afflictions and suffering not to arise, it is said that they are "unborn.

The meaning of "extinction" (*nirodha*) refers to the cessation of delusions and suffering; it should be understood as being fundamentally non-arisen. Because *nirvāṇa* is eternal, it is primordially existent from the beginningless past.

If one relies on this statement to mean that *nirvāṇa* has already been attained, then one must evaluate it as follows: the attainment (*prāpti*) based on the Path is subsumed under the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
