The fruit resembles its cause solely by virtue of being defiled across the nine stages, not by virtue of the distinct categories of the five classes;
if it were by virtue of the distinct categories of the five classes, the fruit would also resemble [its cause].

This fruit is what is called "homogeneous" (sabhāga-hetu) because its cause consists of the defilements of both its own and other classes, whereas the distinct categories of the five classes constitute the "homogeneous" [cause] itself.

For this reason, four propositions are cited as proof. The *Nyāyabindu-ṭīkā* (Treatise on Correct Reasoning) asks: "Is it not the case that the nature of the virile fruit (*puruṣakāra-phala*) arising simultaneously also resembles its own cause?
How then can it be said that a phenomenon resembling its own cause is called a 'concordant fruit' (*niṣyanda-phala')? There is no concordant fruit that does not resemble its own cause;
since the virile fruit differs from its own cause, how can it be certain that only that which resembles its own cause is named a concordant fruit?"
There is no fault of over-extending [the definition] to the result of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).

Is it not also the case that there are results of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda*) from causes of a different type, such as when a universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) belonging to one category takes dharmas of a different category as its result of uniform outflow? [We reply: It is not that they are not similar;

for while the uniform outflows of other categories are similar in being defiled, their nature as causes within their own category is identical. Furthermore, the nature of the result of human effort also possesses distinctions; therefore, it is not [identical] to its cause.

Regarding the statement that "it resembles its own cause," other masters explain this as follows: the effect resembles its cause by possessing two kinds of similarity—first, similarity of essential type (*dravya-jāti*), and second, similarity of nature (*prakṛti-jāti*).
"Essential type" refers to [the similarity of] sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth. "Nature" refers to [the similarity of] being wholesome (*kuśala*), defiled (*kliṣṭa*), and so forth.

Although the nature is the same within the co-arising fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*), there must necessarily be a difference in the essential type; for instance, [while the nature may be the same], the sensations [of the cause and effect] are distinct.

Because they are both *puruṣakāra-phala* (fruits of human effort), and since within the *puruṣakāra-phala* that arises subsequently there may be differences in both substance (*dravya*) and category (*jāti*), one cannot say that the fruit is necessarily similar to its cause.
However, as for the *niṣyanda-phala* (fruit of outflow), its nature must be similar to its cause; among these, there are also cases where the substance is similar to the cause.
Since it is only the *niṣyanda-phala* that is definitively similar to its own cause, there is no fault of confusion [between the two fruits]. If...

The universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) also obtains an outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*); why then is it not admitted that this is simply called a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*)? In reality, with respect to its own category (*nikāya*), it is indeed a homogeneous cause;
however, when viewed in relation to other categories, it is merely universal and not homogeneous. Yet, it is not the case that all universal phenomena are [universal causes] for others.

Rather, according to their respective natures and types, each [universal phenomenon] is a homogeneous cause only with respect to its own category. As for those universal phenomena, when viewed in relation to other categories, they are likewise defiled.
Defiled categories are exclusively universal causes (sarvatragahetu); this is because, with respect to their own category, they possess the two characteristics of a cause.
Thus, although a universal cause has a result that is defiled and of similar outflow (niṣyanda-phala), it cannot be admitted as being a homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu).

From here below is the third section, explaining the characteristics of the fourth phrase, the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*). Because the fetters of affliction are exhausted through wisdom, it is called the fruit of dissociation.

Cessation (*nirodha*) is termed "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*), and discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*) is termed "wisdom" (*prajñā*); thus, analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is designated as the fruit of dissociation.
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "Because one attains this cessation by means of discernment as the cause and thereby becomes free from all fetters, it is called a 'fruit'."

From here below begins the fourth section, the explanation of the fifth and sixth lines concerning the characteristics of the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*). This section contains three parts: first, the explanation of the verse itself;

second, the indication of its specific instances; and third, [the conclusion]. First, regarding the explanation of the verse: if a phenomenon is produced by the power of another phenomenon, that resulting phenomenon is designated as the "fruit of human effort. Second, the indication of its specific instances:

for example, through the power of the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) of a lower stage, the contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena of a higher stage arise immediately following it as their equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

The mind of transformation (*nirmāṇacitta*) arises from the outflow-concentration (*āsrava-samādhi*), the concentration born of cultivation (*bhāvanāja-samādhi*), and the pure concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*) through the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

All such categories are the "virile fruit" (*puruṣakāra-phala*) of the equal-and-immediate condition. Regarding the three types of higher knowledge (*vidyā*) and cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), it should be said that they are obtained by the power of the Path;
this is the unimpeded virile fruit of the Path. The *Nyāyapraveśa* (Treatise on Right Theory) states: "There are four kinds of these: simultaneous, immediate, separated, and distant."
"Simultaneous arising" (*sahaja*) refers to that which arises at the same time through the power of being mutual causes for one another.
"Immediate" (*anantara*) refers to that which arises at the immediately subsequent moment through the power of the cause of the preceding thought-moment.

"Successive" (*viprakṛṣṭa*) refers to that which arises through the power of being an indirect cause over a distant period of time, such as when farmers [act] toward the green sprouts of grain and so forth.
That which is non-arising is called *nirvāṇa*, because it is attained through the power of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*).

Specifically, for one who has not yet entirely abandoned the craving of the desire realm, when entering the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) realized by the "patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkhe-dharmajñāna-kṣānti*)—which abandons the ten latent dispositions (*anuśaya*)—is termed both the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*) and the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).

If, on the other hand, one has already entirely abandoned the craving of the desire realm, when entering the path of seeing, [at the stage of] the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering...

The patience of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) does not sever latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), nor does it realize the fruit of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) as a fruit of dissociation (*visamyogaphala*), because [the practitioner] has already been dissociated from them previously.
It is, however, a fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*), because by the power of this patience, further acquisitions (*prāpti*) arise and one realizes [the cessation] again.

As for those who have completely abandoned desire for the realm of sensuality (*kāmadhātu*), when they enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the patience of dharma-knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkhadharmajñānakṣānti*) either severs or does not sever the ten latent dispositions, as follows:
Next, regarding the second fruit and the first fruit:
below this, in the fifth section explaining the characteristics of the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*) among the seven or eight fruits, there are four parts. First, it explains the root verse:

all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), excluding those already arisen, are the dominant fruits of other conditioned phenomena. Second, it asks about the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*).

Regarding the two superior fruits (*adhipati-phala*), they differ from the other three. To answer: the name "fruit of human effort" (*puruṣakāra-phala*) applies exclusively to the agent, whereas the designation "superior fruit" (*adhipati-phala*) applies universally to both [the agent and the instrument].

To illustrate this with examples: consider objects such as a chariot or a house produced by a craftsman. These objects, relative to the craftsman who produced them, receive the names of both "fruit of human effort" and "superior fruit.

Among the four types of fruits of human effort, those that are temporally separated from their cause are called "separated fruits of human effort" (*vyavahita-puruṣakāra-phala*); these are distinguished from those that are not separated from the craftsman.
It is exclusively the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
From this point on, the following verse distinguishes the causes according to their temporal periods regarding their taking and giving of fruits.

In the text, first the cause is restated as a question, next the verse is cited as the answer, and finally the verse is explained. Within the main body of the explanation, there are six parts; first, the initial phrase is explained: the five causes take the fruit only...

Regarding the present, it is certainly not the past; this should also be stated accordingly. As the *Vibhāṣā* states, among the six causes, the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) takes up its fruit in the present.
This is because unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) cannot take up a fruit, and thus it is not necessarily possessed of a fruit;
for this reason, it is not mentioned here. In the eighteenth fascicle of the *Nyāyānusāra*, other masters state that this efficient cause takes up its fruit.
Because there is no certainty regarding the time of giving the fruit, it is incorrect to claim that there is no distinction between taking and giving [the fruit]. Why is this so?
This cause takes the fruit while being necessarily present; furthermore, there is no sense of "giving" the fruit while it is not yet taking it.

How, then, can one say that the time is indeterminate? However, while the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) takes the fruit only when it is definitely present, its giving [of the fruit] extends [to other times as well].

The past and present [causes] should be understood as being like the two causes—the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*)—in that they do not both possess all types of dominant fruits (*adhipati-phala*).
Since this is established, it is not mentioned here. One might ask: "Does not the capacity of this cause to grasp a fruit also extend to the past?
How then can it be said that the cause which grasps a fruit is strictly limited to the present? Therefore, the treatise states as follows regarding the past: [it does not grasp a fruit].

If all dharmas were capable of serving as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) to produce two minds, then when a mind arises from the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), if it were to grasp [its object] by means of the mind entering the attainment being present, then the two attainments would never manifest again.

Furthermore, since there is no sense of "giving" [a fruit] without first grasping it, it would follow that the taking of a fruit must also extend to the past; however, such a thing does not exist, for the mind entering the two attainments exists only in the present.

At that time, the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and the mind of rebirth (*upapatticitta*) are indeed grasped by the two [preceding] attainments; since these two attainments are what is truly sought, they must necessarily arise first.
Because they serve as an obstacle, the mind of the attainment of rebirth does not arise immediately after the mind of entry [into the attainment].

Therefore, it is said above that this cause grasps its fruit while being present, and that it is not the case that it does not grasp it when there is the sense of "giving" (i.e., bestowing the fruit); such is the principle.

This is universally established as universally established. However, there is such a statement in the *Vibhāṣā*: "The efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) takes up its fruit and gives it forth simultaneously across the past and present;

this is logically untenable. For even when a dharma abides in the present, it likewise takes up birth as its own fruit through both the similar-cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).
The commentary explains: "There are those among the *Vibhāṣā* masters who say that the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*)..."
Because they are subsumed under the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), the efficient cause both takes up and gives forth its fruit across both past and present;

however, the Master of the *Nyāyānusāra* does not accept this, stating that it is logically untenable. Regarding the second phrase, both the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) and the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) likewise give forth their fruits in the same manner, but only in the present time.
It is by virtue of these two causes that the characteristics of duration, change, and cessation take up and give forth their fruits.
Because they must necessarily exist simultaneously, there are ten points in the commentary on the third line of the verse.

First, it explains that the two causes—the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*)—and their results extend across both the past and the present. Second, it raises the question: while the past may be so, how can a present [cause] give rise to a result of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*)?
Third, it answers: there are results of uniform outflow that arise immediately; when these two causes are in the phase of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*), they [give rise to] such results.

Regarding the four categories of the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for the outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the four wholesome [dharmas], there are four permutations.

The first permutation refers to the final acquisition that is relinquished at the moment when the roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*) are severed. The second permutation refers to the acquisition first obtained at the moment when the roots of goodness are reconnected;
it should be explained that at that time, the roots of goodness are reconnected, and the acquisitions of wholesome dharmas from the beginningless past exist in the present.

At the time when [the acquisition] is taken up but not yet given away—at the moment when it first arises and connects with its characteristic—the preceding acquisition was given away but not taken up.
The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "The Sūtra-master has here erroneously made this statement: 'One should say that at the time of connection, the preceding acquisition is conjoined.
A detailed examination of his reasoning shows that this should not be so. Why? Because it is not only at the stage of cessation that the final [acquisition] is relinquished."

The acquisition (*prāpti*) obtained at the initial moment of reconnection [to the wholesome state] is an outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) equal to that [wholesome state], because it is an outflow even of the acquisition already extinguished during the stage of abandonment;
and since the acquisitions of many moments in the preceding stage all serve as similar causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) for the acquisition of the present moment,
yet it is said that only the acquisition of the final moment of that stage yields the fruit of the present acquisition, therefore it should be understood as follows:
This text clarifies that the Master An-hui was a disciple of the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu.

To address the objection that the Sūtra-master merely states "it should be said that at that time the continuity [of the acquisition] occurs," one must ask: whose acquisition is it that extends back through beginningless past lives?

Who says that it refers exclusively to the acquisition abandoned at the very last moment, which is equal to the acquisition at the time of the current continuity, as a flow-on fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*)? Therefore, it should be understood as follows...

5. When the roots of goodness are reconnected (*kuśalamūla-pratisaṃdhi*), the acquisition (*prāpti*) first obtained is said to be wholesome. The third and fourth phrases can be understood according to the text. 6.
Among the similar causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) for unwholesome acquisitions (*akuśala-prāpti*), there are likewise four phrases, which can be understood as in the text.

7. Among the similar causes for acquisitions of obscured-unspecified states (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-prāpti*), there are also four phrases; [this applies] up to the acquisition of the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).

In the time of the Han, regarding what is finally relinquished: it is not the case that one takes from the weak-weak (*mṛdu-mṛdu*) while not giving; nor that one gives at the time of retrogression while not taking;
nor that one both gives and takes when not yet obtained; and as for other Arhats, they neither give nor take. This should be explained according to principle.

Regarding the seven types of non-obscured neutral (*anivṛta-avyākṛta*) acquisitions acting as similar causes (*sabhāga-hetu*), there is a response following the subsequent clause, namely, at the time of giving the fruit.
9. It must also be that which takes the fruit, or at the time of taking the fruit, but is not giving the fruit—namely, the final aggregates of an Arhat in their state of nirvana without remainder.
Regarding the eight [types of causes], for those mental states and mental factors that possess objects, there are three kinds of homogeneous causes according to their three natures;

these can be understood through the four alternatives as explained in the text. 10. Question: What is the meaning of "taking the fruit" (*phalagrahaṇa*) and "giving the fruit" (*phaladāna*)? 10. Answer: It is capable of... [text fragment]

It is called "grasping the fruit" (*phalagrahaṇa*) because it serves as the seed for that [fruit]; it is called "bestowing the fruit" (*phaladāna*) because it directly provides power to that [fruit]. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"To say 'grasping the fruit' means it has the sense of 'drawing forth' (*ākṣepa*), meaning it draws forth the future so that it may arise. Regarding those of the same nature, it can serve as a seed;
regarding those of a different nature, by virtue of having the same fruit; regarding those that are not a single fruit, by virtue of their being of the same class."
Although they are of different categories, because they exist as a continuity of their own respective aggregates, all are termed "projecting" (*ākṣepaka*).

This projecting cause is said to "take up the fruit" (*phalagrahaṇa*). As for "giving the fruit" (*phaladāna*), it means that this cause correctly bestows its power upon that [effect], causing it to arise and so forth.
When the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*) is currently present, its dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*) exists as having already arisen in the present.

The visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) and so forth act as efficient causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*) for the production of various dominant results (*adhipati-phala*), such as visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), which arise without interval,
as in the case of the "supreme mundane dharmas" (*laukikāgra-dharma*) acting as efficient causes for the "patience regarding the dharma of suffering" (*duḥkhe-dharmajñānakṣānti*).
Others arise with an interval, such as the roots of merit conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*) acting as efficient causes for the enlightenment of the three vehicles (*triyāna-bodhi*).
Regarding the four explanations for the phrase "and so forth" concerning the predominant results (*adhipati-phala*), the fourth [explanation] concerns the maturation result (*vipāka-phala*).
A single cause gives its fruit only in the past, because a maturation result neither co-exists with its cause nor occurs immediately after it. Fifth, regarding the other masters:

in addition to the five aforementioned fruits, they establish four further fruits. The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "The masters of the West say there are nine fruits; in addition to the five preceding fruits..."

The separate establishment of the four fruits can be understood according to the text. Regarding the six Vaibhāṣika masters, they subsume these four fruits entirely within the categories of *puruṣakāra-phala* (fruit of human effort) and *adhipati-phala* (dominant fruit):
the second and fourth are *puruṣakāra-phalas*, while the first and third are *adhipati-phas*.

Next, the following verse clarifies the number of causes from which various phenomena arise; within this passage there are six sections. First, it summarizes the previous question and the subsequent answer.
Briefly, there are four types of phenomena: (1) defiled phenomena, (2) phenomena born of maturation, (3) initial untainted phenomena, and (4) phenomena remaining other than the preceding three.
Third, it asks again: what are these "remaining phenomena"? Fourth, it answers: they are those excluding maturation.
The remaining three indeterminate dharmas; excluding the first [category], all other untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas, as well as all other tainted (*sāsrava*) wholesome dharmas—these five.

Thus, these four categories of dharmas are presented by the root verse. Regarding the sixfold explanation of the text of this verse, there are eight sections. First, concerning the defiled (*kliṣṭa*) dharmas, the first line of the verse is explained:
"Defiled [dharmas] arise from the causes excluding the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*). This means that, in succession, they arise from the remaining five causes, excluding the ripening cause.

The fourth phrase concerns the remaining births of the two types of *vipākaja* (fruition-born) dharmas; this explains the first phrase. Regarding *vipākaja*, one excludes the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*);

this explains [the second phrase] as excluding the fruition cause and the remaining five causes. Regarding the birth of the arising cause (*jāti-hetu*), it explains the fourth phrase. Regarding the remaining births of the three [types of causes], it refers to the remaining dharmas; this explains the second phrase.
Regarding the remaining [dharmas] that cover [the others], one excludes the two causes of fruition and universality; this explains [the third phrase] as excluding those two respectively.

The remaining four causes produce [the dharmas]—this explains the fourth phrase. The remaining [causes] produce the four [types of dharmas], beginning with the first untainted dharma—this explains the second phrase.
The noble [dharmas] exclude the previous two [causes] as well as the homogeneous cause; they are produced by the remaining three causes—this explains the fourth phrase.

The remaining [causes] produce the five [types of dharmas]. Question: For what purpose are these four types of dharmas taught? Answer: To indicate the fifth phrase, namely, the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*).

Furthermore, regarding the seven questions on non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) and the four types of matter (*rūpa*), how many causes produce them? The eighth [verse] provides the answer by citing the sixth case:

as with the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), one should know that, apart from the causes excluded therein and excluding the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), the remaining dharmas arise from four, three, or two other causes.
The specific details below can be understood accordingly; among the two aforementioned types of fourfold dharmas, they arise from causes.
The Dharma is definitively non-existent.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā*, Fascicle Six;
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā*, Fascicle Seven.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Shentai of the Great Ci’en Monastery.
Section Two, Part Five: Distinguishing the Faculties (Indriya-vibhaṅga).
Below this, twelve and a half verses distinguish the four conditions (*pratyaya*). Within this, there are three parts; the first consists of one and a half verses.
Regarding the section on the enumeration of the four conditions and the nature of the four conditions: first, the preceding section concludes by posing a question;
next, the root verse is cited; finally, the root verse is explained. Within this explanation, there are six parts. First, the initial phrase is explained. Within this part, first a question is asked:

"Where are these four conditions taught? Next, the answer is given: "They are taught in the *Sūtra*. Finally, the meaning of the term "nature" (*dhātu*) in that *Sūtra* is explained. In this *Sūtra*, "nature" refers to...
The meaning of "kind" (*prakāra*) in these four conditions is the meaning of "nature" (*svabhāva*). This is the second interpretation of the second phrase.
Among the six causes, excluding the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), the remaining five causes constitute the nature of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). This is the third interpretation.

Regarding the third and fourth phrases, the nature of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) includes, therein, the initial nature of arising. According to the root verse, the three [types of] non-existence (*avijñapti*) in the past and present are excluded.
When a learned one known as an Arhat approaches the final moment of the nirvana without remainder,

the last single moment of the mind and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma) takes all other past and present already-arisen minds and mental factors as its equal-and-immediate condition (samanantara-pratyaya).

This is the first of two explanations for the meaning of the term "condition" (pratyaya), which generally describes the sequential arising of minds and mental factors according to the Sarvāstivāda school.
Because they are somewhat similar, they are called "equal" (*saman*); because there is no interval between them, they are called "immediate" (*anantara*).

Based on this meaning, the term "equal-and-immediate" (*samanantara*) is established. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "In a single continuum, two dharmas necessarily arise together with an immediate condition;
therefore, it is called 'equal. Because this condition has no dharma of a similar class intervening between itself and its fruit, it is called 'immediate.'"
It is precisely because of this similarity in degree and sequence between preceding and succeeding moments that the "equal and immediate condition" (samanantarapratyaya) is established;

therefore, it is stated that form (*rūpa*) and so forth cannot all be established as equal and immediate conditions, because their arising in preceding and succeeding moments is not uniform in degree. Below, he points to the specific case:

at the first moment there is only the unmanifest form (*avijñaptirūpa*) of the desire realm, whereas at the second moment, when one enters the first dhyāna with outflows (*sāsrava*), there is [unmanifest form].
Regarding the two types of non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) of the desire realm and the form realm:

when one enters the first dhyāna of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state at the second moment, or when the two types of outflow-free informative matter (*vijñapti-rūpa*) of the desire realm arise immediately thereafter, because the various material phenomena arise from the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) without confusion—whether preceding or succeeding, many or few—the material factors do not establish an equal-and-immediate condition for one another; thus, these two are distinct.
The Venerable Vasumitra stated as follows: Within a single body, the first instance of nourished matter (aupacayika-rūpa) arises in a continuous succession;
subsequently, when it encounters further conditions for nourishment, a second instance of nourished matter arises.

Because this second instance does not conflict with or harm the preceding nourished matter, and because they appear in a state of intermingling, it is impossible to establish [the relationship between them] as one of equal-and-immediate condition (samanantara-pratyaya).

Second, the exposition of the Venerable Bhadanta’s interpretation contains seven parts. First, the exposition of the Venerable Bhadanta’s interpretation regarding how various forms arise immediately [one after another], whether fewer or more.
Second, the question: "Is it not the case that when mental factors (*caitta*) arise immediately [one after another], there are also varieties of fewer or more categories that are not equal?
For instance, in the wholesome category of the desire realm, there are twenty-two; in the unwholesome category of mind, there are twenty-one mental factors."

Regarding the statement that the twelve [factors] are indeterminate, the three natures (trisvabhāva) arise from one another in unequal numbers—sometimes more arising from fewer, or sometimes fewer from more—this refers to cases such as entering the concentration with vitarka and vicāra (*savitarka-savicāra-samādhi*) from the concentration without vitarka but with vicāra (*avitarko-vicāramātra-samādhi*). Answer:

While it is indeed the case that there are more or fewer [factors] when considering different categories (*vijātīya*), within their own respective categories (*svajāti*), there is no sense of inequality; thus, it is said below that "there is none that is fewer."

5. Question: Regarding the four questions on "feeling arising from feeling" and so forth, is it only that which belongs to its own category (*svajātīya*) that can serve as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for what follows?

6. Answer: It is not so. 7. Inquiry: Why is this? 8. Explanation: The dharmas of a preceding mental state (*cittakalāpa*) function collectively as the equal-and-immediate condition for both those of the same category and those of different categories;
it is not only those of its own category. Furthermore, within the specific category of feeling (*vedanā*) itself, there is not even the slightest instance of [one feeling] arising [from another].
Mostly by means of the meaning of "Śākya" and so forth.
Although there have been seven passages above, they are combined as the third section, which describes the Great Virtuous One’s (Bhadanta) interpretation.

Below this is the fourth section, describing the meaning of the "śramaṇa of similar dharma. Within this passage, first, the description of his position asserts that those who maintain the continuity of only homogeneous types [of phenomena] claim that [the person] is merely...
Within their own category, there is the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*); thus, the mind gives rise only to the mind and its concomitants.

Furthermore, if an afflicted state arises immediately after an undefiled state, the afflictions present within that afflicted mind take the previously ceased affliction as their equal-and-immediate condition.

This is explained by analogy with the lower classes: for instance, the mind emerging from the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) takes the mind that had previously entered the attainment of cessation as its condition.

Next, the Master of the Treatise refutes that [position], stating that it is not correct: because there is no preceding uncontaminated mind (*anāsrava-citta*) prior to the first uncontaminated mind, this [first] mind would arise lacking its necessary condition;
thus, the first uncontaminated mind would not be endowed with the four conditions. The *Nyāyabindu* (or *Śāstraviniścaya*) states:

"Furthermore, the first uncontaminated [mind] and so forth would not arise, because the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), acting as the appropriating cause, is absent. Since this is so, [the opponent's] interpretation is resolved.
If one were liberated, would it not be the case that—just as there is no homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for grasping—there could still arise the first untainted moment of mind and so forth?
Likewise, even if there is no equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for grasping, what prevents the first untainted moment of mind from arising?
This analogy does not hold, because the first untainted mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitta*) possess an object of cognition (*ālambana*), just like all other minds and mental factors.
Regarding the doctrine that all phenomena arise from the four conditions (*catur-pratyaya*), both the [opponent’s] position and our own school lack two essential points.

How, then, could this mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitta*) arise? It is not established that there exists any mind or mental factor produced from only three conditions that could serve as a valid example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Therefore, liberation would ultimately be non-existent. If that were so, these minds and mental factors could only arise through the absence of their respective counterparts.

To claim that the intervening conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*) are like those that lack homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*), such that only heterogeneous life-force (*jīvita*) serves as this [condition], is also irrational, because it contradicts the principle of seeds.

Since the establishment of the homogeneous cause implies that contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*) cannot serve as seeds for uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava*), it is not accepted that these possess homogeneous causes.
As for the intervening condition, by virtue of the principle of "opening and yielding," both homogeneous and heterogeneous types possess this capacity to project and produce [subsequent states].

Because there is no distinction in their power, all primary minds (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*), whether of the same or different categories as appropriate, are capable of inducing [a subsequent state];
it is accepted that they all function as equivalent and immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*). This is not contradicted by either scripture or reasoning.

It is not the case that there is no example where the dharma and its illustration differ—namely, that the non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) cannot function as equivalent and immediate conditions because they are neither mind nor mental factors.
When the mind and mental factors are about to cease and emerge, they can indeed take those very same mind and mental factors from the moments of arising and entering as their conditions.

Since there is never even a moment’s lack of the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) during any state involving consciousness—occurring moment by moment—what need is there to laboriously define it as a "discontinuous" equal-and-immediate condition?
Indeed, the equal-and-immediate condition refers to that which provides the immediate impetus for the subsequent arising.

What logic is there in the claim that minds of different categories and so forth share the same meaning as "arising by drawing upon a location" yet are not equivalent to an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*)?

Thus far it has been clarified that only mind and mental factors serve as equivalent immediate conditions; because material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) are disordered, they are not equivalent immediate conditions.
Hereafter, we shall explain by analogy that the fourteen non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) are likewise like various material phenomena in their disordered manifestation.

Therefore, it is not the case that [the life-faculty] is an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), because four types of dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) belonging to the three realms and the unconditioned can manifest simultaneously.
As the *Nyāyānusāra* states: "If that were so, why do you not allow that the life-faculty and the body arise together as an equal-and-immediate condition?
This example is not valid, because both the life-faculty and the body are produced by the power of prior karma. That is to say: this...

The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) does not cease without interval because it is projected by the power of the life-force; rather, it must be produced by the power of the karma performed in a prior state.
Since this is so, the life-faculty should arise all at once in a single moment, as everything arises simultaneously based upon the power of the karma of a single moment.

If that were the case, the arising of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) projected by prior karma would likewise not depend on [the presence of] similar and immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Regarding the immediate conditions and the life-faculties (*jīvitendriya*), there is no fault of their arising simultaneously, because they arise determinately through the power of karma.

It is the nature of cause and effect that a single moment of karma draws forth the arising of many moments of maturation (*vipāka*); furthermore, since it would serve no purpose, the life-faculty does not arise all at once.
This is because the life-faculty is drawn forth for the sake of sustaining the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*); a single continuity of life is sufficient to sustain it.
If many [mental states] were to arise simultaneously, there would be no need for attention;

yet although mental factors are projected by prior karma, they do not arise without depending on the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), as they must rely upon the sense faculties and their objects to come into being. Since they arise through the conjunction of the faculties and objects, it is not useless for many to arise together.
However, because there cannot be a second immediately preceding condition, two of the same kind do not arise simultaneously.
Furthermore, the arising of mind and mental factors is not solely due to the power of prior karma, because they arise as maturation (*vipāka*) and other heterogeneous occurrences;
otherwise, if they did not further depend upon the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), multiple factors would not be able to arise simultaneously within a single moment.

For instance, although the essence of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is exclusively maturation and is produced by the power of prior karma—such that it may be said to be determined by its own kind—it would otherwise fail to function in this manner.
However, regarding the arising of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*), such a phenomenon does not exist;

that is, once the maturation (*vipāka*) has ceased, a similar outflow (*niṣyanda*) arises, and immediately following the outflow, a momentary arising occurs, or a maturation arises. This is because they are not necessarily of the same kind.

Therefore, although mind and mental factors do arise from maturation, one cannot say [of them] that they are identical to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, fascicle 20, states:

Regarding the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), for what reason are they considered "immediately antecedent" (*samanantara*) to the mind, yet not called "immediately antecedent conditions" (*samanantarapratyaya*)?
It is because they are produced by the power of the mind and its mental factors; because their arising is necessarily bound to the cessation of the preceding mind;

because, unlike material phenomena (*rūpadharma*), they cannot coexist with other minds at the same time; and because, unlike acquisitions (*prāpti*) and the like, they do not possess the confusion of simultaneous manifestation.

Because it is not like birth (*jāti*) and so forth, which arise as concomitants of others; rather, since it is produced by the mental application (*manasikāra*) and preparatory effort (*prayoga*), it may be said to be the "immediately preceding condition" (*samanantarapratyaya*) of the mind.

However, because it is definitely contrary to and destructive of the "co-arising" (*sahabhū*) of the mind, it is not the "equal-and-immediate condition" (*samanantarapratyaya*) for the mind and its associates.
Question: Just as names (*nāman*) arise without confusion, the same applies to phrases (*pada*) and syllables (*vyañjana*). Why, then, are they not established as equal-and-immediate conditions?

Answer: It is like a master of transformations and the person he transforms speaking simultaneously; since many names, phrases, and syllables can arise at once, they do not constitute an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

Although the four previous explanations were presented above, they are combined here as the second explanation regarding the substance of the equal-and-immediate condition for names, meanings, and so forth.
This refers to the forty [minds] remaining after excluding the three types of Arhat’s final minds from among the past and present.

The seven [types of consciousness] have mind and mental factors as their substance, yet they lack the "equal and immediate" (samanantara) condition. This is because both "equal" (sama) and "immediate" (anantara) are names for results.
As the subsequent treatise states: "The first 'self' refers to the mind and mental factors emerging from the mindless attainments, and the second moment of the two attainments;
these are the equal and immediate conditions of mind, not the immediate conditions of non-mind. Thus, one knows that both "equal" and "immediate" together constitute [the samanantara-pratyaya].

Regarding the term "immediately preceding" (*samanantara*) as a name for the fruit: since it is the fruit of the *samanantara-pratyaya* (equal-and-immediate condition), this name is derived from both the fruit and its function.
However, concerning the name "immediately preceding" applied to that fruit, the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra* provides five interpretations;
thus, that treatise states: "First, within a single continuum, two dharmas of the same category never arise simultaneously; therefore, it is called 'equal' (*sama*). This..."
Because it is conditioned by a dissimilar [dharma] and lacks a similar dharma intervening between them, it is called "immediate" (*ānantarya*).

If one were to say that this fruit is called "immediate" because it arises from an immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), then the minds and mental factors of the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñin*) and so forth, when compared to what precedes them, would not be "immediate.

Alternatively, if one were to define "equal and immediate" (*samanantara*) as that which arises with no equal dharma intervening, then there could be nothing equal admitted to exist between those two.

Regarding the meaning of the arising of dharmas: the categories of mind and mental factors (citta-caitta) that arise either prior to or simultaneously with another category serve as the condition for the immediately subsequent category;

it is not only those of the same kind. Those who maintain that only the homogeneous stream constitutes [the condition] state that only mind and mental factors, within their own respective classes, can serve as the equal-and-immediate condition (samanantara-pratyaya) for what follows.
Alternatively, a dharma may be "equal" and "immediate" [to another], yet that other dharma [may not be its condition].

That which can be established as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) refers to the presently active mind, as well as the concomitant feelings (*vedanā*) and so forth—whether they are bound to that [mind] or not bound to it—since these are all identical;
thus, they are called "equal. This applies to mental factors such as feeling, which are of the same category and whose two entities arise together.

It is not so for material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*); that is to say, at the time of a single moment of mind, there may be two types of matter: that bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) and that bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).

Because [mental factors] such as desire belonging to the desire realm, or those that are non-bound (unconditioned), arise simultaneously with form, form does not possess the condition of equal and immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

The commentary explains: According to the first interpretation, a subsequent fruit must necessarily be of the same kind; since the mind, feeling, and so forth, do not arise simultaneously with their own kind, and because a fruit of the same kind must necessarily be a single dharma, it is called "equal" (*sama*).
This condition, in relation to its fruit, may involve different kinds separated by an interval, but it never exists without such [an interval].
They are called "immediate" (*ānantarya*) because they are separated by only their own kind; thus, the second [definition] explains it conventionally based on the preceding mind.

This is because, when looking from the preceding mind toward the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) that arise in birth, there is no intervening dharma such as mind or mental factors;
since it is named after the absence of its own kind in the interval, it is called "equal and immediate. The third [definition] explains the aforementioned simultaneity.

Arising minds and mental factors serve as conditions for those that are equal, immediate, of the same kind, and of retribution, just like a gathering [of atoms] and so forth; they are not merely of the same kind.

"Equal" (*samanantara*) has the sense of being equivalent; "immediate" (*anantara*) has the sense of being without interval. These names are derived from their function and the absence of anything else [intervening].
The fourth [position], which maintains only the same kind, asserts that mind relates only to mind, and sensation only to sensation, in three ways.

Because factors such as those that are with-outflows (*sāsrava*) or without-outflows (*anāsrava*), as well as those of the same category, serve as conditions for their immediate subsequent fruits of the same category, they are called "equal-immediate" (*samanantara*);
this name is derived from the perspective of the fruit. The first explanation is that since there is no increase or decrease in those fruits of the same category, they are called "equal.

The fourth explanation is that because the substance, category, and nature of the subsequent fruit are all identical, it is named "equal. The fifth explanation refers exclusively to the manifest activity (*samudācāra*).
Regarding the "single moment" (*ekakṣaṇa*) as the basis for the explanation of the beginning and its commentary on the manifestation of activity:

if a single moment of mind is thus connected to the three realms or not so connected, the concomitant sensations (*vedanā*) and so forth are identical to it; because they share the same meaning as sensation and the rest, they are termed "equal" (*sama*).

Below, this follows the explanation that mindless states (*acittaka*) and sensations and so forth belong to the same category of phenomena. Because the substance of sensation and the rest arise together, they are called "immediately preceding" (*samanantara*).

The term "antara" (interval) refers to being separated by something; because [mental states] arise in succession, interspersed with intervals such as those that are non-intentional, or those that are of the same category—whether outflowing (*sāsrava*) or non-outflowing (*anāsrava*)—they are called *samanantara* (equal and immediate).
Taking these *samanantara* dharmas as conditions is termed the *samanantarapratyaya* (equal and immediate condition).
This name is also derived from the absence of an interval between its own kind. Among these five explanations, the first three and the fifth belong to the Sarvāstivāda school.
The fourth is the meaning of "pseudo-śramaṇa. Furthermore, the first four explanations are all contained within the *Abhidharmakośa* and can be seen there according to the text.

Below this, in the third major section, the question-and-answer analysis begins: first, a question distinguishes that the future [dharmas] are not equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*);
second, from the section on the various arhats, a question-and-answer analysis distinguishes that the final mind of an arhat is not an equal-and-immediate condition.
Regarding the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), it is first explained that it does not exist in the future. Among the six [points], the first asks:

for what reason is it not admitted that the future possesses the immediately preceding condition? The second answers: because future phenomena abide in a state of confusion, lacking priority and posteriority.
The third consists of a question and answer: if there is no priority or posteriority in the future, how did the Blessed One know [it]?
Regarding this dharma in future lives, there is no question that it will arise after passing away from here.

This concludes the fourth section, which contains the explanations of three masters. First, the Sarvāstivāda explanation is stated: because this fault is known through direct perception, it is separated by the mundane knowledge (*sāṃvṛtijñāna*) of the Fourth Dhyāna.
If one argues that the treatise establishes and refutes [this position], then [it follows that] the Blessed One has not seen the prior limit (*pūrvānta*).
The dharmas of the future limit cannot be known [by such means]. Next, the explanation of other schools is presented:

another school further states that within the body of a sentient being there exist the signs of the causes and effects of future lives; these are specific types of formations dissociated from thought (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).

When the Buddha gives rise to knowledge of the desire realm and so forth, he observes only this present sign and does not thereby know the future; it is not necessary for him to rely on the fundamental [dhyāna] to perceive the future.
It is known through the supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*) arising from meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Below, the Master of the Treatise refutes this:
"If that were so, the Buddhas would merely know by means of divination regarding the future. The *Nyāyabindu* states:

Furthermore, other masters have said that within the bodies of sentient beings there currently exist the prior signs (*pūrvanimitta*) of future causes and effects, whether as form (*rūpa*) or mind (*citta*), which are like reflections (*pratibimba*). These do not [arise] independently.
The Buddha, when practicing, perceives this alone and thereby knows the future; it is not necessary for him to rely on present meditative absorption (*samādhi*) or supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*).

However, he does not know it by means of divining signs (*nimitta*), because he directly realizes and sees the future. It is not the power of divination that allows one to clearly perceive and predict what is being divined;
rather, it is as the masters of the Sautrāntika school maintain, following the Sautrāntikas: because he directly realizes and sees it. Thus, like the various teachers of the Sautrāntika school...
As for the statement that the World-Honored One knows all phenomena by merely forming a thought, this is neither like the Sarvāstivāda position nor like the speculative theories of other schools;
rather, this explanation is taken as excellent. Below, a sūtra is cited to prove that the realm of the Buddhas is inconceivable.
Although the above has recounted the three masters combined as the fourth explanation for the third question, from here on is the fifth [section],
which reiterates the previous thesis (*pūrvapakṣa*) and raises an objection by citing specific instances: "If there is no fixed sequence of before and after established in the future,

why is it said that immediately after the 'Supreme Mundane Dharma' (*laukikāgradharma*) only the 'Dharma-knowledge of Suffering' (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) arises, and not other dharmas, up to the 'Golden' [stage]?"

Immediately following the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), only the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) arises, and no other dharmas arise. Regarding this, the Sarvāstivādins explain:

if a resultant dharma arises in dependence upon a causal dharma, that result can only arise immediately after that cause—just as the arising of a result such as a sprout necessarily depends on a seed.
However, because these material dharmas such as sprouts are disordered, they do not possess [the quality of] being an equal and immediate antecedent condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
The same applies to the future *duḥkhe-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti* and so forth;

although they must arise by depending on the *laukikāgra-dharma* and other stages, as stated in the *Vibhāṣā*, for instance, within the future state of the *anāgamya* concentration, both the *laukikāgra-dharma* and the *duḥkhe-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti* exist in great numbers, and it is unknown which *laukikāgra-dharma* gives rise to which *duḥkhe-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*.
Furthermore, because of this confusion, they do not constitute an *samanantara-pratyaya* (equal-and-immediate condition).

The *Pratītyasamutpādādivibhaṅganirdeśa-śāstra* states: "If one maintains that the future exists as having a fixed sequence of before and after, how could the 'Supreme Mundane Dharma' (*laukikāgradharma*) relate to [the truths of] suffering and so forth?
Upon which realm is this fixed sequence based? It cannot be established that the antidotes exist in a fixed sequence within the future;

for it cannot be said that the Supreme Mundane Dharma exists either before or after the 'Dharma-patience regarding suffering' (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*), since that [patience] is fundamentally subsumed under only a single moment."

Therefore, the meaning of "prior" and "subsequent" is established only across successive moments; it is only when the state of the "highest worldly dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) has already arisen that the "patience regarding the knowledge of the dharma of suffering" (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) is termed "subsequent.
Consequently, the relationship of prior and subsequent does not exist in the future, and thus there can be no "equal and immediate condition" (*samanantarapratyaya*) therein.
Furthermore, even if a fixed sequence were to exist in the future, an equal and immediate condition could still not be established, just as in the case of a sprout and so forth.
Because arising is dependent upon seeds and other such factors, although there is a sequence of before and after, this [specific] condition does not exist [in that way].

If a phenomenon arises in dependence upon another phenomenon, it can only arise once that [other] has already arisen; therefore, the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is established only for what has already arisen.

If this were so, there would be no ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) in the future; yet, while the sequence of cause and effect is necessarily fixed as before and after, this [sequence] does not apply to the future.
Because there is a sequence of before and after, this fault does not arise; for although there is a fixed order of before and after, this reason is established without depending upon it.
That is to say, although the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) necessarily has a sequence of before and after, the ripening cause is not established by reference to that sequence.

If this is so, how is this cause-and-effect relationship established? It is established as follows: "Such a karmic cause brings about such a ripening result. This characteristic can indeed be explained.

Since it is also future, it can likewise be established as being in the future; however, this is spoken of in anticipation of the future by way of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Once the cause has arisen, the subsequent state of the effect is established; it is only at that time that "prior" and "subsequent" are called real.
