Question: What is the reason that this [world] does not arise from a single cause? Answer: To answer all three points collectively:

If one were to accept any thesis, reason, or example, or even the reason itself, would one not then abandon the theory that [the world] arises from a single cause? Furthermore, regarding the various worlds, the following specifically refutes the theory that Īśvara is the cause.
Within this, first, the thesis is stated in general: Furthermore, the various worlds are not produced by a self, a god, or the like.

Regarding the claim that [the world] arises from a single cause, such as the desire for pleasure, and that this is further encompassed by sequential causes (*krama-hetu*), as well as the exertion of great effort by a Sovereign Lord (*īśvara*) and the acceptance of all things as being created by Him—within this, first, the sequential cause is refuted;

the text contains eight sections, the first of which restates the position and refutes it through the principle of sequence: "If all worlds were produced from a single cause, such as a Sovereign Lord, etc."
If it were the case at the beginning of the kalpa that all six realms of existence arose simultaneously, they would not arise sequentially;
yet we clearly observe that the various phenomena of the six realms and so forth arise in succession. Therefore, we know for certain that they are not produced by a single cause.
Second, to address the counter-argument: if one maintains that [the world arises] from Maheśvara because of Maheśvara’s desire, then it would follow that...
5. It is not produced by a single cause, because even beyond the celestial realms, it arises through differences in desire (*kāma*). 6. A threefold objection:
since the prior and subsequent differences in desire would have to arise simultaneously, their cause—Īśvara—is without differentiation. 7. A restatement of the rebuttal:
if one argues that the prior and subsequent differences in desire do not arise simultaneously because, apart from Īśvara, they depend on other causes, then...
1. It is not the case that everything has only the single factor of the Lord (*īśvara*) as its cause, for this would contradict your own fundamental tenet;
furthermore, five successive challenges [arise]: if the required cause itself must depend on yet another cause, there would be no end to it. 2. Sixth, by way of a retrogressive inquiry:

if it does not depend on any further distinct causes, then how could the distinction between the prior and subsequent arising of phenomena be established? Otherwise, they would not arise in succession.

7. If one were to grant that the various causes are [infinite], this is a restatement of the reason; it does not refute the reasoning of the Śramaṇa school that [an infinite regress] does not arise. 8. Restating the counter-argument:

if you claim that although the will of Īśvara arises instantaneously, the various worlds do not arise simultaneously because they arise in accordance with the will of Īśvara, this reasoning is also incorrect.
For that will of Īśvara would be identical in its prior state and its subsequent state, arising instantaneously at all times.
Because their arising would be without distinction, the world should also arise all at once.
Although there have been eight passages above, they are combined as the first explanation of the cause for the sequence. From here below is the second explanation of that which is equalized;
furthermore, within this passage there are three parts: first, a refutation based on reasoning; and then [the argument that] that Īśvara exerts great effort.
What benefit is gained by being born into the various worlds of the six realms? Second, regarding the restatement of the premise:
if it is for the sake of generating one's own virtue that beings are born into the various worlds at the beginning of an eon, then this joy is not the means for generating those other worlds.
If one is not sovereign over this joy, then one is likewise not sovereign over anything else.
Because no distinct causes and conditions can be found, [the Lord] gives rise to joy through the suffering of birth and reproaches him;
or, if the Lord were the creator of the hells and so forth, what use would there be for such a Lord?

If the Lord creates the suffering of others, then the verses concerning those who worship him—such as the Brahmins and others—are well-spoken, for those who worship him and the Brahmins speak of themselves [as being under his power].
Regarding the heavens, there are three bodies: first, the *dharmakāya* heaven, which pervades the entire *dharmadhātu*;
second, the *saṃbhogakāya* heaven, which dwells in the palace of the Sovereign Heaven as the Great Brahmā King or as the Heavenly King Maheśvara;

and third, the *nirmāṇakāya* heaven, which exists in the world to protect the lands. As for the statement that "crookedness, treachery, and sharpness can burn," the Master Zhendi said there are three types of *asura*.
He flew through the air with the three kingdoms and passed above the realm of Maheśvara;

the deities there could not endure this and shot flaming arrows at him, burning the three kingdoms until they were all destroyed at once. These flaming arrows were sharp and perilous, capable of incinerating the three kingdoms;
they were terrifying and constantly caused harm. Furthermore, he pierced human bodies with dragons and bound their skulls around his neck.

Because they bind dragons and kill elephants to take their skins—even while still dripping with blood—and wear them as robes, and because those who delight in eating flesh, blood, and marrow consume these very things in all their food and drink, those who perform sacrifices today offer flesh, blood, and marrow; therefore, they are called Rudra.
Regarding "Rudra," Master Xuanzang says that this means "Violent and Wicked" (Bao'e), and it refers to those who worship the Brahmanical heavens.

The Gatekeeper recited this verse regarding the Nirmāṇakāya (Emanation Body). Now, the Master of the Treatise says that because the sufferings of hell and so forth arise, one experiences self-rejoicing;
therefore, we know that this verse also concerns the Sambhogakāya (Enjoyment Body), and its composition as a virtuous discourse is well-founded.

Although there have been three textual passages above, they are combined as the second explanation of the "equalized" [subject]. Furthermore, from below this point is the third explanation of the "equalized" second [subject].
Within that text, there are four parts: first, citing the opponent's position to refute it by challenging their denial of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);
furthermore, if one accepts that all the world arises solely from the single cause of Īśvara, then one is repudiating what is seen through direct perception.
Regarding matters such as human effort, when constructing vehicles or dwellings, or sowing various grains and wheat, one should not require human effort; this is the second point of calculation.

If it is claimed that the *Īśvara* (Lord) depends on other causes and conditions such as human effort—and even if it is merely said that he honors the heavens—then apart from human effort, no function of the Lord is perceived;
this constitutes the third difficulty. Alternatively, that *Īśvara* would consequently not be an *Īśvara*.

Fourth, the refutation of the shifting argument: If one maintains that at the beginning of a kalpa the world arises with Īśvara as its cause, yet at the end of subsequent kalpas it continues to arise depending on other causes, then the initial arising of the world would likewise not depend on other causes;
consequently, the world would have existed from time immemorial without depending on other causes, just as Īśvara has existed from time immemorial.

Above, the fourth section refutes the first argument concerning the Lord (Īśvara). Below this, the fifth section refutes the remaining two arguments concerning the Self (Ātman), supremacy, and so forth.
Sixth, "How marvelous is the world... and following is the lamentation over and critique of false attachments. Seventh, "Let us for now cease the refutation of the heterodox...
and following marks the conclusion of the refutations and the presentation of the established position.
From here below, the fourth section consists of one verse that distinguishes the number of causes formed by the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) acting as the basis for derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*).

In this passage, first the preceding point is restated as a question; next, the verse is cited as the answer; and finally, the verse is explained. Within the main text, there are four parts. First, the initial phrase is explained:
the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states that these primary elements, when viewed in relation to one another, function solely as simultaneous (*sahabhū*) and homogeneous (*sabhāga*) causes.

The distinction between co-arising and previously arisen causes is as follows: because if even one [of these] is missing, the others do not arise, they possess the nature of a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) when viewed in relation to one another.
Although their categories differ, they act as a single cause for one another; thus, there is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).

Regarding the second line of the verse, there are six parts to the explanation. First, the commentary on the root verse: the primary [cause], in relation to its derived effects, can function as five [types of causes].

Regarding the two questions, "What are the five? and "What are the three?", the answers are as follows: namely, the four [conditions] such as the cause of arising (*janana-hetu*), which subsume the five causes;

these five causes enter into the six causes. Thus, these five causes are merely specific distinctions of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*). Fifth, the characteristics of the five causes are explained:

first, that which arises from those primary elements (*mahābhūta*) is called the cause of arising (*janana-hetu*), and so forth, up to the sixth. In this way, it is revealed below in the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (Treatise on the Correct Theory) as a summary.
The great elements (mahābhūta) can serve as five causes for their derived matter (upādāyarūpa). What are these five? They are: arising, supporting, establishing, maintaining, and differentiating.

Although they arise simultaneously, [the great elements] follow along with the derived matter. Just as a shadow arises according to a form, or light is manifested by a lamp’s flame, so too do the great elements possess the status of being causes for their derived matter.
Thus, these five causes are all specific varieties of the efficient cause (kāraṇahetu); this is how the great elements relate to their derived matter.

Since visible form (*rūpa*) is neither a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) nor a single effect, is it not the case that the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and the [four] characteristics such as arising (*jāti*) do not share the same produced derived form (*upādāya-rūpa*) as their effect?
It is not that they do not stand in relation to one another as co-existent causes;

for although they do not obtain the same derived effect through being a cause, there is yet another sense of "sharing a single effect. This is because the primary elements and the derived form necessarily never possess a single effect; thus, they are analogous to the [characteristics].

Principles of equality are certainly not uniform; furthermore, although the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), such as arising, do not result in a single fruit when viewed reciprocally, they nonetheless function as simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) because they are mutually fruits of one another.
This principle does not apply to the relationship between the primary elements and derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*).

Is it not the case that while the mind and its secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) are not mutual fruits, the mind and these characteristics do indeed serve as simultaneous causes for one another? As for the primary elements... [the same applies].
The same should also apply to the derived [matter] (upādāya-rūpa). Why is it that this analogy does not hold?

Because although the primary mind (citta) and its secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇa) do not stand in a mutual relationship of being causes and effects toward one another, there is nonetheless a fixed principle that they stand in a mutual relationship of being causes and effects.

Furthermore, because the secondary characteristics of the mind and the mind itself share a single effect (eka-phala), the mind acts as the co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu) for them. Thus, the meaning of the mind and those [characteristics] being mutual causes and effects is established.
Because there is no such relationship with the derived [matter], the primary elements (mahābhūta) are not the co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu) of that [derived matter].

Furthermore, while derived matter may be wholesome or unwholesome, the primary elements are invariably comprised within the category of the indeterminate (avyākṛta); since they do not possess such characteristics, they do not constitute a co-existent cause.
If that were so, would the primary elements not then become the co-existent cause of indeterminate derived matter? No; for the derived [matter] is wholesome or unwholesome.

Because they are of the same neutral (avyākṛta) category, it is illogical for one portion of the matter of the same class to have the primary elements (mahābhūta) as its cause while another portion does not have the primary elements as its cause;
this is just as there is no such principle that within a single class of phenomena, one portion is associated with the mind (citta-samprayukta) while another portion is not associated with the mind.
Furthermore, you admit that the primary elements exist in the past, yet [you claim] that which is produced by them...
Furthermore, it is logically impossible for matter (rūpa) belonging to the past, future, or present to be a co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu), because their accomplishment is distinct.

That is to say, there are cases where one accomplishes derived matter (bhautika-rūpa) but not the four great elements (mahābhūta); or cases where one accomplishes the great elements that produce [matter] but not the derived matter.
Since there is no such characteristic as a co-existent cause, the great elements and the derived matter are not co-existent causes.

Because they are not associated, they are not associated causes; because they are neither pervasive nor retributive causes, and because the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) by nature, they are not homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*); because they arise simultaneously, even if they were to arise later, they would not be homogeneous;

and although there is a similarity in being neutral, their categories (*jāti*) differ—just as with the mind and its feelings (*vedanā*), etc., whose categories are distinct despite certain similarities.

If it is argued that the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) should likewise be mutual homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) for one another, as they are for their derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), this reasoning is also incorrect.

Although sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth differ from the mind (*citta*) in their specific types, they may still function as causes because they share a single result. From this, one should understand the principle of how [causes] serve as conditions.
Furthermore, there is textual evidence in the *Mūla-śāstra* stating that the primary elements do not possess five kinds of causes in relation to derived matter.
As it is said: "There is a form-base (*rūpāyatana*) that is not caused by the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and is itself not indeterminate," namely, wholesome form-bases.
If the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) were to act as even one of the five causes with respect to derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*), then the meaning of this statement would not be established.
If that were so, it would contradict the Sūtra, which says: "It is designated based on the four primary elements."

The *Rūpaskandha-śāstra* also states that there is no contradiction between the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derivatives (*upādāya-rūpa*) regarding causes such as the "cause of origination" (*janana-hetu*), the "cause of support" (*niśraya-hetu*), and so forth;

for this statement is made with reference to the cause of origination and other such factors. Regarding the fivefold nature of the relationship between the primary elements and their derivatives: they are the "cause of origination" because the derivatives arise from them, just as a mother gives birth to a child.

They are the "cause of support" because the derivatives depend upon them, just as a minister relies on a king. They are the "cause of establishment" (*pratisthā-hetu*) because [the primary elements] are capable of... [establishing the derivatives].
It is a cause of support (*dhṛti-hetu*) because it sustains, like the earth supporting objects, for by its power it maintains them so that they do not cease.
It is a cause of nourishment (*puṣṭi-hetu*) because it causes growth, like food sustaining life; or it is a cause of production (*janana-hetu*), as when the roots of a tree are moistened by water.
Furthermore, all primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are the cause of the production of derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), for derived matter does not arise apart from the primary elements.

Therefore, once derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) has arisen, during the stage of its continuous succession according to its own kind, fire acts as the *āśraya-hetu* (supporting cause), being able to cause it to dry and prevent it from rotting;
water acts as the *pratisthā-hetu* (establishing cause), being able to provide moisture and prevent it from dispersing;

earth acts as the *dhṛti-hetu* (sustaining cause), being able to support it and prevent it from falling; and wind acts as the *puṣṭi-hetu* (nourishing cause), being able to fill and develop it so that it increases.

Therefore, although the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) do not possess the five types of causes—such as the "simultaneous cause" (*sahabhū-hetu*)—in relation to the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), they do possess five distinct causes such as "arising" (*jāti*).
Consequently, there is no contradiction with the Sūtras or Śāstras. The explanation states:

there are those who have attained present *prātimokṣa* vows, for whom the derived matter exists but the past four primary elements do not; or those who have attained [the vows] across six stages (*bhūmi*).
The unconditioned precepts (anāsrava-saṃvara) produced by the four great elements are not necessarily accomplished in relation to the four great elements of a lower stage;
rather, they may be accomplished in relation to the present four great elements that produce them, but not in relation to those of the future.

Furthermore, there is textual evidence in the *Ṣaṭpādābhidharma* (Six-Limbed Abhidharma) stating that, from a broad perspective, there is no association between the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) and its causes, such as the five types of causes [simultaneity, etc.], as explained in this treatise.
There exists a form-base (*rūpāyatana*) whose substance is not indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), and its cause is also not indeterminate;
that is to say, the substance of the indeterminate and wholesome form-bases is not indeterminate, and their causal conditions are likewise not indeterminate.

If the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) were to act as even one of the five causes—such as the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*)—with respect to the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), then the meaning of this passage in the treatise would not be established.
Question: If that were so, it would contradict the Sūtra. As the Sūtra says: "The aggregate of form is designated based upon the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

Since the Sūtra states that it is "based upon" the four great elements, we know that the four great elements stand in relation to derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) as simultaneous causes (*sahabhūhetu*) and so forth.

Furthermore, the *Kātyāyanīputra-śāstra* also states that the great elements are the cause of the derived matter by way of being its dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) and so on. This is because Kātyāyanīputra was referring to the four conditions (*pratyaya*).

Since the treatise states that the great elements (*mahābhūta*) are the cause and the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) for what is derived from them (*upādāyarūpa*), it is known that the great elements, in relation to their derivatives, possess both the causal condition (*hetupratyaya*) and the dominant condition.
The answer does not contradict the previous statement that there are material bases (*rūpāyatana*) which are neither non-neutral causes nor themselves non-neutral;
this does not refer to the five types of causes, such as the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*). Furthermore, the subsequent sutra states: "Based on the four great elements... [and so forth].
The statement that [the five causes] are "increased by predominance" (*adhipati*) is made on the basis of the five causes beginning with "arising" (*jāti*);

however, according to the *Vibhāṣā*, they are included within the "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*) among the ten causes. Furthermore, within the four conditions, these five causes—arising and so forth—are subsumed under the "efficient cause" (*kāraṇa-hetu*).

This is because the meaning of the five causes, such as arising, is explained as being present both before and after [the effect]. The *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Nyāyānusāra* likewise maintain that the five causes, such as arising, are comprised within the efficient cause.
Because they arise simultaneously with the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), the treatise states:

"Although they arise at the same time, because [the primary elements] follow along [with the derived matter], just as a shadow arises when a form is present, or light is revealed when a lamp-flame burns, the primary elements possess the status of being causes for the derived matter.

If the past four great elements produce the present or future *prātimokṣa-avijñapti*, then they serve as the three types of causes—such as the cause of arising (*janana-hetu*)—in relation to their subsequent [effects]. Thus, all derived matters [are produced by the primary elements].

Regarding the third line, it is explained that visible forms (*rūpa*) may mutually serve as three types of causes for one another; regarding the fourth line, it is explained that derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) serves as only one type of cause for the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).

Below this, in five verses consisting of eight lines, the meaning of the mind (*citta*) is extensively clarified, further analyzing the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). In the text:
There are two [sections]. First, restating the preceding [discussion] to introduce the topic:

Although the immediately antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) has already been explained in general terms, it has not yet been determined which mind is followed by how many minds, nor from how many minds does which subsequent mind arise;
therefore, this shall now be definitively explained. Second, the presentation of the verse. Within this, there are three parts: first, five lines of verse that distinguish the twelve types of mind.
Regarding how many times the minds arise from one another, there are two lines of verse that distinguish the arising of the twenty minds;
following this, there is one line of verse that distinguishes how the twelve minds are derived from the three natures within a single realm.

Within the first section concerning the twelve minds, there are again two parts: the first verse describes their prior origination, stating briefly that there are twelve minds, and asking: "What are these twelve?"

The second section consists of two verses that distinguish [the twelve minds]. Within this, the first verse lists the twelve minds, while the subsequent four verses correctly analyze the number of ways these twelve minds arise from one another.
Regarding the commentary on the text of these verses: first, the initial line is explained.

Immediately following a wholesome mind of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), nine minds arise: four of its own realm, two of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) at the time of entering meditative absorption, [and so forth].
Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* on the stages of dependent origination asks: "What kind of wholesome mind arises [at this stage], and by which level (*bhūmi*) is it subsumed?

The answer is: at the initial stage, an acquired wholesome mind (*prāyogika-citta*) arises; if, however, it arises at a later time, it is because one has attained freedom from desire (*vairāgya-lābha*) and dwells in accordance with that state, so there is no possibility for that innate wholesome mind (*upapatti-lābhika-citta*) to arise.
Since this [innate wholesome mind] exists in this realm [the Desire Realm], it cannot cause [the higher wholesome states] to manifest. Some say: [it is because...]
Regarding those included in the stage of the Not-yet-attained (anāgamya), some say they are also included in the first dhyāna; others say they are also in the intermediate dhyāna.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka states that they extend even to the second dhyāna, just as when emerging from meditative absorption, one may emerge by skipping over stages.
Others state that a non-concentrated mind lacks the power to draw forth a mind belonging to a different stage.

Therefore, that explanation is logically untenable. Among the twelve states of mind, six types of mind terminate life but do not lead to rebirth—namely, the wholesome minds of the three realms and the neutral (avyākṛta) minds of the three realms.
Two types of mind lead to rebirth but do not terminate life—namely, the two defiled minds of the desire realm.
Furthermore, two types of mind both lead to rebirth and terminate life—namely, the two defiled minds of the higher realms.

Regarding the statement that "the mind has two types of minds which neither undergo rebirth nor meet their end," this refers to the two untainted (*anāsrava*) minds; the remainder of the text is easily understood.

Next, in the section analyzing the settling of the mind (*cittasthiti*), the text first summarizes the preceding inquiry, then presents a verse as the response, and finally provides an explanation of that verse.

Within the main body of the explanation, there are nine parts: first, the explanation of the second and third lines; then, the explanation of the fourth line, beginning with "the non-obscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) states of the desire realm."
The fifth and sixth phrases explain the three types of non-obscured neutral minds (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*). The seventh and eighth phrases explain the four [types of objects] in this manner.
The first phrase explains the five types of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and so forth. The sixth [phrase] distinguishes the objects of the three types of neutral minds:

the neutral minds of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) take visible form (*rūpa*), odor (*gandha*), taste (*rasa*), and tangible objects (*spraṣṭavya*) as their objective spheres (*ālambana*). Regarding craftsmanship...

In the case of the skillful [minds] and so forth, the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇa-citta*) also takes sound as its object. Thus, if these three types of mind initiate karma, they are exclusively consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Therefore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states: "The minds of deportment (*iryāpathika*) and craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*," meaning the minds capable of initiating deportment and craftsmanship, "are the five consciousnesses;

they are the means for deportment and craftsmanship, but they cannot initiate the minds of deportment and craftsmanship themselves. It is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that [initiates them]."
It can give rise to the mind of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and the mind of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*); it can also give rise to the mind of virtuous conduct (*dharmic*).

Because these minds are associated with mental factors and their textual descriptions are identical to those of the *pravṛtti-citta* (mind of manifestation), it is said that these three minds are exclusively of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). The retributive mind (*vipākacitta*) does not initiate karma;

rather, it is common to all six consciousnesses and takes all twelve bases (*āyatana*) as its objects. Therefore, the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) for deportment is not mentioned here, as it is common to four consciousnesses, and sound is not [an object of the retributive mind].

Because they are modes of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and crafts (*śailpasthānika*), their application (*prayoga*) also extends to the five consciousnesses; this passage is identical to the *Vibhāṣā*.

Regarding the five consciousnesses as the means for crafts and so forth, other masters say that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) induced by deportment and craft can fully perceive objects consisting of all twelve bases (*āyatana*).
Only the *Vibhāṣā* states that the knowledge acquired at birth (*upapattipratilambhika-jñāna*) within the minds of deportment and craft can perceive [these objects].

Because it is another's mind, knowing that it takes all twelve bases (*āyatana*) as its object is the correct principle. Regarding the phrase "In this way, etc.," below is a detailed analysis of how many minds arise from each of the twenty minds.
Among these twenty minds, eight do not undergo death or rebirth:

namely, the wholesome minds acquired by birth (*upapatti-labdha-kuśala*) in the three realms, the retributive minds (*vipāka-citta*) in the three realms, and the deportment minds (*airyāpathika*) in two realms. These two [sets of] minds undergo rebirth but do not terminate life.
"Throughout life" refers to the two defiled minds of the desire realm; "at death" and "at rebirth" refer to the two defiled minds of the higher realms.

Eight minds do not involve death or rebirth: these are the preparatory minds (*prayoga-citta*) of the three realms, the transformation minds (*nirmāṇa-citta*) of the two [upper] realms, the artisanal minds (*śailpasthānika-citta*) of the desire realm, and the two untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*).
The remainder may be understood from the text. This concludes the sixth section: Questions and Answers for Clarification.

Regarding the four pairs that distinguish between the pervasive and the limited: First, for what reason can the preparatory (*prayoga*) and the immediate (*ānantarya*) [minds] produce two types of neutral (*avyākṛta*) minds, whereas those three types of neutral minds cannot produce the wholesome mind of preparation? Answer: Because the ripening-neutral (*vipāka-avyākṛta*) has inferior power;

because it is not produced through the exertion of effort; and because one delights in performing the deportment (*airyāpathika*), the arts (*śailpasthānika*), and the wholesome [preparatory] functions.

Because they function through the arousal of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) and deportment (*airyāpathika*), the three types of neutral minds cannot give rise to a preparatory wholesome mind (*prayoga-kuśala-citta*).

This is because the mind that emerges from meditative absorption functions without effort (*anabhisamskāra*). Since the preparatory mind functions with effort, it is capable of giving rise to those three types of neutral minds immediately after them.
Second pair of questions: If that is so, then a preparatory wholesome mind should not arise immediately after a defiled mind (*kliṣṭa*). Is this not the case?

Because they are concordant, although one may answer thus, there is still weariness regarding the manifestation of afflictions (*kleśa*). This means that after a mind [in which] afflictions are to be known, it is possible for [such a mind] to arise subsequently;

this is like the third pair. Because the *upapatti-labdha* (innate) mind of the desire realm is sharp and clear, it can arise immediately after the preparatory (*prayoga*) mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), whether it be a mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*) or beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). It is not something produced through deliberate effort.
Because it is an *ākṣepaka* (projecting) [attainment], one cannot produce those three minds from this birth-attainment (*upapatti-lābhika*) of the desire realm. Regarding the fourth pair:

furthermore, because the birth-attainment of the desire realm is clear and sharp, it can protect the higher meditative absorptions; thus, it may arise immediately after the defilement of the form realm (*rūpa-rāga*).

However, because the birth-attainment of the form realm is not clear or sharp, it cannot protect the higher meditative absorptions; yet, it is not the case that it cannot arise immediately after the defilement of the formless realm (*ārūpya-rāga*).

And it gives rise to the seven clarities and three types of mental attention (*manasikāra*). Regarding the entry into and exit from the noble path (*āryamārga*), the text first presents the number and lists the names to distinguish the characteristics of the three types of mental attention;
next, it describes the explanations of three masters. The first master explains: "The three types of mental attention enter the noble path;
the three types of mental attention give rise to the noble path. If one speaks thus, it accords with the statement in this sutra regarding impurity (*aśubha*).

Regarding the mindfulness factor of enlightenment that proceeds in conjunction with contemplation: through the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), which is an attention consisting of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*), one enters the Noble Path;

thus, it exists both before and after, as well as simultaneously with it. Second, other masters state that the Noble Path manifests immediately following only the attention to common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-manasikāra*).

Immediately following the Noble Path, all three types [of attention] may arise. As the Sūtra says: "One practices mindfulness and the factors of enlightenment in conjunction with the contemplation of impurity."

Regarding the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*), only after one has subdued the mind by practicing the meditation on impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*) is one able to give rise to the attention to common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇamanasikāra*).
Immediately following this attention to common characteristics, the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) manifests.

It is based on this successive sequence of intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*) that it is said the factors of enlightenment, such as mindfulness (*smṛti*), are practiced together with the meditation on impurity. A third group of teachers further states that they arise solely from the common [characteristics].
Regarding the mutual inclusion of the noble paths (*āryamārga*) and their common production of the noble paths, the *Vibhāṣā* masters refute [the opponent's view] as follows:

If it were the case that only the universal mental application (*sāmānyamanasikāra*) arises immediately after entering the noble path of rightness (*samyaktvaniyāma*) based on the three stages such as the *anāgamya* concentration, then there would be no possibility of arising [such a mind] in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
However, if one enters [the noble path] based on the second, third, or fourth dhyānas...
Regarding the nature of the noble path arising immediately after [the preparatory stage], what kind of mental attention (*manasikāra*) arises?

It cannot be the mental attention to the general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of the desire realm, because that is too remote. If it were the mental attention to the general characteristics of its own level that has not yet been attained, that would itself be the noble path.

Furthermore, there is no previously attained mental attention to the general characteristics of that level other than the previously attained [mental attention] conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).

The aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) can arise and manifest; however, for those who are already noble (*ārya*), the aids to penetration cannot manifest again, because once the fruit has been attained, the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) cannot be generated anew.

If you argue that there is a distinct attention to common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇamanasikāra*) which, being simultaneous with and already cultivated alongside the aids to penetration, belongs to them and thus constitutes their aids to penetration: [this is not so].
Regarding their types: as in the contemplation of the three truths, one contemplates all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as impermanent;

in the contemplation of the single characteristic of the four truths, one contemplates them as non-self, and nirvāṇa as tranquility. Because these are brought forth into manifestation immediately following the noble path through a non-segmented contemplation of the four truths, they do not constitute the "levels of penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
The Vaibhāṣikas do not accept this view, maintaining that within the levels of penetration, there is only...

If one requires that [the preparatory stage] be of the same category as the *nirvedhabhāgīya* (stages leading to penetration), then this is not the *nirvedhabhāgīya*; how then could cultivation have been attained at the time of penetration?

To say so contradicts correct reasoning (*yukti*). Among the three masters, if we rely on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), there are three types of mental attention (*manasikāra*) that enter the noble path (*āryamārga*), and three types of mental attention that give rise to the noble path. If we rely on the view of common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), they enter into the three [stages].

Because [the universal] arises from seeds, the first two masters are both correct in their positions; however, because the position of the third master is incorrect, the Vaibhāṣika masters do not accept it.
In the text, the refutation of the third master concerns only the arising of the universal;

furthermore, even granting that the noble path entering the state of "correct nature and departure from birth" (samyaktva-niyāma) in the three stages such as the *anāgamya* dhyāna could immediately give rise to a universal of the desire realm, [it remains untenable].

Having applied attention (*manasikāra*), one subsequently emerges from the second, third, or fourth dhyāna and realizes the Noble Path (*āryamārga*). However, according to the correct principle, the Noble Path can be realized through all three types of attention;
thus, when emerging from the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), it is identical to that of an Arhat.

If one emerges from the path of seeing by relying on the *anāgamya* concentration, one either gives rise to any one of the three types of attention belonging to the desire realm, or one gives rise to the *anāgamya* itself.

Within the two types of attention (*manasikāra*)—namely, that which focuses on specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and that which focuses on resolution (*adhimokṣa*)—whichever one is practiced, if one emerges from the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) based on any of the other five stages (*bhūmi*), one gives rise to whichever of these two types of attention belongs to that specific stage.
If one were to give rise to the attention focusing on common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), that would itself be the Noble Path (*āryamārga*);

therefore, one cannot give rise to the attention focusing on common characteristics [at that time]. Eighth: Clarifying the distinct mental grounds when emerging from contemplation after first attaining Arhatship.

This is not the same as when one attains the fruit based on the *anāgamya* stage and subsequently gives rise to a contemplative mind (*vipaśyanā-citta*) that belongs either to that same level or to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because it is by means of a desire-realm mind that one first attains the noble path (*āryamārga*). The case of relying on the *ākiṃcanyāyatana* is likewise.

For those in the stages of training (*śaikṣa*) in other levels, they cultivate a mind of another level once they have attained the noble path; however, those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) do not give rise to a mind of another level.

The mind emerges from contemplation. Ninth, within the desire realm there are three types of mental attention (*manasikāra*). Below, the eight types of mental attention across the three realms are explained;
the distinction between their general and specific application to entering and emerging from the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) can be understood. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:

"If one who has been born in the second dhyāna or above gives rise to the three consciousnesses of the first dhyāna, those who have not yet abandoned the defilements of their own level [arise] from that level, whether they be wholesome or defiled."

Immediately following an indeterminate mental application (*manasikāra*), two consciousnesses manifest; immediately following three consciousnesses, the three types of mental applications belonging to their own level arise again.

For those who have already abandoned the defilements of their own level, excluding the mental application associated with abandoning defilement—which is exclusively wholesome or indeterminate in nature—the mental application is exclusively wholesome or indeterminate;

immediately following such a mental application, three consciousnesses manifest, and immediately following these three consciousnesses, only this [wholesome or indeterminate mental application] arises.

Regarding the two types of mental attention (*manasikāra*), there follows one line of the root verse which distinguishes the number of the twelve minds (*citta*)—arising from the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) within the three realms (*tridhātu*).
Among these, there are three lines of verse: the first line is the root verse, while the latter two lines arise as a consequence of the discussion and constitute the commentary (*vṛtti*).

In the commentary on the first verse, there are six parts: first, the initial citation of the preceding [verse] as a question; second, the presentation of the verse as the answer; third, the explanation of the root verse;

fourth, the first [sub-section] explaining that within the defiled minds of the desire realm one obtains six minds; fifth, the fact that these six minds were previously unestablished but are now established through their simultaneous attainment;

and sixth, how a person who has severed the roots of goodness reconnects with them through doubt, or when descending from the upper realms and being reborn in the desire realm, acquires wholesome minds.

Regarding the term "attainment" (*prāpti*), although there are two occasions when the minds attained differ, they are grouped under the single designation "attainment of one mind" because both are wholesome minds of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Furthermore, when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) falls away from the arising of desire-realm afflictions or falls back from the state of an ordinary person, they attain both the unwholesome and the obscured-unneutral minds of the desire realm;
at that time, this is termed the "attainment of these two minds" as well as the attainment of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
First, regarding the acquisition of one obscured mind: as with the four preceding minds, an Aśaikṣa (one beyond training) acquires it either through arising [in that state] or through falling away;

furthermore, they acquire one obscured mind of the formless realm and acquire a Śaikṣa (one in training) mind, as with the four preceding minds. Therefore, six are acquired. Second, regarding the acquisition of defiled minds of the form realm:
ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) acquire six through falling away from their realm, namely, one unobscured-neutral mind of the formless realm and the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇacitta*).

Furthermore, regarding the three minds of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the defiled mind of the form realm arises both through ordinary beings and noble ones, or through falling away and attaining [a higher state];

it also arises from the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) in the form realm, or through falling away and attaining the single obscured-unspecified mind (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) of the formless realm, as well as attaining the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*).

For these reasons, it is said that "six are attained. Regarding the third explanation, within the defiled minds of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), two types are attained; this occurs when a person beyond training gives rise to afflictions.
Because one abandons that defiled mind and attains the mind of a learner (*śaikṣa*), it is called "attaining two. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, fascicle 70, asks:

"Is it not the case that the 'part conducive to decline' (*hāna-bhāgīya*) is abandoned at the time of detachment from the defilements of its own stage? How then can it be that for a non-learner (*aśaikṣa*), when they have not yet declined and a defilement arises, that mind manifests?

The principle is indeed as stated. However, there are three types of the category of the "part conducive to maintenance" (*sthiti-bhāgīya*): first, [the part conducive to decline]; second, the part conducive to progress (*viśeṣa-bhāgīya*); and third, the part conducive to penetration (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*). (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)
1. Slight conformity to decline (*hāna-bhāgīya*); 2. [Slight] conformity to maintenance; 3. Slight conformity to progress (*viśeṣa-bhāgīya*).

Regarding the aforementioned "conformity to decline" within one's own stage (*svabhūmi*), this refers to a small portion of the "conformity to maintenance" (*sthiti-bhāgīya*) that possesses a slight degree of decline; thus, it receives the name "conformity to decline.

However, this meditative mind largely overlaps with the maintenance of its own position and is subsumed under the category of "conformity to maintenance," provided that the practitioner has not yet lost their state of conformity to decline.

If afflictions manifest immediately after that mind, and one abandons that mind to give rise to afflictions from a state conducive to abiding or slightly conducive to decline—because of such retrogression through affliction—there is no contradiction in the meaning of the text.

If one falls away due to the arising of the fetters of desire, it is possible for either of the two minds—the wholesome or the non-obscured neutral—to manifest immediately thereafter; this applies to all those who arise from the stage of training (*śaikṣa*).

Regarding those who fall away from their state of non-delusion (*vairāgya*), when they arise with defilements of the form or formless realms, if they have previously completely abandoned the stains of that level,
they arise immediately after a wholesome mind associated with the *parihāṇabhāgīya* (receding) concentration of that very level.
If they have not yet completely abandoned the stains of that level, both wholesome and defiled minds subsumed under that level may arise immediately after one another.
Regarding those who fall away due to the fetters of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*):

if one has previously completely abandoned the defilements bound to the desire realm, then immediately after either a wholesome or an unobscured-neutral mind of its own level, both [the wholesome and unobscured-neutral minds] may manifest.

If one has not yet completely abandoned the defilements of the desire realm, then immediately after any of the three minds—desire-realm wholesome, defiled, or unobscured-neutral—all [three] may manifest. If they have not yet manifested, they are acquired.

One who has attained pure *dhyāna* or the formless attainments (*ārūpya*) can never fall away from what has been attained by giving rise to the fetters of the form or formless realms, because those afflictions arise immediately after those states.
Rather, one falls away from what has been attained only by giving rise to the fetters of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Furthermore, if one has attained pure *dhyāna* while it is manifest, but has not yet attained pure formless attainments while they are manifest, one can never fall away from them by giving rise to the fetters of the formless realm; rather, one would fall away by giving rise to the desire realm.
Regarding the loss of what has been attained through the fetters of the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*):

if one has already manifested and attained pure meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) or the formless attainments (*ārūpya*), yet falls away from them due to the arising of fetters belonging to the desire realm (*kāma-dhātu*) or the formless realm;

whenever there is such a falling away from what was previously attained—if the higher fetters arise and manifest, one falls away but does not lose the lower wholesome states; if the lower fetters arise and manifest... [the two delusions are not established].

Regarding the loss of a previously attained concentration and the attainment of higher wholesome concentrations, as well as the arising of higher-level afflictions: there are two views on this, one of which maintains that the afflictions of the object must first manifest after one has already regressed from the concentration;

of these two views, the former is considered superior. In the four explanations of the wholesome states of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), three types of wholesome minds of the form and formless realms are permitted to manifest when a wholesome mind of the desire realm is currently present.
Furthermore, at the moment of first attaining the *anāgamya* (threshold) concentration, one attains those wholesome minds of that stage.

Regarding the ninth path of liberation, the acquisition of the transformation-minds (*nirmāṇa-citta*) of the desire and form realms occurs entirely through advancement; thus, there are five explanations for the acquisition of the four minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*).
If one asks how the four minds of those in training are acquired when a mind of one in training is present before them:

it is by virtue of first entering the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*) at the moment of the Dharma-patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*), and by virtue of the ninth path of liberation when the Noble Path (*ārya-mārga*) effects detachment from the defilements of the desire realm.

When one attains the transformative mind (*nirmāṇacitta*) of the desire or form realms, or when the noble path (*āryamārga*) effects detachment from the defilements of the form realm, one simultaneously cultivates and acquires the wholesome mind of the formless realm through a single common object of cultivation (*ekālambana*).
Regarding the remaining cases, it should be understood that they can all be attained as previously questioned. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, fascicle 20, states:
"The acquisition of the six minds and so forth occurs in a single moment; one should not say otherwise. For instance, when the defiled [mind] of the desire realm first arises..."

Regarding the mind, time, or realm—whether there is a regression, the restoration of the roots of goodness, or the loss of superior attainments—in these three states, according to what is possible, a total of six minds are obtained.
At the time of regression, excluding one's own neutral state, one definitely obtains the three minds of one’s own realm, such as the wholesome and so forth;
furthermore, a defiled mind of the form realm may also be obtained. In the state of restoring the roots of goodness, one obtains one’s own wholesome mind, because of doubt.

Because the roots of virtue continue within the mind, one may fall from the state of superior qualities (*viśeṣa-bhūmi*). At such times, both defiled minds of the three realms and minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) can arise.
When a defiled mind of the form realm arises, or when there is a falling away from one's own qualities within that realm, it is possible for six elements to arise;

furthermore, at the time of falling away, one obtains the three types of one's own [elements] as well as the desire-realm *abhijñā-phala* (result of supernormal power). When falling from the state of superior qualities, one obtains the form-realm [elements].

Regarding the formless realm, both the two types of defiled minds and the mind of one in training (śaikṣa) can be attained. When a defiled mind of the formless realm arises, two minds are acquired simultaneously:

namely, the [defiled] mind of training and its own [defiled] mind. In this context, only at the stage of falling away from superior qualities (*viśeṣa-guṇa*) is it possible to attain three minds when a wholesome mind of the form realm is manifest:
namely, its own wholesome mind, as well as the wholesome minds of the desire and form realms.

Regarding the acquisition of the obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) mind through the process of ascending, some say that when one enters the fundamental dhyāna, one simultaneously acquires three types of minds.
While this general explanation is not without merit, at that time one only acquires the latter two [types of mind], because the former type has already been acquired previously.
Otherwise, it would follow that the mind of a learner (śaikṣa) could also be acquired in this state; thus, one should say that four [types of mind] are acquired.

In the state where the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*) is currently manifest, four types of minds may be acquired. If one first realizes the state of "correctness and departure from birth" (*samyaktva-nyāma*), at that time the mind of one in training is what is termed "acquisition.

Furthermore, when one becomes free from the defilements of the desire realm through the Noble Path, the final moment of liberation (*vimukti-kṣaṇa*) acquires the non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) states of the desire and form realms.
When one becomes free from the defilements of the form realm through the Noble Path, one acquires the wholesome (*kuśala*) states of the formless realm. Within this context:

The claim that "detachment is not ultimate" is incorrect, because even when one has not yet completely abandoned attachment to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), wholesome minds of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) can already be attained.
Some say that the wholesome mind of the fundamental stage (*maulabhūmi*) of the formless realm is attained at the time of completely abandoning attachment to the form realm.

If that were so, one should also say that the learner’s mind (*śaikṣacitta*) is attained at the time of abandoning attachment to desire; in that case, one must explain what constitutes the learner’s mind.
"Obtaining the five others" refers to those minds other than the defiled ones previously mentioned;

that is to say, the three types of non-obscured-neutral (*anivṛta-avyākṛta*) minds of the three realms, as well as the wholesome minds of the desire and formless realms and the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). It should be understood that when these minds are manifest, they can only be obtained by themselves.

As for the non-obscured-neutral minds of the form realm, when they are manifest, nothing at all is obtained, because they have already been obtained previously. Therefore, it should not be said that "all are obtained by themselves."
How could it be that when the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is currently arising, it is not also possible to obtain four [types of minds]?

That is to say, at the moment of the first knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), one cultivates the wholesome states of the three realms in the future; since these were not previously possessed, how can it be said that this [attainment] is obtained only by oneself?

Furthermore, when the wholesome states of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are currently arising, one also obtains the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*); how then can it be said that this is obtained only by oneself? These two cases should be stated together.
That which is "attained" (*prāpta*) is not something previously established, as stated in the subsequent verse; therefore, this objection does not apply.
Others, however, state that there are eleven types of mind because the *śaikṣa* and *aśaikṣa* minds are both untainted (*anāsrava*). Based on this meaning, the verse summarizes:
"The wise speak of the defiled mind and so forth. The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "Others summarize this in a verse, saying there are ten [types of mind]."
Master Shi (Śrīlāta) explains this verse in general terms. The master of the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* uses this verse to summarize the twelve minds.

Master Vasubandhu states that regarding wholesome minds, one should say "one attains seven," meaning that at the moment of reconnecting the roots of goodness through right view, when a wholesome mind of the desire realm arises, one simultaneously attains the wholesome and unwholesome minds of the desire and form realms upon reaching the ninth liberation from the defilements of the desire realm.

Adding the two neutral minds of concealment (*nivṛta-avyākṛta*) to the preceding, there are three; when one attains the meditative absorptions of the form and formless realms, those two wholesome minds are said to be attained, and adding them to the preceding, there are five;

when first entering the stage of the state of rightness (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and realizing arhatship, the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are said to be attained, and adding them to the preceding, there are seven.
The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "As the Master of the Sūtras [Vasubandhu] objects, it should be said..."
Since the seven [types of] training and non-training minds are equally untainted (*anāsrava*), there is no fault in speaking collectively of "one mind" or "six [minds].

Regarding the explanation that other masters claim there are eleven types of mind and say there is no fault in speaking of "six," while the master of the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* claims there are twelve types of mind and says there is a fault in speaking of "six":

this is because he intends to include the six [types of] defiled minds of the three realms within the two categories mentioned in the verse. Furthermore, a verse is stated to explain the meaning of these two verses.
It is said that there are five [conditions] by which [the roots of goodness are severed or reconnected]: first, by being reborn into this realm;

second, by entering meditative absorption, namely when wholesome minds of the form and formless realms or the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*) are manifest; third, by the abandonment of defilement, namely when one abandons the defilements of the form and formless realms through the Noble Path;
fourth, by the time of falling away, namely when defiled minds of the three realms arise or at the moment of retrogression; and fifth, by the continuity of the roots of goodness, namely by...
When one continues the roots of goodness through doubt or right view, in these five stages,
the acquisition of the mind is in every case not something previously accomplished. (Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā, Scroll 17)
