If it were not so, what cause would there be for one not to attain mastery within the various concentrations? As for the claim that one does not attain concentration—[it is because of such an obstacle].
It must have a cause; one cannot say that the cause itself lacks its own intrinsic nature (svabhāva), for it would then follow that it could not serve as its own cause.
Alternatively, one might argue that the obstacle of sin (*āvaraṇa*) should likewise be said to lack the nature of being an Arhat-fruit because it does not exist as such.
Since that is not the case, how can this be so? Even the Arhat-fruit lacks its own intrinsic nature because it is not attained through diligent application of effort (*prayoga*).
How could it be that there is no distinct entity for the obstacle of karmic hindrance (*āvaraṇa*)? Therefore, the latter three explanations are all untenable.
One should understand that among these four explanations, the first is the most reasonable.

For what reason would non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*), possessing only a slight power, be able to act as an obstacle such that it causes one to lack mastery over meditative concentration? If this were not the case, by what cause would it [prevent mastery] regarding those [states]?
In meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one cannot attain self-mastery; this refutes the second position.

As for the third position—that which takes the various concentrations as its very essence—since one who fails to attain concentration must have a cause for such failure, it cannot be said that the cause is the non-attainment itself.
This is because a cause cannot logically depend upon itself. Alternatively, even the obstacle of karmic transgression (*āpatti-āvaraṇa*) should likewise be explained in this same manner.
If the fruit cannot be its own nature, and since that is not the case [for the obstacle], how could this be so? This refutes the third position.

Regarding the fourth point—that because one does not diligently seek the preparatory application (*prayoga*) toward it, liberation does not arise, and this very lack is the essence of the obstacle to liberation—the present refutation states:
even the fruit of Arhatship [would fail to arise] due to not diligently seeking it through preparatory application; therefore, its essence [is not distinct from the obstacle].
If one has not yet been born [in the desire realm], how could there be no further distinct body of karmic obstruction? Therefore, the latter three explanations are all unreasonable.
Below this, the sixth section consists of one verse explaining the fulfillment of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). In the text, it first cites the Sūtra and asks:
"The World-Honored One said that the five lower-tier karmic obstructions cannot be drawn back to be born in the desire realm; why then is one not yet called 'fulfilled in training'?"

Because the five higher fetters (*pañca-ūrdhva-bhāgīya*) have not yet been abandoned, [the text] asks: by how many causes is each of the stages of training (*śaikṣa*) and beyond-training (*aśaikṣa*) uniquely designated as "perfected" (*paripūrṇa*) within their respective positions?

It answers with a verse, of which the first two lines clarify the perfection of the stage of training and the last two lines clarify the perfection of the stage beyond training. Following this, in the commentary on the verse itself, the first part explains the first two lines regarding the perfection of training, stating that it possesses three causes: [The text continues: ...namely, the abandonment of the five lower fetters (*pañca-avarabhāgīya*), the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*), and the complete mastery of the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*). These are the three causes for the perfection of training. As for the perfection of the stage beyond training, it is characterized by the abandonment of the five higher fetters, the cultivation of the four right efforts (*catvāri samyakprahāṇāni*), and the complete mastery of the eightfold noble path.

Thus, through these three causes, one is designated as "perfected. Furthermore, because the five higher fetters have not yet been abandoned, one is not yet called "perfected" in the sense of having transcended the desire realm; rather, one is called "perfected" only when one has attained the fruit of Arhatship and is no longer subject to rebirth in the form or formless realms. Therefore, the designation "perfected" is applied uniquely to those who have reached the culmination of their respective stages. This concludes the explanation of the verse.
1. By way of faculty alone: one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta) and is not yet free from passion. 2. By way of fruit alone:

one who is liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta) and is a non-returner (anāgāmin) who has not yet attained the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti). 3. By way of both faculty and fruit: one who has attained vision and is a non-returner who has not yet attained the attainment of cessation.
4. By way of the certainty of fruit: one who is liberated through faith and has attained a different meditative absorption (vairāgya). 5. By way of all three: one who has attained vision.

Upon attaining a distinct meditative absorption (dhyāna), one merely attains it; however, upon attaining the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), it must necessarily be the fulfillment of the fruit (*phala-paripūri*). Therefore, the text does not mention it among the stages of training (*śaikṣa*).

Within the stage of training, there is one who attains one [absorption], two who attain two, and one who attains three; thus, taken together, there are five. One who attains the fulfillment of the absorption necessarily attains the fulfillment of the fruit;
there is no learner (*śaikṣa*) who is designated by the name "fulfilled" solely on account of the absorption or on account of both the faculties (*indriya*) and the absorption.

Therefore, within the first [category], there are only two types of completion; within the second, there are none. Third, the explanation of the latter two lines: in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), there are three fruits.

The first two are not "fulfillment of the fruit"; the third is called "fulfillment of the fruit. In the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), there is only one fruit, and since it is never anything other than the fulfillment of the fruit, the designation "fulfillment of the fruit" is not established for it.

This single case is due solely to the fulfillment of the faculties (*indriya*); that is, the one liberated at any time (*asamayavimukta*) who has not yet attained the supernormal attainments (*vibhaṅga-samādhi*).

Second, [attainment] occurs solely through the perfection of meditative concentration, namely, those liberated by occasion (samayavimukta) who attain the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). Third, it occurs through both [concentration and wisdom], namely, those not liberated by occasion (asamayavimukta) who attain only the attainment of cessation.
Below this, the seventh section consists of fourteen verses that extensively explain the various paths; therein, the first verse explains:

In the passage concerning the four paths, such as the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), first the extensive question is restated and the various distinctions of the paths are explained extensively, up to the point where it is briefly stated how many paths can comprehensively encompass clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
Next, the verse is cited as the answer, followed by the explanation of the root verse. Regarding the path of preparation:

this refers to that which arises immediately prior to the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*). The uninterrupted path: this refers to that which is capable of severing the hindrances. The path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) refers to...
Having already been liberated from the hindrances, that liberation and its attainment arise simultaneously for the first time, as previously explained.

Because there are many moments [of mind] that subsequently arise in relation to the path of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*), it is said to "arise for the first time. As for what is meant by the "path of superior progress," it refers to the three preceding paths;

the remaining paths continue in succession over a long period. Regarding the meaning of the term "path" (*mārga*): the answer is that it is the road to *nirvāṇa*; by means of this, one is able to proceed to the city of *nirvāṇa*.

Therefore, some further explain that "path" (mārga) refers to the basis for seeking; just as a person relies on a path to seek wealth and goods, so too does one rely on the Noble Path to seek the fruit of *nirvāṇa*.

Question: Since the application (*prayoga*), the immediate succession (*ānantarya*), and the attainment (*prāpti*) of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) can be called a "path," how can liberation (*vimukti*) and the path of excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*)—which do not seek analytical cessation—be called a "path"? Answer: Because they are associated with the application and the immediate succession [of the path].
Because they share the same nature as the Path, the superior grades of the preceding preparatory stages (*prayoga*), the immediate succession (*anantara*), the noble liberation (*vimukti*),

and the further progress (*viśeṣa*) are called "liberation" and "further progress"; they are also called "penetration" (*abhijñā*) because the power of each preceding path can reach the subsequent path,
or they are called "path" (*mārga*) because they lead toward entry into *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
From here below, the second section consists of one verse explaining the four paths of practice (*pratipad*).

First, it cites the paths of practice and their commonality, establishing that they receive the name "path" because they are able to penetrate the principles of the truths (*satya*) and proceed toward the fruit of *nirvāṇa*.

First, it asks: how many stages are there? Second, it asks: upon what basis are they established? Next, the verse provides the answer; therein, the first line answers the first question, and the remainder [answers the second].

The three-part response to the second question distinguishes suffering and pleasure according to the stages (*bhūmi*), and distinguishes slowness and speed according to the faculties (*indriya*). Regarding the subsequent explanation of the verse’s main body:
first, the number is stated and the names are listed to explain the first phrase; second, the second phrase is explained as follows:

the path based on the fundamental [dhyānas] is called "pleasant practice" (*sukha-pratipad*) because it is comprised of factors that proceed spontaneously through the equilibrium of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).

The third explanation of the third phrase: The paths based on the formless realm (*ārūpya*), the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), and the intermediate concentration (*dhyānāntara*) are called "difficult progress" (*duḥkhā pratipad*).
They are not comprised of the factors (*aṅga*) [of the higher dhyānas] for two reasons: first, because their correct observation (*samyag-darśana*) is unequal and proceeds with difficulty;

and second, because in the formless concentrations, one observes only cessation (*nirodha*) and thus develops only the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), whereas in the fundamental concentrations, calm abiding (*śamatha*) increases. In the threshold and intermediate concentrations, observation (*vipaśyanā*) increases, and both the paths of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and cultivation are developed together.
Therefore, because the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is like the fundamental [dhyānas], the fourth line is explained as follows:

within these two paths of practice—suffering and pleasure—the dull-facultied (*mṛdvindriya*) are called "slow" because they proceed with a delayed penetration of the object; the sharp-facultied (*tīkṣṇendriya*) are called "swift" because they proceed with a rapid penetration of the object.
Next, explaining by way of persons: the path of practice initiated by a person of dull faculties is called a "slow path."

The "swift" [path] is the opposite of this; it refers to the path of practice arising in those who are both swift and sharp. This is called the "swift path of practice. In the *Nyāyabindu* (Treatise on Right Reasoning), chapter seven, it says:
"By what path of practice do the Greatly Awakened Ones (*mahābuddha*) and Pratyekabuddhas enter the noble state and realize the ultimate fruit?

The Greatly Awakened Ones rely solely upon the 'swift and pleasant' path of practice (*sukha-śīghra-pratipad*). This is because they take the fourth dhyāna as their basis, owing to their extreme sharpness."

Regarding those who enter into right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) through the faculties and attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), becoming like the horn of a rhinoceros among the Pratyekabuddhas, as the Great Awakened One has taught—others are not fixed in this regard.

Among those who have reached the ultimate goal, Śāriputra and others entered the noble state and realized the supreme fruit by means of the "swift path" (*kṣipra-gati*) and the "pleasant-swift path" (*sukha-kṣipra-gati*); they entered based upon the *anāgamya* [concentration].

Because one attains the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) by relying on the fourth dhyāna for the "right determination" (*samyaktvaniyāma*), Maudgalyāyana relies solely on the path of swift progress through suffering (*duḥkhā pratipat kṣepīyasī*);

that is, he enters right determination by relying on the *anāgamya* stage, whereas those who attain the perception of the exhaustion of outflows by relying on the formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samādhi*)— the two types of noble ones who have previously delighted in wisdom and delight in concentration—
realize the ultimate fruit by relying on the realms of form and formlessness, as it is permitted that they reach the finality of the Dharma.
Not only because one must attain the fruits [of the path] in sequence after the outflows have ceased, but because those who enter the Noble Path all rely upon the *anāgamya* (unattained) stage.
Third, the following three verses clarify the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).

Among these, the first verse clarifies the number of factors of enlightenment and explains their nomenclature; therein, it first restates the preceding question: "The path is also called enlightenment."

Regarding the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*): first, a question as to how many kinds there are; second, a question regarding their names and meanings; third, the presentation of the verse as the answer.
Within this, the first two lines answer the first question, and the latter two lines answer the second question.

Following this, in the commentary on the body of the verse, the text first cites a sūtra to state the number, list the names, and explain the first two lines; it then explains the latter two lines. The original Sanskrit term is *bodhi*.

This translation is called "Awakening" (*bodhi*), which refers to the knowledge that conceptualization is non-arising; this is designated as Awakening. Furthermore, for those who follow this awakening, three distinct types of *bodhi* are established:

first, it is called "Awakening" because the昏睡 (*mūrchā*) of ignorance has been forever severed; second, it is called "Awakening" because, having known the objects of the Four Truths as they truly are, one has completed what was to be done;

and third, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) within the causal stage are called "enlightenment" because they are conducive to awakening. Therefore, all these are termed *bodhi*.

The Section on Classification. Second, from here below, is the passage setting forth the essence of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*). First, the question: "Are these thirty-seven factors each distinct in their essence?
Second, the answer: "It is not so. Third, the question: "How is it then? Fourth, the response by verse. Fifth, the explanation of the root verses. [Fifty-five.]
Within the Dharma, based on this verse-text, the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) have ten dharmas as their essence.

Among the seventy-five dharmas, the two types of unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas are not conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); they do not conform to enlightenment and are therefore not factors of enlightenment.

As for the remaining three conditioned [dharmas]—namely, form (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), and that which is neither form nor mind (*cittaviprayukta*)—the latter is excluded by the term "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*). Thus, it is selected from within the aggregate of mind (*cittaskandha*) as the primary fruit.
Regarding the seventy-one outflows (*āsrava*), why is the mind-king (*cittarāja*) not established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*)?

The principle is that it is also subsumed within the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth, because it actually includes all conditioned virtues of application (*prayoga-kuśala*).

However, it is not established separately like wisdom (*prajñā*) and the others, because the mind maintains an equal force and function across both the defiled and purified portions, without partiality; whereas the factors of enlightenment exist only within the purified portion.

Because their functional power is enhanced, the remaining factors are not established [as distinct members]. Furthermore, it is said that most of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) take the common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena as their objects, whereas the mental sovereign (*cittarāja*) mostly takes its own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object; therefore, the remaining factors are not established.

Moreover, it is said that the cultivation of the factors of training (*śikṣāpakṣa*) is fundamentally for the purpose of counteracting all faults (*doṣa*); however, since these faults are mental concomitants (*caitta*) and not the mind itself, the remedial factors must likewise not be the mind.

Because they are established solely through the mutual opposition of the factors to be abandoned (*āvaraṇa*) and their remedies (*pratipakṣa*), some say that the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) assist enlightenment (*bodhi*).

Since enlightenment has the mental factor (*caitta*) of wisdom (*prajñā*) as its essence, it is impossible for a mental king (*citta-rāja*) to assist a mental factor, just as a king cannot be assisted by his ministers;

therefore, the mental king is not established as a factor of enlightenment. Furthermore, regarding other explanations concerning the path of the mind (*cittamārga*) and the world (*loka*) within the realms (*dhātu*):
The cycle of rebirth in the realms of existence has no end; one cultivates the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) in order to sever birth and death.

Because this sovereign mind (*cittarāja*) does not itself constitute the factors of enlightenment, other masters say that from beginningless time the mind has been driven toward various objects by a multitude of sins and defilements, becoming unruly and difficult to tame.
To tame the mind, one cultivates the factors of enlightenment; that which is not yet tamed is itself the means of taming.

Because of this, the "mind-king" (*cittarāja*) is not established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*). For what reason? Among the great mental factors (*mahābhūmika-caitasika*), only four dharmas are established as factors of enlightenment.

This is because they truly encompass all [virtues] within the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth; they truly include all the wholesome qualities of application (*prayoga-kuśala*).
Nevertheless, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom are established separately because the power and function of these three accord with the side of purification (*viśuddhi-pakṣa*).

The factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) can only be established [for those] who are capable; one should consider that among the defiled factors, contact and desire possess particularly strong functional power, and thus they are not separately established as such.
Since the factor of enlightenment of resolve (*adhimokṣa*) increases specifically within the contemplation of the true reality (*bhūta-pratyavekṣā*), it is subsumed only under that.

Therefore, this resolve is not included among the factors of enlightenment. Other masters say that resolve only increases upon reaching the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*); the Sūtra merely establishes it [there].
Because they constitute the factors of one beyond training (*aśaikṣāṅga*), the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) increase during the stage of training (*śaikṣāvasthā*);

for by the power of these as causes, one is able to bring forth the three types of enlightenment (*trividhabodhi*). Therefore, resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) is not included among the factors of enlightenment, as its function is to initiate the mind toward an object, making it prone to detachment and instability.
Mental attention (*manaskāra*), however, is a factor of enlightenment because it scrutinizes the object with precision, causing the mind to become single-pointed.

Because it contradicts the first [definition], this *manasikāra* (attention) is not included among the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*). If that is so, why then establish *vitarka* (applied thought) as a factor of enlightenment?

Although *vitarka* indeed stimulates the mind toward its object, its purpose is to cause the mind to investigate the ultimate reality, rather than to cause the mind to be flighty or easily distracted from the object.
Regarding the observation of the truths (*satya*), it possesses the power of stimulation; it is said that this power can stimulate right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).

Therefore, one must not analogously infer from this that other statements regarding whether [attention] is defiled or pure—based on the power of attention increasing during the stage of apprehending an object—are incorrect.
Attention that has reached its object in a continuous stream is established as either irrational or rational;

however, because its force is weak, it is not established as an affliction (*kleśa*) or a factor of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*). For afflictions and factors of enlightenment must exist in a state of continuity once they have reached their respective objects.

Because feeling increases within the category of affliction (saṃkleśa), and because its functional power increases within the categories of both affliction and purification (vyavadāna), it is established as a factor of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga).

Consequently, among the links of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), it is established as the link of feeling (vedanā); and among the factors conducive to awakening (bodhipakṣadharma), it is established as the factor of joy (prītisambodhyaṅga).
Other masters say that although feeling is predominant in affliction, it is also associated with the pure category (vyavadānapakṣa).
Performing acts of benefit is also a functional capacity; for example, although the nature of a *caṇḍāla* is base and inferior, they are able to perform acts of benefit for noble lineages.
Therefore, in the sense of being a factor of benefit, the factor of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) is established among the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).

For what reason are all three types of feeling (*vedanā*) common to the untainted (*anāsrava*), yet only joy (*prīti*)—and not the other two—is designated as a factor of enlightenment? [The answer is that] the factors of enlightenment can serve as objects of mental cultivation (*saṃskāra*).

Because their characteristics are sharp while those that have not yet abandoned [the afflictions] are dull, they do not exist [as such]. Other masters say that because the two sensations have not yet been abandoned, they are obscured by the equanimity of the practice of bliss;
thus, their characteristics are not clear, and for this reason, they are not established [as factors of enlightenment].

For what reason, among the great wholesome mental factors (*cittamahābhūmika-dharma*), are only four established as factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*)? In reality, they are all subsumed within the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth. They are included therein.

In reality, these [factors] collectively encompass all wholesome preparatory practices (*prayoga-kuśala*). Nevertheless, faith (*śraddhā*), diligence (*vīrya*), pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are established separately because these four accord with awakening (*bodhi*) most powerfully.
How do these four accord so strongly with the function of awakening? Faith is the supreme path for setting out toward enlightenment;
it is the initial foundation for practicing all deeds, the cause for the fruit of purity, and has faith as its very root. If one lacks faith, [one cannot practice].
Because the [other] faculties do not fulfill this function, the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) is established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).

As for what others have said—that placing a water-clearing jewel into turbid water causes the water to become clear and pure, so that those with eyes may discern various forms and images—likewise, by placing faith within the mental complex (*cittapakṣa*), it enables the co-arising mental factors to become limpid and pure;
through this, one is able to gradually perceive the principles of the Four Noble Truths.
Next, because it increases and brings about the attainment of enlightenment (*bodhi*), faith should be established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).
Diligence (*vīrya*) is capable of exerting effort in the various practices and can spur one on to swiftly advance toward the enlightenment of the three vehicles.

If there were no right diligence, even if one had already set out, one would eventually become weary and abandon the path midway, and nothing would ever be accomplished. Therefore, diligence is established as a factor of enlightenment. There are other explanations regarding its beginninglessness.

The reason why those who have arrived [at this stage] are unable to see the Four Noble Truths is due to their indolence and lack of delight in hearing and correctly contemplating the principle of the Four Noble Truths.
Diligence (*vīrya*) is able to counteract that [indolence], causing them to delight in hearing and correctly contemplating the principle of the Four Truths;
because it enables one to see the Four Truths and swiftly realize *bodhi*, diligence should also be established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*). Tranquility (*praśrabdhi*)...
By ceasing worldly activities, the mind is made pliant; through the practice of equanimity (*upekṣā*) and rectitude, the mind is rendered impartial.

Thus, one is able to increase all supramundane practices and cause them to swiftly proceed toward the enlightenment (*bodhi*) of the three vehicles. For this reason, equanimity is established as a factor of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*).

Other masters say that from time immemorial, the mind has been disturbed by lethargy and agitation, and because of this failure to perceive the Truths (*satya*), one does not realize the three vehicles.

Bodhi-lightness (praśrabdhi), equanimity (upekṣā), the application of equanimity toward torpor (styāna), and the abandonment of agitation (auddhatya)—because through these one sees the truths and swiftly proceeds toward Bodhi, they too should be established as factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma).

If that were so, then shame (hrī) and dread of blame (apatrāpya), which are subsumed under the category of natural wholesomeness (svabhāva-kuśala) and receive the name "pure dharmas" (śukladharma) among the various classes of wholesome qualities, should also be established as factors of enlightenment.
They should not be so established, because shame and dread of blame exist merely for the sake of... [the restraint of body and speech].

All states associated with unwholesome minds constitute the most significant obstacles among the distractions that delude; as for their obstruction regarding the principle of seeing the truths (*satyadarśana*), their obstructive power is slight.

Those qualities which are the opposite of these are termed *hrī* (shame) and *apatrāpya* (modesty). They are subsumed under the nature of the wholesome (*kuśala-svabhāva*) and receive the designation of "pure dharmas" (*śukla-dharma*).

Although they possess superior efficacy in countering distracted delusions, their auxiliary power for meditative excellence (*samādhi-kuśala*) is slight. Within the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*), they are categorized as those that accord with [the path].
Because they assist meditative concentration (*samādhi*) in realizing the truth of the principles of awakening, those [other wholesome factors] are not established [as the limbs of enlightenment].

If that were so, one should also establish non-attachment (*alobha*) and non-hatred (*adveṣa*), since they are wholesome by their very nature as roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*). Yet, they too should not be so established;

for attachment and hatred are associated with all six consciousnesses, pervade all five fruits, are of the nature of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and act as the primary preparatory stages (*prayoga*) for the commission of coarse and evil karma, thereby severing the roots of virtue and obstructing the tranquility of the mind.

Because "wholesome strength" (kuśala-bala) and "far-sighted vision" (dūradarśana) are superior, their opposites are established as "non-greed" (alobha) and "non-hatred" (adveṣa), which receive the designation of "wholesome roots" (kuśalamūla) as they are subsumed under intrinsic wholesomeness (*svabhāva-kuśala*).

Although their power is strong within the context of scattered wholesome karma (*vikṣipta-kuśala-karma*), their functional efficacy is weak within the context of meditative wholesome states (*samāhita-kuśala*).

This is because the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) are taken to be favorable to meditative wholesome states and assist in awakening to the principles of the Truths; therefore, those two are not established [as roots]. If that were so, then "heedfulness" (*apramāda*) should also [not be established].
Because heedfulness (*apramāda*) is established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), all practices lead to Buddhahood; therefore, one should always praise and encourage its cultivation.
Furthermore, one should not establish heedlessness (*pramāda*) within the state of non-concentration, allowing the mind to wander toward the five desires.

Since the power of these [desires] to obstruct generosity and other wholesome qualities is strong when the mind is distracted, and since this obstructive function is more prominent than that [of the hindrances] during the state of non-concentration, heedfulness is established specifically as the antidote to it. However—

Because one is able to guard the mind against the five desires so that it does not wander, and can single-mindedly cultivate generosity and the like, the power of these scattered virtues (*vyākṣepa-kuśala*) is indeed strong;

however, within the context of the power of concentrated virtue (*samādhi-kuśala*), their efficacy is weak and inferior. Since the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) grasp those that accord with concentrated virtue to assist in awakening to the principles of the Truths (*satya*), they do not establish [non-harming] therein.
If that were so, non-harming (*avihiṃsā*) should be established as a factor of enlightenment, for harming (*hiṃsā*) is capable of causing affliction.

Since it is measured that sentient beings fall into the three evil realms, [non-harming] is established as their antidote; therefore, harming should not be established as a condition for the arising of affliction.

Furthermore, while harming obstructs the cultivation of mundane wholesome states (*vibhava-kuśala*), non-harming is the opposite of this. Because it assists the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is also not established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
Other masters say: "Among the great wholesome dharmas, if a dharma is superior by nature to its respective counteractive object (*vipakṣa*), it is established [as a factor]."
They are factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*), whereas others are not. Those that are "strong in their opposition" (*pratipakṣa*) are those associated with all defiled minds (*kliṣṭa-citta*).

Those that are "superior by nature" (*svabhāva-śreṣṭha*) are those that assist the practice of insight (*darśana-carita*). As previously stated, faith (*śraddhā*), diligence (*vīrya*), tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) possess both of these two meanings.
Among the six beginning with shame (*hrī*), five—namely, shame and so forth—possess neither of the two meanings. Only heedfulness (*apramāda*) possesses one of the two meanings.

If it is asked: "Why are the two [factors]—delight (*abhinandana*) and aversion (*daurmanasya*)—not included among the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), given that they are otherwise lacking in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)?

In truth, they are indeed subsumed within the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth, because those [applications of mindfulness] collectively encompass all wholesome states of preparatory application (*prayoga-kuśala*). However, they are not established separately as factors of enlightenment for three reasons:

first, because the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of these two are mutually contradictory; second, because neither is universal across all four noble truths (*catvāry āryasatyāni*); and third, because there is no single stage (*bhūmi*) in which either could be present at all times.
Because they are included within the preceding category of mind (*citta*), they are not established as separate factors; thus other masters say:

"As for joy (*prīti*) and disenchantment (*daurmanasya*), since these are produced by the power of wisdom (*prajñā*) observing its objects—meaning they function to accord with the arising of awakening and insight—they should not be established separately, as their characteristics are contrary [to those factors].

For what reason are both *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought) capable of being cultivated (*prayoga-kuśala*) and even untainted (*anāsrava*), yet [are not included] among the factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*)?

The distinction between one being correct and the other incorrect is not ultimate, as both meanings are applicable as previously explained. Nevertheless, *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought) are established separately because *vitarka* exerts a powerful influence on right view within the Noble Path;
when it arises, its mode of activity (*ākāra*) is so sharp and intense that it assists the vision in seeking the principles of truth, thereby qualifying it as a constituent of the path (*mārgāṅga*).
*Vicāra*, however, is not like this, for its mode of activity arises with an extremely subtle and weak intensity.
Therefore, some other masters say that when both [vitarka and vicāra] function together, the coarse aspect of vitarka obscures vicāra;

because the aspect of functioning is subtle when only vicāra arises, it is not established separately among the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa). Since right effort (samyag-vyāyāma) itself exerts and impels right view (samyag-dṛṣṭi), why establish vitarka as a separate factor of enlightenment?
For the exertion of right view differs from vitarka; thus, it is established as a limb of the path (mārgāṅga).

In the middle [of the path], both should be established; that is to say, diligence (*vīrya*) exerts them to cause rapid progress in cultivation, while investigation (*vicāra*) exerts them to cause rapid contemplation of the Noble Truths.

For what reason is manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*) not established as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*)? Because factors of enlightenment are exclusively wholesome states conducive to meditative concentration (*samādhi-anukūla-kuśala-dharma*), consisting of unmanifest action (*avijñapti*) co-arising with the mind that possesses superior conduciveness;
manifest action is not so. Therefore, it is not established. For what reason are the dissociated factors (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) not established [as factors of enlightenment]?
Since the formations (*saṃskāra*) lack a distinct superior capacity to assist awakening (*bodhi*), they are not established as separate factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*).

This is because, unlike the unmanifest (*avijñapti*), which—though dissociated [from mind]—serves as the hub for the wheel of the Path, these formations do not have such a function regarding awakening.

Furthermore, other masters state that the two mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*) are contrary to awakening because they suppress the mind, and thus the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source].

Since these factors are established based on their respective characteristics (*lakṣya*), they function reciprocally; because they function equally toward both defilement and purification, and because their activity toward purification increases as factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), they are not established separately [from the universal mental factors].

However, among these ten factors, four belong to the "universal ground" (*mahābhūmika*)—namely, mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and feeling (*vedanā*)—while four belong to the "great wholesome ground" (*kuśalamahābhūmika*)—namely, faith (*śraddhā*), diligence (*vīrya*), tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
One factor belongs to the "indeterminate ground" (*aniyata-bhūmika*), which is vitarka (applied thought). As for form (*rūpa*)...

Regarding the factors of the Dharma: there is one [factor] that is co-existent with the mind, namely the morality (śīla) associated with it; ten are the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa), as clarified by the [chapter on] outflows (āsrava);

the remaining ones are not factors of training (śaikṣa), as explained previously. Within these ten, six are opened up to become eight and four, differing in number; thus, a verse says: "Wisdom, concentration, and effort open into eight;
Mindfulness and the faculties are divided into four; The category of morality is divided into three; The faculty and power of faith are two; Tranquility [is one]."

Because joy (*prīti*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and investigation (*vicaya*) each have their own distinct nature, there are thirty-seven [factors]. Now, in this text, the doctrine is first presented in summary.

Although these factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) are named thirty-seven, their actual entities (*vastu*) are only ten—namely, faith (*śraddhā*), diligence (*vīrya*), and so forth. Next, the thirty-seven are subsumed into these ten entities:

because the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), the power of wisdom (*prajñābala*), and the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicayasaṃbodhyaṅga*), they are identical to right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*); thus, these eight [are one entity].

The factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) have wisdom (*prajñā*) as their essence; furthermore, the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*), the power of energy (*vīryabala*), the factor of enlightenment of energy (*vīryasaṃbodhyaṅga*), and right effort (*samyagvyāyāma*)—these eight factors of enlightenment have diligence (*vīrya*) as their essence.

Furthermore, the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the faculty of concentration (*samādhindriya*), the power of concentration (*samādhibala*), the factor of enlightenment of concentration (*samādhisambodhyaṅga*), and right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*)—these eight factors of enlightenment have concentration (*samādhi*) as their essence.
Because the force of these wisdom, diligence, and concentration is most powerful, they are established separately as distinct categories throughout the four stages [of the path].

Because there are four gates, these three types are each further divided into eight. Furthermore, among the factors of awakening, both the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) and the power of faith (*śraddhābala*) have faith as their essence.

Both the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*) and the power of mindfulness (*smṛtibala*), as well as the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛtisambodhyaṅga*) and right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*), these four awakening factors have mindfulness as their essence.

Right speech (*samyagvāc*), right action (*samyakkarmānta*), and right livelihood (*samyagājīva*), these three awakening factors have ethical discipline (*śīla*) as their essence. Furthermore, there are diligence (*vīrya*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), and right intention (*samyaksaṃkalpa*).

In terms of their essential function, each awakening factor has its own distinct factor as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Thus, the actual entities (*vastu*) of these factors of enlightenment are only ten:
namely, the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), plus joy (*prīti*), tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), the bodhisattva precepts, and applied thought (*vitarka*).

The teacher Viśeṣaśīla asserts that there are eleven, because bodily action (*kāyakarman*) and vocal action (*vākkarman*) are not intermingled and are therefore each divided into two; the remaining nine are the same [as the previous view].
The preceding section thus contained eleven [verses].

Below this, the second section consists of one verse explaining that the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*), and the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) have wisdom (*prajñā*), effort (*vīrya*), and concentration (*samādhi*) as their essential natures.
In the text, it first asks: do the three—foundations of mindfulness and so forth—refer to the associated, co-existent, and common foundations of mindfulness?

The term "universally encompassing" refers to all wholesome qualities of application (*prayoga-kuśala*) which have no separate affiliation; why then are only wisdom, diligence, and concentration mentioned in sequence?
The verse provides the answer, and the subsequent commentary explains the body of the verse. First, there is a general explanation of the root verse;

then, the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), and the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*)—these three categories of wholesome qualities—are based upon the foundations of mindfulness and so forth, and their substance as wholesome roots truly encompasses everything.

All preparatory wholesome states are indeed wholesome roots of superior strength according to their respective categories; these are designated, respectively, as wisdom (*prajñā*), diligence (*vīrya*), and concentration (*samādhi*).

Regarding the explanation of the name "application of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the initial question asks: for what reason is wisdom established as the application of mindfulness? The subsequent answer states that the Abhidharma masters (*Vibhāṣā-ācāryas*) explain it thus:
because wisdom is maintained and made to abide by the power of mindfulness, it is named after its cause; therefore, it is called the "application of mindfulness."

The Master of the *Smṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* explains: "In reality, it is by means of wisdom (*prajñā*) that the mind is made to abide upon its object; because wisdom perceives things as they truly are, it causes the mind to clearly remember them.

Thus, the name 'application of mindfulness' (*smṛtyupasthāna*) is derived from the result. This has already been established at length in the previous [section] on the four applications of mindfulness.
Regarding the three explanations for the term "right abandonment" (*samyak-prahāṇa*), the text first asks: "For what reason is diligence (*vīrya*) called right abandonment? Next...

Answer: Because this power of diligence (*vīrya*) is able to eliminate laziness within the two virtuous states of right cultivation—namely, the diligent abandonment [of unwholesome factors] and the diligent cultivation [of wholesome factors]—these four are collectively termed "right abandonments" (*samyak-prahāṇa*) or "right strivings" (*samyak-pradhāna*). Furthermore, because this diligence is preeminent among the right application and exertion of body, speech, and mind, it is so named.
Regarding the explanation of the name "bases of psychic power" (*ṛddhi-pāda*) in the text, the initial question asks: for what reason...

The establishment of the bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*) is explained as follows: the various wondrous and sublime qualities, such as the five supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*), are called "supernormal" (*ṛddhi*).

Because meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is that upon which these depend, it is called a "base" (*pāda*). Since they are named after their fruit and their function, they are termed "bases of supernormal power.

These very bases of supernormal power are pursued for accomplishment through four factors; because they are named according to their causes, their fruits, and their functions, they are called the "four bases of supernormal power" (*catvāra ṛddhipādāḥ*).

Other masters assert that the "bases" (*pāda*) are precisely concentration (*samādhi*), meaning that when mindfulness (*smṛti*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are absent, there is concentration alone. The Master of the Sūtras (Śrīlāta) refutes this, stating:

"According to them, the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) would number thirteen, and the factors of the *vibhaṅga* (or *vibhajyavādin*) would number eleven; furthermore, by adding desire (*chanda*) and mind (*citta*), they would reach thirteen.

This is because the two bases of mindfulness and wisdom are already included within the previous eleven, whereas the two bases of desire and mind are not included within those eleven, and thus must be added."
Regarding the desire-mind (*chanda-citta*), the masters of antiquity have all stated that the essence of the basis of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) is meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

If this were so, there should be only an increase in desire; however, since it is said that both desire and mind increase, we know that the "desire-mind basis of psychic power" refers to the mental sovereign (*citta-rāja*).

Furthermore, if the supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) were identical to concentration, it would contradict the scriptural teachings, as the Sūtra says: "I shall now explain for you the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) and so forth."
"Rddhi" (supernatural power) refers to the various enjoyments of the rddhi-pādas, such as "dividing one into many," and so forth; thus we know that *rddhi* is supernormal power (*abhijñā*).
"Pāda" (basis/foot) refers to the four *samādhis*, such as the desire-based and others; thus we know that the *samādhi* which is the support for supernormal powers is called a "pāda.

In this context, the Buddha taught that the supernormal powers which are the fruits of meditative concentration are called *rddhi*, and they are produced by the four categories, beginning with desire.

Samādhi is termed the "basis" (*pāda*). Here, the name "basis" is established for samādhi as the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala*), while the essence of that concentration is called the "basis.
Since these bases serve as the productive causes for the four factors—desire and so forth—and there are four such causes, they are spoken of as "four.

Because these are named according to their fruit, their functional application, and their causal nature, they are called the "four bases of psychic power" (*ṛddhipāda*). 5. Explanation of the Faculties (*indriya*) and Powers (*bala*).

In the text, the initial question asks: "For what reason are the five dharmas, such as faith and the rest, which are identical in essence, first called 'faculties' (*indriya*) and later called 'powers' (*bala*?

The subsequent answer states: "Because these five dharmas depend on their superior or inferior grades, they are first faculties and later powers; furthermore, those that can be categorized [as belonging to a specific stage] are called faculties, while those that cannot be so categorized are called powers.
It further asks: "For what reason is the sequence of the stages, such as 'dwelling' (*sthiti*), as it is? That is to say, regarding cause and effect, [it begins] from the inferior..."
The answer can be understood according to the text.
From here below is the third section, consisting of one verse that establishes the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) by way of their stages. In the text, first there is a question:

"At which stage should it be said that which factor of enlightenment increases? Next, the verse is cited as the answer; finally, the root verse is explained, beginning with the five cessations (*pañca-nivaraṇa-pratipakṣa*), both collectively and individually.

Within the stage of karma, up to the point where it is said that the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) increase during the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*), one is able to realize the various categories of merit belonging to the "Aids to Penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
It is said that the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) increase during the stage of "Summits" (*mūrdhan*), because one attains the state of "Patience" (*kṣānti*) and achieves non-retrogression.

It is said that the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) increase during the stage of "Dharma-Patience" (*dharmanidhyānakṣānti*), because one attains the sense of non-falling back. It is said that the faculties (*indriya*) increase during the first stage [of the Path of Seeing].

Because they possess the sense of being unyielding, the powers (*bala*) are said to increase during the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); because they assist awakening as one draws near to the state of enlightenment, the factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*) are said to increase;
and because they proceed with rapidity during the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are said to increase.

However, in the sūtras, they are taught according to their numerical order—first seven and then eight—and not according to the sequence of their cultivation. This is as explained by the masters of the Vibhāṣā.
Regarding this fixed interpretation, other masters say that it does not contradict the sequence taught in the sūtras for establishing the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth.

They maintain that when a practitioner is about to engage in cultivation, their mind first scatters among many objects; therefore, they first cultivate the foundations of mindfulness to subdue that mind.
For this reason, the foundations of mindfulness come first, and by their power, [the practitioner proceeds] up to the right [concentration].
The abandonment of the second [hindrance] is due to diligence; up to the third, the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), which take superior concentration as their basis;
up to the fourth, the faculties (*indriya*), for once the meaning of the faculties is established; up to the fifth, the powers (*bala*).

On the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) are established, because one realizes the four noble truths as they truly are. Throughout both the stages of ordinary beings and the noble ones, the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are established, as they apply universally to both the direct and the indirect paths.

Because the Dharma is the city of Nirvāṇa, as stated in the sūtras, those who cultivate the eight factors of the path to perfection—beginning with the four foundations of mindfulness and culminating in the seven factors of enlightenment—also cultivate them to perfection;
thus, it is known that the path-factors pertain to both the stages of ordinary beings and the noble ones. Furthermore, a sūtra states:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that one who speaks words of reality is metaphorically said to proclaim the Four Noble Truths. By means of the Four Noble Truths...
Because the Truths (*satya*) are the principle of reality as it is, they are called "reality" (*yathābhūta*); this is a metaphorical explanation of the Four Noble Truths.

The phrase "causing one to quickly exit by way of the original path" is a metaphor for causing one to cultivate the eight factors of the Noble Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), because the eight path-factors are the path upon which all Buddhas of the past traveled.
Since the Sūtra speaks only of the eight factors of the Noble Path as the road for exiting birth and death, it is known that these eight branches apply universally.
Generally, from the perspective of the stages of both ordinary beings and noble ones, these are established according to their respective levels.

However, when taken as a whole, the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), and the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*)—whose essential natures are wisdom (*prajñā*), energy (*vīrya*), and concentration (*samādhi*)—are subsumed within the five faculties (*pañcendriya*). These faculties of wisdom, energy, and concentration are precisely what constitute the five faculties;

when these five faculties reach the stage of "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*), they are collectively termed the five powers (*pañcabala*). Among these five faculties, the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) exists only prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), while the others...

The four faculties (*indriya*) pertain to both the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). Because these [faculties] serve as roots, the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*) are established.

Specifically, right speech, right action, and right livelihood belong only to the path of seeing. Joy (*prīti*), tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) belong only to the path of cultivation. Effort (*vīrya*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) pertain to both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.

The faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) belongs exclusively to the path of seeing. Therefore, the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* asks: "For what reason are joy, tranquility, and equanimity established as factors of enlightenment?"

Are the factors of the path—right intention, right speech, right action, and right livelihood—not established as factors of the path, yet not factors of awakening? And are they also not associated with faith?

Answer: Because they are conducive to awakening. From the knowledge of conditions up to the constant arising of joy, and from the constant arising of joy up to the arising of awakening—namely, by ceasing all activities and through equanimity, awakening constantly arises. Because they are not conducive to progress, they are not the path; they depart from it.

That which is not pleasing to the Path does not depart because it dwells with attachment; since "reliance on equanimity" (*upekṣā*) and "departure" (*niḥsaraṇa*) are diametrically opposed, [the former] is not called a factor of the Path.

As for the defilements, they serve as the hub for the wheel of the Path, and thus they are established as factors of the wheel of the Path; however, because they are not associated [with the Path], they are not factors of enlightenment.

Because right effort (*samyagvyāyāma*) and right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) are the awakening [of the mind], and because they are conducive to departure and progression rather than to awakening, they are established as factors of the Path and not [as factors of enlightenment].

Regarding the awakening factor of faith (*śraddhā-saṃbodhyaṅga*): for those who have first begun their practice, it is a joy; for those who have already traversed the path, it is a state of transcendence. Therefore, in both cases, it is not established [as a separate factor]. The *Nyāyapravēśa-śāstra* asks:
"Why is faith not established as a factor of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*) or a factor of the path (*mārgāṅga*)? The answer is:

at the time of the initial setting forth, faith functions with predominance (*adhipati*) for entering the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*). However, at that time, its power and function are weak and inferior; therefore, it is not established as a factor of awakening or of the path.

Among the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), for what reason are joy (*prīti*), pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) established there, yet they are not likewise established within the path (*mārga*)?

Because they accord specifically with enlightenment and do not accord with the path. How do they accord with enlightenment? Furthermore, within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), in each stage one cultivates nine grades of superior enlightenment;
as one repeatedly awakens to the truths in accordance with that [cultivation], so too does superior joy arise.

Because of the arising of superior joy, one has not yet discerned the Truths; it is like a person who, having dug the earth and obtained treasure, feels joy. Because of that arising joy, one no longer digs further.

Through the power of *vitarka* (applied thought) which accords with awakening, and through the power of tranquility (*praśrabdhi*) which lightens and pacifies all activities, as well as through the power of equanimity (*upekṣā*) which renders the mind even, one is finally able to observe the object with precise discernment. Therefore, tranquility and equanimity are established within *vitarka*.
Regarding the [factors] within the limbs: why do these three not accord with the swift progression of the Path? This is the meaning of the Noble Path.

Since these [three] are slightly inconsistent with swift progression, yet they all enable faith to abide in tranquility, for what reason are *vitarka* (applied thought) and the *śīla-skandha* (limb of morality) established among the limbs of the Path, but not likewise established among the limbs of Awakening (*bodhyaṅga*)?
It is because they are particularly conducive to the Path and not conducive to Awakening. Why is this so?

Since *vitarka* (applied thought) and *śīla* (ethical discipline) conform to the Path and facilitate the swift observation of the eight truths—the upper and lower objects—within the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), they are established as branches of the Path;
for *vitarka* acts as the hub and *śīla* forms the wheels, enabling the wheel of the Path of Seeing to revolve swiftly among the truths.
Why, then, would these not conform to Awakening (*bodhi*)? Furthermore, why is it that *vitarka* is not tranquil regarding the truths?

Because *vitarka* (applied thought) operates by seeking the characteristics of the principles of the Noble Truths, whereas *vicāra* (sustained thought) operates with tranquility through the vision of those truths, there is a slight contradiction between them.

Since *vicāra* is associated [with the mind], possesses an object of perception (*ālambana*), and has a basis and mode of activity (*ākāra*), it contradicts the definition of *bodhyaṅga* (factor of enlightenment).
Therefore, it is not established as a factor of enlightenment. Furthermore, the fact that it functions pervasively as a path (*mārga*) cannot be used as a precedent for its inclusion here.

From here below is the fifth section, consisting of one verse that distinguishes between the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*). In the text, first the previous question is restated regarding the stages of increase (*anuśaya*);
since the sequential order has already been explained, it is logically appropriate to state: "Of these thirty-seven [factors], how many pertain to both [the outflowing and the outflow-free]?

This is the first question. "How many are outflow-free? This is the second question. Next, the verse is cited as the answer; therein, the first two lines provide the response to the questions that follow.
The two lines answer the first question; the subsequent portion explains the content of the verse. First, the upper two lines are explained here:

among these, the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and the eight branches of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*), because they are established only within the stages of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
Prior to the path of vision, mundane phenomena such as right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) and so forth do exist, but because they are tainted (*sāsrava*), they do not qualify as "noble" (*ārya*).

Regarding the sequence of the names of the factors of the path, the remaining two [factors], the third and fourth, and the five factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) all pertain to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) stages.
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Treatise on Correct Reasoning) states: "In the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the seven factors of enlightenment increase as they are proximate to awakening;
because they counteract the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), the essence of the factors of enlightenment is exclusively uncontaminated. All factors of enlightenment assist toward awakening; however—
The reason this alone is designated by the name "limb of enlightenment" (*bodhyaṅga*) is that it is most proximate to the fruit of awakening (*bodhi*).

By this principle, one should understand that the seven limbs of enlightenment are established based solely on their function as antidotes to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). This is taught as the primary class of antidotes for the lower stages.
If one does not accept this, why would they not apply to both [the Peak of Existence and the lower stages], or rather, why would they not apply to all?
Within the [seven] factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), the designation "enlightenment-factor" is established based on proximity to awakening during the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Since this state of proximity to awakening within the path of cultivation is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*), it is only the untainted path of cultivation that is designated as a "factor of enlightenment. Within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the eight factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are predominant;

therefore, they are consistently subsumed under the nature of being untainted. Although right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) and the others also extend to the tainted (*sāsrava*), [in this context, they are understood as untainted].
However, those [factors] do not receive the name "limbs of the noble path" because the term "limbs of the noble path" refers exclusively to the untainted (*anāsrava*).

Furthermore, regarding the outflows (*āsrava*), it is accepted that the factors belonging to the limbs of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*)—which are mentioned after the limbs of enlightenment—are necessarily untainted. Some say that if they were mentioned before, they would pertain to both types (tainted and untainted);
however, since the limbs of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are taught only after the limbs of enlightenment, the limbs of the path are invariably untainted, while the remaining factors pertain to both.

The second point is already established: among the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*), those that increase in an earlier stage also increase in their functional power in subsequent stages, whereas those that increase in a subsequent stage do not [necessarily] increase in an earlier stage.

Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* states: "From the stage of a beginner up to the stage of non-arising of ideation (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) constantly increase," and so forth at length.

From here below, the sixth section consists of two verses concerning the possession of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) across the stages (*bhūmi*). In the text, first there is a question as to how many of these thirty-seven factors exist in which stage;

this is answered by citing the verses. Subsequently, the original intent of the verses is explained: the first [stage] possesses all thirty-seven; the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*) excludes joy (*prīti*);
and the two dhyānas exclude applied thought (*vitarka*). Thus, these two stages each possess thirty-six. Regarding the third stage and the subsequent ones...

In the intermediate [dhyāna], both [joy and applied thought] are excluded, leaving thirty-five factors; in the first three formless attainments, visible form and the three moral precepts are excluded, and joy and applied thought are further excluded, leaving thirty-two;

in the desire realm and the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), the factors of enlightenment and the path are each excluded, leaving twenty-two in each, because these two stages lack the untainted (*anāsrava*) factors.
As the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "In these various stages, the factors of enlightenment are present according to their respective requirements."

The manifestation [of these factors] is indefinite as to whether they are few or many; that is to say, according to their respective positions, those listed later necessarily include those preceding them.

Since a single entity can be divided into multiple aspects, there may be multiple [factors] arising simultaneously. It is not only the four applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) that are concerned here;

they certainly do not arise together, because they are divided into four based on their respective objects (*ālambana*). If even two types of wisdom (*prajñā*) cannot arise simultaneously, how much less could all four arise at once?
Wisdoms arise simultaneously and cannot be one; wisdom is divided into many based on its objects.
If they are subsumed under the total mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), it is because there is never a single wisdom that arises in a single moment with four objects and four aspects.
By this principle, although the first intention summarizes them as possessing all thirty-seven factors, at most, they manifest instantaneously in a single moment.
However, there may be thirty-four [categories]. In the *Chengshi lun* (Tattvasiddhi-śāstra), fascicle 22, the "Chapter on Śamatha and Vipaśyanā" states: Question:

The Buddha has taught in various places that one should be mindful of two dharmas, namely śamatha and vipaśyanā. If all dharmas such as the various dhyānas and samādhis should be objects of mindfulness, why does he speak only of śamatha and vipaśyanā? Answer:
"Śamatha" refers to meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and "vipaśyanā" refers to the four kinds of verified confidence (*avetyaprasāda*). First, the preceding question is restated.

When the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) are about to arise, one necessarily attains the "purity of conviction" (avetyaprasāda). There are four questions: first, how many types are there;
second, in what stage is it attained; third, what is its substantial nature (dravya); and fourth, is it contaminated (sāsrava) or uncontaminated (anāsrava)? Next, the verse provides the answers:
the first two lines answer the first question, the next four lines answer the second question, and the seventh line answers the third question.
The eighth phrase answers the fourth question. Following this, the commentary on the verses begins by first citing the number and listing the names to explain the first two lines;

second, it explains the third, fourth, fifth, and sixth lines. Regarding the stage of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), when one perceives each of the three truths (*satya*), one attains only the "pure confidence in the Dharma" (*dharma-prasāda*).
This is because the objects of the three truths realized therein are the Jewel of the Dharma (*dharmaratna*) as ultimate reality (*tattva*); therefore, [the other two purities] do not exist there.

The substance of the purification by faith (*śraddhā-saṃprasāda*) is called the "purification of the Dharma. At the same time, the morality concomitant with the Path (*mārga-sahabhū-śīla*) is the "purification of morality.

During the stage of the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*), one simultaneously attains the two purifications of the Buddha and the Saṅgha; that is to say, at that time, one also attains the qualities of a Buddha that have not yet been awakened and the qualities of the Bodhisattva-Saṅgha consisting of the *śaikṣa* and *aśaikṣa* dharmas.
Although these are indeed dharmas, they do not increase the purification [of the Dharma-purification]; rather, one cultivates them as distinct objects of focus.
Because the Three Jewels are real, one further separately attains the two types of indestructible confidence (*aveṇika-prasāda*) in the Buddha and the Saṅgha.

The word "furthermore" (*kāma*) is used to indicate that at the time of seeing the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), one also attains the verified confidence (*saddhā*) in the Dharma and the precepts; subsequently, one further attains the verified confidence in the Buddha and the Saṅgha.

This is because one attains the cultivation of untainted faith (*anāsrava-śraddhā*) which specifically conditions the two faculties of a Bodhisattva and the three faculties of a Pratyekabuddha. This faith in the Dharma is verified confidence, while that which specifically conditions the [other] various [faculties] is [verified confidence in the Buddha and Saṅgha].

The Buddha’s faculty of knowing fully (ājñātendriya) and his faith constitute the specific object of the purification of faith in the Buddha; the three faculties and faith of a Bodhisattva constitute the purification of faith in the Saṃgha;

and the simultaneous possession of the essence of the precepts co-arising with the Path constitutes the purification of faith in the Dharma. Regarding the Dharma that is the object of this faith, there are briefly two types:

the specific and the general. The general encompasses all four truths, as they are all the Dharma; the specific refers only to the truth of suffering, the truth of origination, and the other [two] truths, excluding the truth of cessation.

Because the path of the two types of bodhisattvas and the three faculties of the pratyekabuddha is comprised solely within the Jewel of the Dharma, at the time of seeing the Four Truths, they all attain the verified confidence in the Dharma (*dharma-avetyaprasāda*).
Since the morality beloved by the Noble Ones accompanies the clear realization (*abhisamaya*), there is no time when it is not also attained;

thus, they all likewise attain the verified confidence [in the Sangha]. This is the third explanation of the seventh phrase: one should know that it is called "possessing faith" because of the distinction in what is believed, and that this is the reality.

The entities are of only two kinds: namely, the three kinds of verified clarity regarding the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, which have faith as their essence; and the verified clarity of the noble precepts, which has the precepts as its essence.
Therefore, there are only two. This is the fifth explanation of the eighth phrase. These four kinds are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*), because tainted phenomena are not verified clarity.

Fifth, regarding the explanation of the name "verified clarity" (*avetyaprasāda*), the text first poses a question: [...]* *Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment from a commentary on Abhidharma, specifically concerning the categories of verified clarity.*
In what sense is the term "clear confidence" (*avetyaprasāda*) established? Answer: Because one thus sees and knows the principle of the Four Noble Truths, it is called "realization.
Right faith in the Triple Gem and sublime ethical discipline (*śīla*) are both termed "clear" (*prasāda*) because they are pure within the aggregates of form and mind.

Since they are free from the stain of lack of faith and the stain of broken precepts, and because these four kinds of purity are attained through the realization of the principle, the name "clear confidence through realization" is established. (6)

The sequence is clarified by the order in which they manifest upon emerging from meditative absorption; thus, the internal sequence of the contemplation is explained. Question: What is the sequence of manifestation when one emerges from meditative absorption? Answer:
It is said that at the stage of emerging from absorption, one first places faith in the Buddha and so forth.

This can be understood through the following analogies: the Buddha is like a guide, the Dharma is like the path, and the Saṅgha is like a caravan leader. This sequence continues up to the precepts (*śīla*). These four types [of qualities] are as follows: the Buddha is like a guide, the Dharma is like the road, and the Saṅgha is like a merchant.
The precepts of the companions are like a vehicle.

From here below, the ninth section contains three stanzas that clarify the establishment of the ten factors of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), namely the factors of right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) and right liberation (*samyag-vimukti*).

Within this, the first two stanzas distinguish the essential nature of these two factors. In the text, it first cites the Sūtra and poses questions regarding the eight factors of the stage of training (*śaikṣa*).

The factors of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) constitute eleven; why, then, are the two questions regarding right liberation (*samyagvimukti*) and right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) not mentioned among the factors of one in training (*śaikṣa*)?
What is the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of right liberation and right knowledge? Next, a verse is cited in response:

[Verse omitted] Regarding this, the first two lines answer the first question, while the remaining six lines answer the second question. Below, the commentary on the verse itself begins with the explanation of the first part.
Regarding the first two phrases: because within the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) there remain further dharmas from which one has not yet attained liberation, there is no "limb of liberation.

Since one in the stage of training cannot be called "liberated" while still bound by even a slight fetter, it is not the case that the stage of training lacks the essence of liberation—that is, *nirvāṇa*.

One can establish the "knowledge of liberation" (*vimukti-jñāna*) upon having realized [that essence]; because those in the stage beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) have already severed all faults, the "limb of liberation" is established, after which they are able to give rise to [this knowledge].
Because there are two types of knowledge regarding liberation—the conditioned and the unconditioned—the "body of knowledge and vision of liberation" (vimukti-jñāna-darśana-kāya) is established.

It is designated as "right knowledge" (samyag-jñāna) because it is manifested through the two factors of liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation in the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa).
Since these two factors do not exist for those in training (śaikṣa), they possess only eight [factors]. The second and fourth lines of the verse clarify the essence of liberation; liberation is...
The essence [of liberation] is twofold, namely conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Conditioned liberation refers to the supreme resolve (*adhimokṣa*) and the liberation (*vimukti*) of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), which consist in the cessation of all afflictions (*kleśa*). Regarding the third [point], there are three explanations for the fifth and sixth phrases:

conditioned liberation is called an "untrained limb" (*aśaikṣāṅga*) because the designation of "limbs" is based upon what is conditioned; furthermore, the untrained limbs include two kinds of liberation, namely:

It should be understood that when other sūtras speak of the two deliverances of mind and wisdom (*citta-prajñā-vimukti*), these are actually the factors of resolve (*adhimokṣa*) associated with mind and wisdom.

Within the fivefold aggregate body (*pañca-skandha-kāya*), these two deliverances of mind and wisdom constitute the aggregate of deliverance (*vimukti-skandha*). Regarding the sequence, an external objection states:
"If the essence of the aggregate of deliverance is resolve, then why does the Sūtra say: 'How is deliverance pure and supreme?'"

The superior answer is that the mind is liberated from the defilement of greed and liberated from the defilements of hatred and delusion, and so on, until it is called the "aggregate of liberation" (*vimukti-skandha*) because it is truly liberated;
this is not merely the state of resolve (*adhimokṣa*). Next, twenty-eight [objections] are raised: if that is so, what is it? Other masters say:
by the power of true knowledge (*tattva-jñāna*), greed, hatred, and delusion are dispelled; this very meaning of the mind being free from stain is what is called the "aggregate of liberation. Fourth.
The explanation of the seventh and eighth phrases: First, the preceding section concludes as follows.

Thus, it has already been stated that the essence of right liberation (*samyag-vimukti*) has as its essence twenty types of predominant resolve (*adhimokṣa*), or according to other masters, the mind-king (*citta-rāja*). As for the essence of right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*), it is as explained previously among the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*);
namely, the aforementioned "knowledge of the non-arising of phenomena" (*anutpāda-jñāna*) is designated by the name "body of the knowledge and vision of liberation" (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana-kāya*).
The essence of liberation and right knowledge is designated as "liberation" because it is associated with the body of the knowledge and vision of liberation;
thus, it exists only in the stage of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) who is free from bonds, and not in the stage of one still in training (śaikṣa) who remains bound.

From here below is the second [section], which explains that because the factors of liberation (*vimokṣāṅga*) are established for one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), it clarifies the moment of the mind’s liberation of one beyond training.
Regarding the text: at what time does the initial mind truly attain liberation such that it is called "the mind of one beyond training attains liberation"?

Next, a verse is cited as an answer, followed by an explanation of the verse’s basis as taught in the *Ṣaṭpādābhidharma-śāstra*. It states that the first mind of one beyond training is still in the future.
