Question: What is meant by "obstructions" regarding liberation from the state of being about to arise (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*)? Answer: They are called "attainments of transgression" (*āpatti-prāpti*).

By virtue of those attainments of transgression, one is able to obstruct this mind of an Arhat (*aśaikṣa-citta*) from being in the state of being about to arise. Since beginningless time, the sovereign mind of an Arhat has not been able to abide in the state of being about to arise.
When the Diamond-like Samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*) is in its present state of ceasing, those attainments of transgression are precisely [being overcome].

Because the abandonment cannot pull the future acquisition (*prāpti*) into the state of arising, it cannot prevent the future mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) from being in the state of arising;
thus, at the stage when the initial mind of one beyond training is in the process of arising in the future, that acquisition of the offense is correctly abandoned.
In the past state where the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) has already ceased, that acquisition of the offense has already been severed by the initial mind of one beyond training.
In the present state of having already arisen, it is called "already liberated.

At the moment when the first mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is currently arising—the time of its actual liberation—the future mind of one beyond training, which has not yet reached the characteristic of arising, as well as the conventional mind within the mundane body of one beyond training, shall also be called "liberated" at the time when that mind of one beyond training is in the state of the characteristic of arising. For now, we speak only of the actual [moment] in the world.

Regarding the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*), when that which is determined to arise has already arisen, at that very moment, the first mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) comes into operation within the present body and operates within the present time.
Therefore, it is asked: from what obstacle is the future conventional mind (*laukika-citta*) of those beyond training liberated?
The answer is: it is also from that very [obstacle], namely, from the fault that obstructs the arising of the mind. It is asked: in the state prior to liberation, this world...

Question: Is it not the case that no wholesome mundane mind fails to arise? Answer: In the state of one who is not yet liberated, although a mundane mind already arisen exists within the body of a trainee (śaikṣa), it is not like the mundane mind that arises within the body of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) as it is now.

Question: To what is it similar? Answer: It is similar to all other minds that are either associated with or acquired simultaneously with [attainment]. If this mundane mind follows after the mind of one beyond training...
It is called "liberation" because it arises together with the acquisition of non-possession (*aprāpti*).
Third, the latter half of a verse explains the time when the path severs the obstructions. In this passage, first the question is posed:

at what stage does the arising of the path cause the obstructions to be severed? Next, the verse is cited as the answer; finally, the root verse is explained. Regarding the phrase "at the very moment of cessation," this indicates that [the path] abides in the present.

Because the world [of conditioned phenomena] possesses both the characteristic and function of cessation simultaneously, it is called "presently ceasing. The term "presently arising" indicates the future world; thus, that which is in the present is called "presently ceasing.
The Path (*mārga*) is able to sever obstructions only while residing in the present at the time of the characteristic of "presently ceasing";

it causes afflictions such as ignorance to be unable to arise subsequently, which is termed "severing obstructions. In other stages, there is certainly no severing of obstructive afflictions; therefore, it is not like [the case of other states].
When liberation arises in the world, it also extends to that which has not yet arisen; for both the already arisen and the not yet arisen are alike in being free from hindrances.

The three preceding verses together constitute the ninth section, clarifying the establishment of the ten factors of the Aśaikṣas: right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) and right liberation (*samyag-vimukti*).
Below this, the tenth section consists of one verse clarifying the cessation, separation, and abandonment—the three [aspects of liberation]—the first of which is cited in the text as follows:
The Sūtra asks regarding the three—namely, abandonment (*prahāṇa*), detachment (*virāga*), and cessation (*nirodha*): first, what is their essential nature;
second, what is their distinction? Next, a verse is cited in response. Within this, the first line answers the first question, and the following three lines answer the second.

Subsequently, the commentary explains the content of the verse: first, it explains the initial line concerning the three—abandonment and so forth—which are identical to the previously explained unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena.

Taking liberation as its essential nature, the next [section] explains the remaining three phrases: "separation" (*visamyoga*) refers to the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) obtained through the mere separation from the binding afflictions and the phenomena bound by them that are associated with greed;
"abandonment" (*prahāṇa*) refers to the analytical cessation obtained through the remaining eight fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the phenomena bound by them that are associated with them;
and "cessation" (*nirodha*) refers to the extinction of the remaining nine [afflictions], such as greed and so forth.

Regarding the objects (*vastu*) in which the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) increase through association and objectification: at the time one is freed from the binding of the object (*ālambana-bandhana*) when abandoning the nine fetters, the entity of that object-bound state attains liberation through analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

This is because these three [types of cessation] are all, in essence, analytical cessation. Thus, the *Sūtra* states that these three are themselves the unconditioned liberation (*asaṃskṛta-vimukti*).
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, fascicle 63, states: "However, while the three are identical in essence, they differ in terms of conventional designation (*prajñapti*). If one considers..."
In reality, there is no distinction. How, then, can it be said that there are differences based on conventional designation? To be "detached" means to be free from the fetter of greed;

to be "abandoned" means to have severed the remaining eight fetters; and to be "extinguished" means that the substantial entities bound by all other fetters, such as greed and so forth, have been extinguished.
For what reason are these three thus distinguished? It is because of the general summary of contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*).
There are three [types of factors]: first, those that bind but do not defile; second, those that both bind and defile; third, those that are neither.

The unconditioned (*asamskrta*) realized through the abandonment of these three types of factors conducive to bondage and defilement is, respectively, called "abandonment" and so forth—the three [fruits].

Furthermore, other masters maintain that only the abandonment of that which binds constitutes a distinct unconditioned state, whereas the abandonment of the others does not; this is their explanation.

The eight fetters that have objects (*sālambana*) capable of binding [to existence] and the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) that has objects—when these three types of objects are abandoned, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) realized therein is called, respectively, "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*) and so forth.
Furthermore, other masters say that there is a distinct unconditioned state of abandonment for that which is capable of defiling;
as for the remaining objects, those masters maintain that the eight fetters that have objects and the fetter of craving that has objects are indeed objects of craving.
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) realized through the abandonment of these three types of objects is, respectively, termed "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*) and so forth.

This is because the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is attained prior to the specific object to which one is bound. Among these three explanations, the first is considered the best interpretation.

It is said that while the substance (*svabhāva*) is one, they are conventionally designated as three based on differences in meaning; thus, although their names differ, from the perspective of the reality of the unconditioned, they are fundamentally one.
Regarding the statement that there are three types of unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) [liberation] at the highest level, this is because there is no distinction [in their nature].

However, liberation is attained according to the measure of the specific objects to which one was bound; it is like a person who, when released from bondage, is said to have attained liberation only with respect to the person who was bound, and not with respect to the severing of the bond itself.
This is the position of the *viniścaya* (the definitive school). Therefore, the preceding treatise follows the... [text truncated]

Because the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is attained separately for each bound entity (*saṃyojana-vastu*), among the three explanations, the first is considered the best; this opening passage represents that first explanation.

How is it that there is a difference based on the conventional (*prajñapti*)? The answer is as follows: regarding a single atom (*paramāṇu*), from the perspective of being free from the fetter of greed (*rāga-saṃyojana*), it is termed "freedom" (*virāga*);

from the perspective of severing the remaining eight fetters, it is termed "severance" (*prahāṇa*); and from the perspective of extinguishing the substantial entity (*dravya-vastu*) that is perceived, it is termed "cessation" (*nirodha*).

It is called "cessation. [The interlocutor] asks: "By what causes and conditions are these three distinguished in such a way? [The respondent] answers: "Contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are, in brief, of three types:
first, the eight fetters (*saṃyojana*) which are capable of turning one away [from liberation] but are not themselves defiling, because they are not objects of craving;

second, the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*), which is both capable of binding and itself defiling; third, those whose nature is neither capable of binding nor defiling, namely, those that are conducive to bondage (*anulomika-bandhana*)."
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) realized through the abandonment of these three factors of defilement is, respectively, conventionally designated as "abandonment" and so forth.

That is to say, although these three are in reality not distinct in essence, the first master asserts that they are established as distinct unconditioned states based on the difference in the quantity of the objects to which one is bound.
This is just as, for example, when matter is bound by atoms, a distinct unconditioned state is attained for each individual atom; this [position] is the correct one.

Furthermore, another second master asserts that there are nine distinct unconditioned [attainments] (asaṃskṛta) solely for the severance of the nine fetters (saṃyojana) that bind; it is not so for the severance of others. He says:

"Regarding the nine fetters that bind—namely, those with objects consisting of the eight fetters, those with objects consisting of craving (tṛṣṇā), and those with objects consisting of other matters—the unconditioned attainments realized through the severance of these three types each consist of nine kinds. These are, respectively, called the three: severance (prahāṇa), and so forth. That is to say:
The third master asserts that the unconditioned (*asamskrta*) which constitutes the abandonment of the defiling craving alone is distinct; the abandonment of the remaining [fetters] is not so.
That master maintains that craving has eight objects, while the other fetters have various other things as their objects.

The unconditioned realized through the abandonment of these three types [of objects] is, respectively, termed "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*) and so forth—the latter two masters asserting that the three, "abandonment" and the rest, are each distinct in their essential nature (*svabhāva*), and none of them are [identical].

The Master Nyāyānusārin now critiques the [other] masters' positions: because one attains distinct *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through deliberation) for each individual dharma bound by a fetter, at the time the fetter is abandoned and at the time it is liberated, among the three [previous] explanations, the first is superior.
This is because the three [aspects] are merely conventional designations;

in reality, there is no difference in their single essence. However, when the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) arises, the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering...

When one attains the ten types of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), because one has already abandoned the immediate fetters of their own kind, it is said that the objects bound by the ten latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are [now] liberated.
Although there remain unabandoned pervasive latent dispositions of the origin-view (*samudaya-dṛṣṭi*) that can still bind them, these are of a different kind and are remote;

therefore, regarding the objects bound by what is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), it is stated that they are liberated from the bonds abandoned through the vision of suffering. The remainder [is as follows].

The four *parijñās* (full knowledges) are likewise: because the lower [levels of] suffering can bind other categories with a degree of remoteness, when the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) arises, although it severs the remaining four categories of fetters, one has not yet attained liberation from the fetters bound by the remaining four *parijñās*.
Within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the nine grades of mutual binding are also like this; because they can bind within their own category with intimacy, they sever their own [category].
When the ninth grade [of defilement] is able to bind, the corresponding grades within its own class that are bound attain the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Because the binding capacity of different classes in relation to one another is remote, even if the binding [defilements] are severed, those bound by different classes do not attain the unconditioned. However, regarding dharmas that are not bound by [the ninth grade], it is necessary that the binding [defilements] be completely severed by the ninth grade;
subsequently, each bound dharma individually attains the unconditioned.
From here below, the eleventh section consists of one verse that clarifies the nature of "manifestation" (*ākāra*) in terms of its distinction from and correspondence with "detachment" (*vairāgya*).

In the text, first, the question is asked: "If one is able to manifest [the truths], must one necessarily be able to become detached? Second, the answer is given: "No. Third, the question is asked: "How so? Fourth, the verse is cited as the answer. Fifth, the verse is explained.

Within the explanation of the verse, the first line is explained first: only the patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) that arise by taking suffering (*duḥkha*) and origin (*samudaya*) as their objects are designated as "manifestation."

The others are not so. Second, according to one interpretation, those *kṣāntis* (patiences) and *jñānas* (knowledges) arising within the objective sphere of the Four Truths that are capable of severing the afflictions all receive the name "detachment" (*vairāgya*).

Third, according to another interpretation, because there are differences in breadth and narrowness regarding the remaining two phrases, they constitute four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*), which may be understood according to the text.
